verdict.summary: GetHintFormat dereferences hmhd->type before the NULL check; a parsed track with NULL InfoHeader (a state the function's own later 'if (!hmhd ...)' anticipates) causes a NULL pointer dereference and crash on attacker-supplied input.

GF_HintMediaHeaderBox *hmhd = (GF_HintMediaHeaderBox *)trak->Media->information->InfoHeader;
	if (hmhd->type != GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_HMHD)
evidence.reason: hmhd is dereferenced (hmhd->type) with no NULL check in execution order. The only NULL guard, 'if (!hmhd || !hmhd->subType)' at line 7, executes after the dereference, proving the code itself anticipates hmhd == NULL yet reads it first. An attacker-supplied file whose track's Media->information->InfoHeader is NULL (no media-info header box) reaches line 4 with hmhd = NULL and crashes the parsing process.

assumptions: InfoHeader is populated during MP4 box parsing based on file content; a minf without a media-info header box leaves it NULL. The code's own 'if (!hmhd || !hmhd->subType)' check confirms NULL is an anticipated state, making the trigger instantiable without caller misbehavior.
GF_Box-style structures place 'type' as a common leading field, so reading ->type on a mis-cast InfoHeader is in-bounds; the defect is strictly the NULL case.
limitations: trak->Media->information->sampleTable and ->SampleDescription (line 8) are also dereferenced without NULL checks, but no statement in this code documents whether the parser guarantees they are non-NULL for tracks reaching this function, so that crash path is speculative.
The 'if (!hmhd) return a ? a->type : 0;' arm at line 9 is dead code for the NULL case because the dereference at line 4 precedes it; it is a symptom of the misordered guard, not a separate defect.

verdict.summary: ReadPSDChannelPixels advances the raw pointer p by 1, 2, or 4 bytes per column for image->columns iterations with no length parameter and no bounds check, so a PSD whose row pixel buffer is shorter than columns*packet_size bytes causes a heap out-of-bounds read inside PushShortPixel/PushFloatPixel/*p++, leaking adjacent heap memory into the decoded image.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop bounds iterations on x (columns) but never bounds p against the pixels buffer; the function receives no length, so a crafted PSD row buffer shorter than columns*packet_size bytes makes p read past the heap allocation at *p++ / PushShortPixel / PushFloatPixel (lines 35, 39, 47), an out-of-bounds read whose values are written into the output image (disclosure). Trigger: PSD header declaring columns C with packet_size 2 or 4 and a short row data buffer.

Origin of the tainted traversal: p is initialized to the attacker-file-derived row buffer with no recorded length anywhere in the function, and packet_size (1/2/4) is derived from the file-parsed image, fixing the per-iteration read width that drives p past the buffer.

assumptions: The allocation and sizing of the pixels buffer (and the compressed-data decode that fills it) happen in the caller (psd.c channel-reading code) and are not shown; nothing in the given code quotes a guarantee that it holds at least columns*packet_size bytes, so per guard-anchoring that guarantee does not exist.

GetPSDPacketSize, PushShortPixel, PushFloatPixel, GetAuthenticPixels, SetPSDPixel, GetAuthenticIndexQueue semantics assumed per their standard ImageMagick roles (raw memory readers / cache accessors).
indexes from GetAuthenticIndexQueue is assumed non-NULL for colormapped images; its use happens in SetPSDPixel (not shown).
limitations: Whether a specific caller path actually produces an undersized buffer is decided in code not given; if every caller always allocates columns*packet_size bytes, the over-read would not trigger there — however, historically this exact function (ImageMagick psd.c) exhibited a heap over-read fixed by adding exactly the missing length parameter and p bound check, corroborating reachability.
The depth==1 branch changes read consumption (one 1-4 byte read covers up to 8 columns) but is still unbounded; it is covered by the same missing-guard defect.

Trigger fully instantiated: line 6's guard checks only the outer signature_def lookup, so a MetaGraphDef with the signature key present but its outputs map lacking the key passes the guard and reaches the dereference.

assumptions: init_op_name is assumed to be a valid non-NULL out-pointer per calling convention; no statement in the code asserts it.

The end-iterator dereference may, on some implementations, read out-of-bounds node data rather than crash cleanly; a disclosure chain beyond the crash could not be simulated with the given code, so impact is recorded as a crash/DoS on the model-loading process.

verdict.summary: This is the patched form of the TF bincount kernel. The three OP_REQUIRES guards on splits (num_batches > 0, splits_values(0) == 0, splits_values(num_batches) == num_values), placed before the loop in execution order, mathematically bound the batch_idx walk: since idx < num_values == splits_values(num_batches), the while loop can never push batch_idx past num_batches, and since splits_values(0) == 0 it always advances at least once (batch_idx >= 1), so per_batch_counts[batch_idx-1] stays in [0, num_batches-1]. The weights shape-equality check bounds weight_values(idx). No reachable input produces an out-of-domain index, size, or offset at any sink.

assumptions: BatchedMap is a sized container constructed with num_batches elements (constructor call quoted: BatchedMap<W>(num_batches)); its element indexing by [batch_idx-1] is bounded by the proven batch_idx range.

OP_REQUIRES aborts the kernel (returns from Compute) when the condition fails, so the quoted checks run before the loop on every path.
limitations: int num_batches = splits.NumElements() - 1 and int num_values = values.NumElements() truncate int64 counts; a wrap requires tensors with >= 2^31 elements (>= 16GB for int64), and even then truncation only makes the int smaller than the real element count (never larger), and a negative wrap is rejected by 'num_batches > 0' or skips the loop via 'idx < num_values' — no out-of-bounds access is reachable, so this is not instantiated as a vulnerability.

Intermediate splits values are not checked for monotonicity or non-negativity; this can produce an incorrect bincount assignment (values attributed to the wrong batch) but all memory accesses remain in bounds, a correctness issue, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad::Compute uses raw int64 values from row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor as the START of the pooling loops (in_row_start, in_col_start) without any lower-bound validation; only the loop END values are clamped via std::min. Origin of the tainted value: in_row_start/in_col_start are taken verbatim from attacker-controlled tensors; the only clamps present (std::min on the END values) bound the loop terminators, and no statement anywhere bounds the START values, so the missing guard is the absence of e.g. in_row_start = std::max(in_row_start, 0) / a rejection of negative or >= in_rows sequence values.

A crash-only impact was not demoted: the instantiated trigger produces out-of-bounds WRITES (memory corruption), not merely a crash.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read allocates the content-script-types buffer with gf_malloc(sizeof(char) * (s->size+1)) using the attacker-controlled u64 box size with no bound. When the file declares s->size = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, s->size+1 wraps to 0, gf_malloc(0) returns a minimal non-NULL chunk, the NULL check passes, and gf_bs_read_data(bs, p->content_script_types, s->size) copies the remaining stream bytes (attacker-chosen length and content) into the ~0-byte heap buffer, yielding a heap buffer overflow write; the terminator write p->content_script_types[s->size] is also out of bounds.

evidence.reason: s->size is the attacker-controlled 64-bit box size from the parsed file with no range check anywhere in this function. The allocation length sizeof(char) * (s->size+1) wraps to 0 when s->size = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (u64 overflow, CWE-190), so gf_malloc(0) returns a minimal non-NULL chunk and the line-6 NULL check passes. gf_bs_read_data is then called with the raw s->size (UINT64_MAX) as copy length, writing the remaining attacker-supplied stream bytes into the undersized heap buffer — an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) with attacker-chosen length and content; p->content_script_types[s->size] = 0 on line 8 is likewise out of bounds. The only guard in the code checks the allocation pointer for NULL, not the size relationship between the allocation and the copy.

assumptions: gf_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal allocation (glibc/standard allocator behavior); if it returned NULL the code would safely return GF_OUT_OF_MEM for this exact value.
gf_bs_read_data copies min(requested, bytes-remaining-in-stream) bytes, so the overflow length equals the remaining attacker-supplied file content.

The container parser (not shown) passes the file's box size field into s->size at full u64 width; no check in this code bounds it, so per guard-anchoring rules the unbounded u64 value is treated as attacker-reachable.
limitations: Unchecked gf_bs_read_data return: when the stream holds fewer bytes than s->size, the malloc'd buffer stays partially uninitialized between the bytes actually read and index s->size, so the stored string can embed uninitialized heap bytes (CWE-908). Trigger is instantiable in this code, but the consumer that would surface the string (output/serialization) is not shown, so the disclosure impact chain is not instantiated here.

On 32-bit builds, any s->size whose low 32 bits of (s->size+1) are small (e.g., s->size = 0xFFFFFFFF) also yields an undersized allocation followed by a huge read; this is a width-truncation variant only exercised on a 32-bit target while the code declares a u64 size, so it is recorded as an additional 32-bit-only trigger, not the primary.
A NULL dereference of s or p is not considered: no path in this code dereferences s before the callee-provided box object, and no statement in this code can produce s = NULL for this handler.

assumptions: GF_AV1_OBUArrayEntry.obu_length width and GF_AV1Config field types are not shown; assuming obu_length is wide enough that a->obu_length = obu_size (line 68) does not truncate inconsistently with the (size_t)obu_size allocation.

The underflow causes over-consumption bounded by the remaining bitstream (reads stay inside the gf_bs buffer); no out-of-bounds memory access or corruption was demonstrable within this function, hence low severity.

verdict.summary: The exported parameter `size` is attacker-data, but every instantiable boundary value (negative, zero, INT_MAX) leads to a safe NULL return before any memory write: the malloc-NULL check `if (!ret) return ret;` executes before `ret->size = size;` on the only path. The `if (alloc_size <= 0) return NULL;` check is a dead test for negatives (size_t is unsigned), but its failure is neutralized because a negative size produces a huge allocation size and malloc fails, yielding the same safe NULL sentinel. The only corruption scenario — an undersized allocation via unsigned wrap — requires the unshown internal callee's arithmetic and a 32-bit size_t, so it is not instantiated by this code.

assumptions: The behavior of the internal callee `TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size)` (not shown) is assumed to be the conventional `sizeof(TfLiteIntArray) + (size_t)size * sizeof(int)`; per discipline 3 its exact arithmetic, and any wrap therein, is an assumption, not a quotable fact.

The layout of `TfLiteIntArray` (that `ret->size = size;` writes within `sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)` bytes and that `alloc_size` covers at least the struct) is assumed from the type name; the struct definition is not given.
limitations: Speculative: `if (alloc_size <= 0)` can never be true for a negative-derived value because `alloc_size` is `size_t`; a negative `size` therefore bypasses the intended early rejection, but the huge resulting allocation makes malloc fail and the function returns NULL — no memory corruption occurs in this code.

Speculative (not a vulnerability here): on a 32-bit platform, if the unshown callee computes `sizeof(TfLiteIntArray) + (size_t)size*4` and `size` is a multiple of 2^30, the product could wrap to 0, allocating only `sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)` bytes while `ret->size` records a huge count; any resulting out-of-bounds write would occur in caller code not given, and the wrap depends on unshown callee arithmetic and platform width — preconditions not instantiated.

Returning NULL for negative `size` is indistinguishable from the ordinary allocation-failure path; if an unseen caller fails to check the return value, that defect would live in that caller, not in this code.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read copies attacker-supplied box payload bytes into the fixed 1024-byte stack buffer str with an unbounded read loop; the loop only terminates on a NUL byte, so a diST box payload longer than 1024 non-NUL bytes writes attacker-controlled data past the end of str, corrupting the stack frame.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop writes gf_bs_read_u8(bs) output (attacker-controlled box payload bytes) into char str[1024] at index i with no bound on i. The only exit condition, 'if (!str[i]) break;', tests the byte content for NUL and never checks i against 1024. Trigger: an attacker-supplied diST box containing >1024 non-zero bytes makes the first out-of-bounds write at str[1024] with attacker-chosen content, continuing until the terminating NUL, overwriting the stack frame; the subsequent gf_strdup(str) additionally reads out of bounds.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_u8(bs) returns each payload byte of the box being parsed (bitstream semantics per discipline 3); its content is fully attacker-controlled via the input file.
At end-of-stream gf_bs_read_u8 returns 0, which terminates the loop only after the out-of-bounds writes have already occurred.
limitations: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(p, i) with the oversized i could additionally corrupt box size accounting, but the macro body is not shown, so its impact is not part of the instantiated chain.
Exploitability (control-flow hijack vs. crash) depends on the target stack layout, but the attacker-controlled stack out-of-bounds write itself is the confirmed memory-corruption primitive.

verdict.summary: simplifyBroadcast indexes shape_and_rank_for_dim[0] after an is_splat check that is vacuously true for an empty vector. When every input shape has rank 0 (or shapes is empty), maxRank stays 0, the vectors are zero-sized, and line 36 performs an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read whose garbage Value may be returned as the canonicalization result, injecting attacker-influenced uninitialized data into the compiled IR.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds/uninitialized read: llvm::is_splat is vacuously true for an empty SmallVector, so the short-circuit does not prevent indexing [0]. Trigger: attacker-supplied IR where all broadcast shape operands have rank 0 → maxRank = 0 (lines 6/11) → shape_and_rank_for_dim is empty → element 0 is read out of bounds (or from uninitialized storage), and the resulting garbage Value can be returned as the simplification result. No emptiness/maxRank>0 guard exists anywhere in the function.

Origin of the harmful value: maxRank is initialized to 0 and equals 0 whenever every analyzed shape has rank 0 (line 9 only rejects a disengaged Optional, not an empty shape), so both joined_dimensions and shape_and_rank_for_dim are constructed with zero elements while the code later unconditionally indexes [0].

assumptions: llvm::is_splat returns true for an empty container (all_equal/adjacent_find semantics: an empty range is vacuously splat) — relied on per documented STL/LLVM convention.

ShapeComponentAnalysis::GetValueInfo can return an engaged Optional containing an empty (rank-0) shape description for shape values describing scalars, making maxRank == 0 reachable from attacker-supplied IR; no code shown prevents this.
In release builds, SmallVector::operator[] performs no bounds check (assert is compiled out), so the empty-vector [0] access is an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read rather than a guaranteed assertion.
limitations: shapes[0].getType().cast<RankedTensorType>() (line 45) would abort on a non-ranked-tensor shape operand, but triggering it requires GetValueInfo to succeed for such a value while maxRank > 0 — a caller/analysis contract that cannot be quoted from the given code, so it is speculative.

The int-vs-size_t comparison at line 41 and the unsigned wrap at line 52 were analyzed and are benign: the line-11 max guard keeps the computed extract index within [0, rank-1], and rank > INT_MAX is not instantiable in this code.
In debug builds the defect manifests as an assertion crash inside SmallVector::operator[] rather than a silent OOB read.

verdict.summary: lsquic_qeh_settings handles peer-supplied QPACK settings (max_table_size, dyn_table_size, max_risked_streams) but every in-code sink is guarded and fail-closed: the double-settings path returns early, the dynamic-table minimum is clamped, the TSU buffer is sized from its own sizeof before being passed, and a nonzero lsqpack_enc_init result logs and returns -1 before QEH_HAVE_SETTINGS is set. The attacker-controlled values reach only the arguments of the checked lsqpack_enc_init call; no memory, copy, indexing, format, injection, or authorization sink in this code consumes them unguarded, and any misuse would occur inside the not-shown callee, whose behavior is an assumption. No instantiable vulnerability exists in the given code.

assumptions: qeh is non-NULL and QEH_INITIALIZED per the caller's contract; the only in-code enforcement is `assert(qeh->qeh_flags & QEH_INITIALIZED);`, which is typically compiled out under NDEBUG, so it was not relied on as a runtime guard (crash-only, not attacker-instantiable).
QENC_MIN_DYN_TABLE_SIZE is assumed a positive compile-time constant; its numeric value is not shown.
The behavior of lsqpack_enc_init (whether it validates or allocates based on max_table_size/dyn_table_size/max_risked_streams) is not shown and was not relied upon in either direction.
max_table_size, dyn_table_size, and max_risked_streams were treated as attacker-controlled peer SETTINGS data per the trust model, i.e., the worst-case provenance was assumed.
limitations: max_table_size, dyn_table_size, and max_risked_streams are passed to lsqpack_enc_init with no upper-bound check and no dyn_table_size<=max_table_size normalization anywhere in this code. If the not-shown callee sizes an allocation from these peer-controlled values, a malicious peer could inflate per-connection memory usage (potential CWE-400) or trigger an internal fault; the impact link lies entirely inside the unshown callee, so it cannot be confirmed or refuted from the given code.
A hypothetical concurrent second SETTINGS frame could race the QEH_HAVE_SETTINGS check; no two interleavable ordered operations are exhibited in this code path, so this remains speculative.
Potential truncation of a 62-bit QUIC SETTINGS varint into the 32-bit `unsigned` parameters would occur in the not-shown caller before this function is entered.
The `qeh_begin_out(qeh)` callee and the qeh_enc_sm_out state are internal; no attacker-derived argument is passed, so no defect was assessable there.

verdict.summary: ValidateInputs' only memory sinks are the indexed reads a_shape_flat(i) and b->dim_size(i). Both are provably in bounds: 'if (a_shape->NumElements() != b->dims()) return errors::InvalidArgument(...)' executes before the loop and equates the flat vector's length to the loop bound's expression b->dims(), so 'for (int i = 0; i < b->dims(); ++i)' keeps every index in range on every iteration, including the dims()==0 edge. The contents of a_indices/a_values are never read in this code, so the downstream risk of unvalidated sparse-index values cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: Tensor pointers a_indices, a_values, a_shape, b are non-null — no NULL check or assert is quotable in this code; this is a framework-caller contract.

a_shape's dtype matches the template parameter Index so that a_shape->flat<Index>() (line 21) does not trip a framework CHECK — this is enforced by the op registration (not shown), not by any statement in this code; a mismatch would be a crash-only DoS at equal privilege.

In the real TensorFlow kernel, the caller subsequently reads a_indices values to index into dense buffers; an attacker-supplied out-of-range index could cause an OOB read/write there. That consuming statement is not part of the given code, no call site here passes a raw index/size to a memory operation, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this snippet and the candidate is not counted as a vulnerability in this code.

IsVector/IsMatrix checks (lines 3, 8-9) constrain ranks but not dtypes; a dtype-mismatched a_shape would abort on a framework CHECK inside flat<Index>() — speculative given the unshown op-signature contract, crash-only impact.

verdict.summary: This FromProto intake validates the shape (TensorShape::IsValid), rejects DT_INVALID, rejects unhandled dtypes via CASES_WITH_DEFAULT, and checks the decode failure sentinels (dtype_error, p == nullptr) before any use of p — and NULL-checks buf_ before its only dereference. The attacker-controlled mismatch between shape.num_elements() (N) and tensor_content() size is passed unchecked to the not-shown Helper<T>::Decode / FromProtoField<T> callees, where any out-of-bounds would actually occur; the impact chain is not instantiated in this code, so no vulnerability is confirmed here.

assumptions: Helper<T>::Decode and FromProtoField<T> (not shown) are assumed to validate content size against N·element_size and return nullptr on mismatch; this code's own sentinel handling (if (dtype_error || p == nullptr) return false;) is consistent with but does not prove that contract.
TensorShape::IsValid is assumed to reject syntactically invalid/overflowing shapes; its exact bounds are not shown.
limitations: Shape/content size mismatch: an attacker can supply tensor_shape with N=1000000 and a 4-byte tensor_content; this code passes both to Decode/FromProtoField with no consistency check anywhere in the given code. Any OOB read/write would occur inside the not-shown callee, so the impact link is uncharacterizable (discipline 3) — recorded as a cross-function validation gap, not a confirmed vulnerability of this code.

Out-of-range dtype enum: with N==0 the decode block is skipped, so only DT_INVALID (0) is rejected; set_dtype(proto.dtype()) can store any nonzero enum value (e.g., 999). Any harmful use (e.g., dtype-table indexing) occurs in consumer code not given; trigger impact not instantiated.
Huge shapes: potential int64 overflow in shape.num_elements() or oversized allocation depends on TensorShape::IsValid semantics not shown; the allocation itself happens inside the callee.

verdict.summary: Unsigned integer underflow at `size -= 4;`: the attacker-controlled u32 payload size is never checked to be >= 4 (the only prior checks, `if (!size)`, pass values 1-3), so sizes 1-3 wrap to ~0xFFFFFFFD. The wrapped value drives `while (size)` and defeats the only remaining bounds guard `if (size<obu_size)`, causing the parser to read, allocate, copy and retain OBUs from the entire remainder of the bitstream, far beyond the declared box boundary.

evidence.snippet:

	while (size) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: unguarded unsigned underflow. Attacker-controlled size in {1,2,3} (crafted av1C box payload size; the 32 config header bits are read from the bitstream without bounding by size, so validation at line 28 passes) makes `size -= 4` wrap to ~0xFFFFFFFE. The wrapped value keeps `while (size)` alive and neutralizes the `if (size<obu_size)` guard at line 72, so the loop parses and retains every OBU in the rest of the file beyond the declared box. The fix guard (`if (size < 4) return NULL` before the decrement) appears nowhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `size` is the exported function's payload-size parameter, derived from the attacker-supplied media file (ISOBMFF box size). No documented or asserted lower bound on it exists; the only checks on it before the decrement are `if (!size)`, which pass values 1-3 into the wrap.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int/gf_bs_read_data/gf_bs_seek behave as GPAC bitstream accessors: reads past the logical box but within the stream buffer are memory-safe and return available data/partial reads; this bounds the impact of the over-read to within the input buffer.
gf_av1_parse_obu (not shown) returns GF_OK only after consuming the OBU; its exact acceptance of oversized or zero-size OBUs is unknown and therefore never used to instantiate a trigger.

Potential non-advancing (infinite) loop if a successfully parsed OBU has obu_size == 0 and gf_malloc(0) returns non-NULL; requires unshown callee behavior.
`assert(obu_size == gf_bs_get_position(bs) - pos)` at line 53 can abort in debug builds on a parse/consumption mismatch; debug-only, callee-dependent.

verdict.summary: BiasAndClamp performs no runtime validation that bias_size <= array_size (and that bias_size divides array_size); the only invariant check, TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ((array_size % bias_size), 0), is a debug-only macro compiled out of release builds and checks divisibility, not bounds. An attacker who supplies a model file with a bias tensor larger than the output array (or sizes that do not divide evenly) makes the NEON/scalar loops write up to bias_size floats per iteration past array_data's end — a heap out-of-bounds write (and, on the NEON path, a non-terminating loop that keeps writing past the buffer because the loop condition tests array_ptr != array_end_ptr at block start).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: stores write array_ptr[0..bias_size-1] each outer iteration, but no check ensures array_ptr + bias_size <= array_end_ptr. Trigger (simulated): attacker-derived sizes bias_size=8, array_size=4 with a 4-float array_data buffer; at i=4 the store writes array_data[4..7], past the buffer, and the outer loop (which only tests the block start against array_end_ptr) never terminates, continuing to corrupt the heap.

evidence.snippet: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ((array_size % bias_size), 0);
evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the sole invariant on the two attacker-derived sizes is a debug-only DCHECK (no-op in release builds) and even when active it only asserts divisibility of array_size by bias_size, never that 0 < bias_size <= array_size. The scalar path (lines 58-62) has the same unguarded out-of-bounds write at array_data[array_offset + i].

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ is a debug-only assertion that is compiled out (no-op) in release builds of TensorFlow Lite; if evaluated in a debug build it aborts rather than validating, so it provides no production enforcement.

bias_size and array_size are treated as attacker-data: this inline helper is called by TFLite kernels with sizes derived from tensor shapes in a parsed model file, and no caller-side contract is quotable in the given code.
ActivationFunctionWithMinMax(float, float, float) is assumed to be a pure scalar clamp helper with no memory side effects.
limitations: A negative bias_size (e.g., -4) is not rejected (line 4 only checks == 0): the NEON/scalar inner loops skip due to negative bounds but the outer loops never terminate (array_ptr += bias_size walks backwards; array_offset decreases indefinitely), giving an infinite-loop CPU denial of service with no out-of-bounds write. Its reachability depends on a negative size flowing from the shape pipeline, so it is recorded as a secondary robustness/DoS issue, not a primary memory-corruption finding.

Out-of-bounds READ of bias_data beyond its own buffer is possible only if the caller passes a bias_size exceeding the bias buffer's extent; that particular mismatch is a caller contract that cannot be quoted here and is subsumed by the primary array_data overflow.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety, injection, or validation defect is instantiable within this function. All bitstream-derived scalars are masked or sentinel-checked before use (nal_hdr & 0x1F; 'if (ret < 0) return ret'; 'if (avc->last_ps_idx < 0) return -1'; 'if (!avc->s_info.sps) return -1'), struct copies are same-type/size memcpy, and ret is initialized on every path. The one asymmetric guard (checking avc->s_info.sps but dereferencing n_state.sps) cannot produce NULL here because n_state.sps is inherited non-NULL from the checked value and only the unshown internal callee avc_parse_slice could clear it while returning >= 0, which its checked failure sentinel ('if (ret < 0) return ret;') covers.

assumptions: Behavior of internal callees not shown (avc_parse_slice, svc_parse_slice, SVC_ReadNal_header_extension, avc_compute_poc, gf_avc_read_sps_bs_internal, gf_avc_read_pps_bs_internal) is assumed per GPAC conventions; none of it is quotable contract.
gf_bs_read_u8/gf_bs_read_ue are assumed to return 0/underflow-safe values at end-of-bitstream (standard GPAC bitstream semantics).
avc points to a caller-owned, parser-initialized AVCState; its internal pointers (s_info.sps) were produced by this parser's own earlier code paths.
limitations: Speculative: 'avc->s_info.sps->poc_type == n_state.sps->poc_type' dereferences n_state.sps while only avc->s_info.sps is NULL-checked. The trigger requires avc_parse_slice to return >= 0 while leaving/setting n_state.sps NULL — no statement in this code can produce that state, and the callee's failure channel is guarded by 'if (ret < 0) return ret;'. Would be CWE-476 if the callee contract allowed it.

Speculative/fail-open parse-state: '/*ret = */svc_parse_slice(bs, avc, &n_state);' discards the failure sentinel and proceeds to avc_compute_poc(&n_state) and state commit regardless; all subsequent uses in THIS code are in-bounds stack-field accesses, and any NULL/OOB would occur inside unshown callees receiving in-domain arguments.

avc->last_ps_idx (set from gf_bs_read_ue for SEQ_PARAM_EXT) is stored but never used as an index in this code; if a not-shown consumer indexes an SPS array with it, bounds enforcement there is unverified here.

verdict.summary: The kernel computes loc via std::inner_product over attacker-controlled group indices (from the *_indices tensors) and writes output_t(loc) at five sites. The only guard, 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, loc < output_elements, ...)', is a signed upper-bound-only check: a negative loc (produced by a negative group index or overflowing stride product) passes it, so output_t(loc) performs an out-of-bounds heap write before the output buffer. evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: dir->length (attacker/caller-supplied size_t from the exported function's parameter) enters here, and is used unchecked as an array index at line 18.

Potential path traversal via info->name depends on name validation not shown here; not instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: The Quantize op validates only axis_ > -1 and input.dims() > axis_, both of which admit axis_ = 0; axis_ - 1 = -1 is then passed to flat_inner_outer_dims<float,3>, producing a malformed tensor view used for OOB reads when quantizing slices.

evidence.reason: axis_ = 0 (attacker-controlled op attribute) passes every guard (`if (axis_ > -1)`, `input.dims() > axis_`, range checks on min/max), reaches this sink with argument axis_ - 1 = -1, an invalid negative dimension index; flat_inner_outer_dims/chip then build an out-of-bounds tensor view consumed by QuantizeSlice — OOB read in the host process from attacker-supplied graph attributes.

verdict.summary: Prepare reads weights_time->dims->data[1] (and input/weights_feature dims->data[1], dims->data[0]) without validating the tensors' dimension counts; the only NumDimensions check in the function applies to the state tensor. A malicious .tflite model supplying a rank-1 (or rank-0) weights_time/input/weights_feature tensor causes out-of-bounds reads past the TfLiteIntArray dims allocation during graph preparation.

evidence.snippet: const int memory_size = weights_time->dims->data[1];
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: dims->data[1] is read with no check that NumDimensions(weights_time) >= 2 anywhere in the function (the only rank check, TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2), applies to a different tensor). Trigger: an attacker-supplied model with weights_time of rank 1 (dims = [N]) passes the inputs->size and modulo checks (rank=1, num_filters%1==0) and reaches this line, reading one int32 past the end of the size-1 TfLiteIntArray heap allocation; the leaked value flows into the state-shape comparison.

Same defect class, additional sinks: input->dims->data[1] and weights_feature->dims->data[1] are read with no dimension-count validation on either tensor. Trigger: a model whose input (or weights_feature) tensor has rank 1 makes these statements read past the dims allocation before any shape check runs.

assumptions: GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe validate tensor presence and index only; they do not enforce dimension counts or shapes (no quotable statement in this code documents such a precondition).
Tensor dims (TfLiteIntArray) are parsed from the attacker-supplied .tflite model file and can have any size, including 0 or 1.
params->rank, tensor dims entries, and quantization params are all flatbuffer-controlled by the model author.
limitations: Negative rank: TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, rank != 0) allows rank < 0 (e.g., rank=-4, num_filters=8 → num_units=-2 written into output_size_array->data[1] and passed to context->ResizeTensor). Impact depends on how the not-shown interpreter ResizeTensor handles negative dims; no quoteable guard here, but the harmful consumption occurs entirely inside the unshown callee — impact chain not instantiated.
Signed overflow of memory_size * num_filters at the state-shape comparison affects a comparison only in this code; no memory use of the wrapped value is shown here.
Results of TfLiteIntArrayCreate/TfLiteIntArrayCopy are not NULL-checked, but triggering requires allocation failure, which an attacker cannot induce.

Quantization params pointers (input_params, etc.) are dereferenced after type checks but scale->data[0] access depends on unshown TfLiteAffineQuantization contents; not independently triggered by a quoteable flow in this code.

verdict.summary: The afra box parser bounds its local-entry loop with an exact arithmetic check (ptr->size / entry_size < entry_count is rejected), and every bitstream read — including the global-entry loop whose global_entry_count lacks an arithmetic pre-check — is preceded by a same-width ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE guard that terminates the loop once the box's remaining size is exhausted. No unguarded memory, size, or injection sink is reachable.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) checks ptr->size >= N, returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE on failure, and otherwise decrements ptr->size by N; its body is not shown in the given code. Under this standard GPAC macro semantics every read is bounded and the global-entry loop is capped by the remaining box size.
gf_bs_read_* on truncated streams returns without memory corruption (standard GPAC behavior); gf_list_insert on a growing list at index i behaves as append.
ptr->size reflects the remaining bytes of the box as maintained by the box-reading framework.
limitations: Memory leak: in both loops, if ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE fails after gf_malloc succeeded (e.g., a truncated afra box), the just-allocated GF_AfraEntry/GF_GlobalAfraEntry is not inserted into the list and leaks on the error return. Impact is a single small struct (~24-40 bytes) per parse attempt with no attacker-scalable amplification — robustness, not a security vulnerability.
gf_list_insert return value is unchecked; failure would only occur on out-of-memory, which is environment failure not attacker-induced.
The entry_count arithmetic check would only be bypassable with a box of roughly 51-68GB to satisfy entry_count = 0xFFFFFFFF; not producible from this code's own flow at realistic sizes.

verdict.summary: Internal compiler codegen routine; all consumed values are compiler-internal (AST contract, symbol IDs, stack slots, arity n in 0..15) bounded by this code's own guards; no memory, copy, or injection sink operates on attacker-derived raw offsets/sizes in this snippet.

assumptions: The AST (tree/rhs) is produced by the compiler's own parser not shown here and conforms to its node grammar (e.g., tree->cdr and tree->cdr->cdr non-NULL for NODE_CALL/NODE_COLON2 paths).

limitations: Potential defects inside the not-shown callees (gen_move, genop_*, gen_hash, gen_vmassignment, codegen) could not be examined; this code passes only in-domain arguments per its own arithmetic.

If the upstream parser (not shown) could emit malformed AST nodes (e.g., NULL tree->cdr->cdr for NODE_CALL), dereferences like `tree->cdr->cdr->car` could crash; that producer is outside this snippet, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled PCL byte stream's only memory sink, the command[MagickPathExtent] accumulation loop, is correctly bounded by the guard '((size_t) (p-command) < (MagickPathExtent-1))' together with the '*p="\0"; p=command;' flush, verified in execution order and at the exactly-at-limit boundary; all other attacker-derived values (CropBox/MediaBox dimensions, density) flow only into bounded string formatting, numeric-only delegate arguments, and image metadata, with no memory, allocation, or injection sink inside this function.

In ping mode, 'image->magick_columns*=image->resolution.x/2.0;' can inflate stored image dimensions when resolution.x > 2; the result is metadata only and any consequent allocation happens in code not shown.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable vulnerability. The only size-bounded sink, EVP_DigestUpdate(md.get(), hash_buffer, hash_length), is guarded in execution order by RELEASE_ASSERT(hash_length == SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH, ...), which runs after X509_digest sets the length and before the use, pinning it to 32 bytes within the EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64) buffer. The loop sinks are streaming digest updates over vectors whose extent equals their data size, with no reachable overflow (byte-sized value_type) and no injection surface; the format string is a constant literal. All assert failures are fail-closed process aborts triggered only by configuration-derived values, with no attacker-controlled path in this code.

assumptions: RELEASE_ASSERT aborts the process in all build types; a failed check never allows execution to continue.
X509_digest writes the digest and *len on success (OpenSSL documented semantics); EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE = 64 >= SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH = 32.

ca_cert_, verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ are populated outside this snippet from TLS validation configuration; this function itself performs no network/file/peer parsing.
The caller supplies a buffer of the size documented in the parameter declaration uint8_t hash_buffer[EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE] and an initialized digest context (interface contract quoted in the signature).
limitations: Session-ID digest completeness cannot be judged from this snippet: if the validator holds other validation-relevant settings (e.g., CRL, verify depth, subjectAltName matching) that are not hashed, a resumed session could be validated against stale settings; those members and the code that consumes the session ID to skip revalidation are not shown, so the fail-open-resumption impact chain is not instantiated here.

RELEASE_ASSERT failures (e.g., X509_digest or EVP_DigestUpdate returning 0) abort the process; the trigger requires a configuration-derived certificate or hash-list entry to fail digesting, and no attacker-controlled input path in this code produces that state.

A hypothetical 'X509_digest returns 1 without setting *len' leaving hash_length indeterminate is precluded by documented OpenSSL semantics and, in any case, is gated by the RELEASE_ASSERT(hash_length == SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH) check before the digest update.

For an equation with an empty input side (e.g. "->i"), num_inputs = input_str.size() = 0, input_label_counts is resized to 0 (empty), and (*input_label_counts)[0][label] at line 51 performs an out-of-bounds read (std::vector::operator[] on an empty vector, then indexing through the garbage inner vector), an attacker-instantiated memory-safety defect in the process consuming the einsum equation.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds read: with num_inputs == 0 (equation with empty input side, e.g. "->i"), input_label_counts was resized to 0 at line 27, so (*input_label_counts)[0] indexes an empty std::vector via unchecked operator[]. The only related text, 'num_inputs == 1 ||', short-circuits only the [1] operand when num_inputs is exactly 1 and does not constrain the num_inputs == 0 case; no check, clamp, at() accessor, or error arm rejecting num_inputs == 0 exists anywhere in the function.

int num_inputs = input_str.size();

evidence.reason: Taint origin: num_inputs is derived from the attacker-supplied equation string parsed at line 11 and is never validated to be >= 1 before it sizes input_label_counts (line 27) and is used as an index precondition at lines 51-52.

assumptions: ParseEinsumEquation (line 11) is an internal callee not shown; the trigger assumes it accepts an equation with an empty input side (e.g. "->i"), yielding input_str.size() == 0. No statement in this code documents or enforces a minimum-operand precondition, so per guard-anchoring this unquotable contract cannot dismiss the candidate; the defective unchecked index itself is in this code.

MapToLabels (lines 21, 23) is assumed to assign consecutive integer labels in [0, label_mapping.size()) with kEllipsisLabel as an out-of-range sentinel, per the quoted comment 'Map from single character labels to (consecutive) integer labels' (lines 13-14) and the containers sized from the same map (lines 26, 30, 38). Under this contract the label-indexing sites are in bounds.
kEllipsisLabel's numeric value is not shown; the guards 'label != kEllipsisLabel' (lines 32, 40) and 'label == kEllipsisLabel' (line 49) are taken to exclude it from indexing.

If ParseEinsumEquation in the actual codebase were modified to reject equations with an empty input side, the OOB trigger would be unreachable in deployment; however, no such rejection exists in the given code, and this function is the intake point for the equation string.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad's Compute never validates out_backprop's batch/depth dimensions (out_batch, out_depth, from input 1) against the original input shape (in_batch, in_depth, from input 0). The inner loops index the in_backprop temporary matrix, sized in_cols*in_rows*in_batch x in_depth, with in_index=(b*in_rows+in_r)*in_cols+in_c where b is bounded only by out_batch and a row index d bounded only by out_depth. An attacker supplying mismatched shapes (e.g. input shape [1,4,4,1] with out_backprop shape [2,1,1,1]) causes an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced double values at line 132.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write sink. The matrix in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat is sized in_depth rows x (in_cols*in_rows*in_batch) columns (lines 86-88, from input 0), but the write index in_index uses b bounded only by out_batch (line 96) and row d bounded only by out_depth (line 128), both from input 1. With orig_input_tensor_shape=[1,4,4,1] and out_backprop shape [2,1,1,1], iteration b=1 produces in_index up to 31 against a 16-element buffer, writing attacker-influenced doubles out of bounds. No OP_REQUIRES anywhere relates out_batch/out_depth to in_batch/in_depth.

evidence.snippet: const int64_t in_index = (b * in_rows + in_r) * in_cols + in_c;
evidence.reason: Computation directly producing the faulty index: b iterates to out_batch-1 (input 1's batch) while in_rows/in_cols and the destination buffer extent derive from input 0's in_batch; the row/col terms are provably in range (clamps at lines 102/112 plus checks at 103/115), so the batch term b*in_rows*in_cols is the sole out-of-domain component.

evidence.snippet: const int64_t out_batch = out_backprop.dim_size(0);
evidence.reason: Origin of the unvalidated taint: out_batch is taken from out_backprop (context->input(1)) with no subsequent check tying it to in_batch from context->input(0) (lines 55-70 only assert in_* != 0); it feeds the loop bound at line 96 and the OOB index at line 126.

assumptions: out_backprop, row/col_seq_tensor, and orig_input_tensor_shape are op inputs supplied across a trust boundary (graph/session data, e.g. an untrusted saved model or serving request); their contents and shapes are attacker-controlled.
Eigen Map::coeffRef performs raw column-major memory access at (row + col*rows) with no bounds checking (characterizable standard-library semantics).
TensorShape::AddDim and Tensor::dim_size semantics for degenerate inputs (negative dims, tensors with fewer than 4 dims) are not shown; their behavior is an assumption.
limitations: Negative in_batch/in_rows/in_cols/in_depth values pass the != 0 checks and reach in_shape.AddDim (line 76) and the Eigen maps; whether this CHECK-crashes inside TensorShape or corrupts memory is not shown in this code, so the trigger impact is not instantiated here.
int64 overflow of in_index requires shape magnitudes (~2^63 scale) for which the temp allocation at line 81 would fail first via OP_REQUIRES_OK; speculative.
out_backprop with fewer than 4 dimensions relies on dim_size behavior not shown; if it returns a sentinel the loops may simply not execute — no separate impact instantiated.

If a crash were the only impact (it is not — the confirmed defect is an out-of-bounds WRITE with attacker-influenced values), crashing a model-serving process with attacker-supplied tensors would still be a denial of service.

verdict.summary: The Assign kernel's unlocked copy path re-fetches the ref tensor with mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false) after the guarding mutex scope has ended, and copies rhs into it without re-validating its size. The only numel/shape checks (old_lhs.shape().num_elements() == rhs.shape().num_elements() and the validate_shape_ OP_REQUIRES) run inside the mutex on a different tensor object, so a concurrent attacker-driven Assign can replace_ref_input a smaller tensor between the check and the out-of-lock Copy, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled contents and length.

evidence.snippet:
Tensor old_unlocked_lhs = context->mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false);
    Copy(context, &old_unlocked_lhs, rhs);
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: after the mutex_lock scope closes, the ref tensor is re-fetched (line 85) and rhs is copied into it (line 86) with no shape/num_elements/dtype re-validation anywhere on this path. A concurrent attacker-controlled invocation of the same op can swap the ref to a smaller tensor first, so the copy writes attacker-sized data into an undersized heap buffer (heap OOB write).

evidence.snippet: context->replace_ref_input(0, copy_tensor, /* lock_held */ true);
evidence.reason: Origin of the racing value: this statement (in the shortcut-2 path, sized by the concurrent op's own rhs.shape() at line 69) atomically replaces the ref with a tensor of arbitrary attacker-chosen num_elements; executed by a second thread between the victim thread's mutex release (line 80) and its unlocked Copy (line 86), it produces the undersized destination that the sink at line 86 then overflows.

evidence.snippet:
mutex_lock l(*context->input_ref_mutex(0));
      const Tensor& old_lhs = context->mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ true);
evidence.reason: The only size guards (lines 38-39 numel check, lines 21-28 validate_shape_ OP_REQUIRES) are scoped to old_lhs, fetched here under the mutex; because the mutex is released at line 80 and a different tensor (old_unlocked_lhs) is consumed at line 86, these checks do not constrain the sink in execution order.

assumptions: Copy(context, dst, src) is a project-internal helper not shown; per the call-site rule the defect is recorded at line 86 where the attacker-derived size reaches a copy with no validation on any path in this code, even though the faulting write lands inside the callee.
Tensor buffers are refcounted (shallow copies at lines 44 and 85 keep the buffer alive), so no use-after-free is claimed; the defect is the size mismatch, not object lifetime.

mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false) is assumed to acquire and release the lock internally and return the current ref tensor; no internal size validation by it is assumed or relied upon (none quotable).
limitations: Dtype confusion candidate: shortcut 1 checks num_elements (elements) but the copy is byte-sized, so mismatched dtypes with equal element counts would overflow; no statement in this code produces a mismatched-dtype operand pair (kernel instantiation is dtype-bound in the runtime, not shown), so this trigger could not be instantiated here.

CHECK(reshaped_old_lhs.CopyFrom(old_lhs, rhs.shape())) at line 46 can abort the process, but only after the numel guard at lines 38-39 makes CopyFrom succeed; at most a same-privilege crash, not instantiated as corruption.
Hard-coded DEVICE_MEMORY in forward_input (line 58) may cause the buffer-reuse shortcut to be skipped on CPU; robustness/performance only.

Without concurrency (single-threaded execution), the unlocked Copy at line 86 always sees a ref whose shape was just set to match rhs (lines 44-48, 74); a deployment guaranteeing serialization would neutralize C1, but no such guarantee is quotable from this code.

verdict.summary: BiasAndClamp performs out-of-bounds writes on array_data whenever array_size is not a multiple of bias_size. The only divisibility check is TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ((array_size % bias_size), 0), a debug-only assertion compiled out in release builds. On the NEON path, the outer loop for (; array_ptr != array_end_ptr; array_ptr += bias_size) uses pointer equality, so a non-divisible array_size steps the pointer past array_end_ptr and it can never equal it, producing an unbounded loop of vst1q_f32 stores writing ever-farther past the end of the array buffer. On the non-NEON path, the inner loop for (int i = 0; i < bias_size; i++) writes array_data[array_offset + i] with array_offset < array_size, overshooting the buffer by up to bias_size-1 elements on the final iteration. Both bias_size and array_size are data-carrying parameters of a non-static function and are attacker-influenced (tensor sizes derived from untrusted input); no runtime guard exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Root cause and NEON trigger: the divisibility precondition is enforced only by a debug-only DCHECK (no-op in release). The outer loop terminates on pointer equality (!=) while stepping by bias_size, so with e.g. bias_size=4, array_size=6: iteration 2 stores via vst1q_f32(array_ptr + i, x) at array_ptr = A+4 writing A[4..7] (A[6], A[7] OOB), and array_ptr (A+8) can never equal array_end_ptr (A+6), yielding an unbounded out-of-bounds heap write loop. No runtime bounds check, clamp, mask, corrected comparison, or error arm exists on any path.

Same defect on the non-NEON path: with bias_size=4, array_size=6, the outer loop enters at array_offset=4 (4 < 6) and the inner loop writes array_data[4..7], so indices 6 and 7 are out-of-bounds writes past the array_size-element buffer. The loop bound 'array_offset < array_size' does not bound the maximum written index array_offset + bias_size - 1, and no other guard exists.

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ is a debug-only assertion that is compiled to a no-op in release/NDEBUG builds (standard, universally known TensorFlow Lite macro semantics); it is therefore not a runtime guard.

No caller is shown; per the analysis rules bias_size and array_size are treated as attacker-controlled data-carrying parameters of a non-static function, and this code is judged as the last line of defense.
bias_data is assumed to hold at least bias_size readable floats; the reads bias_data[i] for i <= bias_size-1 are in bounds relative to that contract.
limitations: bias_size == 0 causes a division by zero inside TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ in debug builds only (line 9); in release builds it yields an infinite non-writing loop (hang) — a crash/hang of the process ingesting the input with no corruption, so it does not drive the verdict.

Written values are floats clamped to [clamp_min, clamp_max], so payload controllability is partial (clamped sums of OOB-read array data and attacker-supplied bias); the OOB write itself is unconditional memory corruption.
The 16-wide NEON block reads bias_data up to index bias_size-1 (i <= bias_size-16 yields max index bias_size-16+12+3 = bias_size-1), which is in bounds; no OOB read of bias_data was confirmed.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi trusts the attacker-controlled RTCP length field without checking it is >= 2: rpsi_len = (ntohs(hdr->length)-2)*4 underflows to a huge pj_size_t, and the subsequent guard 'length < rpsi_len + 12' wraps back to 4, passing for any packet of exactly the 4-byte common header. The parser then reads padlen and pt at buffer offsets 4 and 5 (out-of-bounds reads past the received packet) and exports rpsi->rpsi with slen ≈ 2^61 pointing 6 bytes into the packet. Additionally, padlen (0-255) is never validated, so rpsi_len*8 - 16 - padlen underflows even for well-formed length fields, producing a pj_str with an out-of-domain length that drives downstream over-reads. Reachable by any network peer via a crafted RTCP PSFB/FMT=3 packet.

evidence.snippet:
rpsi_len = (pj_ntohs((pj_uint16_t)hdr->length)-2) * 4;
    if (length < rpsi_len + 12)
evidence.reason: Root cause: hdr->length (attacker-controlled 16-bit RTCP length field) is decremented by 2 with no >= 2 check. For length field 0, rpsi_len becomes (pj_size_t)-8; the guard then computes rpsi_len + 12 which wraps to 4, so 'length < 4' is false for any packet of exactly 4 bytes and the size check is bypassed.

Sink: with length field 0 and length == 4 (the only bound the code enforces is 'length >= sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common)'), p = hdr+4 is one past the buffer; 'padlen = *p++' reads buf[4] and 'rpsi->pt = (*p++ ...)' reads buf[5] out of bounds. Line 25 also underflows whenever padlen > rpsi_len*8-16 (padlen 0-255 is unvalidated), and line 26 exports a string with slen ≈ 2^61 anchored 6 bytes into the packet, causing downstream out-of-bounds reads.

assumptions: sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common) is 4 bytes (V/P/Count+FMT byte, PT byte, 16-bit length) — standard PJSIP definition; if it were larger, the same trigger holds with hdr->length chosen so that rpsi_len+12 wraps to sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common).

pj_size_t is unsigned (pj_uint32_t or size_t), pj_strset only stores ptr/slen without copying, and rpsi->rpsi_bit_len is pj_size_t — per PJSIP headers; the underflow analysis holds for either width since -8 + 12 wraps to 4 modulo 2^32 as well.
limitations: The full over-read of the exported rpsi->rpsi string (slen ≈ 2^61) happens in downstream consumers not shown; however the direct out-of-bounds reads at lines 23-24 occur within this function and alone establish memory-safety impact.
The PJ_EINVAL/PJ_ENOTFOUND/PJ_ETOOSMALL checks and the pt/count gate (lines 11-15) were examined and are correct; no other candidate survived STEP 5.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow: attacker-controlled lengths (credential_id_len, cert_x_len, cert_y_len) from the WebAuthn/FIDO registration message are memcpy'd into the fixed 200-byte stack buffer data_signed with no bounds check on any path, allowing out-of-bounds stack writes with attacker-controlled content.

verdict.summary: Compute() never validates that the sparse-tensor rank is at least 2. With an attacker-supplied rank-1 truth/hypothesis shape, group_dims is empty, output_shape has 0 dims, and the statement `output_strides[output_shape.dims() - 1] = 1;` indexes a zero-size vector with -1 (wrapping to SIZE_MAX), performing an out-of-bounds write at data()-1 where data() is nullptr — a wild-address write that crashes the op-hosting process; the only guard present (`output_elements > 0`) passes because a scalar shape has num_elements()==1.

The same expression with an empty (rank-0) shape tensor would construct a vector of SIZE_MAX elements.

assumptions: ValidateShapes (lines 15-18) and sparse::SparseTensor::Create are project-internal callees not shown; per analysis rules no guard was credited to them. The trigger assumes only that Create accepts a standard rank-1 sparse tensor (indices [nnz,1], shape [N]), which is documented SparseTensor semantics.

If ValidateShapes in the unshown implementation happens to require rank >= 2, the primary trigger would be blocked by code outside this excerpt; no such check is quotable here, so the candidate stands per guard-anchoring rules.

`end_value_index - 1` would index outside the input list if N < 2; that contract is enforced by the op definition upstream, not in this code.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates only the rank of the indices tensor (IsMatrix) and the total element counts (NumElements). evidence.reason: The loop bound uses indices->dim_size(0) but the element access reads column 0, valid only if dim_size(1) > 0. No check anywhere constrains dim_size(1). With indices shape [3,0] (NumElements=0) and an empty values vector, all prior guards pass (IsMatrix true; 0==0 emptiness check passes) and each iteration reads flat index i*0+0 of a 0-element tensor — an out-of-bounds heap read of an int64, with the read value also used in the comparison at line 45 (error-oracle disclosure path).

Whether sparse::SparseTensor::Create or the later Dataset iterator bounds-checks them is not shown, so the downstream OOB impact of this candidate is not instantiated here.

limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds access itself occurs inside the not-shown SparseTensor::Create / Dataset iteration code; the instantiated defect here is the missing index-vs-shape bound at the loop and the unvalidated pass at the Create call site.

verdict.summary: The FIDO U2F attestation verifier validates the type of attStmt, its keys, x5c, and sig, but never validates the CBOR type of the x5c array element 'att_cert' before calling cbor_bytestring_handle/cbor_bytestring_length on it and passing the resulting (pointer, length) to gnutls_x509_crt_import. An attacker submitting a registration with attStmt {'x5c': [<CBOR integer/map/etc.>], 'sig': <bytestring>} makes the bytestring accessors read mismatched union members of the libcbor item, yielding an attacker-influenced length and a garbage/uninitialized pointer that gnutls dereferences as DER data — an out-of-bounds read / type confusion, crashing the authentication service (remote DoS) and potentially reading out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing CBOR type check on att_cert. The code checks att_stmt ('!cbor_isa_map(att_stmt) || cbor_map_size(att_stmt) != 2'), x5c ('!cbor_isa_array(x5c) || cbor_array_size(x5c) != 1'), and sig ('sig == NULL || !cbor_isa_bytestring(sig)'), but att_cert = cbor_array_get(x5c, 0) can be any CBOR item the attacker places in the registration response. Instantiated trigger: attStmt = {'x5c': [CBOR uint 0x4141410000000042], 'sig': h''} passes all checks; cbor_bytestring_handle/length applied to the integer item read mismatched union members, producing a garbage pointer and an attacker-influenced size, which gnutls_x509_crt_import dereferences to parse DER — out-of-bounds read at an attacker-influenced address/length, crashing the process (remote DoS of the WebAuthn authentication endpoint). The one missing guard — cbor_isa_bytestring(att_cert) before line 53 — appears nowhere on any path (verified by exhaustive search over all fix forms).

assumptions: att_stmt, credential_id/cert_x/cert_y lengths, and client_data originate from the client-supplied WebAuthn registration response; this function is the structural validation intake point (it validates attStmt/x5c/sig structure itself), so their content is attacker-data.

libcbor accessors (cbor_bytestring_handle/cbor_bytestring_length) only assert their item type in debug builds; on a non-bytestring item they read mismatched union members of the cbor_item_t struct (undefined behavior).
o_base64_encode is assumed to either fail closed on *out_len==0 or write within its 64-byte target; 32 input bytes produce 44 output chars either way, so no overflow.
generate_digest_raw with digest_SHA256 writes exactly 32 bytes (client_data_hash[32] is sized for it).
limitations: Speculative: size_t overflow of the allocation sum 'rpid_hash_len+client_data_hash_len+credential_id_len+cert_x_len+cert_y_len+2' would make o_malloc undersize the buffer and let the memcpys overflow, but it requires individual lengths at SIZE_MAX-scale (e.g. credential_id_len ≈ SIZE_MAX-100); a CBOR bytestring of such declared length cannot be decoded from any bounded request the upstream parser consumes, so the trigger could not be instantiated.

Logic laxness with no security effect: keys are matched by prefix ('o_strncmp(..., "x5c", MIN(3, cbor_string_length(key)))' matches any key starting with 'x5c' or the empty string); both matched values are still fully validated and any mid-flow error is captured in j_error, so the final 'if (json_array_size(j_error))' fail-closes with G_ERROR_PARAM.

If o_base64_encode requires the output capacity in *out_len, cert_export_b64_len initialized to 0 makes the function always take the 'Internal error' path — a functional fail-closed bug, not a security vulnerability.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer unregisters codec->scenegraph->global_qp and then unconditionally overwrites the parsed node's reference count (num_instances = 2) without checking that the bitstream-controlled node (which BIFS may encode as a NodeID reference to the very node currently stored in global_qp) is not that same object, and without preserving its existing references. Since gf_bifs_dec_node parses attacker-encoded BIFS, a NodeID reference in the bitstream makes 'node' the same pointer as codec->scenegraph->global_qp; the unregister then drops a reference on (and can free) the object that lines 22-34 continue to use and write through — the missing guard 'node != codec->scenegraph->global_qp' appears nowhere in the code.

No statement on any path checks the node's existing reference state.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the decoded node comes directly from the attacker-controlled BIFS bitstream; its identity (a fresh inline node or a reference to any previously declared NodeID, including the current global QP node) and its registration state are chosen by the stream originator, driving the trigger at lines 11 and 27.

assumptions: gf_bifs_dec_node can return a previously registered node when the BIFS stream encodes a NodeID reference, and registers nodes carrying a NodeID in the scene graph's node table — standard GPAC/BIFS decoder semantics, not shown in the snippet.

gf_node_unregister(node, NULL) decrements the node's instance count and destroys the node when it reaches zero, and gf_sg_command_del / scene-graph teardown unregister node fields and registered nodes — the same semantics this code relies on at line 11.
limitations: gf_sg_command_new (line 29) and gf_sg_command_field_new (line 30) return values are unchecked; a NULL 'inf' at line 31 would be a NULL dereference, but this requires an allocation failure the attacker cannot induce — robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The exact statement at which the premature free lands (command destruction vs. scene-graph teardown vs. an UnregisterNode command) lies in code not shown; the corruption primitive (refcount undercount plus the possible free at line 11 with subsequent uses at lines 22-34) is fully within this function.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel validates only that positions tensor indices are non-negative (lines 7-13) but never checks them against the input tensor's dimension size along the gather axis, then passes the raw attacker-controlled indices to optimized_ops::Gather (lines 18-21). evidence.snippet: ctrl->data_port = e * 256 + f;
evidence.reason: Sink computing the connection port from unvalidated ints e, f: no 0-255/0-65535 range check exists anywhere in the function, and e*256 overflows signed int (UB) for attacker input e >= 8388608 (e.g. 'PORT 127,0,0,1,8388608,0'); when the sscanf at line 14 fails to assign e or f, this line also consumes uninitialized values.

assumptions: handle_PORT is invoked by the FTP command dispatcher with str pointing at the client-supplied PORT argument (client command content is attacker-data across the network trust boundary).
send_msg, uev_io_stop, ERR, and DBG behave as conventional helpers/logging macros.

str == NULL would crash sscanf, but whether the unseen dispatcher can pass NULL is an unquoted caller contract — not counted as a vulnerability.
%d in scanf on values exceeding INT_MAX has implementation-defined matching behavior; the overflow finding at line 25 uses e within INT_MAX, so it does not depend on that.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-influenced value reaching a memory write, the flat index idx computed from group coordinates and shape-derived strides, is provably bounds-checked by 'OP_REQUIRES(ctx, idx >= 0 && idx < out_flat.size(), ...)' immediately before 'out_flat(idx) = reduced_val();' on every loop iteration, with the group-size/strides-size equality also pre-checked by an OP_REQUIRES. No other unguarded memory, injection, authz, or crypto sink exists in this kernel.

assumptions: ValidateInputs(shape_t, reduction_axes_t) (project-internal, not shown) is assumed to validate the shape and reduction axes; no memory-unsafe use in this code depends on it because the flat write index is independently bounds-checked.

SparseTensor::Create, SparseTensorReduceHelper, sp.Reorder<T>, sp.group(), and Op::Run are project-internal callees whose validation/write semantics are not shown; their contracts are assumed, but none of them is passed a raw attacker offset/size/pointer into a memory operation at a call site in this code.
Op::template Run<T> is assumed to write reduced_val before it is read each iteration; the read follows the Run call in execution order.
limitations: Potential int64 signed overflow in output_strides construction ('output_strides[d+1] * shape_vec(...)') and in CoordinatesToFlatIndex ('idx += coords[i] * strides[i]') is undefined behavior for extreme attacker shapes, but any resulting wrapped index still passes through the 'idx >= 0 && idx < out_flat.size()' check before the write, so the impact is at worst an in-bounds wrong-slot write or a clean error return, not memory corruption.

CHECK_EQ(coords.size(), strides.size()) in CoordinatesToFlatIndex would abort the process on mismatch, but the preceding OP_REQUIRES on 'output_strides.empty() || (g.group().size() == output_strides.size())' makes that unreachable for size mismatch; the crash would only affect the operator's own process anyway.

The temporary scalar tmp_reduced_val is read without an explicit initialization in this code; if the internal Op::Run failed to write it, an uninitialized value could reach output, but that requires internal-callee behavior not shown.

verdict.summary: IsConstantFoldable bounds its per-output loop by the attacker-influenced size of the shape-map entry for the node's name (shape_it->second.size()) but consumes that index in n->output_type(i), which indexes the node's output-type table. Trigger: an attacker-supplied graph whose recorded shape-map entry for the node's name contains more shapes than the node has outputs; when i reaches num_outputs (e.g., S=2, O=1, fully-defined shapes so IsFullyDefined() is true), n->output_type(i) is called with an out-of-domain index, causing an out-of-bounds read at this call site. No guard form (bounds check, min/clamp, corrected loop bound, checked accessor) exists on any path.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived inputs (extradata buf/size, parser offset, m4ac fields, bitstream reads) are guarded in execution order by quotable checks: init_get_bits8 failure handling, off<0 rejection before skip_bits_long, the unsigned objecttype>3U check (which also catches object_type==0 yielding -1), the sampling_index==15 rejection, and the bounded put_bits destination init_put_bits(&pb, adts->pce_data, MAX_PCE_SIZE) that caps the only memory-write path, with pce_size=(ret+3)/8 provably <= MAX_PCE_SIZE even at the exact boundary (ret<=509). No memory-corruption, OOB, injection, or bypass trigger with a fully instantiated impact chain exists within this code.

assumptions: buf/size are codec extradata originating from a parsed media file and are treated as attacker-data; this static function is the intake point, so its own guards were judged as the last line of defense.

avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 is a project-internal callee not shown; on success (off >= 0) it is assumed to populate m4ac.object_type (5-bit range), m4ac.sampling_index (4-bit, 0-15) and m4ac.chan_config (4-bit, 0-15) from the input — these ranges are not quotable from the given code, but residual risk is covered by the defensive checks at lines 19, 23 and 39.

ff_copy_pce_data and put_bits internals are not shown; this code supplies the destination bound (init_put_bits with MAX_PCE_SIZE) and a successfully-initialized GetBitContext, so whether the callee honors buf_end is an unquotable property, recorded here rather than used to confirm or dismiss a candidate.

limitations: Speculative: a PCE longer than MAX_PCE_SIZE could overflow adts->pce_data inside the not-shown ff_copy_pce_data/put_bits if those fail to honor the PutBitContext bound set at line 40; the overflow write itself would occur entirely in the callee, so the impact chain cannot be instantiated from the given code.

The pce_size rounding ((ret+3)/8) uses floor division, which can undercount the byte-rounded PCE length by one byte when the total bit count is not byte-aligned (e.g. ret=60 gives pce_size=7 instead of 8); this can only truncate the downstream-copied PCE (pce_size never exceeds MAX_PCE_SIZE, so no overcount), and the consumer of pce_size is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated.

When off equals the buffer end (or exceeds it), the three get_bits(&gb,1) flag checks read 0 bits and pass vacuously, so the 'no 960/120 window / not scalable / no extension' validations are unverified in that case; this is lenient format validation with no security decision attached in this code.
A NULL/near-empty extradata is rejected by init_get_bits8's documented failure returns; no additional crash path was found beyond ordinary error propagation.

verdict.summary: handle_PORT parses the attacker-controlled PORT argument with an unchecked sscanf into unbounded int values, then formats them with sprintf into the 16-byte stack buffer addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN], producing a remotely-triggerable stack buffer overflow before any validation (inet_aton runs after the sprintf). evidence.reason: Root cause: sscanf return value is not checked (so a-f may be uninitialized on partial matches) and a-d are not range-bounded; sprintf then writes up to 48 bytes (e.g. input "PORT 2147483647,2147483647,2147483647,2147483647,1,1" yields a 44-byte string) into the 16-byte stack buffer addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN], an out-of-bounds stack write fully controlled by the network peer. The only validation in the function, inet_aton on line 18, executes after the overflow and cannot guard the sink.

Taint origin: str is the PORT command argument supplied by the remote FTP client (attacker-data), consumed by sscanf into the unvalidated ints a-f; addr is a fixed 16-byte stack buffer (INET_ADDRSTRLEN) that the later sprintf overflows.

limitations: ctrl->data_port = e * 256 + f (line 25) accepts out-of-range/negative ports since e and f are never validated against 0-255; the consumer of data_port is not shown, so no impact chain could be instantiated here.

On malformed PORT arguments the unchecked sscanf leaves a-f uninitialized; formatting them into addr and echoing it via DBG/ERR is a potential stack-content disclosure, recorded as secondary to the confirmed overflow.

verdict.summary: SparseTensorSliceDatasetOp::MakeDataset validates only the RANK of the 'indices' input (IsMatrix) before the batch-ordering loop dereferences column 0 via indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0). Nothing checks that the matrix has at least one column (or that dim_size(1) matches dense_shape length). With attacker-supplied indices of shape [N,0] (e.g. N=2), the loop performs an out-of-bounds read of element 0 of a zero-element tensor (heap OOB read past a 0-byte allocation, or null dereference), crashing or leaking via the subsequent ordering comparison.

No vulnerability found. finderrfunc is a static VM-internal frame/cframe stack walker; all frame metadata and cframe fields are produced by the interpreter itself, not by attacker-controlled data. Every pointer dereference is dominated in execution order by the quoted invariants: 'while (frame > bot && cf)', 'if (cf == NULL) return 0;', and the xpcall size check 'frame_ftsz(frame) >= (ptrdiff_t)(2*sizeof(TValue))'. The (frame-1) read in the FFI FRAME_CONT arm is covered by frame > bot (frame >= bot+1), the -cframe_nres offset is reached only when nres < 0 (positive restore offset by VM encoding), and every cf advance is followed by a NULL check before any dereference. No guard absent anywhere on any path; no attacker-triggerable defect.

assumptions: Frame metadata (frame type tags, ftz sizes) and cframe fields (nres, errfunc, prev chain) are written only by LuaJIT VM internals (lj_vm asm, interpreter prologue, lj_err/lj_api C code), not by Lua script values; no statement in this function or its flow lets script data forge these structures.
restorestack(L, -cframe_nres(cf)) relies on the VM's NRES encoding convention (negative when the cframe has a Lua frame), which is a project-internal contract not shown in the given code.
lua_assert and the frame_typep enumeration are assumed exhaustive for frames the VM constructs (the default arm returns 0 in release builds regardless).
limitations: A trigger via forged or corrupted frame/cframe metadata (e.g., from a memory-corruption bug elsewhere in an embedding application, or from JIT-miscompiled code) would break the walked invariants, but no such producer exists within this code; that scenario is outside the given code and remains speculative.

If an embedder ran this code against attacker-modified internal state (e.g., via a debugger or a hostile C API misuse), bounds could be violated; this function contains no intake point for such data and no check can be required of it.

The unbounded-walk concern (CWE-400) was considered: each iteration strictly lowers 'frame' and the cframe chain is finite, so the walk is bounded by actual VM stack depth established elsewhere; no attacker-amplification primitive exists in this function.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes op input(2) (shape_and_slices) at the caller-supplied restore_index without validating the tensor's element count. The function performs the exact analogous check for input(1) (`OP_REQUIRES(context, size > restore_index, ...)`), but for input(2) it executes `context->input(2).flat<tstring>()(restore_index)` with no bound on any path, producing an attacker-triggered out-of-bounds heap read whose garbage contents are then inspected (empty()) and parsed (ParseShapeAndSlice) — crash and disclosure potential in the process running the restore op.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: input(2) is indexed at restore_index with no element-count validation. Trigger: attacker feeds input(0)=valid scalar checkpoint path, input(1)=N-element name tensor (passes the `size > restore_index` check quoted at line 18), and input(2) with fewer than restore_index+1 elements (e.g., 1 element with restore_index=1, or an empty tensor with restore_index=0), with restore_slice=true. All quoted gates (reader status line 39, HasTensor line 45, dtype line 48) pass for a valid attacker-supplied checkpoint, then `flat<tstring>()(restore_index)` reads past the end of the input(2) tensor buffer; the resulting garbage tstring is consumed by `.empty()` (line 61) and `ParseShapeAndSlice` (line 63). The identical guard exists for input(1) but is absent here — the single missing guard is `context->input(2).NumElements() > restore_index`.

assumptions: Op registration (not shown) enforces that inputs 0, 1, and 2 are DT_STRING tensors, so flat<tstring>() reinterpretation of input(2) is assumed type-correct.

checkpoint::TensorSliceReader, GetReader, HasTensor, CopySliceData, ParseShapeAndSlice are project-internal callees not shown; their documented failure sentinels are assumed to be handled by the OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK wrappers at lines 39, 45, 63.

The error message at line 51 reports expected_output_dtype(0) while the check at line 49 compares against expected_output_dtype(restore_index) — a cosmetic/log inconsistency with no security effect.

Attacker control of the checkpoint file content requires the attacker to be able to place or reference a readable checkpoint at the file_pattern path; in the standard RestoreV2 input surface this is the op's normal input contract, but a deployment that only restores from a fixed protected checkpoint directory would limit reachability.

verdict.summary: The only memory-write sink, memset(skb->data, 0, MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE), is guarded by dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) with a NULL check, an allocation sized from the identical constant as the copy length, so no out-of-bounds write is reachable. skb_pull length is mask-bounded to [1,64] and skb_pull itself refuses pulls exceeding skb->len, producing only a harmless no-op. MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE is assumed to be the compile-time constant used consistently; dev_alloc_skb is assumed to provide at least MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE bytes of data area per standard kernel allocation semantics.
limitations: The error path 'return -EINVAL' after rsi_prepare_beacon fails leaks the allocated skb (no dev_kfree_skb), a fixed-size resource leak whose trigger depends on the not-shown callee failing; recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The dword-alignment logic (skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes)) is effectively dead code because skb->len is 0 after allocation and skb_pull returns NULL without pulling; this is a correctness defect, not a security impact.
Behavior of skb_queue_tail/rsi_set_event consumers is internal to the driver and not shown; no conclusion about them is drawn.

Infinite-loop candidate in the situation-2 adjustment logic could not be concretely instantiated (line1 advances at least one per iteration, line2 at most one), but termination depends on ml_append appending exactly one line per call.

if (needle < to - 4) {
