verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr parses attacker-supplied RTCP XR report blocks but validates only that a block's length field is nonzero (`if (rb_len)`); it never checks that the block's fixed-size struct fits within the received packet. A remote peer can place a short report block at the end of the packet so that post-loop field reads (rb_rr_time->ntp_frac, rb_stats->lost/jitter_*/toh_dev, rb_dlrr->item.*, voip metrics fields) read up to ~36 bytes past the end of the packet buffer (out-of-bounds read; values are stored in session statistics).

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: report block pointers are saved with only a nonzero-length test (`if (rb_len)`); no statement verifies that the block's struct (12 bytes for RR Time, ~40 for Stats, ~32 for VoIP Metrics) fits inside the packet, and rb_hdr can be the last word of the packet. Trigger: 12-byte packet, pkt_len=2, block bt=BT_RR_TIME with rb_len=1 at offset 4 passes all checks, so subsequent fixed-offset struct reads run past the buffer.

sess->rx_lrr = ((pj_ntohl(rb_rr_time->ntp_sec) & 0x0000FFFF) << 16) | 
		       ((pj_ntohl(rb_rr_time->ntp_frac) >> 16) & 0xFFFF);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: with the 12-byte trigger packet (size=12, pkt_len=2, BT_RR_TIME block header as the last word with rb_len=1), rb_rr_time->ntp_sec reads pkt[8..11] (in bounds) but rb_rr_time->ntp_frac reads pkt[12..15], 4 bytes past the end of the 12-byte packet buffer; the value is retained in sess->rx_lrr.

Second OOB read sink: attacker sets flag bit 7 of rb_stats->header.specific, so rb_stats->lost (struct offset 8) is read even when the block extends past the packet; jitter and toh flags drive reads up to struct offset ~39, reading up to ~36 bytes past the buffer end.

assumptions: Report-block struct layouts (pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rb_rr_time = 4-byte header + ntp_sec + ntp_frac; rb_stats ≈ 40 bytes; rb_voip_mtc ≈ 32 bytes; rb_dlrr header + ssrc + item{lrr,dlrr}) are the standard pjproject definitions, which the field accesses in this code match.
TRACE_ is a debug macro typically compiled out; its constant format strings and extra arguments are not security-relevant.
pj_get_timestamp, pjmedia_rtcp_get_ntp_time, pj_math_stat_update are trusted internal helpers.
limitations: Lines 14/17 read rtcp_xr->common.pt and common.length before any size check; with size < 4 this is a 1–3 byte OOB read, but instantiating it requires a caller that passes sub-4-byte packets — a contract not quotable in this code, so it is not counted as primary.
The advance `rb_hdr + rb_len + 1` can jump up to ~256KB past the buffer, but the while-condition immediately ends the loop, so the wild pointer is never dereferenced.

The unsigned wrap in `eedelay = now - lrr - dlrr` only affects RTT statistics and is constrained by the quoted sanity checks (`if (now-dlrr >= lrr)`, `if (eedelay <= 30 * 1000 * 1000UL)`); no memory-safety effect.

verdict.summary: ReadPCLImage parses attacker-controlled CropBox/MediaBox coordinates from the input file via sscanf and converts them to page dimensions with no sign or magnitude validation: a negative or huge extent becomes a near-2^64 size_t (negative long cast to size_t), which flows unclamped into the GhostPCL delegate command '-g<width>x<height>' executed by ExternalDelegateCommand. A ~24-byte crafted PCL/PS prolog forces the delegate to render/write multi-gigabyte output and the process to consume it — attacker-scalable resource exhaustion (DoS) with no guard anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-file-derived bounds are converted to size_t with no range/sign check. Trigger: file containing 'CropBox [0 0 -100 -100 ]' yields bounds.x2-bounds.x1 = -100, so width = (size_t)(-100) = 18446744073709551516; the 'if (width > page.width)' max-update stores it in page.width. No clamp, range check, or bound exists on any path; the value sizes the delegate render request '-g%.20gx%.20g' passed to ExternalDelegateCommand, causing unbounded render/output work from a tiny input (CWE-400 via CWE-191).

evidence.snippet:
count=(ssize_t) sscanf(command,"CropBox [%lf %lf %lf %lf",
          &bounds.x1,&bounds.y1,&bounds.x2,&bounds.y2);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: file bytes accumulated in command[] are parsed with %lf into bounds, accepting arbitrary attacker magnitudes and signs; the only subsequent validation, 'if (count != 4) continue;', checks the parse count, never the value range.

assumptions: CastDoubleToLong is an internal callee not shown; it is assumed to convert doubles to long with sane clamping for NaN/out-of-range — the defect does not depend on this since any reasonable conversion of -100.0 yields -100, which casts to a huge size_t.

ExternalDelegateCommand and ReadImage semantics (execute command / read image file) are assumed standard for the delegate pipeline; the amplification follows directly from the arguments this code passes.
The pcl:color/mono/cmyk delegate (GhostPCL) is assumed configured per delegates.xml; if absent the function fails closed at the delegate_info NULL check.
image_info fields (page, density, ping, monochrome) are operator-supplied, not file-derived, and were treated as trusted content.
limitations: Command-buffer fill loop is guarded: 'if ((c != (int) '/') && (c != '\n') && ((size_t) (p-command) < (MaxTextExtent-1))) continue;' — edge-tested: max write index MaxTextExtent-2, NUL at MaxTextExtent-1, p reset each segment; no overflow.
The ignored return of '(void) AcquireUniqueFilename(read_info->filename);' (line 215) only matters on environment/temp-dir failure an attacker cannot induce, and the failure path is fail-closed.
'geometry' is formatted (lines 168-169) but never used afterwards — dead code, no security effect.

In-process OOM when re-reading the delegate's giant output may be capped by ImageMagick resource policies not shown here (assumption); the primary amplification occurs in the delegate render/write step this code invokes.
The ping-path multiplications of image->columns/rows use operator-supplied resolutions and only modify metadata; no instantiated security impact.

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads an attacker-controlled field count (nbFields, up to 2^31-1) directly from the BIFS bitstream with no sanity bound and uses it both as the allocation count for gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc and as the decode loop bound. A ~36-bit input can force multi-gigabyte heap allocations retained in the scene graph and hundreds of millions of decode iterations, enabling memory-exhaustion/CPU denial of service of the decoder process.

evidence.snippet:
NbBits = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 5);
	nbFields = gf_bs_read_int(bs, NbBits);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: nbFields is read straight from the attacker-controlled bitstream (up to 2^31-1 when the 5-bit NbBits equals 31) with no range, cap, or sanity check on any path.

Sink: the unvalidated attacker count nbFields sizes the MF allocation (line 29) and bounds the decode loop (line 32). The only quoted guard, 'if (e) return e;', tests allocation failure, not magnitude. Instantiated trigger: NbBits=31, nbFields=2^28 yields a ~1 GiB heap allocation retained in the scene graph (and up to 2^28 decode iterations) from ~36 bits of input, repeatable per BIFS command — attacker-scalable memory/CPU exhaustion (CWE-400).

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int(bs, n) returns a value in [0, 2^n-1] (GPAC bitstream accessor semantics); with the 5-bit NbBits this makes nbFields reachable up to 2^31-1.
gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc either succeeds with memory proportional to nbFields times the per-item size or returns an error; the per-item width is internal to GPAC and not shown.
Behavior of gf_bifs_dec_sf_field and gf_bs_read_int on an exhausted stream (silently returning zeros vs. erroring) is not shown; either way the allocation at line 29 is already retained.
codec->ActiveQP / force_keep_qp / pCurrentProto are decoder state shaped by previously decoded attacker commands.
limitations: Potential u32 count*size overflow inside the unshown gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc (e.g. 2^31 items of 4 bytes wrapping the computed size) would yield a heap out-of-bounds write via the loop at line 32; the overflowing arithmetic is not quotable in this code, so it is recorded as speculative (CWE-190), not as the primary finding.

Decoded node leak when node==NULL and codec->pCurrentProto==NULL (new_node is registered but never attached to any list): reaching the call site with node==NULL is not instantiated by any statement in this code.

The QP branch's 'gf_node_register(new_node, NULL); gf_node_unregister(new_node, node);' refcount shuffle and gf_bifs_dec_qp_remove/qp14_set_length behavior rely on unshown callees; no misuse of an out-of-domain argument is provable at these call sites.
The MFNODE-branch loop is partially self-limiting because each iteration must consume node-coding bits from the stream; the MF-alloc path is the dominant amplification sink.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_xr_rx_rtcp_xr reads the RTCP XR common header fields rtcp_xr->common.pt (line 14) and rtcp_xr->common.length (line 17) before any statement bounds the size parameter; the only size check, `if ((pkt_len + 1) > (size / 4))`, executes after these reads. A caller-supplied packet with size < 4 (attacker-controlled datagram length at this exported parsing entry point) causes a 1-3 byte out-of-bounds read. All subsequent block parses are correctly bounded by the quoted per-case sizeof checks, so impact is confined to this overread: no disclosure (the value only feeds a comparison that returns regardless), no write, worst case a remotely induced fault.

In find_pattern_in_path(), the ACTION_EXPAND path computes i = (int)(p - aux) as the length of a keyword taken from the (attacker-supplied) current buffer line or included-file line, and copies it with STRNCPY(IObuff, aux, i) into the fixed global IObuff[IOSIZE] without any bound on i. Buffer lines can contain keywords longer than IOSIZE (1024), so editing a crafted file and triggering insert-mode completion in 'adding' state overflows IObuff with attacker-controlled bytes (also IObuff[i++] and the IOSIZE - i clamp at line 456 misbehave once i >= IOSIZE). No check or clamp of i against IOSIZE exists anywhere on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: i is the length of the matched word in the buffer/included-file line (aux = p = startp at line 406, p = find_word_end(p) at 414), which is unbounded and attacker-controlled via file content. STRNCPY(IObuff, aux, i) copies i bytes into the fixed 1024-byte global IObuff with no bounds check; the comment 'IOSIZE > compl_length' is an assumption, and the later clamp 'if (p - aux >= IOSIZE - i) p = aux + IOSIZE - i - 1;' only guards the second copy and assumes i < IOSIZE. Trigger: a buffer line containing a keyword longer than IOSIZE bytes completed with insert-mode completion in 'adding' state (i == ins_compl_len() both equal the long word length) -> out-of-bounds global-buffer write with attacker data.

assumptions: STRNCPY behaves as strncpy (copies up to n bytes); IObuff is the fixed-size global char_u IObuff[IOSIZE] with IOSIZE = 1024, per the code's own comment 'IOSIZE > compl_length' and its use of vim_snprintf(... IOSIZE ...) elsewhere.
ptr/len come from Vim's completion machinery (len = strlen(ptr), non-negative, bounded by line length), so alloc(len + 5) with sprintf "%.*s" is an exact fit (2 + len + 2 + NUL).
Buffer and included-file line lengths are unbounded in Vim (ml_get / vim_fgets lines can exceed IOSIZE), so words longer than IOSIZE are producible from attacker-supplied file content.
limitations: Speculative: when the ALLOC_MULT for the bigger stack fails (line 251 returns NULL), the code intentionally writes files[depth+1] and vim_free(files[old_files].name) at index old_files == max_path_depth, one past the allocated array (lines 270-284). Trigger requires an allocation failure the attacker cannot reliably induce; recorded as a robustness/OOM-path defect, not a primary finding.

Speculative: sprintf(pat, ..., len, ptr) into alloc(len + 5) overflows only if len were negative or near INT_MAX; no caller shown passes such values, and len is strlen-derived in the assumed calling convention.

Recursive include scanning is bounded by the already-searched scan over indices [0, depth] ∪ [old_files, max_path_depth) (lines 123-150), which remembers popped files, so cyclic includes do not produce unbounded re-push in this code as written.

verdict.summary: mruby VM main interpreter loop. All sinks consuming runtime-variable mrb_value data are guarded by quoted, execution-order-preceding type dispatches with fallback/error arms (OP_MATH TYPES2 switch with L_SEND_SYM fallback, OP_GETIDX type switch with getidx_fallback, OP_RESCUE type check raising E_TYPE_ERROR, OP_KARG/OP_KEY_P/OP_KEYEND kidx short-circuit checks rejecting kidx<0 before regs[kidx]). Remaining candidates require malformed bytecode (operands beyond nregs/pool/syms, out-of-range JMPUW jump) or a minimally-sized REnv with kd=1 (OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` permits a one-past read when kd=1), none of which is producible by any statement in this code: the function neither parses nor loads bytecode, and the compiler well-formedness contract is documented by in-code assertions (mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen), mrb_assert((pool[b].tt&IREP_TT_NFLAG)==0)). No injection, format-string, crypto, or fail-open defects found.

assumptions: ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE macro (not shown) normalizes argc/a and fetches blk before L_SENDB_SYM uses them
uvenv() returns a valid REnv or NULL; mrb_stack_extend() allocates at least the requested register count; catch_handler_find() returns handlers whose unpacked begin/end/target are within irep
irep/pool/syms are built by the in-process compiler/loader; this function receives an already-constructed RProc and never parses an external format
mrb_assert is a debug assertion removed in release (MRB_NDEBUG) builds; it documents invariants but does not enforce them at runtime
limitations: Latent off-by-one (not triggerable from this code): OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH guard `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` allows len == m1+r+m2+2, while a kd=1 encoding accesses e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] (one past the end) — requires a kd=1 bytecode encoding with a minimally-sized env, producible only from hand-crafted irep, not from the trusted compiler flow shown

If an embedding application ever executes untrusted bytecode (.mrb), the absence of per-operand validation becomes exploitable: e.g. OP_MOVE `regs[a] = regs[b]` with operands >= irep->nregs (stack sized only via mrb_stack_extend(mrb, (irep->nregs < 4) ? 4 : irep->nregs)) gives OOB read/write; OP_JMPUW `pc = irep->iseq + a;` has no runtime check against irep->ilen on the main path (only the assert in the CHECKPOINT_RESTORE arm). mruby does not support executing untrusted bytecode, and no statement in this code produces malformed irep

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes input(1) and input(2) with the unvalidated restore_index parameter (tensor_name_t.flat<tstring>()(restore_index) and context->input(2).flat<tstring>()(restore_index)) without any NumElements/bounds check, unlike input(0) which is explicitly checked (OP_REQUIRES(context, size == 1, ...)). An attacker across the trust boundary who controls the op inputs and the index value can cause an out-of-bounds read of heap memory past the tensor buffer; the out-of-bounds string content is then used in HasTensor lookups and concatenated into attacker-visible error messages, giving an out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential.

evidence.snippet:
const Tensor& tensor_name_t = context->input(1);
  const string& tensor_name = tensor_name_t.flat<tstring>()(restore_index);
evidence.reason: Root cause and primary sink: restore_index is used to index input(1) with no check that restore_index < tensor_name_t.NumElements(). The code checks input(0) with OP_REQUIRES(context, size == 1, ...) at lines 5-12 but performs no equivalent validation here. Trigger: attacker supplies tensor_name_t with fewer elements than restore_index+1 (e.g., 1 element, restore_index=1, or a 0-element tensor with restore_index=0, or a negative restore_index); flat<tstring>()(restore_index) then reads one-past-the-end / before the tensor's heap buffer (Eigen's bounds assert is compiled out in release), and the OOB tstring content is used at line 38 and embedded in error messages at lines 39-40/46, leaking out-of-bounds heap data to the invoker.

evidence.snippet:
const tstring& shape_spec =
        context->input(2).flat<tstring>()(restore_index);
evidence.reason: Second instance of the same defect: input(2) is indexed by restore_index with no NumElements or range check anywhere on the path (only gated by the restore_slice flag). An attacker controlling the size of input(2) independently of the index value triggers the same out-of-bounds read; the OOB shape_spec then flows into ParseShapeAndSlice.

evidence.snippet: int preferred_shard, bool restore_slice, int restore_index) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: restore_index is an unvalidated 32-bit int parameter of this non-static function; no documented, asserted, or checked precondition bounds it, so it is attacker-data per the parameter-intake rule and indexes both input(1) and input(2) with no guard on any path.

assumptions: checkpoint::TensorSliceReader::HasTensor / CopySliceData and checkpoint::ParseShapeAndSlice are not shown; their behavior (e.g., validating slice_to_load against saved_shape before copying into t) is assumed, not quoted.
Eigen TensorMap::operator() (the accessor behind flat<T>()) performs bounds checking only via eigen_assert, which is compiled out in release builds — characterized per standard-library semantics.
The behavior of the real callers of RestoreTensor (which may bound restore_index) is not shown and therefore cannot be quoted; per the analysis rules the index parameter is treated as attacker-data.
context->expected_output_dtype and context->allocate_output are assumed to validate the slot index restore_index (framework-managed accessors).
limitations: If a caller outside this code provably bounds restore_index below both input(1) and input(2) NumElements, the OOB read would require that caller's cooperation; no such caller is shown, so this could not be verified.
The dtype error message at line 44 uses expected_output_dtype(0) instead of expected_output_dtype(restore_index) — a cosmetic message bug with no security effect.

Whether slice_to_load can exceed saved_shape and cause an OOB write inside CopySliceData depends on the not-shown ParseShapeAndSlice/CopySliceData validation; only parsed_shape.IsSameSize(saved_shape) is enforced in this code.
CHECK_NOTNULL(reader) and the new TensorSliceReader allocation can abort on OOM, an environment failure no attacker induces.

verdict.summary: In pcx_write_rle, the run-length scan increments 'from' past the last pixel (from += step can set from == end, or overshoot end when step does not divide the row length) and then dereferences it in 'if (data != *from || from == end)'. Because || evaluates the dereference before the bounds test, the code reads one or more bytes past the end of the row buffer on every final pixel of a row, a heap out-of-bounds read reachable from attacker-controlled image data (potential crash at an allocation/page boundary).

evidence.snippet:
from += step;
        if (data != *from || from == end) {
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: 'from += step' advances from to (or past) 'end' on the last pixel of a row, and the left operand 'data != *from' dereferences 'from' before the 'from == end' bounds test is evaluated. The only guard, 'while (from < end)', was checked before the increment and is stale. Trigger: encode any row whose pixel content is attacker-supplied; when from reaches end exactly, *end is read one byte past the buffer.

assumptions: gp_fputc has standard fputc semantics (int byte, FILE-like stream); its return value is unused.
'step' is a positive bytes-per-pixel constant supplied by the device configuration, not by parsed file data.
limitations: If 'step' could be 0 or negative (caller contract violation not producible from this code's own flow), the loop would not advance or would read backwards before the buffer; speculative, not counted.

When end - row_start is not a multiple of 'step', 'from += step' overshoots end and line 14 reads up to step-1 bytes past it; this misalignment depends on caller geometry, but the aligned one-byte overread at from == end is unconditional on every row.
The overread byte never reaches the output when from == end (both comparison results take the same branch), so impact is memory-safety violation/crash potential rather than information disclosure.

verdict.summary: The loop indexes bin->segment_entries with a bound taken solely from the attacker-parsed SegCount field and no guard in this code ties the array size to that count, and bin->ne_header is dereferenced without a NULL check. However, neither the allocation of segment_entries nor the state ne_header==NULL is produced by any statement in this code, so no trigger with a concrete security-impact chain (corruption, disclosure, bypass) is instantiated within this snippet.

assumptions: segment_entries is allocated by the NE file loader (not shown) with a count related to SegCount; this code contains no statement sizing or validating it.
__translate_perms and r_str_newf behave per their documented semantics.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read at 'NE_image_segment_entry *se = &bin->segment_entries[i];' if the loader allocates fewer entries than ne_header->SegCount — the allocation site is outside this code, so the mismatch state could not be instantiated; a count-consistency guard is the natural fix.

NULL dereference of bin->ne_header at 'bin->ne_header->SegCount' — the NULL-check 'if (!bin || !bin->segment_entries)' omits ne_header, but producing ne_header==NULL requires loader behavior not shown, and impact is only a crash of the parsing process.

verdict.summary: Ragel-generated HTTP/1.1 parser. All buffer dereferences are guarded in execution order by the quoted 'p == pe' checks at machine entry and at every state entry, keeping p within [buffer+off, buffer+len) given the asserted off <= len. All callback pointer/length arguments are in-domain slices of the buffer; the tr22 edge case yields (one-past-end pointer, length 0) which is in-domain. Remaining candidates (off > len under NDEBUG, stale mark offsets across buffers, nread accumulation) require caller behavior or compile-time configuration this code neither produces nor documents beyond asserts, so they are speculative.

assumptions: Macros MARK, PTR_TO, LEN and functions snake_upcase_char, puma_parser_has_error, and the parser->request_method/request_uri/http_field/header_done etc. callbacks are not shown; assumed to store/reconstruct offsets within the current buffer and to consume (pointer, length) slices without exceeding the given length.

assert() is assumed active; under NDEBUG the guards 'assert(off <= len)', 'assert(parser->nread <= len)', 'assert(parser->mark < len)', 'assert(parser->field_start < len)' disappear, but the operative dereference guard (if (p == pe)) is real code, not an assert.
Callbacks invoked with attacker-derived in-domain arguments; per discipline 3 the defect cannot be located at these call sites since pointer and length are provably inside the buffer.
limitations: If a caller passes off > len with NDEBUG defined, 'p = buffer+off' forms an out-of-bounds pointer and 'pe - p' underflows; the code only guards this with assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer"), which is a documented contract check, not a runtime guard. Trigger requires caller contract violation not producible by this code's own flow.

On multi-invocation parsing with a different buffer per call, persisted parser->mark / parser->field_start offsets from a previous buffer would make LEN(mark, p) compute across buffers (potentially huge size_t). This requires an unstated caller pattern; this code never instantiates it.

'assert(parser->nread <= len)' can be violated when nread accumulates across invocations against a smaller per-call len, indicating an unstated single-buffer/resume contract; impact limited to the assert (no memory access derives from nread here).

The commented-out 'assert(*pe == '\0')' indicates the buffer is not required to be NUL-terminated; all reads are length-guarded, so no OOB read results, but consumers relying on NUL termination are outside this code.

An error-state parser (cs == 0) re-entered with data falls through the switch to '_test_eof2: cs = 2;' without consuming bytes and without a memory-safety effect; possible caller-visible loop behavior is not shown.

verdict.summary: This static helper allocates an skb of MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE bytes and memsets exactly the same constant, so the only bulk write is provably within the allocation; the alignment pull is masked to at most 63 bytes and is in fact a no-op on a zero-length skb; all other values are kernel-allocator outputs or constants, and no attacker-controlled data enters the function. The failure and success paths handle the skb exclusively (free vs queue), so no double free or UAF is possible in this snippet.

assumptions: MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE is a compile-time constant from a header not shown; the analysis does not depend on its value because it is used identically as the allocation size (line 6) and the memset length (line 10).

rsi_prepare_beacon() (not shown) is assumed to write within the skb's remaining tailroom; any overflow would be a defect inside that callee, not at this call site, since this code passes only a valid skb and no attacker-derived size, offset, or pointer.
limitations: The return value of skb_pull() at line 14 is ignored; on a freshly allocated (zero-length) skb skb_pull is a no-op, so the intended 64-byte alignment of skb->data is never actually established. This is a functional/robustness issue in this snippet, with no memory-safety consequence in the code shown.

If the unseen callee rsi_prepare_beacon() assumes the skb retains the full MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE tailroom or assumes 64-byte-aligned data, an out-of-bounds write or misaligned hardware access could occur inside that callee; the callee is not part of the given code, so no trigger could be instantiated here.
Beacon content/configuration carried in struct rsi_common never flows through any statement of this snippet, so no attacker-data taint could be traced within the given code.

verdict.summary: Ragel-generated HTTP parser FSM is memory-safe for all in-contract inputs: every byte dereference is guarded in execution order by 'if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;' and the entry 'if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;', all LEN/PTR_TO uses are dominated by MARK on the same path, and all asserts (off <= len, mark < len, body_start <= len) hold by construction. The only OOB paths require the caller to violate the asserted precondition off <= len (unbounded when NDEBUG disables the assert) or to pass a different buffer without re-initializing parser state; neither is produced by this code's own flow.

assumptions: MARK/LEN/PTR_TO macros (not shown) are assumed to be parser->mark = p - buffer, LEN(m,p) = p - (buffer + m), PTR_TO(m) = buffer + m, per the Mongrel/Puma lineage; if LEN used unsigned subtraction, the cross-call scenario in limitations would underflow.
puma_parser_has_error(parser) is assumed to test the error state (cs == 0); it is not shown.
The callbacks (request_method, request_uri, http_field, header_done, etc.) are assumed not to write through the const pointers/lengths handed to them; they are not shown.
puma_parser_init (not shown) resets cs, mark, field_start, field_len, nread between requests.
limitations: Contract-gated OOB read: if the caller passes off > len and the build defines NDEBUG (disabling 'assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer")'), then p = buffer+off is past pe, the 'p == pe' guards never match, and 'switch ((*p))' reads out of bounds without bound, and callbacks receive pointers/lengths past the buffer. Trigger requires caller violation of a precondition this code asserts, so it is not a vulnerability in this code. Note the second assert, 'assert((size_t)(pe - p) == len - off)', passes even when off > len due to identical underflow on both sides and provides no protection.

Cross-call stale offsets: parser->mark/field_start/field_len/query_start persist across calls and this code never resets them; if the caller reuses the parser on a different buffer without re-init, LEN(mark, p) can underflow to a huge size_t passed to http_field/fragment/query_string. Trigger depends on caller behavior not instantiated by this code.

snake_upcase_char((char *)p) casts away const and modifies the caller's buffer in place; a read-only buffer would crash the server process on a header field (equal-privilege crash, no corruption) — deployment-dependent, not instantiated here.
High-bit bytes (signed char, negative) bypass some grammar exclusions (e.g. case 23/24 'if (0 <= (*p) && (*p) <= 31) goto st0;'), affecting only which characters are accepted, not memory safety.

verdict.summary: call_qftf_func safely marshals a user-configured callback invocation: the allocation failure sentinel is checked before use, the callback return is type-guarded before dereference, the list refcount is incremented before clear_tv so no use-after-free occurs, and the dict reference bump balances dict_unref. No attacker-reachable sink consumes unvalidated data in this code.

assumptions: call_callback (project-internal, not shown) sets rettv on non-FAIL return; this contract cannot be quoted from the given code, but the != FAIL and v_type == VAR_LIST checks guard every use of rettv regardless.

The quickfixtextfunc callback is configured by the vimrc/plugin owner (operator-privilege user config, not settable via modeline), so its return content is not treated as cross-trust-boundary attacker data.
A typval with v_type == VAR_LIST always carries a non-NULL vval.v_list per Vim's value model; the given code cannot produce a VAR_LIST-with-NULL itself.
limitations: The function is written without an explicit return type; taken literally as C implicit int, `return NULL;` / `return qftf_list;` would truncate a 64-bit list_T* to int. The impact requires a caller not shown in this excerpt, so the chain is not instantiated; this is consistent with an excerpted `static list_T *` signature and is recorded, not confirmed.

If the internal call_callback could return non-FAIL while leaving rettv uninitialized, the v_type read could consume stale stack data; this depends entirely on an unquoted internal-callee contract and could not be instantiated from this code's own flow.

verdict.summary: pj_scan_get_char validates the cursor against scanner->end before every buffer read: 'if (s >= scanner->end || !*s)' rejects out-of-range and NUL positions before 'chr = *s', and after the increment the pointer can reach at most end, where the short-circuited PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF(s) prevents the second dereference. verdict.summary: parallels_open parses an untrusted Parallels disk image header and stores ph.tracks and ph.nb_sectors into driver state with no sanity/domain checks, unlike the validated catalog_entries field. An attacker-supplied image with tracks = 0 (or arbitrary geometry) is accepted (only magic/version and catalog_size are checked), leaving the driver in a state whose read path divides/strides by the unvalidated tracks value and indexes via unvalidated catalog offsets — the historical QEMU Parallels block-driver vulnerability, whose fix is exactly the missing check at this intake point.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled header fields ph.nb_sectors and ph.tracks are stored into driver state with no nonzero/bounds check anywhere on any path (the only guards in the function cover ph.magic/ph.version at lines 16-21 and ph.catalog_entries at lines 28-32), even though the next field is explicitly checked. Trigger: a crafted image passing the magic/version check with ph.tracks = 0 reaches line 25 unconditionally, leaving a zero geometry stride in BDRVParallelsState that the driver's read path consumes as a divisor/stride (divide-by-zero / miscomputed cluster index), crashing or corrupting the process that opened the attacker-supplied image. Root cause: missing input validation of header geometry at the trust-boundary intake point.

assumptions: bdrv_pread is assumed to read the full requested amount or return a negative error (standard QEMU block-layer contract); under this semantics the ret < 0 checks at lines 12 and 36 make the header and catalog reads safe and the partial-read/uninitialized-ph scenario unreachable.

The declared type of BDRVParallelsState.catalog_size is not shown; in QEMU it is uint32_t. Even under a hypothetical signed declaration, an oversized le32 value would become negative, pass the > INT_MAX/4 check, cause g_malloc to abort (glib aborts on failure) rather than corrupt memory, and skip the loop — so no corruption primitive arises from the catalog_size handling either way.
HEADER_MAGIC and HEADER_VERSION are fixed constants, so an attacker can trivially satisfy lines 16-21 to reach the unvalidated stores at lines 23/25.
limitations: The concrete divide-by-zero / out-of-bounds use of s->tracks and of the catalog bitmap entries occurs in the driver's read path (a sibling function not included in the given code); the defective intake/store is in this code, and the downstream impact is asserted from this driver's known semantics (historical QEMU block/parallels CVE), not from a quoted statement.
The catalog bitmap entries themselves are attacker-controlled 32-bit values accepted verbatim; their use as file offsets is likewise in code not shown.

verdict.summary: On the tree-ensemble parse-failure path, BoostedTreesCreateEnsemble's Compute() calls result->Unref() — which frees the newly created BoostedTreesEnsembleResource via its RefCounted base when the count reaches 0 — and then unconditionally returns via OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...). The local std::unique_ptr still holds the raw pointer and its destructor executes delete on the already-freed object, producing a heap-use-after-free write and double free. The trigger is fully attacker-controlled: an attacker who can supply op inputs (e.g., an untrusted model/graph author) feeds a malformed tree_ensemble_serialized string, making InitFromSerialized return false and entering the defective arm.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the error arm frees the resource via Unref() (RefCounted deletes 'this' when the count drops from 1 to 0) and then unconditionally returns via OP_REQUIRES with literal false; the surviving std::unique_ptr then performs a second delete on the freed pointer. Trigger: attacker-supplied malformed 'tree_ensemble_serialized' op input makes InitFromSerialized return false, entering this arm — heap-use-after-free write plus double free (heap corruption).

evidence.snippet:
std::unique_ptr<BoostedTreesEnsembleResource> result(
        new BoostedTreesEnsembleResource());
evidence.reason: Origin of the conflicting ownership: the unique_ptr holds sole ownership of the freshly allocated resource (refcount 1), yet the error path also frees it manually via Unref() without resetting the unique_ptr — no reset/release/custom deleter exists on the failure path, so the destructor double-deletes.

assumptions: BoostedTreesEnsembleResource inherits TF's core::RefCounted semantics: Unref() deletes the object when the refcount reaches 0 (new object starts at 1).
OP_REQUIRES unconditionally sets the context status and returns from Compute when its condition is false; the literal false makes the return certain.

InitFromSerialized returns false for input bytes that fail protobuf parsing (documented ParseFromString semantics); the code's own error arm demonstrates this false value is an expected, reachable result.
Op inputs ('stamp_token', 'tree_ensemble_serialized', handle input 0) are attacker-controlled per TensorFlow's threat model where graphs/models are supplied across a trust boundary.
limitations: Memory leak on the ALREADY_EXISTS path: at line 24 result.release() unconditionally transfers ownership to CreateResource; if CreateResource returns ALREADY_EXISTS without taking ownership the resource is orphaned (per-call leak, CWE-400 candidate) — but CreateResource's ownership behavior on ALREADY_EXISTS is a callee not shown, so this is speculative here.

Potential out-of-bounds read if the attacker supplies a non-scalar or empty 'stamp_token'/'tree_ensemble_serialized' tensor: scalar<T>()() performs at most a DCHECK in release builds and reads element 0 — the fault would land inside TF's tensor accessor (not shown), trigger not fully instantiable from this code alone.
stamp_token is passed unvalidated into InitFromSerialized, a callee whose body is not shown; no sink for it is visible in this code.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor never validates that the column count of input_indices_in matches the rank of input_shape before invoking ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor with both. An attacker supplying an indices matrix {nnz, k} with k < input_shape.dims() causes the functor to read input_indices(i,j) for j in [k, rank) past the heap allocation; the leaked out-of-bounds int64 values are folded into the flat index and returned in the attacker-visible output indices tensor (info disclosure / SIGSEGV in the op-serving process). No check, clamp, mask, or allocation on any path in this code constrains the relationship between the matrix's second dimension and input_shape.dims().

Instantiated trigger: input_shape_in=[3,4,5] (r=3, dense_size=60), input_indices_in={1,1} content [[7]] (k=1, nnz=1), target_shape_in=[60] passes every guard (IsMatrix/IsVector lines 6-17; product=60>0; line 66: 60==60; line 74: [3,4,5] != [60]; line 96: 60>0 && 60>0), then the functor reads input_indices(0,1) and input_indices(0,2) at offsets 8 and 16 past the 8-byte allocation — heap out-of-bounds read whose values flow into the returned output indices tensor.

Origin of the tainted value: input_shape's rank r is fixed by the attacker-controlled length of input_shape_in (line 20), while line 22 reads only dim_size(0) (nnz) of the indices matrix; no statement in the function ever reads or validates dim_size(1) against input_shape.dims(), so the mismatched column bound r reaches the functor call at lines 101-104 unvalidated.

assumptions: The functor ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor reads input_indices(i,j) for j < input_shape.dims() using strides derived from input_shape: this is not shown verbatim but is forced by the call signature and reshape semantics (the only role of the input_shape argument is to define the rank and strides for interpreting the indices matrix); Eigen's .matrix<int64>() accessor (line 103) checks rank==2 only, not column extent.
output_indices_idx/output_shape_idx are wired by the op registration and are not attacker-controlled; op-declared dtypes make vec<int64>()/matrix<int64>() dtype checks framework-enforced.

The caller (op kernel) passes the op's input tensors directly to this exported function; no upstream validation of the indices/shape consistency is shown, so per the trust model this function is the last line of defense.
limitations: int64 overflow in product *= size (line 44) lets inconsistent shapes satisfy lines 50/56/66/96 (e.g. sizes (2^63-1,3) wrap to a positive value), but all functor writes are bounded by the line-92 allocation and zero strides are impossible (any suffix wrapping to 0 forces the full product to 0, rejected at line 96 when nnz>0), so this yields wrong output values, not memory corruption, in this code.

Index values in input_indices_in are not validated against input_shape (only shape-level checks exist), so output indices can be out-of-range for output_shape; any memory misuse of those values would occur in downstream ops not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

for (int d = 0; d < output_rank; ++d) (line 30) uses an int loop counter against an int64 bound; overflow requires a target_shape vector with more than 2^31 elements (~17GB input) — huge-input DoS only.
Behavior for negative values inside input_shape_in (TensorShape constructor internals) and the exact dtype-check behavior of Tensor accessors are not shown and were treated as framework contracts.

Internal callees tabstop_set(), tabstop_fromto(), tabstop_count(), tabstop_first(), ml_replace(), ml_get() follow their documented Vim semantics (reject invalid vartabstop lists, return t+s <= virtual span, take/copy ownership correctly); their implementations are not shown.

If ml_replace() failed after taking ownership of new_line, 'ptr = new_line' could read freed memory, but that requires an allocation failure inside ml_replace (environment/OOM only, not attacker-inducible); the success path is covered by 'new_line = curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_ptr'.

Return values of TfLiteIntArrayCreate/TfLiteIntArrayCopy (lines 53, 64-72, 74, 118, 149, 163, 171, 184ff) are not checked for NULL; this fails only on allocator exhaustion at small fixed sizes, which an attacker cannot induce.
