verdict.summary: This is mruby's core VM interpreter. All runtime attacker-influenced values (register contents, argc, indices into arrays/envs) are contained at their sinks by quoted guards (integer-overflow checks in OP_MATH/OP_MATHI, REnv length checks in OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR/OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH, kidx sign checks in OP_KARG/OP_KEY_P/OP_KEYEND) or are routed into bounds-safe documented accessors (mrb_ary_entry/ref/set, mrb_hash_get/set). The remaining unguarded memory sinks (regs[a], syms[b], pool[b], irep->reps[b]) consume compiler-generated bytecode operands; no statement in this code can admit an attacker-crafted irep (procs are created only via MRB_METHOD_PROC, mrb_proc_new, cipush), so no trigger is instantiable.

assumptions: FETCH_*/CASE/INIT_DISPATCH/NEXT/JUMP macros decode operands within their declared widths (uint32_t a, uint16_t b/c) but their definitions are not shown; operand range validation against irep->nregs/pool/syms sizes is performed by the mruby compiler, not by this function.

ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE (macro not shown) is presumed to assign the local `blk` before its uses at `m = prepare_missing(mrb, recv, mid, &cls, a, &c, blk, 0);` and `if (mrb_proc_p(blk))`; if it did not, `blk` would be read uninitialized, but that precondition lies in unshown code.

mrb_assert guards (e.g. `mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen);` in OP_JMPUW, `mrb_assert((pool[b].tt&IREP_TT_NFLAG)==0);` in OP_STRING) are compiled out in release builds; the values they check are produced in-range by this code's own statements (e.g. THROW_TAGGED_BREAK stores a pc-derived offset), so their removal is not reachable with a bad value.
Callees mrb_ary_entry/mrb_ary_ref/mrb_ary_set/mrb_hash_get/mrb_div_int are assumed to implement their documented bounds-safe/raising semantics per discipline 3.
limitations: If an attacker could supply a crafted irep (e.g. via an application calling mrb_load_irep on untrusted data — not in this code), this function performs NO validation of register indices (regs[a], regs[b], regs[a+1], regs[a+3]), pool indices (pool[b], pool[a]), symbol indices (syms[b]), rep indices (irep->reps[b]), or jump offsets (pc += (int16_t)a), yielding trivial out-of-bounds read/write. This is mruby's documented design (bytecode is trusted compiler output) and the trigger is not instantiable from any statement in this code.

OP_ARGARY and OP_BLKPUSH on the lv==0 branch (`stack = regs + 1`) index the register frame using masked operand fields (m1<=63, m2<=31) with no runtime length check against irep->nregs; safe only under compiler-validated bytecode.
OP_ENTER's argument-shuffling (`value_move`, `stack_clear`, `regs[blk_pos] = blk`) assumes irep->nregs exceeds len+kd+1, an invariant guaranteed by the compiler, not asserted here.

verdict.summary: This is the Linux kernel BPF ring-buffer reserve routine. The attacker-controlled u64 size is bounded by the quoted check `if (unlikely(size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ)) return NULL;` and the reservation is bounded by `if (new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask)`, both of which execute before any memory access or state update. Stale consumer_pos read before the lock is conservative (cons_pos only increases), header offset is masked and 8-aligned, and the space check prevents both over-reserve and unsigned-subtraction wraparound. No trigger for truncation, busy-bit collision, or out-of-bounds access could be instantiated from values this code can reach.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is not defined in the given code; per upstream Linux (include/linux/bpf.h) it is (UINT_MAX >> 2), which keeps size below 2^31 and keeps size + 8 (8-aligned) within u32 range, making the u32 len assignment and hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT lossless.

struct bpf_ringbuf fields (mask, data, producer_pos, consumer_pos, spinlock) are established at map-creation time in code not shown; mask is assumed to be ringbuf_size - 1 with ringbuf_size a power-of-two multiple of pages, and the data pages are assumed double-mapped so wrapping records are contiguous (standard bpf_ringbuf design).
bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off() is an internal helper not shown; assumed to derive an in-range page offset from the already-masked hdr pointer.
hdr->len and hdr->pg_off are assumed to be u32 fields of struct bpf_ringbuf_hdr per the kernel definition.
limitations: Candidate u64-to-u32 truncation in `len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` and busy-bit collision in `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT` are SPECULATIVE only because the numeric value of RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is not defined in this snippet; if the macro permitted size >= 2^31 (busy-bit collision corrupting the recorded length) or >= 2^32-8 (len truncation to a small value, allowing a reserve whose space check passes while hdr->len records a truncated size), those would become memory-safety defects. The upstream kernel definition (UINT_MAX >> 2) forecloses both.
Potential write past the first data-page mapping for records that wrap the ring end was not instantiated: safety depends on the ringbuf double-mapping construction performed in code not shown.
The function is static; the reachable attacker model is a BPF program invoking bpf_ringbuf_reserve (attacker-controlled register value) under kernels permitting the relevant BPF program load.

verdict.summary: This is the mruby VM interpreter core. Every memory access driven by runtime (attacker-influenced) values is guarded by an explicit, execution-order-correct check — env-length checks in OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR (`b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e)`), OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH (`MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` rejection), keyword-argument sentinel checks (`kidx < 0`), NULL checks (`mrb->exc == NULL`, `!e`, `!target`, `!irep`), fully enumerated argc-packing arms in OP_ENTER, and integer-overflow checks (`mrb_int_*_overflow`) before every arithmetic store. The remaining indexing (register operands a/b/c, syms[b], pool[b], irep->reps[b]) consumes compiled program representation whose invariants this code itself documents via mrb_assert statements; no statement in this code parses or fabricates bytecode from external data, so no malformed-irep trigger is instantiated here.

assumptions: Bytecode operands (a, b, c) and irep tables (syms, pool, reps, nregs, ilen) are treated as the compiled-program contract, not attacker data: mrb_vm_exec executes an irep handed to it and never parses one. The contract is documented in this code by mrb_assert statements, e.g. `mrb_assert((pool[b].tt&IREP_TT_NFLAG)==0);` and `mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen);`, though no explicit register-bounds assert exists — reliance on compiler-generated operand consistency is an assumption recorded here.

Internal callees (mrb_stack_extend, cipush/cipop, uvenv, mrb_div_int, mrb_ary_entry/set, mrb_str_aref, mrb_hash_*, stack_clear, ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE, FETCH_* macros) are assumed to honor their documented mruby semantics per discipline 3; ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE and the FETCH macros are not shown and could not be analyzed.
limitations: Unvalidated bytecode-operand indexing (regs[a], syms[b], pool[b], irep->reps[b]) would yield register/symbol/pool out-of-bounds access, but only for a maliciously crafted precompiled irep. No such loader exists in this code; the trigger is speculative (precondition uninstantiated). Upstream mruby explicitly treats mrb_load_irep on untrusted input as unsupported.

OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH env guards admit a by-one edge (kd=1 with MRB_ENV_LEN(e) == m1+r+m2+2 accesses e->stack[m1+r+m2+2]); identical to upstream mruby and only reachable when the env length mismatches the compiler-emitted calling convention, i.e., malformed bytecode.
OP_JMPUW's restore-path bound `mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen)` is compiled out without MRB_DEBUG; same malformed-bytecode-only exposure.
OP_APOST casts `ARY_LEN(ary)` to int; truncation requires a >2^31-element array (~16 GB of mrb_values), not producible at realistic scale by any statement in this code.
OP_ASET asserts the array on regs[a] while mrb_ary_set reads the array from regs[b]; debug-only asymmetry, no runtime-content trigger without malformed bytecode.

verdict.summary: The BPF ring-buffer reserve path is correctly guarded: size is rejected above RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, the rounded record length is rejected above the ring size ('len > rb->mask + 1'), the in-flight space check 'new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask' runs under the spinlock against an acquire-loaded consumer position (fail-closed on stale values), and the record header is placed at 'rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask)' with wrap handled by the double-mapped data area. No trigger for memory corruption or denial of service could be instantiated within the given code.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is assumed to be ((u32)~0U >> 2) = 0x3FFFFFFF (upstream value, not present in the given text); with this bound, round_up(size + 8, 8) reaches at most 0x40000008, which fits the u32 'len' without truncation, and the busy bit (0x80000000) never collides with the stored length in 'hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT'.

rb->mask is assumed to be (ringbuf_size - 1) with ringbuf_size a power of two well below 2^32, so 'rb->mask + 1' does not wrap and 'prod_pos & rb->mask' is always a valid offset; the rb->data area is assumed double-mapped so wrap-around header/data writes land in the duplicate mapping (standard ringbuf construction).

Invariant producer_pos >= consumer_pos and monotonic consumer advance are maintained by consumer-side code not shown; a stale or concurrently-read consumer position errs toward rejecting the reservation, never toward overflow.
bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off is an internal helper not shown; its return value is only stored in the header's pg_off field and is not used as an offset in this code.
limitations: Speculative candidate (not instantiable from the given code): if RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ were >= 2^32 - 7, the assignment 'len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8);' would truncate the u64 result into u32, wrapping to a small len that passes 'len > rb->mask + 1' and the space check, causing a heap overflow when the caller writes 'size' bytes. The bound constant is not present in the given text, so per discipline 1 this trigger could not be proven; with the universally known upstream constant 0x3FFFFFFF it is unreachable.

Speculative candidate: u32 wrap of 'rb->mask + 1' would disable the length check, but it requires a 4 GiB ringbuf allocation that this code never creates (rb arrives pre-constructed) and that the mmap-based layout precludes.

Unchecked-concurrency reasoning relies on the consumer-side protocol (acquire/release pairing noted in the comment 'pairs with consumer's smp_load_acquire()') whose implementation is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: gen_hash's stack accounting is internally consistent: the per-iteration flush (if (val && cursp() >= slimit) { pop_n(len*2); ...; len = 0; }) resets len and keeps register usage bounded, every pop_n/pop count exactly matches the pushes performed on all simulated paths (including kw-rest-first-element, consecutive kw-rests, and flush-after-kw-rest boundary cases), and len*2 cannot overflow int given the flush bound. The unused 'limit' parameter deviates from the upstream slimit selection policy (upstream conditions slimit=INT16_MAX on 'limit'), but within this function the change only shifts when flushing occurs; any security consequence would require caller or VM register-encoding behavior not present in the given code, so no impact could be instantiated.

assumptions: push/pop/pop_n/cursp/genop_1/genop_2/codegen are codegen-scope helpers not shown; their standard semantics (sp increment/decrement, operand emission with automatic extension for wide values, recursive codegen pushing exactly one value when val is true) were assumed and were in fact forced by the internal consistency of every pop_n/genop_2 pairing in this code.

The AST representation consumed via tree->car->car->car (element = cons(key-node, value-node), key-node = cons(node-type, ...), kw-rest element carrying the expression in tree->car->cdr) is produced by the parser, which is not shown; well-formedness of every element is a contract of that producer.
GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX are compile-time constants assumed to be within 16-bit operand-encodable ranges, consistent with the code's use of INT16_MAX as the loose bound.
limitations: Candidate: the 'limit' parameter is never used; upstream mruby conditions the loose stack limit on it (limit && cursp() >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX). Its omission changes only the flush threshold (bytecode register usage / size), and the accounting remains balanced for either threshold; a memory-safety or operand-range failure would have to occur in non-shown caller codegen (e.g., OP_SEND argument encoding) or in VM register handling, so the trigger and impact chain could not be instantiated in this code.

Candidate: NULL dereference on the tree->car->car->car / tree->car->cdr chains for a malformed AST element (at most a crash of the compiler process itself, at equal privilege with the party supplying the source) — the malformed node cannot be produced by any statement in this code; it depends on the not-shown parser, so the trigger is speculative.

When val == 0, len grows without bound (no flush executes), but no statement in this code uses len as a size, count for a memory operation, or loop bound in that mode; the returned count is consumed only by non-shown caller logic.

verdict.summary: GroupedConvolutionFunctor computes num_groups = in_depth / patch_depth from attacker-controlled tensor shapes with no validation. With filter.dim_size(2)==0 (or > in_depth, giving num_groups==0 used later as a divisor in pre_shuffle/post_shuffle), the op divides by zero and crashes the host process (DoS). With in_depth not divisible by patch_depth (e.g., 8/3), the per-group input depth (in_depth/num_groups=4) differs from the filter channel depth (3), and the unvalidated, mismatched slices are passed to functor::SpatialConvolution, forcing an out-of-bounds read at the call site. On the EXPLICIT path, explicit_paddings[2..5] are indexed with no size check (std::vector operator[] is unchecked), a further OOB read.

evidence.reason: Root cause: num_groups is derived from attacker-controlled tensor dims with zero validation. Trigger 1: filter shape [1,1,0,1] gives patch_depth=0 and line 12 executes in_depth/0 → SIGFPE, crashing the process running the attacker-supplied model. Trigger 2: patch_depth=5 > in_depth=3 gives num_groups=0, which then reaches the divisions `tensor.dim_size(3) / num_groups` in pre_shuffle (line 20) / post_shuffle (line 26), first evaluated at the allocate_temp call on line 37 → SIGFPE. No statement in the code checks patch_depth != 0, num_groups != 0, or in_depth % patch_depth == 0.

evidence.snippet:
functor::SpatialConvolution<CPUDevice, T>()(
            ctx->eigen_device<CPUDevice>(), output_slice, input_slice,
            filter_slice, row_stride, col_stride, row_dilation, col_dilation,
            static_cast<int>(explicit_paddings[2]),
            static_cast<int>(explicit_paddings[3]),
            static_cast<int>(explicit_paddings[4]),
            static_cast<int>(explicit_paddings[5]));
evidence.reason: Sink: with in_depth=8, patch_depth=3 (num_groups=2), input_slice has channel depth 4 while filter_slice has channel depth 3; the channel contraction performed by the convolution indexes the smaller operand out of range — heap OOB read (or CHECK abort) caused by out-of-domain arguments passed at this call site with no divisibility/depth check anywhere in the code. Additionally, explicit_paddings[2..5] are indexed with no size check in this code; with padding==EXPLICIT (attacker-selectable attr) and a short/empty vector, std::vector::operator[] reads out of bounds and the garbage value is passed into the convolution.

assumptions: The behavior of functor::SpatialConvolution (not shown) is project-internal; the OOB read in candidate C3 is inferred from the universally known contraction semantics of convolution plus the unvalidated mismatched channel depths passed at the call site, per the wrapper rule.

Candidate C5 (uninitialized output channels when out_depth % num_groups != 0, leaving output[...,out_depth-1..] unwritten at line 90 and returning uninitialized heap to the model consumer) rests on the unquoted assumption that framework output allocation is not zeroed.
DCHECK on data_format (line 6) is a no-op in release builds; no reachability conclusion relies on it.
limitations: Validation that may exist in the op's shape function or dispatcher (e.g., explicit_paddings size when padding==EXPLICIT, or Conv2D depth constraints) is outside the given code and could not be quoted; per guard-anchoring it was treated as absent, which slightly raises the likelihood of the explicit_paddings OOB candidate beyond what production TF may permit.

The exact OOB locus for the depth-mismatch candidate (C3) lies inside the unshown SpatialConvolution callee; the defect is recorded at this code's call site, where the unvalidated out-of-domain argument is produced and passed.

verdict.summary: All memory writes in uECC_sign_with_k are sized from internal-trusted curve constants and guarded by quotable, execution-order-correct checks (0 < k < n check on the scalar; the numBits-vs-num_bytes*8 check before storing s into the signature). The only attacker-derived raw size, hash_size, is passed unvalidated into the internal helper bits2int, and the unshown regularize_k return value carry indexes k2[carry] without a {0,1} bound; but both harmful uses land inside or depend on callees not shown in the given code, so no trigger is fully instantiated within this code. No primary defect found.

assumptions: bits2int(message_hash, hash_size) clamps its input to the curve's octet count before writing into the uECC_MAX_WORDS-word destination; its implementation is not part of the given code, so this is an assumption, not a verified guard.
regularize_k returns exactly 0 or 1, making k2[carry] and k2[!carry] in-bounds indices into the 2-element array k2; the callee is not shown.
EccPoint_mult reduces its output below curve->p and writes at most 2*num_words words into p (which aliases signature in the native little-endian build).

The internal caller supplies signature with at least 2*curve->num_bytes bytes and an alignment suitable for the (uECC_word_t *)signature cast, and private_key with at least BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes; these contracts are not quotable in the given code.
curve and its num_words/num_n_bits/num_bytes/num_n_bits fields are library-internal constants (≤ uECC_MAX_WORDS words), not attacker data.
limitations: hash_size is passed with no validation on any path in this code to bits2int, whose destination tmp is a fixed uECC_MAX_WORDS-word stack array. If bits2int copies min(hash_size, capacity) bytes (as in the reference uECC implementation), the code is safe; if it copies hash_size bytes unclamped, a caller-supplied oversized hash_size causes a stack buffer overflow. The write itself is not a statement in the given code, so the trigger cannot be instantiated here — this remains a latent contract requirement on the not-shown callee and its callers.

carry = regularize_k(...) is used as k2[carry] and k2[!carry] with no in-function bound; an out-of-range return would produce an out-of-bounds pointer read followed by a wild write via uECC_generate_random_int, but the producer's behavior is not shown.

If no RNG function is configured (g_rng_function == 0), the blinding factor is the constant 1, weakening the countermeasure against side-channel analysis of uECC_vli_modInv; this is a configuration-dependent hardening gap, not a memory-safety defect.

The native little-endian path casts the uint8_t* signature buffer to uECC_word_t*; an unaligned or undersized buffer from a caller violating the (unquoted) API contract would cause misaligned/OOB access.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor never validates that the rank of the attacker-controlled input_shape_in vector equals the second dimension (column count) of the attacker-controlled input_indices_in matrix, nor that the index values are consistent with input_shape, before passing both into functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor. A crafted op input (e.g., input_shape_in=[1,1,1,1,1] with input_indices_in a 1x2 matrix and target_shape_in=[1]) passes every check in the function (IsMatrix/IsVector, output_shape.num_elements()==dense_size) and reaches the functor, which indexes the indices matrix by the input rank, reading past the matrix heap allocation. The out-of-bounds-read-derived values are written into the op's returned output tensor, enabling heap memory disclosure or a crash; the read distance is attacker-scalable via the input_shape vector length.

evidence.reason: Sink: the functor call passes input_shape (whose rank is the attacker-controlled length of input_shape_in) together with input_indices_in.matrix<int64>() (whose column count is the independent attacker-controlled dim_size(1)) into an indexing operation with no validation on any path. Simulated trigger: input_shape_in=[1,1,1,1,1], input_indices_in=[[0,0]] (1x2), target_shape_in=[1] passes all OP_REQUIRES checks (output_shape.num_elements()=1 == dense_size=1) and reaches this call, where the rank-5 shape is used to index the 2-column matrix, reading past the 16-byte heap allocation into the returned output tensor.

Origin of the tainted values: input_shape is constructed solely from the attacker-controlled vector input_shape_in (its length becomes input_shape.dims(), the input rank) with no comparison to input_indices_in.shape().dim_size(1) anywhere in the function, while nnz is taken independently from the attacker-controlled indices matrix; this unvalidated rank/width mismatch is the root cause consumed at the line 95 sink.

assumptions: The behavior of functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor (not shown) is assumed to iterate over the input rank, indexing input_indices(n, i) for i < input_shape.dims() and decomposing the flat index by output dims via div/mod, which is its documented role; per discipline 3 the defect is assigned at the call site in this code because the out-of-domain rank/width pair is passed there with no validation on any path.
TensorShape::num_elements() is assumed to compute the element-count product used by the line 66 check; TensorShape/AddDim overflow semantics (not shown) are project-internal.
limitations: Secondary facet of the same missing validation: when no target dim is -1, the guard 'product > 0' (line 50) is bypassed, so a target dim of 0 combined with input dense_size==0 and nnz>0 (e.g., input_shape_in=[0,5], target_shape_in=[5,0], indices=[[0,0]]) passes output_shape.num_elements()==dense_size (0==0) and reaches the functor, where a mod/division by a zero-size output dim would fault. The faulting statement lies entirely inside the unshown functor, so it is not the driver of the verdict.

product *= size (line 44) is int64 signed multiplication bounded only below by 'size >= 0' (line 41); target_shape_in=[INT64_MAX, INT64_MAX] overflows it (UB, CWE-190). No memory-corruption or bypass link could be instantiated from the given code because the line 66 element-count check and in-bounds div/mod writes in the functor consume the result only within the allocated matrices.

Index VALUES within input_indices_in are never validated against input_shape.dim_size(i); the derived output indices stay in-bounds via div/mod, so this yields incorrect (silent wrong) results rather than a memory-safety defect in this code.

verdict.summary: The GSER parser issuerAndThisUpdateCheck() advances the cursor past the parsed value with x.bv_val += <len> + 1; x.bv_len -= <len> + 1 without verifying that a closing double quote was found. When the issuer or thisUpdate value scan loop exits because it consumed all remaining bytes (is->bv_len == x.bv_len / tu->bv_len == x.bv_len), the unsigned ber_len_t x.bv_len underflows to (2^width - 1) and x.bv_val moves one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied LDAP attribute buffer. Subsequent space-eating loops and strncasecmp/x.bv_val[0] dereferences (lines 30, 35, 83, 122, 130) then read out of bounds — potentially scanning far into the heap until an unmapped page — giving a remotely triggerable heap out-of-bounds read / denial of service against the slapd process handling the attacker's directory data.

evidence.reason: Root cause (issuer branch): the scan loop at lines 65-77 can exit via its condition with is->bv_len == x.bv_len when the attacker-supplied issuer value contains no terminating '"' (e.g. input "{issuer rdnSequence:\"AAAA...AAAA}" of length >= 39 ending in '}'). No statement checks that a closing quote was found, so x.bv_val += is->bv_len + 1 moves the cursor one byte past the heap buffer and x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1 underflows the unsigned ber_len_t to (2^width - 1). The following dereferences at lines 30/122 ((x.bv_val[0] == ' ') && x.bv_len), line 130 (x.bv_val[0] != ','), and lines 35/83 (strncasecmp(x.bv_val,...)) then read out of bounds, potentially walking the heap until a fault — remote DoS via heap overread.

Identical defect in the thisUpdate branch: the scan loop at lines 107-111 breaks only on a '"' and otherwise leaves tu->bv_len == x.bv_len with no closing-quote check; the pointer/length update at lines 112-113 then advances x.bv_val one byte past the input buffer and underflows x.bv_len, making the later space-eating loop (line 122) and ',' check (line 130) read out of bounds. Trigger input: "{thisUpdate \"AAAA...AAAA}" with length >= 39.

assumptions: ber_len_t is an unsigned type (as in OpenLDAP), so x.bv_len -= (x.bv_len + 1) wraps to the maximum value rather than becoming -1; the OOB read occurs even without wrap since x.bv_val already points past the buffer.
The input berval is not guaranteed NUL-terminated or padded, so reads at x.bv_val[0] past bv_len-1 access memory outside the value.
limitations: ber_dupbv_x (line 142) and slap_sl_malloc (line 148) return values are not checked for NULL; impact requires allocation failure, which no attacker input induces, so this is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The underflowed x.bv_len (huge) is rejected by the final 'if ( x.bv_len ) return LDAP_INVALID_SYNTAX;' (line 139), so parsed OOB data is never returned to the attacker — disclosure is limited to the OOB read itself (crash oracle / DoS), not a direct info leak.

The deref-before-length-test order in the space-eating loops (lines 30, 47, 96, 122) reads the in-bounds '}' byte in non-underflowed flow and is only harmful via the confirmed underflow defects; not counted separately.

verdict.summary: suggest_trie_walk() writes into fixed stack arrays compflags[MAXWLEN], tword[MAXWLEN] and preword[MAXWLEN*3] using traversal counters (ts_complen, ts_twordlen, depth, ts_prewordlen) that are incremented during compound/split/insert traversal with no MAXWLEN bound on any path: the only depth check (depth < MAXWLEN - 1) applies solely to the prefixtree branch, and the compound-count check is short-circuited when slang->sl_compsylmax < MAXWLEN. A long attacker-typed bad word compounded from 1-byte compound-flagged words drives ts_complen past MAXWLEN, producing an out-of-bounds stack write (compflags[ts_complen], compflags[ts_complen+1]); the same unbounded growth writes tword[ts_twordlen++] past tword[MAXWLEN] in STATE_PLAIN/STATE_INS.

evidence.reason: Root cause: ts_complen is incremented once per accepted compound word ('if (try_compound) ++sp->ts_complen;') with no bound against MAXWLEN. The only textual cap, '(slang->sl_compsylmax < MAXWLEN || sp->ts_complen + 1 - sp->ts_compsplit < slang->sl_compmax)', is short-circuited TRUE whenever sl_compsylmax < MAXWLEN (the typical configuration), so ts_complen can reach and exceed MAXWLEN-1 while compounding a long attacker-typed bad word, writing one byte past compflags[MAXWLEN] and beyond (stack out-of-bounds write).

Second sink of the same root cause: ts_twordlen is incremented with no MAXWLEN check on this path (nor in the STATE_INS 'tword[sp->ts_twordlen++] = c;' path); growth is gated only by the TRY_DEEPER score test, whose budget (su->su_maxscore) scales with the attacker-controlled bad-word length, so tword[ts_twordlen] writes past tword[MAXWLEN]. The depth counter incremented in the same block ('++depth; sp = &stack[depth];') is likewise unbounded outside the prefixtree branch, overflowing stack[MAXWLEN].

assumptions: TRY_DEEPER()/go_deeper() are score-based gates only (macros not shown); no statement in the given code shows they bound depth, ts_twordlen or ts_complen against MAXWLEN, and for early low-score steps of a long word they pass.
The loaded spell file supplies compound flags on short words, sl_compminlen = 0, sl_compprog != NULL and sl_compsylmax < MAXWLEN, i.e. the short-circuiting configuration of the compound-count check.
su->su_badlen can reach MAXWLEN-scale values (no smaller cap is quoted in this function).
limitations: The DEBUG_TRIEWALK sprintf(changename[depth], ...) sites are compiled out by default; if DEBUG_TRIEWALK were defined they would add format/bound issues but are excluded.

Exact MAXWLEN-step reachability depends on the not-shown su_maxscore computation; the overflow direction and unbounded counters are established from this code alone, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

verdict.summary: In get_visual_text, every index access to the selected text is preceded, in execution order, by quoted guards: the lnum equality check with early `return FAIL`, `if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0;`, and `if (*lenp > 0)`, and the strict LT_POS ordering forces the computed `*lenp` to be at least 1 with both endpoints on the valid cursor line, so the byte at `*pp + *lenp - 1` is at worst the line's terminating NUL (inside the buffer). No statement in this code can produce a column beyond the line length or a negative length; the only remaining OOB trigger requires editor-global cursor state that no shown statement produces. No vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: The core Vim invariant that cursor/visual column never exceeds the current line length (maintained by cursor adjustment and virtualedit's coladd mechanism outside this snippet) is assumed; it cannot be quoted here.
ml_get_pos()/ml_get_curline() return a valid NUL-terminated line pointer for the checked cursor line (callee not shown).
unadjust_for_sel() keeps VIsual.col within the line (callee not shown); with 'selection'=exclusive it is assumed not to drive the column negative.
Callers of this internal helper pass valid non-NULL pp/lenp output pointers (callers not shown); the function itself never dereferences them for input.
limitations: Speculative: a heap out-of-bounds read at `(*mb_ptr2len)(*pp + (*lenp - 1))` would require a cursor or VIsual column beyond the line's terminating NUL (e.g., blockwise-`$` MAXCOL or broken cursor state); no statement in this code produces such a state, so the trigger is not instantiated.
Speculative: integer underflow in `VIsual.col - curwin->w_cursor.col + 1` requires near-INT_MAX columns (MAXCOL-scale); not produced by any statement here.

In the has_mbyte path the trailing-NUL trim is skipped, so a selection ending on the line's NUL can return a length that conceptually includes the NUL byte; the access stays in-bounds and callers treat the text as a C string, so this is a robustness/cosmetic issue, not memory corruption.

Behavior of ml_get_pos and unadjust_for_sel is internal to Vim and not shown; arguments passed to them here are positions validated against the cursor's own line, so no out-of-domain argument crosses the call sites.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the FTPWHO shared-memory filename copy: when the client-supplied filename length equals sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, the guard `sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename` (line 149) is false at exactly that boundary, and the else-arm computes the source pointer as `&name[sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U]` = `&name[-1]`, reading one byte before the filename buffer; the else-arm also copies the field's full width without writing a NUL terminator. No guard on any path bounds the start index or terminates the field.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated computed source index. With sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (the exact boundary admitted by the `sl < sizeof ...` check at line 149 being false), `sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U` evaluates to -1, so memcpy reads from name[-1], one byte out of bounds before the attacker-supplied filename, and copies the full field width without writing any NUL terminator. Trigger instantiated: an FTP client issuing STOR with a filename of exactly the shm filename-field size reaches this arm after the quoted guards (shm_data_cur != NULL at line 140, sl computed at line 141).

evidence.snippet: const size_t sl = strlen(name);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: sl is the length of the client-controlled filename parameter; when it equals sizeof shm_data_cur->filename the branch guard at line 149 selects the unguarded else-arm.

assumptions: checknamesanity permits ordinary filenames at least sizeof shm_data_cur->filename characters long; the existence of the else-arm handling sl >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename indicates this is a designed-reachable case.
The FTPWHO block is compiled in (the defect exists only when FTPWHO is defined) and shm_data_cur is non-NULL at runtime (guarded at line 140).
name points to the client's command argument string; the byte at name[-1] is copied into the shared-memory field, observable by the ftpwho monitor process (not shown).
limitations: Uninitialized read: ulhandler.total_uploaded (local declared line 3, initialized only inside unshown ul_init) is read at lines 192 and 250 even when ul_init fails (else arm at 170-172 sets ret=-1). Cannot confirm ul_init leaves it uninitialized; if it does, a stack value is leaked into the 451/displayrate reply (CWE-457). Trigger not fully instantiated.

FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 179 (SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE) uses fd f after (void) close(f) at line 173; in this single-threaded flow no fd reuse occurs between them, so it degrades to EBADF with no attacker-controllable effect — robustness issue.
TOCTOU between checknamesanity (line 33), open (57-61), and rename (46): no two ordered attacker-interleavable operations exhibitable in this code; O_NOFOLLOW is used at both opens.
The impact of the missing NUL terminator beyond the one-byte OOB read (over-read of shm struct fields by consumers such as pure-ftpwho) lands in code not shown.

verdict.summary: The function gates every packet handed to the internal reassembly sink ipf_handle_frag with a family-matched validity check (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag paired with the correct dl_type constant) executed under the ipf mutex; non-fragment packets are simply refilled. No memory, injection, authz, or crypto sink with an absent guard exists in this snippet; all parsing happens in internal callees whose bodies are not given.

assumptions: ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag and ipf_handle_frag are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics (including whether the validity checks fully validate packet headers and offsets before ipf_handle_frag parses them) cannot be quoted, so any latent parsing defect inside them is out of scope for this snippet.

dl_type is treated as per-batch metadata supplied by the caller; if the caller could supply a dl_type that mismatches a packet's actual ethertype, the validity callee is the only defense — its correctness is unverifiable here.
DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH is assumed to produce in-bounds pb_idx and to tolerate packets consumed (not refilled) by ipf_handle_frag, per its documented iteration contract.
limitations: Candidate (a)/(b): a malformed or family-mismatched packet could be misparsed by ipf_handle_frag if the validity check is insufficient — the harmful access would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee and the guard's strength cannot be verified, so the trigger is speculative and not attributable to this snippet.
The implicit return type (missing 'void'/'bool' before ipf_extract_frags_from_batch) is a code-hygiene/compilation concern with no attacker-controlled security effect in the given code.
This function is a known hotspot in OVS IPF processing; real-world CVEs in this area live in ipf_handle_frag/ipf_reass internals, which are not included in the given code.

verdict.summary: In AssignOp::Compute, when use_exclusive_lock_ is false the copy of rhs into the variable is performed after releasing input_ref_mutex: line 86 ends the lock scope, line 91 re-fetches the current ref tensor with no shape validation, and line 92 copies rhs into it. A concurrent execution of this same op on the same variable (attacker-supplied graph with validate_shape=false, use_locking=false, parallel while-loop iterations, and non-forwardable rhs tensors so forward_input returns nullptr) can replace_ref_input a smaller-shaped tensor inside the exhibited window; the post-lock fetch then returns that smaller buffer and Copy writes rhs-sized data into it — a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled contents (or a CHECK-fail abort, i.e., DoS of the process running the attacker's graph). No statement anywhere in the code re-validates the fetched tensor's shape/size against rhs before the unlocked Copy.

evidence.snippet:
Tensor old_unlocked_lhs = context->mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false);
    Copy(context, &old_unlocked_lhs, rhs);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the destination tensor for the unlocked copy is re-fetched from the variable after the mutex (held by `mutex_lock l(*context->input_ref_mutex(0));`, line 24) was released at the end of the scope (line 86), and its shape is never re-validated against rhs. A concurrently running Assign on the same variable can install a smaller-shaped tensor in the window between the lock release and this fetch (both endpoints are statements of this code), so Copy receives a destination buffer smaller than rhs — heap out-of-bounds write (or CHECK-fail DoS) with attacker-controlled data. Trigger instantiated with validate_shape=false, use_locking=false, parallel while-loop iterations, rhsA=[1024] float32 and rhsB=[4] float32, each rhs given a second consumer so forward_input returns nullptr.

Origin of the trigger value: this replace_ref_input atomically swaps the variable to a newly allocated rhs-shaped tensor under the mutex, but with use_exclusive_lock_ false the function then exits the lock scope (line 86) instead of copying under it. A second execution of this same code can perform its own replace_ref_input between this thread's lock release and its post-lock `mutable_input(0, /* lock_held */ false)` fetch, changing the variable's shape so the subsequent Copy at line 92 uses a smaller destination than rhs.

assumptions: Copy(context, lhs, rhs) is a copy routine whose precondition is that the destination buffer holds at least the source's byte count; its implementation is not shown.

Concurrent execution of two Assign ops on the same variable is attainable via standard executor parallelism (e.g., while-loop parallel_iterations or tf.data), configured by the attacker who authors the graph; executor code is not shown.
validate_shape_, use_exclusive_lock_, and relax_constraints_ are graph attributes settable by the graph author (op constructor not shown).

Dtype equality between old_lhs and rhs at the allocate_temp/Copy sites is presumed enforced by the Assign op's shared type attribute at graph construction — framework code not shown; this is the only reason the dtype-confusion variant is not itself a trigger here.
limitations: Dtype-confusion candidates (e.g., allocate_temp(old_lhs.dtype(), ...) at line 75, or Copy with mismatched dtypes) could not be instantiated: triggering them requires ref/value dtype mismatch, which the unshown op-registration type contract prevents; recorded per guard-anchoring rules as relying on an unquotable contract.
CHECK(reshaped_old_lhs.CopyFrom(old_lhs, rhs.shape())) at line 52 is protected by the num_elements equality at lines 44-45 on the same path; unreachable failure.

A concurrent reader observing the uninitialized allocate_temp buffer during the window between replace_ref_input (line 80) and the completed Copy (line 92) would disclose uninitialized heap, but the triggering ReadVariable-type op is not part of the given code; recorded as a secondary speculative finding.

If the internal Copy helper re-validates shape equality before copying, the impact degrades from heap out-of-bounds write to a CHECK-fail abort — still denial of service of the process executing the attacker-supplied graph.

verdict.summary: The PCX RLE encoder dereferences the attacker-controlled raster buffer only under quoted, execution-ordered bounds checks (outer 'while (from < end)', short-circuit 'from >= end ||' before '*from', and '(from < end) && (*from == data)' in the scan loop), and the emitted run-count bytes are provably clamped to 0xc1..0xcf by the 'while (from - start >= max_run)' chunk loop with max_run = step*15. No memory, injection, or amplification sink is reachable with attacker-controlled pixel data. The only unquoted contract is that 'step' (bytes-per-pixel stride) be positive; a non-positive stride would cause a hang (step==0) or backward out-of-bounds read (step<0), but no statement in this code and no trust-boundary party can supply such a value — the stride is device configuration, while the attacker controls only the buffer contents, which are fully guarded.

assumptions: 'step' is the PCX device's bytes-per-pixel stride supplied by internal device code (call sites not shown); no statement in this code documents or checks step > 0, so this is an assumption, not a quoted contract.
gp_fputc is the standard Ghostscript file-putc interface writing its int argument as a byte; no memory or injection semantics at the call site.
The pixel bytes between 'from' and 'end' are attacker-derived content (rendered document data); the pointers and stride are produced by the enclosing device code, not shown.
limitations: Non-positive 'step' is unguarded: step==0 causes an infinite loop at 'while ((from < end) && (*from == data)) from += step;' (from never advances); step<0 walks 'from' backward with 'from < end' remaining true, reading below the buffer start (CWE-125) and hanging. Recorded as a robustness/contract issue: the trigger requires a caller passing step <= 0, which neither this code's own flow nor any trust-boundary input surface can produce (the attacker controls pixel content, not the stride), so it is speculative here.

'int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT' (line 8) could overflow signed int, but reaching the run path requires step <= (end - from), so overflow would need a >143 MB-stride scanline of identical bytes — not producible by any quoted data flow.

The remainder-encoding arithmetic (15-byte chunks plus (from-start)/step+1 remainder copies) was verified arithmetically correct at the boundaries from==start, from-start==max_run, and from-start==max_run-step; no output-correctness defect found.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans guards only num_spans == 0 but the do-while body unconditionally reads spans[1] (line 15) and, after spans++, spans[0] post-loop (line 92). With num_spans == 1 both reads go one element past the span array (CWE-125); the garbage value read into len then flows into memset(m, coverage, len) at line 85, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Additionally, for any intermediate coverage the memset length spans[1].x - spans[0].x is completely unvalidated on every path in this code.

evidence.snippet:
do {
	int len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x;
evidence.reason: Sink: with num_spans == 1 the do-while body executes once and reads spans[1] one element past the span array (OOB read). The read value becomes len and is later used as a memset length. No statement in the code constrains num_spans to >= 2.

evidence.snippet:
if (num_spans == 0)
	return CAIRO_STATUS_SUCCESS;
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the only num_spans guard in the code rejects exactly 0 (operator ==), leaving num_spans == 1 unhandled although the loop body requires at least 2 valid span elements. The minimal fix (a num_spans < 2 check) appears nowhere in any form.

Impact sink: len is the attacker-derived (or, for num_spans == 1, out-of-bounds-read) difference spans[1].x - spans[0].x. It is passed unvalidated as the memset size into the mask buffer returned by pixman_image_get_data(r->mask); neither len nor m - base is bounded on any path, giving a heap out-of-bounds write for any intermediate-coverage span whose length exceeds the mask capacity.

assumptions: The capacity of the mask buffer returned by pixman_image_get_data(r->mask) (line 6) is not shown; whether candidate B's memset overflows for a given span length depends on that allocation, which per guard anchoring is recorded here rather than relied on.

The span array is assumed to hold exactly num_spans valid elements; if upstream rasterizers always append a terminating span or guarantee num_spans >= 2, that contract is not quotable from this code and does not demote the finding.

pixman_image_composite32 is treated per its documented semantics as clipping composite geometry to destination image extents, so composite calls with garbage x/width values are not treated as the primary corruption sink.
limitations: For num_spans == 1, the memset out-of-bounds write requires the out-of-bounds-read value V to satisfy V - 10 > 1 (i.e., adjacent heap byte pattern); the OOB read at lines 15 and 92 triggers unconditionally and is the fully instantiated primary impact.
Composite calls at lines 43-49 etc. receive attacker-derived coordinates/widths, but clipping inside pixman bounds the impact to at most the OOB reads already counted.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse reads sizeof(struct capability) bytes from the peer-supplied capability stream after only verifying 3 bytes remain (line 16 checks pnt+3 > end), causing an out-of-bounds read at the memcpy (line 26); additionally, when PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is set, the `continue` at line 57 skips the only pointer-advance statement `pnt += cap.length + 3;`, producing an infinite loop and CPU-exhaustion DoS on the BGP daemon.

evidence.snippet: memcpy (&cap, pnt + 1, sizeof (struct capability));
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: the only preceding bounds check is `if (pnt + 3 > end) ... return -1;` which guarantees just 3 in-bounds bytes, but the memcpy reads sizeof(struct capability) (> 3, since struct capability contains code, length, mpc.afi, mpc.safi) from the attacker-controlled BGP peer message buffer. No statement anywhere bounds the copy length to the remaining message length.

evidence.snippet:
if (CHECK_FLAG (peer->flags, PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY))
	    continue;
evidence.reason: Infinite loop / CPU exhaustion: this `continue` returns to `while (pnt < end)` without executing the loop's only pointer-advance statement `pnt += cap.length + 3;`, so when the operator sets override-capability and a peer sends an MP capability, pnt never advances and the loop spins forever, wedging the BGP daemon (attacker-supplied capability triggers it).

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability) > 3 — inferred from its members code, length, mpc.afi (2 bytes via ntohs) and mpc.safi being read; the exact struct definition is not given.
cap.length is a single-byte field (promoted to int, max 258), so `cap.length + 3` cannot wrap — inferred from typical struct capability definition.
limitations: peer->host logging of cap fields could disclose parsed out-of-bounds bytes only when BGP_DEBUG normal is enabled; the primary impact is the OOB read itself, not a proven disclosure.
The infinite-loop trigger requires the operator-configured PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY flag, which is a documented quagga/FRR option and is read directly from the peer struct in this code.

verdict.summary: The function is a well-formed dispatcher over a packet batch: it iterates with the refill-safe macro, takes/releases ipf_lock symmetrically, and on every path either refills the packet at its macro-produced in-range index or deletes the still-live pointer exactly once. No attacker-derived size, index, offset, or length is computed or consumed in this code; all fragment-header parsing and validation occur in callees not shown (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag), so no trigger for memory corruption, injection, or bypass can be instantiated within the given statements.

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH produces pb_idx in [0, pb_cnt) and pkt as a live in-batch pointer, per its container-accessor role; the macro definition is not shown.
dp_packet_batch_refill and dp_packet_delete are standard OVS batch helpers with the documented refill/free semantics; their definitions are not shown.

dl_type, zone, now, and hash_basis arrive from the OVS datapath classification layer already consistent with the packet's flow; no quotable contract for this appears in the given code, but these values are used here only as opaque comparison/dispatch scalars, never as bounds or offsets.
limitations: C1 (double-free): if ipf_handle_frag returned non-zero after having freed pkt, dp_packet_delete(pkt) would be a double-free; whether that happens is entirely inside the not-shown callee — the given code keeps pkt live on every path it controls, so the trigger could not be instantiated here.

C5 (fragment validation gap): historical OVS IP-fragmentation defects (e.g., the CVE-2022-4337 family in ipf_dpif.c) live in ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag/ipf_handle_frag, which are not part of the given code; analyzing those functions requires their source.
C3 (amplification): per-packet lock acquisition is O(1) per packet and bounded by the batch size; any attacker-scalable cost would have to originate inside ipf_handle_frag, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: In crun_command_exec, the argument-duplication loop is bounded by `i < argc - first_arg`, so its last iteration computes the argv index first_arg + (argc - first_arg - 1) + 1 == argc and passes argv[argc] — the C-standard NULL sentinel — to xstrdup, dereferencing NULL and aborting the container runtime's exec process on every standard `crun exec CONTAINER CMD` invocation; no bound of argc - first_arg - 1 or NULL check exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one loop bound: the loop condition `i < argc - first_arg` runs argc - first_arg iterations, and the last iteration evaluates argv[first_arg + i + 1] with i = argc - first_arg - 1, i.e. argv[argc], which is guaranteed NULL by the C standard. That NULL is passed unvalidated into the string-duplication call xstrdup, dereferencing NULL inside the copy and crashing the runtime for any attacker-supplied exec invocation without --process (e.g. argv=["exec","mycontainer","/bin/ls"], first_arg=1, argc=4: i=1 already passes argv[3]=argv[argc]=NULL). The required guard — bounding the loop at argc - first_arg - 1 or NULL-checking the element — appears nowhere; the only nearby check, crun_assert_n_args(argc - first_arg, 2, -1), is a minimum-count check and does not bound the index.

assumptions: xstrdup has standard string-duplication semantics (strlen-based copy); its exact NULL handling is not shown, but per the call-site rule the out-of-domain NULL argument is the defect here regardless of where the fault lands.
argv[argc] is the NULL sentinel per the C standard calling convention, and argp_parse sets first_arg to the index of the first unconsumed argv element per documented libc semantics.
crun_assert_n_args (internal, not shown) enforces the minimum argument count, presumably exiting on failure; its return value is ignored at line 17.
limitations: process->args_len = argc (line 41) overstates the actual duplicated argument count (argc - first_arg - 1 real strings); its impact depends on libcrun_container_exec_with_options (not shown) and is pre-empted by the earlier NULL-duplication crash, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
LISTEN_FDS parsing via strtoll (lines 30-31) can yield 0, negative, or overflowed values folded into preservefds; the only consumer is the not-shown exec callee, so no in-code sink was instantiated.

process->env/env_len and capabilities->effective/..._len pairs (lines 49-50, 64-77) copy array/size pairs produced by the not-shown argp parser; array-length consistency cannot be verified from this code.

The returned value of crun_assert_n_args at line 17 is ignored; if it merely returned an error instead of exiting, argc - first_arg < 2 would still reach the same NULL-duplication sink (same crash), so this does not change the verdict.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks in string_scan_range are provably bounded in this code: the eating loop is capped by 'i < sizeof (tmp) - 4' with per-iteration rc clamped to at most 4 (utf32 arm forces rc=4, escape arm rc=2), so tmp writes and the terminating NUL stay inside the stack buffer even at the boundary iteration; heap reads via buf + needle - from are gated by the loop condition 'needle < to' with remaining length 'to - needle' passed to every decoder, and 'needle' never drops below 'from'; the wide-detection reads w[0..8] are covered exactly by '(to - needle) > 8 + rc'; allocation extent is the same checked 'len' bounded by 'len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX'; and BOM lookbacks are guarded by 'str_start - from > 1' and '> 3'. The int truncation of 'len * 4' cannot produce an out-of-bounds write because calloc(len, 4) always allocates at least the truncated bound, and it requires the operator-set RABIN2_CHARSET variable, not attacker input. No attacker-reachable memory corruption, OOB access, injection, or authz failure was instantiated.

assumptions: r_utf8_decode / r_utf16le_decode / r_utf32le_decode honor their length argument and return 0 when fewer than the needed bytes remain (documented radare2 UTF API semantics); every decode call in this code passes 'to - needle' as that length under the loop condition 'needle < to'.

r_charset_encode_str honors its out_len bound; regardless, this code's 'calloc (len, 4)' allocation is always >= any 32-bit truncation of 'len * 4', so the callee's bound can never exceed the allocation.
r_utf_block_list returns parallel, -1-terminated block and frequency arrays of equal length; the 'if (!block_list[j])' lookup inside the freq_list loop assumes this parallelism (callee not shown).
r_buf_read_at clamps reads to the RBuffer's extent; since buf comes from calloc it is zero-filled even on short reads, so no uninitialized data reaches output.

R_STR_ISEMPTY tolerates a NULL charset from r_sys_getenv; r_charset_new/r_charset_use handle NULL allocations internally (callee not shown, and the path is gated on the operator's RABIN2_CHARSET environment variable, not attacker input).
limitations: 'int outlen = len * 4;' can truncate when len > 2^30-1 (len is bounded by ST32_MAX), producing a wrong encode bound and incorrect scan results when RABIN2_CHARSET is set. Not attacker-triggerable (operator environment variable) and not memory-unsafe here, since calloc(len, 4) >= outlen always holds; correctness defect only.

The return value of 'r_buf_read_at (bf->buf, from, buf, len);' is ignored (comment 'may oobread' refers to reading past mapped file data into the zero-filled local buffer); a short read silently scans zeros — robustness, no disclosure or corruption.

'if (!block_list[j])' indexes block_list with a bound derived from freq_list's sentinel; an OOB read would require the two callee-returned arrays to have different lengths, which could not be instantiated from this code.
bs->vaddr = str_start - pdelta + vdelta + baddr can unsigned-underflow to a huge key for ht_up_insert if str_start < pdelta; value-only, no memory access, no security effect shown.
section/bf struct contents are dereferenced after only NULL checks; their integrity is a caller contract this code does not assert beyond 'r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1)'.

evidence.reason: First use of the unvalidated index parameter `facet` (line 1): it indexes stl->facet_start with no range check anywhere in the function (the only pre-use check, `if (stl->error) return;` at line 12, constrains an unrelated flag). For any facet >= number_of_facets or < 0 this memcmp reads out of bounds — attacker-file/parameter data crossing the trust boundary induces an OOB read.

neighbor1 = stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge1];
  neighbor2 = stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge2];
evidence.reason: Origin of the write indices: neighbor1/neighbor2 (and neighbor3/vnot1-3 at lines 55-58) are read from stl->neighbors_start[facet] using the same unbounded `facet`; with facet out of range these become arbitrary heap garbage that the checks `neighbor != -1` (lines 60/64/71) do not bound.

Simulated trigger: facet = N+K passes line 12, reaches line 45 with neighbor1 = attacker-influenced adjacent heap value G (G != -1), and line 61 writes neighbor2 to stl->neighbors_start[G] — heap memory corruption with attacker-influenced index and value.

assumptions: stl_remove_facet and stl_update_connects_remove_1 (internal callees, not shown) are assumed not to re-validate their facet/neighbor index arguments; their contracts cannot be quoted from the given code, so lines 22, 49, 52, 69, and 72 are additional call sites receiving potentially out-of-domain indices.

limitations: Candidate C3 (negative which_vertex_not making (vnot+1)%3 a negative index even with a valid facet) is speculative: the producer of which_vertex_not values is not shown, so a value <= -2 could not be instantiated from the given code; it remains plausible but unproven.

If a hidden caller always passed facet in [0, number_of_facets) the OOB read would not fire — but no such contract is documented or asserted anywhere in this code, and the function is non-static/exported, so the parameter is treated as attacker-data per the analysis rules.

verdict.summary: In QPaintEngineEx::stroke, the element-processing loops are bounded only by the coordinate pointer (while (points < lastPoint) with lastPoint = points + 2*elementCount). When the final element(s) of an attacker-supplied path is a CurveToElement with fewer than 3 elements (6 coordinates) remaining, the CurveToElement arm reads points[0..5] — up to 4 qreals past the end of the path's coordinate buffer — and passes them to cubicTo(); the identical pattern repeats in the cosmetic-pen branch. No bounds check on either the points or types array exists on any path, yielding an out-of-bounds read whose values are stroked into visible output.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the enclosing loop's only guard is 'while (points < lastPoint)' where 'lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1)', which guarantees merely 2 readable coordinates, yet the CurveToElement arm consumes points[0..5] (6 coordinates) and advances points by 6 with no check that 6 coordinates or 3 type entries remain. Trigger: an attacker-supplied QVectorPath with elementCount()==1 and elements()[0]==CurveToElement (or any path whose last CurveToElement is not followed by two more elements) enters the loop (points < lastPoint true), reaches cubicTo(points[0]..points[5]) and reads 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the 2-qreal buffer; the same defect exists in the cosmetic branch's '((const QPointF *)points)[0..2]' reads. The OOB values are stroked/rasterized, giving a read of adjacent process memory into rendered output.

assumptions: QVectorPath::isEmpty() is assumed equivalent to elementCount()==0 so that a 1-element path is not rejected earlier; the definition is not shown.
The hooks qpaintengineex_moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo (not shown) are assumed to grow d->strokeHandler->pts/types storage, so output-side capacity is not the defect here.
state(), QTransform::inverted(), and the dasher/stroker callees are assumed to behave per Qt semantics.
limitations: The 'default: break;' arm advances neither points nor types; a ElementType value outside the four enum constants would make 'while (points < lastPoint)' loop forever (CWE-400). However, no statement in this code produces such a value and it is not instantiable from the shown input surface, so it is speculative.
The 'default' arm in the cosmetic-pen branch also stalls similarly and is speculative for the same reason.
Actual disclosure impact depends on how the stroked OOB coordinates propagate into visible pixels in code not shown.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node recurses once per attacker-supplied nested element (line 83, also tail-recursive PI/comment paths at lines 24/40) with no depth limit anywhere in the function: a ~1MB document of repeated '<a>' open tags produces ~350k stack frames and stack-exhausts the parsing process (attacker-scalable denial of service). Additionally, the raw dereferences '*scanner->curptr' and '*(scanner->curptr+1)' at lines 80-81 (and 93) lack the pj_scan_is_eof guard that the same function applies at line 88, so a document ending exactly at an open tag ('<a>') leaves curptr == endptr after line 76 consumes the final '>' and causes a one-byte out-of-bounds read at line 80.

No depth counter, limit parameter, or terminating branch exists anywhere in the function; PJ_CHECK_STACK() (line 6) is not quotable as enforcement and no branch acts on it to stop recursion. N ~ 350k (~1MB document) exceeds any default thread stack -> stack overflow crash of the process parsing the attacker's document (CWE-674, DoS).

while (*scanner->curptr == '<' && *(scanner->curptr+1) != '/'
				   && *(scanner->curptr+1) != '!')
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: this while condition dereferences scanner->curptr and scanner->curptr+1 with no pj_scan_is_eof check, although the same function proves the required guard form at line 88: 'if (!pj_scan_is_eof(scanner) && *scanner->curptr != '<')'. The same unguarded dereference pattern appears at line 93 (CDATA test) and lines 8, 53, 68.

assumptions: pj_scan_* and pj_scan_is_eof semantics (EOF when curptr >= endptr; get/scan functions advance curptr and throw on EOF) are inferred from line 88's usage, not from shown definitions.

on_syntax_error is assumed to throw/longjmp (pjproject PJ_THROW convention); if it returned, additional unguarded dereferences (e.g., line 12's curptr+1 after line 9) would become reachable - unprovable either way from the given code.

The scanner buffer is assumed to have no readable sentinel byte at endptr (i.e., endptr is one past the last valid byte), per the (pointer,length) scanner model implied by line 88; if a NUL sentinel always exists at endptr, the OOB read at lines 80-81/93 is defanged but the recursion finding stands unchanged.

node->content.slen = scanner->curptr - node->content.ptr (line 102) may include the first ']' of ']]>' in content - a parsing-accuracy defect with no demonstrated security impact.

The tail-position recursions at lines 24 and 40 (PI/comment) may be optimized into jumps by the compiler; the non-tail recursion at line 83 (result used at line 84) cannot be, so the stack-exhaustion trigger rests on line 83.
If pj_scan_get_until_ch does not advance past its delimiter, the CDATA while-loop (lines 98-101) could spin; this depends on unshown callee behavior - speculative.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf uses the caller-controlled int parameter len as the memcpy length without validating it is non-negative: 'if (remain >= len) { rlen = len; }' passes a negative len straight into rlen, and 'memcpy(buf, (void *) ((char *) dp->data + dp->pos), rlen);' converts it to a huge size_t, causing massive out-of-bounds read from dp->data and out-of-bounds write to buf. The only EOF guard ('if (remain <= 0) return EOF;') sits in the else branch that a negative len never reaches.

evidence.snippet: memcpy(buf, (void *) ((char *) dp->data + dp->pos), rlen);
evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy length is rlen, which can be the raw negative parameter len converted to a huge size_t, producing out-of-bounds read and write (memory corruption). Simulated trigger: logicalSize=100, pos=10, len=-1 -> remain=90; 90 >= -1 true -> rlen=-1 -> memcpy with size ~SIZE_MAX.

Origin of the faulty value: 'rlen = len' copies the attacker-influenced read length into rlen with no len > 0 check; the comparison 'remain >= len' only bounds rlen from above and is trivially satisfied by any negative len, while the only rejection guard 'remain <= 0' is in the else branch that a negative len never enters.

assumptions: ctx is a valid gdIOCtx/dpIOCtx and dp points to a valid dynamicPtr; the data buffer is at least logicalSize bytes (allocation/growth logic in dynamicPut is not shown).

len is a data-carrying parameter of a function installed as a gdIOCtx callback and invoked by image decoders parsing untrusted data; the specific caller that can pass a negative len is not shown in the given code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read past the allocated data buffer would additionally require logicalSize to exceed the real allocation; that producer is not in the given code.
dp->pos could only be negative or exceed logicalSize via a not-shown seek helper; positive-len paths are correctly rejected by the EOF branch, so no separate finding is claimed for pos handling.
len == 0 results in a zero-byte memcpy and is harmless.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder clamps x and y only against the upper image bounds (if (x >= im->sx), if (y >= im->sy)) and never checks y < 0. An attacker calling this exported function (e.g., via a binding such as PHP imagefilltoborder) with a negative y passes it unchanged into gdImageGetPixel(im, i, y) and gdImageSetPixel(im, i, y, color), which index the pixel array at row y — an out-of-bounds read and an out-of-bounds write of an attacker-chosen color value. Negative x is safe only by accident of the loop condition i >= 0 plus the leftLimit == -1 early return.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the only clamp on y enforces the upper bound (y >= im->sy -> y = sy-1). There is no y < 0 check or clamp anywhere in the function, so an attacker-supplied negative y (parameter of an exported function) passes through unchanged to the pixel access sinks.

Sink: with attacker input y = -1 (and x = 5, border = 1, color = 0 on a 10x10 image), the loop runs with i=5..0 and calls gdImageSetPixel(im, i, -1, 0), indexing pixel row -1 — an out-of-bounds row-pointer dereference and write of the attacker-chosen color (memory corruption). gdImageGetPixel(im, i, -1) on the previous line performs the matching out-of-bounds read. No guard on any path bounds y >= 0.

assumptions: gdImageSetPixel/gdImageGetPixel are the standard libgd accessors that index im->pixels[y][x] / im->tpixels[y][x] without internal bounds checks (bounds are the caller's documented responsibility); even if a deployed version bounds-checks internally, the call site passes an out-of-domain attacker-derived index with no validation in this code, which per analysis rules is a defect at the call site.
im, im->sx, im->sy are well-formed per gdImage contract; im->sx/im->sy are attacker-influenced when the image was decoded from attacker data.
limitations: Unbounded recursion: fill recursion depth is bounded only by image height (recursion at y-1/y+1, lines 51/70), so a crafted image with a very large sy can cause stack exhaustion (DoS) in the image-processing process; trigger requires a huge image produced by code not shown, so it is not counted as the primary finding.
Negative x is safe only incidentally: the loop condition i >= 0 plus the leftLimit == -1 early return abort before any pixel access; a negative x reaching other code paths would not be guarded.

verdict.summary: No primary vulnerability was instantiated. The recursion-depth guard (recurse == 1000 check with a fully paired ++recurse/--recurse on the single post-increment exit) is present and verified in execution order; name length len is checked (len <= 0) before every use; one-past reads stay inside the NUL-terminated buffer. The two defects whose guards are genuinely absent — the register-name validation that applies only in vim9script (and only emsg's rather than failing), and the '@' error arms that leave ret == OK with rettv at VAR_UNKNOWN — cannot have their impact chains instantiated: get_reg_contents and the downstream consumers of a VAR_UNKNOWN typval are project-internal callees not shown, and the passed value is a register-name character, not a raw offset, size, index, or pointer.

assumptions: get_name_len produces an (s, len) pair where s (either *arg origin or the alias string) contains at least len characters; this contract is internal and not quoted in the given code, but both values come from the same call so no divergence is produced here.
get_lambda_tv returning OK implies rettv->vval.v_partial is a populated partial (pt_func deref at 'ufunc_T *ufunc = rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func;') — internal contract, not quotable here.
rettv->vval may contain garbage when v_type is set to VAR_UNKNOWN (the code's own comment implies this); clear_tv is designed to treat VAR_UNKNOWN as inert.
Expression text (*arg) originates from attacker-influenced sources (scripts, registers, options, user input) — treated as attacker-data throughout.
limitations: Legacy-script path: `rettv->vval.v_string = get_reg_contents(**arg, GREG_EXPR_SRC);` is reached with an unvalidated register-name character; the only guard, `else if (in_vim9script() && !valid_yank_reg(**arg, FALSE)) emsg_invreg(**arg);`, is gated by in_vim9script() and does not set ret = FAIL. The impact (any mishandling inside get_reg_contents) is entirely inside a not-shown internal callee and the argument is an identifier character, not a raw offset/size/index/pointer, so the candidate is speculative — not counted as a vulnerability.

In vim9script, the '@' error arms (semsg for whitespace, emsg_invreg for invalid register) leave ret == OK and rettv at VAR_UNKNOWN with untouched vval, which then flows to handle_subscript and eval7_leader and back to the caller. No statement in this code fails on those arms; whether any downstream consumer mishandles VAR_UNKNOWN cannot be shown here, so the impact chain is not instantiated.

STRCMP-family comparisons (STRNCMP(s, "true", 4) etc.) rely on get_name_len's internal guarantee that the name buffer holds at least len bytes; if that internal contract were broken the reads would be out-of-bounds, but the contract violation cannot be triggered by any statement in this code.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability found. The two memory-critical sinks in this JIT compiler function are provably guarded: the 32-byte class-map read is preceded in execution order by 'jump = CMP(SLJIT_GREATER, TMP1, 0, SLJIT_IMM, 255);' (char <= 255 implies index char>>3 <= 31, strict operator verified at the 255/256 boundary), and the UCD stage-1/stage-2 table chain is bounded by the quoted 32-bit clamp 'jump = CMP(SLJIT_LESS, TMP1, 0, SLJIT_IMM, MAX_UTF_CODE_POINT + 1);' plus UNASSIGNED_UTF_CHAR replacement, together with mask forms ('& UCD_BLOCK_MASK', '& 0x7', '& UCD_SCRIPTX_MASK', '& UCD_BPROPS_MASK'); in 8-bit non-utf mode the omitted >255 guard is safe because the code-unit width bounds chars at 0xFF (0xFF>>3 = 31 <= 31). Remaining candidates (unbounded cc[1] indices into PRIV(ucd_*) tables, min>max wrap of 'max - min' from an inverted range, unbounded 'while (*cc != XCL_END)' scans, and compares/jump-list routing tallies for PT_SCX XCL_NOTPROP) all require out-of-domain opcode bytes or truncated pattern memory that no statement in this code can produce, or have impacts (regex match semantics) that land outside this code; they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Macros and callees not shown are relied on only for documented semantics: GETCHARINCTEST, SET_CHAR_OFFSET, SET_TYPE_OFFSET, read_char, optimize_class, compile_char1_matchingpath, is_powerof2, OP_FLAGS.

The opcode stream cc is produced by the not-shown pcre2_compile stage; opcode-type bytes carry a quoted asserted contract (SLJIT_ASSERT(*cc == XCL_PROP || *cc == XCL_NOTPROP)), but the domain of property values cc[1] is fixed only by that unshown producer.
XCLASS_NEEDS_UCD is tested but never assigned in this snippet; it is assumed to be a composite mask of the XCLASS_HAS_* bits defined outside this code.
SLJIT_ASSERT is assumed compiled out in release builds, so the quoted asserts document contracts but do not enforce them at runtime.

PRIV(ucd_stage1/2), PRIV(ucd_records), PRIV(ucd_script_sets), PRIV(ucd_boolprop_sets), PRIV(ucd_caseless_sets) are assumed sized by the Unicode range 0..0x10FFFF and the validated property/script indices, as is standard for these const tables.
limitations: C1 (speculative): property values cc[1] index PRIV(ucd_script_sets)/PRIV(ucd_boolprop_sets) via cc[1]>>5, PRIV(ucp_typerange) via cc[1]*2, and PRIV(ucd_caseless_sets)+cc[1] with no bound check anywhere in this code; an out-of-domain index would cause an out-of-bounds read in the generated machine code or in the compile-time scan. The trigger requires pcre2_compile (not shown) to emit an out-of-domain opcode byte — e.g. via a corrupted or unvalidated serialized pattern buffer — which no statement in this code can produce; precondition not instantiated.

C2 (speculative): an inverted XCL_RANGE would set min > max and wrap 'max - min' in the no-map quick check; simulation shows the wrapped guard merely skips the quick check (control still reaches the per-entry comparisons, which reject the empty range correctly), so no memory effect, and the producer rejects out-of-order ranges at pattern-compile time.

C3 (speculative): the three 'while (*cc != XCL_END)' loops walk pattern memory with no bound; a truncated opcode stream (no XCL_END) would read out of bounds, but producing it requires upstream memory corruption not instantiated here.

C4 (impact not instantiated): the compares tally for PT_SCX with XCL_NOTPROP (extra compares++ in the scan loop vs. decrements in the SCRIPT/SCRIPT_EXTENSION/main loops) may affect whether the last generated jump targets 'list' vs 'backtracks'; any error would alter accept/reject semantics of the generated matcher, but proving a concrete wrong-accept requires the unshown compiled-format contract (e.g. whether negated xclass maps are stored complemented) and a consumer of the match result, neither of which is shown.
STEP 6 short-snippet sweep was not run: no primary candidate survived, but the code exceeds ~50 lines.
