evidence.snippet:
name = elf_map + shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + dyn[i].d_un.d_val;
                    snprintf(value, 50, "Shared library: [%s]", name);
evidence.reason: In the DT_NEEDED arm of the dynamic-entry loop, name is computed as elf_map + attacker-controlled shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + dyn[i].d_un.d_val with no validated_offset or any other range check on this path (validated_offset appears only in the earlier section-name loop), and dynstr itself is uninitialized if no '.dynstr' section exists; snprintf's %s then reads memory until a NUL, giving an out-of-bounds read of the mapping/adjacent memory.

assumptions: validated_offset(name, elf_map, elf_map + st.st_size) (line 184) is assumed to validate that the name pointer and its string lie within the mapping; its internals are not shown. Even granting this, it covers only the section-loop name pointers, not the header offsets (lines 176-178), the DT_NEEDED name, or the shdr/phdr table bounds.
get_elf_class and the PRINT_* macros are assumed to be plain accessors/printers; any bounds enforcement they might perform cannot be quoted from the given code and is therefore not relied upon.
Line numbers were counted treating the first line of the provided code ('int parse(char *elf) {') as line 1; the 64-bit branch duplicates the same defects at corresponding positions.
limitations: strcpy(&name[15 - 6], "[...]") (line 260) writes into the mmapped file data, but the preceding strlen(name) > 15 check plus validated_offset (line 184) constrain the write to bytes already inside the mapping; it mutates only the private MAP_PRIVATE copy and no out-of-bounds write could be instantiated.
Impact is bounded to out-of-bounds reads / information disclosure from adjacent memory and process crash of the parsing process; no attacker-controlled write was instantiated.

verdict.summary: All StatusOr and pointer uses in BuildXlaCompilationCache are guarded by quoted, execution-order-verified checks (metadata presence, platform.ok(), client.ok(), GetCompilationDevice). The only unchecked dereferences (tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads() at line 41 and config_proto() at line 44) cannot be shown to receive NULL from any statement in this code, and no memory, size, index, format-string, command, or injection sink consumes attacker-derived data. A non-NOT_FOUND compiler lookup error is silently swallowed (fall-through at line 36), but no security state is misrepresented and no unvalidated value reaches a sensitive sink.

assumptions: ParseVisibleDeviceList, tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads(), config_proto(), xla::Compiler::GetForPlatform, and XlaOpRegistry::GetCompilationDevice are internal callees not shown; their return contracts (including possible NULL returns) could not be quoted and were treated as assumptions, not as trigger producers.
Callers are assumed to pass non-NULL device, flr, and cache out-pointers; no documented precondition is quotable in this code, but no statement here can make them NULL either.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference at line 41 ('device->tensorflow_cpu_worker_threads()->num_threads') if the not-shown accessor returns NULL for non-CPU devices; trigger requires callee behavior not instantiated by any statement in this code, and the worst case is a same-process crash with no corruption.
Potential NULL dereference at line 44 ('flr->config_proto()->gpu_options()') under the same un-instantiable precondition.

Fail-open error handling: when compiler_for_platform holds a non-OK status other than NOT_FOUND, the error is silently ignored and execution continues past line 36 to build a client and cache anyway; recorded as a robustness/logic defect, not a security vulnerability, since no security state is presented and any genuinely unusable platform fails independently at GetOrCreateLocalClient.

verdict.summary: The peer-controlled ticket length ticklen is bounded to 0..65535 by n2s and pinned exactly to the received message length by the guard 'if (ticklen + 6 != n) ... goto f_err', which executes before the free, allocation, memcpy, and digest; the destination is allocated from the same expression as the copy length with the NULL result checked before use. No out-of-domain value is reachable at any memory sink. The only latent defect (tlsext_tick left dangling after free on the malloc-failure path, enabling a later double free) requires an allocation failure of at most ~16KB that the remote peer cannot induce, so it is not an instantiated vulnerability.

assumptions: ssl_get_message (project-internal, not shown) is assumed to return in n the body length of the message present in s->init_msg and to enforce the 16384 maximum passed to it; no statement in the given code establishes this, but no statement in the given code can produce an n larger than the delivered message either.
n2l/n2s are assumed to have their standard OpenSSL macro semantics (4-byte and 2-byte big-endian loads advancing p), bounding ticklen to 0..65535.
SSL_MAX_SSL_SESSION_ID_LENGTH is assumed to be 32 (SHA-256 output size), matching the EVP_Digest write into s->session->session_id; the array declaration is not in the shown code.
ssl_session_dup and EVP_Digest are assumed to have their documented failure behavior (NULL return / fixed-size output), which the code checks or safely consumes.
limitations: Double-free latent defect (CWE-415-class): 'if (s->session->tlsext_tick) { OPENSSL_free(s->session->tlsext_tick); s->session->tlsext_ticklen = 0; }' frees without setting the pointer to NULL; if the immediately following 'OPENSSL_malloc(ticklen)' fails and control goes to 'goto err', the session retains a dangling tlsext_tick that SSL_SESSION_free will free again. Trigger requires an allocation failure of at most 16378 bytes (ticklen = n-6, n <= 16384), which a remote peer cannot induce, so it is not an instantiated vulnerability here.

Edge case: when ticklen == 0 (n == 6), OPENSSL_malloc(0) may return NULL on some platforms, causing a spurious handshake abort via the '!s->session->tlsext_tick' error arm; this is platform-dependent allocation behavior of a zero-size request, not attacker-induced memory unsafety.
Candidate C4 (integer overflow in 'ticklen + 6') was dismissed by computation: ticklen's reachable maximum from n2s is 65535, so ticklen + 6 max is 65541, well within int range.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability in the given code. Attacker-controlled PNG-derived dimensions (decode.width/height) are fully validated by the quoted guard (truncation round-trip equality, >0, < 2^27 per dimension, int64 total_size < 2^29), which sits before every allocation/copy sink in execution order; the output tensor, row stride, and row count passed to png::CommonFinishDecode are all derived from the same decode fields and are provably consistent, and the 2^29 bound guarantees height*width*channels*2 stays within int range for channels <= 4. Remaining concerns are speculative or bounded: decode.channels has no in-function guard (safety depends on the not-shown CommonInitDecode/op registration bounding it to 1-4), and large-but-admitted dimensions allow a bounded (~4 GB cap) allocation amplification from a tiny PNG.

In Node::RunForwardTypeInference, the index ix taken from edge->src_output() is validated against the source node's experimental_type args_size() only by a DCHECK, which is compiled out in release builds; node_t.args(ix) then indexes the protobuf repeated field out of bounds. Both ix and args_size() originate from an attacker-supplied GraphDef (NodeDef.input strings and NodeDef.experimental_type), yielding an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds read whose result is dereferenced as a FullTypeDef by the forward type inference function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: ix (attacker-controlled edge src_output) is compared against node_t.args_size() (attacker-controlled NodeDef experimental_type arg count) only by a DCHECK, which is a no-op in release builds, and then passed directly to node_t.args(ix), whose RepeatedPtrField contract requires 0 <= ix < args_size(). Trigger: a GraphDef where the source node has experimental_type with type_id != TFT_UNSET and args_size()=0 (e.g., TFT_PRODUCT with no args) while an edge into the current node carries src_output()=0 (or any k >= args_size, chosen via the 'src:k' input string); the simulation reaches line 45 with ix=0, args_size()=0 and no active check, producing an out-of-bounds read whose bogus FullTypeDef& is dereferenced by props_->fwd_type_fn at line 56.

evidence.snippet: input_idx.at(i) = edge->src_output();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: edge->src_output() is derived from the attacker-supplied GraphDef edge (NodeDef input string 'src:idx') and is stored unvalidated into input_idx; .at() only bounds-checks the destination slot i, never the stored value, which later becomes ix at line 40.

assumptions: DCHECK is compiled out in release builds (Google logging macro semantics; aborts only in debug builds) — no release-build enforcement of line 41 exists.

Protobuf generated accessor args(int index) is unchecked in release and its documented contract requires 0 <= index < args_size(); the code's own DCHECK at line 41 corroborates that no check occurs inside the accessor.
props_->fwd_type_fn is non-null for ops registered with a forward type inference function (TF op registry, not shown); the code's own null-check at line 4 shows this is a designed path.

in_edges_ and node defs originate from a parsed GraphDef/SavedModel (untrusted model file) and the importer preserves NodeDef fields including experimental_type; this code is the last line of defense for those values.
limitations: input_nodes.at(i)/input_idx.at(i) (lines 16-17) throw std::out_of_range when dst_input >= input_types.size(); .at() is a bounds-safe accessor so there is no memory corruption, but the uncaught exception aborts the process (denial of service on malformed graphs). The trigger depends on whether graph import rejects such input indices — producer code not shown, so not counted as a primary finding.
In debug builds, the DCHECKs at lines 14 and 41 abort the process before the sink — a debug-only crash, not a release vulnerability.

infer_type.ValueOrDie() (line 57) aborts if props_->fwd_type_fn returns an error Status; whether any registered inference function can return an error on attacker-shaped input is not shown, so this is speculative.

Turning the out-of-bounds read at line 45 into memory disclosure (versus a crash) depends on heap layout; the directly instantiated consequence is the out-of-bounds read and dereference of the out-of-bounds-derived reference.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. All numeric values reaching code-emission sinks are guarded or clamped in this code (idx > 0 check, n < 0 sentinel check, n bounded to 0..15, n == 14 repackaging, n == 2 arity check for OP_SETIDX, and default arms calling codegen_error in both switches). Remaining candidates depend on stack discipline of not-shown callees (gen_values, gen_hash, pop/push) or parser AST invariants and are speculative.

assumptions: codegen_error does not return (aborts codegen) and unknown lhs types never reach the second switch's gen_* sinks.
gen_values, gen_hash, gen_move, pop/push/cursp, genop_* maintain the virtual stack discipline documented by their use here; their bodies are not shown.
NODE_CALL AST nodes always carry tree->cdr with a method-id child, so nsym(tree->cdr->car) never dereferences NULL.
limitations: Candidate 1: possible stack-pointer imbalance in the NODE_CALL keyword-argument repackaging path (pop_n(n) when n == 14 followed by OP_ARRAY) depends on the stack effects of gen_values and gen_hash, which are not shown; trigger not instantiable.

Candidate 2: gen_setupvar called with caller-supplied sp when rhs == NULL for NODE_LVAR/NODE_ARG relies on the caller's stack-slot convention; no attacker-controlled out-of-domain value demonstrably reaches it.
Candidate 3: dereference of tree->cdr->car without a NULL check assumes a parser invariant not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: In the CP950 PUA path of the Big5 wchar conversion filter, k is a linear-scan index over cp950_pua_tbl; when the attacker-controlled code point c2 = c1<<8|c matches no table row, the loop exits with k equal to the row count, and the very next statement reads cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] (and later [k][0]) with no post-loop bound, causing an out-of-bounds read of attacker-forced index in the process converting the attacker-supplied byte stream. The bytes c1 (cached lead) and c (second byte) are attacker data; no check, clamp, found-flag, or error arm on k exists on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the scan loop bounds k only while inside the loop; if the attacker-derived c2 matches no cp950_pua_tbl row, k exits at exactly the row count (one-past-limit boundary), and line 53 then reads cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] — and lines 54–55/57 read [k][2] and [k][0] — with no k < N check, clamp, found-flag, or error arm anywhere on the path. Trigger: attacker sends a CP950 byte pair (lead 0x81–0xfe cached at lines 19–20, second byte 0x40–0x7e/0xa1–0xfe per line 31) for which the table lookup yields w <= 0 and c2 falls outside every table row; the loop runs to completion and the immediately following statement performs the out-of-bounds read; the resulting garbage feeds w, which is emitted via the output callback (line 67), and the access itself can crash the process consuming the attacker input.

Origin of the tainted value: c1 (cached attacker lead byte) and c (attacker second byte) are combined into c2, which solely determines whether the unbounded scan loop at lines 47–51 breaks or exits with k == row count; the branch is entered whenever the Unicode table lookup returns w <= 0, which the attacker arranges with any unmapped CP950 pair.

assumptions: is_in_cp950_pua(), cp950_pua_tbl, big5_ucs_table, big5_ucs_table_size, the CK macro, and output_function are defined in the same module but not shown; their semantics could not be quoted.

The existence of a (c1,c) pair that passes is_in_cp950_pua() yet whose c2 falls outside every cp950_pua_tbl row is not provable from the snippet alone; in the real php-src mbfilter_big5.c this mismatch exists and upstream fixed this exact function by adding the missing post-loop bound on k, which supports but does not quote-verify the instantiation.

The conversion filter is assumed to run on attacker-supplied byte streams (e.g., mb_convert_encoding on user input), consistent with its role as an mbfl filter callback consuming one attacker byte per call.
limitations: The exact triggering byte pair depends on the unshown table and helper; any concrete pair named here would rely on the unshown module constants.

Impact is an out-of-bounds read of a static const table (a few bytes past its end): the strongest direct effects are a crash/DoS of the converting process and possible disclosure of adjacent read-only data through the computed w emitted by the output callback; no out-of-bounds write is claimed.

big5_ucs_table[w] at line 38 was verified safe via the quoted guard at line 37 (w >= 0 && w < big5_ucs_table_size, correct operators, same variable, no bypass); other arithmetic (c1<<8|c, negative (c1-0xa1)*157) flows only into guarded branches or value output and was dismissed.

verdict.summary: qf_fill_buffer captures qfp (qfl->qf_start) and qfl before invoking the user-controlled 'quickfixtextfunc' callback via call_qftf_func(); the callback can free or replace the quickfix list (e.g., setqflist(...,'r')), leaving qfp and qfl dangling. No revalidation exists anywhere between the callback and the loop's dereferences (qfp->qf_fnum at lines 65-66/69, qfp->qf_next at line 71, and qf_buf_add_line's internal reads of qfp fields), producing a use-after-free whose freed-memory contents the attacker can groom, leading to a wild-pointer read chain — memory corruption in the editor process.

evidence.reason: Sink: qfp is dereferenced (qfp->qf_fnum, qf->qf_next, and qfp passed into qf_buf_add_line which reads its fields) with no validity check after the 'quickfixtextfunc' callback invoked at line 46 has had the opportunity to free/replace the quickfix list. Trigger: attacker-influenced vimrc/plugin sets quickfixtextfunc to a function that calls setqflist([{'lnum':1,'text':'x'}], 'r') while being invoked, freeing the node qfp points to while keeping qf_count=1; the loop then reads freed heap memory at line 66/69 and loads an attacker-groomable qf_next at line 71, dereferencing it on the next iteration — use-after-free memory corruption. The only pointer guard present, `if (qfp == NULL)` at line 72, runs after the dereference and only catches NULL, not freed memory.

Origin of the invalidation window: this call hands control to user-script code ('quickfixtextfunc') after qfp was captured at line 34 (qfp = qfl->qf_start) and before any use of qfp/qfl; the script can free or replace the quickfix list and buffer during this call, and the given code never re-reads qfl->qf_start nor revalidates qfp/qfl/buf on any subsequent path (the while condition at line 51 itself reads the possibly-reallocated qfl).

assumptions: call_qftf_func invokes a user-configured VimL callback ('quickfixtextfunc') whose body is script-controlled — Vim-documented semantics of an option name visible in this code's flow (call to call_qftf_func with qftf_list consumed as a typval list).

The callback can invalidate the captured state via documented Vim commands such as setqflist(...,'r')/':cnew' (freeing qfline_T nodes and/or reallocating the quickfix stack) or wiping the quickfix buffer — the exact freeing is engine-internal and not shown in this snippet.
Attacker control is via crafted vimrc/plugin/config plus a crafted quickfix-producing file, the standard Vim CVE threat model.
limitations: dirname[MAXPATHL] overflow inside qf_buf_add_line: potential harm would occur entirely inside a not-shown callee with no out-of-domain argument passed from this code; speculative, not counted.
ml_delete(lnum + 1) (line 81) stays in bounds even if the callback alters the buffer, because lnum counts only successful appends and the append path breaks on FAIL; dismissed after edge testing.

The 'quickfixtextfunc' function being benign in a stock configuration reduces real-world reachability but does not restore a guard this code can quote; per the analysis rules the callback body is not a contract this code enforces.

verdict.summary: All shape-vector indexing sinks are preceded by quoted empty/size guards; the unguarded spots (unchecked node_map_->GetNode results for the conv children, and conv_node->attr().at("data_format") without an existence check) cause at most a same-privilege abort/NULL-deref of the process loading the attacker-supplied model, with no memory corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: node_map_->GetNode, IsReallyConstant, MaybeRemoveControlInput, MaybeAddControlInput, AddPrefixToNodeName, UpdateInput, AddNode, NodeExists, ShapesSymbolicallyEqual, IsValidConstShapeForMulConvPushDown, IsConv2D/IsConv3D/IsAnyMul, and GraphProperties accessors are internal helpers whose semantics are not shown; assumed to behave per TensorFlow grappler conventions.
properties.GetOutputProperties/GetInputProperties are assumed to return references to containers whose lifetime covers the function scope.
limitations: conv_node->attr().at("data_format") is called without checking the attribute exists; a Conv2D/Conv3D node lacking this attr causes std::out_of_range/abort — crash-only robustness issue for the party loading the malicious model.

conv_left_child and conv_right_child (results of node_map_->GetNode on conv inputs) are dereferenced in IsReallyConstant without NULL checks, unlike mul_left_child/mul_right_child which are checked; a malformed GraphDef referencing a nonexistent node name yields a NULL dereference — crash-only, equal privilege.

The graph-mutation control flow (MaybeRemoveControlInput/MaybeAddControlInput/UpdateInput) could in principle introduce cycles or mis-wire nodes, but the callee implementations are not shown, so no memory-unsafe or correctness-violating impact can be instantiated from this code alone.

verdict.summary: The PNG dimension values derived from attacker input are rigorously validated before any allocation or copy: a 64-bit round-trip cast check catches int truncation, `width <= 0 || width >= (1LL << 27)` (and the symmetric height check) bound each dimension, and `total_size >= (1LL << 29)` bounds the product. At the extreme passing values, the allocation sizes and the row strides passed to CommonFinishDecode (decode.channels * width * sizeof(uint16), new uint16[height*width*decode.channels]) provably fit in int32 and match each other, so no integer overflow, buffer-size mismatch, or out-of-bounds write is reachable from this code.

assumptions: png::CommonInitDecode (internal callee, not shown) is assumed to set decode.channels to a small valid value (1-4 per PNG color type) and to fail (return false) on malformed PNG data; no statement in this file bounds decode.channels.

png::CommonFinishDecode is assumed to consume the caller-provided row stride and to write within the supplied buffer dimensions (its failure is checked via OP_REQUIRES, but its internal writes are not shown).
OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK abort the kernel with an error status on failure (standard TF macro semantics).
limitations: If png::CommonInitDecode could ever produce decode.channels outside 1..4, the stride decode.channels * width * sizeof(uint16) and the allocations would be sized inconsistently; no statement in this code could prevent that, but no path in this code instantiates such a value, so the trigger remains speculative (callee behavior not shown).

An attacker may request dimensions yielding a very large (up to ~4 GB) but strictly bounded allocation; allocation failure is handled via checked status for the tensor path, and the worst case is resource consumption bounded by 2^31 elements, not unbounded amplification.

A failed `new uint16[...]` in the DT_FLOAT path would throw std::bad_alloc rather than return an error status; it requires an allocation of up to 2^31-4 elements (~4 GB) and is a crash-of-own-process robustness concern, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: PQconnectPoll validates all server-controlled values that reach memory-sizing or indexing sinks: the auth message length msgLength is range-checked per message type ('R' limited to [8,2000], 'E' to [8,30000] with the >30000 case routed through the pre-3.0 re-read path) and gated by 'if (avail < msgLength)' plus pqCheckInBufferSpace before any body consumption; negotiation response bytes are validated against fully enumerated arms with a rejecting else; port numbers are clamped to [1,65535]; Unix socket paths are length-checked with the correct >= operator; host indices are bounded by 'conn->whichhost + 1 < conn->nconnhost' with an nconnhost > 0 check on reset; and errorMessage tail accesses are short-circuit-guarded against len == 0. No trigger with a fully instantiated in-code impact chain survives.

assumptions: Behavior of not-shown internal callees is assumed per their documented semantics: pqGetc/pqGetInt bounds-check against the input buffer, PQgetvalue performs tuple/column bounds checks and may return NULL out of range, getHostaddr initializes host_addr[0] on failure, pqGets_append safely handles a missing NUL terminator, pqReadData manages conn->inBuffer/inCursor/inEnd consistently, and pg_getaddrinfo_all returns family-appropriate addrinfo with ai_addrlen <= sizeof(sockaddr_storage).

pg_getaddrinfo_all output addrlen is bounded by the address family (system resolver contract), so the memcpy into conn->raddr.addr cannot overflow; no statement in this code lets a raw attacker-supplied addrlen reach that memcpy.

ch->type values are confined to the enumerated CHT_* constants by the connection-string parser (not shown); an out-of-enum value would simply leave conn->addrlist NULL after release_conn_addrinfo, causing an orderly advance to the next host.
limitations: Speculative: a malicious PostgreSQL server could return a TUPLES_OK result with one tuple but zero columns, so that 'val = PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0)' yields NULL and 'strncmp(val, "on", 2)' / 'strncmp(val, "t", 1)' dereferences NULL (client crash / DoS). Not confirmed: PQgetvalue's NULL-return behavior is not shown in the given code, so the trigger producer is an unquotable internal callee, and even granting it the impact is only a same-privilege client crash (robustness).

Speculative: if getHostaddr failed without initializing the stack buffer, 'if (host_addr[0])' and emitHostIdentityInfo would read uninitialized memory (CWE-457); the callee is not shown so this precondition cannot be instantiated.

Speculative: areq and the decremented msgLength are passed to pg_fe_sendauth without a further in-code range check; any mishandling would occur inside that not-shown callee, which per its known contract consumes them for auth-request dispatch.

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line writes attacker-controlled file content into the fixed 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv using index j whose only bound is the input line length (strlen of the attacker's line, up to lineSize-1). In the win-CP conversion branch each input byte can emit two output bytes, so a file line of >=512 non-UTF8 high-bit bytes drives j past 1024, and any line longer than 1024 bytes overflows regardless of encoding. No check, clamp, or sized allocation bounds j anywhere, producing a stack out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced byte values in the text/subtitle import path.

evidence.reason: Sink: szLineConv[j] is written with j only ever incremented and never bounded against the fixed 1024-byte stack buffer declared at line 5. Simulated trigger (unicode_type=0, line of 1023 bytes of 0xE9, lineSize=1024): line 17's test (0xE9 & 0xc0) != 0x80 is true for every byte, so lines 18-20 emit 2 bytes (0xC3, 0xA9) per input byte; after 512 input bytes j=1024 and line 53 writes out of bounds, continuing to j=2046 with the NUL terminator at szLineConv[2046] on line 56 — an attacker-file-driven stack buffer overflow.

evidence.snippet:
len = (u32) strlen(szLine);
		for (i=0; i<len; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin: the sole loop bound len is strlen of the line read from the attacker-supplied file via gf_fgets (line 9), up to lineSize-1, with no relation enforced to the 1024-byte szLineConv; the expansion in the win-CP branch (lines 17-21) makes the write count j reach up to 2*len, exceeding 1024 whenever len >= 512 (or whenever a line exceeds 1024 bytes), with no guard on j on any path.

assumptions: lineSize is assumed to be at least 513 (realistically 1024, matching the internal buffer) so that a line long enough to overflow can be read; no statement in the code binds lineSize to szLineConv's 1024 bytes, and even lineSize==1024 suffices for the simulated trigger.

gf_utf8_wcstombs is an internal GPAC callee whose exact return convention (whether it can return 1024 when the output exactly fills the buffer) is not shown; standard wcstombs-like semantics assumed for paths B/C.
gf_fgets is assumed to behave like fgets (store up to lineSize-1 bytes plus a NUL terminator), which is what keeps the szLine[i+1] reads in path A within the caller's buffer.
limitations: Line 62 'szLineConv[i] = 0;' could write one byte past szLineConv if gf_utf8_wcstombs returns exactly 1024 (full buffer); reachability depends on the callee's unshown return convention, so it is speculative.

The UTF-16 byte-swap while(1) loop (lines 51-59) scans szLine in u16 pairs with no explicit bound and relies on finding two consecutive zero bytes; a line filling the buffer exactly could read 1-2 bytes past szLine, but the trigger edge (line length == lineSize-1 with a nonzero final byte under UTF-16 framing) was not fully instantiated.
The szLine[i+1] read at line 17 when i == len-1 reads the fgets NUL terminator and is in bounds; no separate finding.

verdict.summary: In the CP950 PUA path of mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar, the linear scan over cp950_pua_tbl can complete without break, leaving k equal to the table's row count; k is then used to index cp950_pua_tbl[k][0..2] with no bounds check, causing an out-of-bounds read of attacker-triggered static data whose value flows into the converted output stream.

evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the attacker-controlled pair (lead byte cached at lines 19-20, trail byte c) yields c2 (e.g. 0x8f50 for input bytes 0x8f 0x50 in CP950, admitted by the entry predicate at lines 45-49 covering c1 in [0x81,0x8d],[0x8e,0xa0],[0xc7,0xc8],[0xfa,0xfe]). When no table row's range [2]..[3] contains c2, the loop exits with k equal to the row count, and nothing resets or bounds k.

Out-of-bounds read sink: cp950_pua_tbl[k][2]/[0] is indexed with k == rowcount (one past the end of the static const array) because no bounds check on k exists between the loop (line 55) and this use; the garbage-derived w, when > 0, is emitted via (*filter->output_function)(w, filter->data) at line 71, leaking/corrupting converter output from adjacent static memory.

assumptions: The contents of cp950_pua_tbl and big5_ucs_table_size are not printed in the snippet; the concrete gap value 0x8f50 relies on the known upstream table layout whose rows straddle the 0x8f40-0x8fa0 gap. The structural defect (no post-loop bound on k) is independent of this and was verified absent.
The CK macro is assumed to be the standard mbfl check-return wrapper; it is not shown.
filter->status is assumed initialized to 0 by the filter framework before first call (standard mbfl contract), so filter->cache is always set before case 1 reads it.
limitations: big5_ucs_table[w] at line 38 is correctly guarded by the quoted 'w >= 0 && w < big5_ucs_table_size' (line 37); negative indices from CP950 low lead planes (c1 < 0xa1) fall through to w = 0 — no defect there.
The OOB read is limited to a fixed small region (one row past the table); worst case is disclosure of adjacent read-only data via converted output, not arbitrary-index access.

verdict.summary: This is libpq's PQconnectPoll state machine. Server-controlled protocol values (message type byte, 4-byte message length) are fully validated in execution order: beresp must be 'R' or 'E', msgLength is rejected if <8 or >2000 (auth) / >30000 (error), which also excludes negative values, and buffer space is ensured via pqCheckInBufferSpace before the message body is consumed. The ai_addrlen memcpy is sized by getaddrinfo results for the client's own host parameters, not attacker bytes, and fits sockaddr_storage. The one genuinely missing check — no PQnfields validation before PQgetvalue in CONNECTION_CHECK_WRITABLE/CHECK_STANDBY — has a trigger whose NULL-producing step lies in a callee not shown and yields at most a same-privilege crash; it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: The UNIXSOCK_PATH macro (not shown) writes into portstr[MAXPGPATH] without overflowing; the given code only checks strlen(portstr) >= UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN after the write and before use.

pg_getaddrinfo_all/getaddrinfo return ai_addrlen values that fit within sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage) for AF_INET/AF_INET6/AF_UNIX, so memcpy(&conn->raddr.addr, addr_cur->ai_addr, addr_cur->ai_addrlen) cannot overflow.
conn->sslmode and conn->gssencmode are non-NULL, NUL-terminated strings established by libpq's connection-parameter parsing (code not shown), so conn->sslmode[0] derefs are safe.
getHostaddr(conn, host_addr, NI_MAXHOST) always NUL-terminates host_addr including on non-IP address families (callee not shown).
PQgetvalue returns NULL for an out-of-range field index (callee not shown); see limitations.
limitations: In CONNECTION_CHECK_WRITABLE and CONNECTION_CHECK_STANDBY, only PQntuples(res) == 1 is checked before PQgetvalue(res, 0, 0); there is no PQnfields check. A malicious/misbehaving server answering 'SHOW transaction_read_only' or 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()' with a zero-field result would make strncmp(val, "on", 2) / strncmp(val, "t", 1) dereference NULL (potential crash of the client process). The NULL value is produced inside the not-shown PQgetvalue callee, so the trigger could not be fully instantiated from the given code, and the impact is at most a same-privilege crash with no corruption — robustness issue, not promoted to a vulnerability.
ch->type switch has no default arm; an out-of-range ch->type would fall through silently, but ch->type is set by libpq's own connection-string parsing (not shown) and is not attacker-byte-derived.
Behavior under USE_SSL/ENABLE_GSS disabled (goto error_return arms) was treated as fail-closed; verified those arms return FAILED rather than continuing.

verdict.summary: In send_response_data, the x-amz-tagging-count header is emitted from obj_tags.count() AFTER the try/catch block; when decode of the attacker-influenced RGW_ATTR_TAGS attribute throws buffer::error, the catch only logs and falls through, so dump_header at line 161 outputs a value that no statement on that path ever initialized (uninitialized stack data reaching HTTP response output / info disclosure), and no success check, initializer, or error arm exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the use of obj_tags.count() at the sink is outside the try block and no statement initializes obj_tags or tests decode success before it. Trigger: a GET of an object whose RGW_ATTR_TAGS attribute is malformed so that obj_tags.decode(it) throws buffer::error (a failure path the code itself anticipates, as shown by the catch handler); the catch logs and falls through, so dump_header emits a never-initialized count value in the x-amz-tagging-count response header — uninitialized stack memory reaching output. The parallel retention/legal-hold branches correctly keep their dumps inside the try, confirming the guard form (success test or dump-inside-try) exists in the codebase but is absent on this path.

assumptions: RGWObjTags's default constructor is assumed not to zero-initialize its count member and decode is assumed to throw before assigning count on truncated input; the class definition and decode implementation are not included in the given code.
s->auth.identity is assumed non-NULL after authentication; no null check is present in the given code.
dump_header / dump_range / decode_attr_bl_single_value are project-internal callees whose sanitization and clamping behavior is not shown.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read at line 205: dump_body(s, bl.c_str() + bl_ofs, bl_len) performs no bounds check against bl.length() in this code, but bl_ofs/bl_len are computed by the internal read pipeline (derived from the Range header) which is not shown; no statement in this code produces an out-of-range offset, so the trigger is speculative here.

Potential HTTP response-header injection (CWE-113): attacker-supplied values (response-* query params for authenticated requests, user x-amz-meta-* attributes) are passed to dump_header without visible CR/LF sanitization, but dump_header is not shown, so the impact link is uncharacterizable.

The anonymous-request check at line 112 correctly prevents unauthenticated response-header manipulation; the remaining authenticated override of response headers matches documented S3 behavior and is not a defect.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in BuildInputArgIndex are guarded by quoted, execution-order-verified checks: the loop bound 'i < dtypes.size()' bounds every dtypes[i] access, 'dtypes.size() < size_t{1}' rejects the empty-dtype edge, 'if (arg_attrs)' guards the nullable pointer, and the invariant check 'arg_index != result_.nodes.size()' aborts any index/count divergence (including the theoretical size_t-to-int truncation path, which is unreachable at realistic scale). No trigger with a fully instantiated security impact chain survives.

assumptions: ArgNumType, AddItem, AddNode, AddAttr, and MakeRefType are internal callees not shown; their error-return and non-NULL contracts could not be quoted and are treated as assumptions. No statement in this code's own flow produces a failure sentinel or NULL from them.
result_ member state (nodes, arg_types) is assumed to be manipulated only via AddItem/AddNode as reflected by the quoted invariant check on result_.nodes.size().
limitations: Speculative: 'int arg_index = result_.nodes.size();' narrows size_t to int; a truncation would require result_.nodes.size() to exceed INT_MAX (~2.1 billion nodes), unreachable before massive resource exhaustion, and the quoted check 'if (arg_index != result_.nodes.size())' converts any divergence into an Internal error return before further use.

Impact not instantiated: the loop 'for (const auto& arg_attr : arg_attrs->attr()) AddAttr(arg_attr.first, arg_attr.second, gnode->mutable_attr());' would overwrite the just-set 'T' and 'index' node attributes if arg_attrs contains those reserved keys (a concretely reachable state), but the memory-safe proto map insert has no security consequence within this code; any type-confusion effect would occur in downstream consumers not given.

verdict.summary: The exported allocation-sizing function takes a signed `int size` with no range check; at `sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size` a negative size is converted to size_t and the multiplication wraps, so the function returns a byte count far smaller than required (e.g., size=-1 yields computed_size=0 on the non-MSVC path). Callers using this return value to allocate TfLiteIntArray buffers then under-allocate, enabling heap out-of-bounds writes; no guard of any form exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the signed parameter `int size` (line 1) is unvalidated; on line 4 it is implicitly converted to size_t for the multiplication `sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size`, which wraps for negative inputs (size=-1 -> computed_size=0 on the non-MSVC path, 8+(-4)-4=0 on MSVC). The returned value is the heap allocation size consumers use, so an attacker-supplied negative (or, on 32-bit, huge) count yields an under-sized allocation leading to heap out-of-bounds writes. No bounds check, clamp, mask, error arm, or any other guard form appears anywhere in the function body.

assumptions: Callers allocate a buffer of TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size) bytes and then write the size field and up to `size` elements into it — this is the function's sole documented purpose, but the callers themselves are not part of the given code.

sizeof(dummy.data[0]) == sizeof(int) == 4 and sizeof(dummy) is 4 (flexible-array definition) or 8 (data[1] MSVC definition); either way the wrap simulation for negative size holds, differing only in whether the final result is 0 or 4 minus 4.
limitations: The final heap out-of-bounds write occurs in callers not shown; within the given code the instantiated defect is the wraparound producing a wrong allocation-size return value, which memory-allocation sizing is.

The large-positive-size overflow trigger (e.g., size >= 2^30 overflowing 4*size) requires a 32-bit size_t target; on 64-bit it instead yields a huge but non-wrapping value. This secondary trigger is target-width-dependent and did not drive the verdict.
MSVC path with size=0 was edge-tested: computed_size = sizeof(dummy) - sizeof(dummy.data[0]), which is consistent with the one-element-included sizeof; no independent defect found there.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety, injection, or trust-boundary defect is instantiable in gen_assignment. All value-carrying sinks are guarded in execution order: the lv index is gated by 'if (idx > 0)' before gen_move, gen_values' failure sentinel is tested by 'if (n < 0) { n = 15; push(); }' immediately after production, and every n-derived operand (OP_SEND/OP_ARRAY counts, pop_n amounts) is confined to [0,15] by the quoted increment/clamp chain. Remaining candidates (NULL deref on tree->cdr->cdr, stack-pointer underflow in pop_n, cursp()-1 underflow, out-of-range lv_idx) all require misbehavior of not-shown internal callees (parser node construction, gen_values/gen_hash/push/pop conventions, lv_idx) whose contracts cannot be quoted from this code, and this code's own statements cannot produce those trigger states.

assumptions: push()/pop()/pop_n()/cursp() and gen_* helper semantics are project-internal and not shown; stack-accounting analysis of pop_n(13/14/2/14) relies on their conventional behavior.

gen_values(s, tree->car, VAL, limit) is assumed to return either a non-negative count ≤ limit or a negative sentinel for variable-length arguments; only the sentinel handling is quotable here ('if (n < 0) { n = 15; push(); }').
lv_idx(s, sym) is assumed to return a valid local-variable register index (>0) or a non-positive sentinel for upvars; only the 'if (idx > 0)' routing is quotable.
The parser is assumed to emit well-shaped NODE_CALL/NODE_COLON2 nodes (non-NULL cdr chains); this code contains no statement that constructs or mutates node structure.
limitations: Candidate: NULL dereference at 'tree = tree->cdr->cdr->car;' (and 'nsym(tree->cdr->car)') if the parser emitted a truncated NODE_CALL chain. Speculative: trigger requires a parser defect outside this code; no in-code statement produces malformed trees.

Candidate: s->sp underflow via pop_n(n)/pop_n(2)/pop_n(14) if gen_values or gen_hash push fewer stack slots than the pops assume, leading to negative register operands in generated ops. Speculative: mismatch depends on unshown macro/callee behavior; no quotable mismatch was found in the given statements.

Candidate: 'int recv = cursp()-1;' underflow on the safe-call (NODE_SCALL) path if s->sp were 0. Speculative: entry stack state and push()/codegen() semantics are not shown; the enclosing statements make cursp()==0 unreachable from quoted code.

Candidate: lv_idx returning 0 routes to the upvar path (gen_setupvar) — a potential miscompilation for a zero-indexed local; no memory-corruption impact instantiable from given code, and lv_idx semantics are unshown.

verdict.summary: In gopherToHTML, a malicious Gopher server response line makes llen reach TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (either directly, or via the clamp at lines 79 that produces exactly that value), and the terminator write `line[llen + 1] = '\0'` then writes one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte `line` buffer — a remotely triggered off-by-one out-of-bounds NUL write (memory corruption) in the proxy process.

evidence.reason: Sink: the NUL terminator is written at index llen+1, but every guard only bounds the copied byte count to TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1. With a Gopher line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes (attacker = the Gopher server controls inbuf/len), llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 and line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE] = '\0' writes one byte past LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE).

Insufficient guard: it clamps gopherState->len + llen to at most TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (the copy length), never llen+1 (the terminator index); moreover its clamp arm itself produces llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 when gopherState->len == 0, which then feeds the off-by-one write at line 99.

assumptions: LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) declares a buffer of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes (standard Squid macro semantics); TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the compile-time constant used consistently for line/tmpbuf.
gopherState->buf is at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes (structure not shown); the clamped memcpy at line 86 is bounded by the same expression otherwise.
inbuf/len carry the raw Gopher server response (standard Squid gopher flow); regardless of caller, these parameters are the trust-boundary data this function parses.
limitations: atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) NULL-dereference candidate in the CSO branch was dismissed on a quotable guard: `if (!result) break;` executes before the atoi calls, and strtok monotonicity means an earlier NULL token implies result is also NULL.

In the extreme off-by-one edge, port[2] can read line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE+1]... at most 1 byte past (port[2] ≤ line[llen+1]); this shares the same root cause as the primary finding and is not counted separately.
line[llen] is left uninitialized between the copied bytes and the terminator on each iteration; the read is in-bounds and only feeds parsing, no security-state impact found.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable sinks are guarded: the empty-tensor check before flat<ResourceHandle>()(0) is exact and in execution order, FindDeviceFromName's failure is checked before its result is used, and nullptr device pointers are handled on every branch. Remaining concerns (variant mismatch at absl::get<Device*>(op.Device()), dtype consistency between handle and tensor) depend on unquotable internal contracts and could not be instantiated as triggers in this code.

tensor_handle->Tensor(&tensor) always yields a valid Tensor* on OK status (internal contract).
ctx.HostCPU() is non-null (internal contract).
op.is_function() == false implies op.Device() holds the Device* variant alternative (internal EagerOperation contract, not shown).

Potential dtype confusion in tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>()(0) if a handle's declared dtype ever diverged from its tensor contents; no statement in this code produces such a state.
The TODO-noted blocking call tensor_handle->Tensor(&tensor) is a synchronization/performance concern, not an attacker-scalable security effect.

verdict.summary: updateHandshakeState only transfers already-derived cipher objects into the connection state. Every transfer is gated on the same optional it moves (if (zeroRttReadCipher), if (oneRttWriteCipher), etc.), *clientParams is null-checked with a thrown QuicTransportException before dereference, and the amplification limit is cleared only after a 1-RTT read cipher is derived (validated-CFIN condition). The two CHECK assertions (handshakeReadHeaderCipher, conn.oneRttWriteCipher) can only fire if the not-shown handshake layer returns internally inconsistent state; no attacker-instantiable memory-safety, injection, or fail-open defect exists in this code.

assumptions: getZeroRttReadCipher/getOneRttReadCipher/getHandshakeReadCipher and the paired header-cipher getters are assumed to be derived together by the handshake layer (not shown), so CHECK(handshakeReadHeaderCipher) reflects a real invariant.

isHandshakeDone() is assumed to imply a 1-RTT write cipher was exported on some earlier invocation, making CHECK(conn.oneRttWriteCipher) an internal invariant rather than an attacker-triggerable abort.
getClientTransportParams returning transport parameters means they were validated at the TLS layer; processClientInitialParams (not shown) is assumed to enforce parameter validity.
limitations: CHECK(handshakeReadHeaderCipher) aborts the process if the handshake layer returns a read cipher without a header cipher; trigger requires callee inconsistency not producible from the given code — speculative.
