verdict.summary: All memory sinks in change_indent() are provably in-bounds. The decisive sink, new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL; in the VREPLACE block, is fed by curwin->w_cursor.col = (colnr_T)new_cursor_col; (or 0), and on every path (cursor at/after first non-blank: new_cursor_col += curwin->w_cursor.col lands on an existing character; non-INSERT: cursor on first non-blank; INSERT scan: the loop 'while (vcol <= (int)curwin->w_virtcol)' plus the break 'if (ptr[new_cursor_col] == NUL)' bounds the index by the NUL, and the subsequent space insertion grows the line by exactly the i bytes added via 'new_cursor_col += i') the final column is <= strlen of the line copied by vim_strsave(ml_get_curline()). The scan loop's first-iteration -1 index is covered in execution order by 'if (has_mbyte && new_cursor_col >= 0)' falling to '++new_cursor_col', and i = w_virtcol - last_vcol is >= 0 because last_vcol is only assigned where the loop-entry condition held. The only way to reach the write with cursor.col > line length requires the user's 'virtualedit' option to place the cursor virtually past end-of-line at entry — a state neither attacker data nor any statement in this code produces — so it is recorded as speculative, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: colnr_T/int widths behave as declared; screen columns and byte columns stay below MAXCOL for reachable lines.

set_indent()/shift_line() place the cursor on the first non-blank, as documented by this code's own comment: '// Set the new indent. The cursor will be put on the first non-blank.' — treated as a quoted contract.
mb_ptr2len/lbr_chartabsize/vim_strsave follow documented vim semantics (advance by whole characters never past NUL; strsave returns a strlen+1 copy or NULL).
ml_replace(lnum, orig_line, FALSE) takes ownership of orig_line (no double free).
limitations: Speculative OOB write: with the user option 'virtualedit' (insert/all), w_cursor.col can exceed the line length at entry; Path A ('new_cursor_col += curwin->w_cursor.col') would then propagate a virtual column into new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL, writing past the vim_strsave allocation. The precondition (cursor past end-of-line) requires a user edit-mode option, not attacker file content, so it was not instantiated.
Memory leak: if orig_line = vim_strsave(...) succeeds but 'new_line = vim_strsave(...)' fails and the early 'return' fires, orig_line is leaked — only on allocation failure, not attacker-inducible.

The replace-stack loops (replace_join(0) / replace_push) rely on the stack-depth invariant maintained by the edit loop, which is not shown; no raw attacker-derived index/size is passed at these call sites.

Insstart.col / ai_col adjustments after 'Insstart.col -= insstart_less' can land at the line's NUL slot when the indent grew; consumers of these fields are outside this code (bounded by the new line length by the shift-in-bytes argument, so no overrun was proven).

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML processes an untrusted Gopher server's response with three fully instantiated defects: (1) the bound check `gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE` permits llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, but the sink `line[llen + 1] = '\0'` then writes one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE `line` array (off-by-one out-of-bounds write, reachable in every conversion mode); (2) `port = strchr(host, TAB)` can return NULL for a telnet-type line with no third TAB, and `*port` is dereferenced unconditionally in the telnet HREF branch, crashing the proxy (remote DoS); (3) the attacker-controlled `host` field is appended raw into HREF attributes in the http://standard-link branches, enabling HTML/script injection in the page served to the browsing client.

This TensorFlow tensor-handle creation op consumes one attacker-data item (the input tensor), but it flows only through framework-typed accessors: the output dereference 'handle' is guarded in execution order by 'OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ctx->allocate_output(0, TensorShape({}), &handle));', the output is always a 1-element scalar matching the scalar()/flat() accessors used, and the dtype branch 'if (ctx->expected_output_dtype(0) == DT_RESOURCE)' matches the dtype allocate_output allocates. The two residual weaknesses — the unchecked return status of 'ctx->input(0)' and reliance on expected_output_dtype being only DT_RESOURCE or DT_STRING — have triggers that no statement in this code can produce (the dtype comes from static kernel registration, and a missing input yields a valid default tensor per the framework contract), and their worst simulated outcomes are a controlled CHECK abort or a valid-but-empty tensor in session state, neither of which is memory corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification.

assumptions: ctx->input(0), OP_REQUIRES_OK, allocate_output, AddTensor, MakeResourceHandle<Tensor>, and Tensor accessor semantics follow the documented TensorFlow framework contracts (input() returns a valid Tensor reference even on missing input, allocate_output sets an error status on failure, scalar<T>()/flat<T>() CHECK the dtype and element count) — per discipline 3 these are framework accessors, not project-internal callees.

ctx->expected_output_dtype(0) is derived from the op's kernel registration, fixed at process build; the given code contains no registration statement, so I cannot quote the set of possible dtypes — but no statement in this code derives it from graph or input data.
limitations: C1 (speculative): if this op were ever registered with a non-string/non-resource output dtype, 'handle->flat<tstring>().setConstant(tk.GetHandle(name()));' would CHECK-fail (controlled abort, DoS at most). The trigger value (a third dtype) cannot be produced by any statement in this code, and CHECK failure is an abort, not corruption.

C2 (robustness): 'const Tensor& val = ctx->input(0);' does not check the status; on a missing input a valid default empty Tensor would be stored into the tensor store under a new session id. All simulated consequences (retrieving an empty, well-formed Tensor) are handled by the framework's type system; no memory-safety, disclosure, or authorization impact could be instantiated.

verdict.summary: The shape-inference callback's only security-relevant sink, the dimension access c->Dim(c->input(0), 1), is guarded in execution order by the quoted rank check TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(0), 2, &unused));, which fails and returns before the access for every input rank other than 2 (or unknown rank, which WithRank resolves to a rank-2 shape). All other statements pass dimension handles to InferenceContext constructors with no raw indices, sizes, or pointers, so no attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect exists in this code.

Attacker-controlled index values from the `indices` input tensor are passed raw into the mutating scatter functor calls (ScatterScalarFunctor line 42-43 / ScatterFunctor line 61-62) with no bounds validation anywhere before the scatter executes; the only out-of-range check, `OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...)`, inspects the functor's return value only AFTER the functor has already run, enabling an out-of-bounds write into the resource-variable tensor `params` at an attacker-chosen index.

The only bounds-reaction, `OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...)` on the next line, executes after the scatter has already run, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds write at the attacker-supplied index. Same pattern at lines 41-44 for the scalar branch.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: the `indices` op input is attacker-controlled across the trust boundary; its element values flow via `indices_flat` (line 36) directly into the unvalidated scatter calls, with only count (line 22) and bound-width (line 29) checks — never value checks — along the path.

Dtype-mismatch CHECK-fail in `indices.flat<Index>()` is a process crash of the caller's own TF process at equal privilege; recorded as robustness, not promoted.

CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation (not shown) is assumed to validate sparse_feature_values_inputs.size() and to handle the case where num_sparse_features_with_values == 0 leaves an empty OpInputList.
The TensorFlow executor is assumed to enforce tensor dtypes against the OpDef before Compute, so example_weights_t->flat<float>() cannot be reached with a mismatched dtype.

Trigger is instantiable via graph attributes, but num_features_ has no use in the given code, so the impact chain is not instantiated. If later code indexes with num_features_, this would become CWE-190/CWE-787.

Potential dtype-confusion CHECK crash at flat<float>() relies on the framework NOT enforcing the OpDef dtype; this is an environment behavior not provable from the given code.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety defect is instantiated in this code. isor_reader_get_sample/isor_reader_get_sample_from_item set ch->sample/ch->last_state; isor_reader_release_sample releases the current sample so the stsd-reconfig 'continue' path does not refetch the identical sample indefinitely.
PROP_DATA copies the supplied buffer while PROP_DATA_NO_COPY borrows it; gf_filter_pck_get_data returns a pointer valid for the lifetime of the packet with a correct size.
isoffin_push_buffer, isoffin_configure_pid, isoffin_setup, and gf_isom_* behave as their names/contracts suggest; none of their bodies are shown.

'assert(ch->sai_buffer_size);' is the only guard before PROP_DATA(ch->sai_buffer, ch->sai_buffer_size); in release builds a non-NULL sai_buffer with size 0 is passed through — no corruption link is shown for a zero-size property, so not treated as a defect.

'isoffin_push_buffer(filter, read, pck_data, data_size)' forwards raw input-packet data and size with no validation at this call site; any defect would live in the not-shown callee, and pck_data/data_size are the accessor's own valid outputs, so the call site itself passes in-domain arguments.
The stsd-reconfig 'continue' does not decrement nb_pck, but each iteration releases and refetches a sample, bounding the loop by the sample count in the file (linear, non-amplifying).

subs_buf (PROP_DATA_NO_COPY) and finfo.moof_template are borrowed pointers set as packet properties; no free/realloc of their storage occurs in this code before the packet is sent, so no UAF link is quotable here.

verdict.summary: In callback_glewlwyd_user_auth, an attacker with any valid session cookie can bind an arbitrary attacker-supplied username into that session without any authentication or authorization of the username: the no-password branch (lines 49-53) only validates the session (get_users_for_session -> G_OK) and then calls user_session_update with the raw request-supplied username 'to set as default', and the failed-password branch (line 37) performs the same session update even after auth_check_user_credentials explicitly failed. No statement in the code verifies the username belongs to the session, enabling session takeover / authentication bypass.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing authorization check on the request-supplied username before it is bound into the session. Trigger: attacker holding a valid session cookie POSTs {"username":"admin"} with no password field; line 17's password-length test is false, line 46's else-if is false (key absent), so the refresh path runs; get_users_for_session validates only the SESSION (line 50-51), never the username, and line 53 then executes user_session_update binding the unauthenticated attacker-chosen username as the session default (per the code's own comment 'Refresh username to set as default'), with the raw cookie value passed as session id. No membership/authorization check exists on any path.

Second instantiation of the same missing-authorization defect: on a FAILED password authentication (auth_check_user_credentials did not return G_OK, and response->status is set to 401 at line 41), the code still updates the attacker's existing session (any valid cookie) with the just-rejected attacker-supplied username via user_session_update, with the only condition being that a session cookie exists — no check that the username is authorized within that session.

assumptions: user_session_update, get_session_id, get_users_for_session, auth_check_user_credentials are project-internal callees not shown; the effect of user_session_update setting the session's default/acting username is documented only by this code's own comment '// Refresh username to set as default' (line 52).
o_free tolerates NULL; session_uid is assigned on every path that frees it (lines 20-21, 37, 49, 81-82, 114-115), so no free of an indeterminate value was found.
config->session_key / cookie_domain / cookie_secure come from server configuration, treated as internal-trusted.
limitations: Log forging (CWE-117): attacker-controlled username and ip_source flow into y_log_message %s sinks (lines 28, 35, 74, 89); format strings are constants so no CWE-134, but newline injection into logs is plausible; impact depends on the not-shown y_log_message implementation, so not counted as primary.

get_ip_source/get_client_hostname may return NULL, and session_uid may be NULL if get_users_for_session(config, NULL) could return G_OK; both consequences rest on unshown callee semantics (NULL handling in y_log_message / ulfius_add_cookie_to_response) and were not instantiated.
strftime(expires, 128, ...) into expires[129] was edge-tested and is safe (max ~29 bytes for the format); no memory-safety defect found in this function.

verdict.summary: send_control_msg copies a host-sized control message of length `len` into the guest-provided iovec elem.in_sg (filled by virtqueue_pop) without ever checking that the guest-supplied destination capacity (elem.in_num segments, per-segment iov_len) is at least len. A guest can post a 1-byte device-writable descriptor on the control queue; when the host then sends an 8-byte virtio_console_control message, iov_from_buf writes past the end of the mapped destination segment — an out-of-bounds write in the host emulator process (memory corruption). The code itself acknowledges the missing check: '/* TODO: detect a buffer that's too short, set NEEDS_RESET */'.

evidence.snippet:
/* TODO: detect a buffer that's too short, set NEEDS_RESET */
    iov_from_buf(elem.in_sg, elem.in_num, 0, buf, len);
evidence.reason: Sink: iov_from_buf copies len (host-fixed, e.g. 8-byte control message) bytes into elem.in_sg, whose per-segment lengths and count (elem.in_num) are guest-controlled and never validated against len anywhere in the function. Trigger: guest posts a device-writable descriptor of length 1 on c_ivq; virtqueue_pop succeeds (in_num=1, iov_len=1); iov_from_buf writes 8 bytes into the 1-byte mapped segment, overflowing past the region end in the host process. The TODO comment is the developer's own admission that the bounds check is absent; no iov_size()/length check, clamp, or detach-on-short-buffer exists on any path.

evidence.snippet: if (!virtqueue_pop(vq, &elem)) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: virtqueue_pop fills elem.in_sg and elem.in_num from descriptors the guest placed on the control queue, making the destination capacity of the line-15 copy attacker-controlled; the surrounding checks only test pop success and queue readiness, never the popped buffer's size.

assumptions: iov_from_buf is taken per its documented QEMU semantics: it copies up to `bytes` (len) into the iovec segments without bounding the total against the iovec's aggregate capacity — the upstream fix for this exact function added an explicit `if (iov_size(elem.in_sg, elem.in_num) < len)` check before the call, confirming the helper does not self-bound and the caller must validate.
virtqueue_pop populates elem.in_sg (base pointers and iov_len) and elem.in_num from guest-written virtqueue descriptors; vser->c_ivq is the guest-configured control queue.

Callers of this static helper pass fixed host-defined lengths (e.g., sizeof(struct virtio_console_control) = 8); the content of `buf` is host-generated, so the attacker-controlled side is the destination capacity, not the source length.
limitations: Secondary (folded into the primary finding, not independent): virtqueue_push(vq, &elem, len) at line 17 reports len bytes written even if the destination was shorter, so the guest also receives a misstated byte count.
If virtqueue_pop could return true without fully initializing elem, elem would be uninitialized at line 15; its boolean success contract at line 10 is treated as reliable per the pop success check.

verdict.summary: All sinks in this op are guarded in execution order: session_state is NULL-checked with OP_REQUIRES before use, and both AddTensor and allocate_output results are consumed through OP_REQUIRES_OK failure-sentinel tests before handle is first read. The output tensor is a fixed scalar (TensorShape({})) whose dtype matches the branch condition via op registration, so scalar<ResourceHandle>() and flat<tstring>() writes are in-domain. No attacker-derived size, index, offset, or pointer reaches any memory or injection sink.

assumptions: Op registration (not shown) fixes the output dtype such that expected_output_dtype(0) is DT_RESOURCE for the V2 op and DT_STRING for the V1 op; the code relies on this for flat<tstring>()/scalar<ResourceHandle>() type agreement, otherwise an internal CHECK would abort (controlled failure, not type-confused write).
ctx->tensor_store() is non-NULL whenever session_state() is non-NULL, since both are populated together by the session-run framework; no in-code statement can produce the divergent state.
Op arity guarantees ctx->input(0) exists; enforced by the executor, not in this snippet.

MakeResourceHandle<Tensor>, TensorStore::AddTensor, and SessionState::GetNewId are internal callees whose semantics are not shown; only strings and framework handles are passed to them, no raw attacker-derived sizes/indices/pointers.

The input tensor's lifetime is deliberately extended via the tensor store; this is the op's documented purpose, not a use-after-free.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element declares `zval fname, retval;` without initializing retval, calls call_user_function_ex() to invoke __wakeup() without checking its return value, then unconditionally calls zval_ptr_dtor(&retval). An attacker-controlled WDDX packet can place an attacker-named class object (e.g. a nonexistent class resolving to __PHP_Incomplete_Class) on the stack; when that object lacks a __wakeup method the call fails without writing retval, and zval_ptr_dtor() then operates on uninitialized stack memory — reading a garbage type tag and potentially dereferencing/freeing a wild pointer (wild free / memory corruption in the host process).

evidence.reason: retval is declared uninitialized, call_user_function_ex() at line 45 is invoked with its return value unchecked, and zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) at line 48 executes unconditionally. When the attacker-created object on the stack has no __wakeup method (guaranteed reachable via a nonexistent class name in the packet, see second evidence entry), the call fails and retval keeps uninitialized stack garbage; zval_ptr_dtor reads a garbage type tag and can dereference/free a wild pointer. No initialization, return-value check, or method-existence check exists anywhere on any path.

Origin of the trigger value: the class name string comes from the attacker-supplied WDDX packet (<var name="php_class_name"><string>...</string>). When the named class does not exist, an attacker-uncontrolled-to-exist object of __PHP_Incomplete_Class is created (object_init_ex at line 79) and placed on the stack (ZVAL_COPY_VALUE at line 94); this class defines no __wakeup, so the later call_user_function_ex() for __wakeup deterministically fails, leaving retval uninitialized for the sink at line 48.

assumptions: Zend engine contract assumed for call_user_function_ex/zend_call_function: when the target method does not exist, it returns FAILURE without writing *retval. This engine behavior is not shown in the given code and is the one unquoted link in the trigger; confidence reflects this.

wddx_stack_top is assumed to return elements[stack->top - 1] and push-side handlers (php_wddx_push_element, not shown) create entries with the types this pop handler tests for (ST_STRUCT, ST_FIELD, varname from the packet's name attribute).
php_base64_decode is assumed to never return NULL (the PHP 7 implementation always returns an allocated zend_string); this is internal-callee behavior not shown in the given code.
limitations: Potential UAF/double-free: in the IS_UNDEF branch (lines 22-29), when stack->top == 1 the entry is efree'd at line 28 while stack->top stays 1, leaving a dangling elements[0] that a later pop could read and double-free. Not reported as primary: no statement in the given code produces an IS_UNDEF top entry at top==1 (UNDEF entries originate in the not-shown push handler), so the trigger could not be fully instantiated.

php_base64_decode result at line 33-36 is used via ZVAL_STR without a NULL check; a NULL-producer could not be instantiated from the given code (CWE-476 only if the callee can fail), so it is recorded as speculative.

The EL_FIELD branch (lines 120-124) pops and efree's whatever entry is on top without verifying it is a ST_FIELD entry; a stray </field> tag frees an arbitrary entry and leaks its zval. Impact is bounded memory leakage (request-scoped), not memory corruption, because the subsequent closing tag hits the stack->top == 0 guard and returns.

Ownership transfers at lines 106 and 110 insert ent1->data into a hash without a matching zval_ptr_dtor, causing refcount leaks bounded by the packet size and reclaimed at request shutdown; no attacker-scalable retention beyond the input itself.

The __wakeup invocation itself on attacker-deserialized objects is an inherent deserialization-gadget surface of WDDX, but that is a design property of the API, not a defect localized to a missing guard in this function.

verdict.summary: The OpKernel reads an attacker-supplied integer from input(0) into `index` (line 7) and passes it unchecked into `buf->Peek(index, &tuple)` (line 9) with no range or negativity validation anywhere on any path; a negative or out-of-range input tensor value (e.g. -1, becoming 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF after the size_t conversion) drives an out-of-bounds access inside the buffer's queue, whose result tuple is then exported via set_output, enabling out-of-bounds read/crash of the shared runtime process. The only related check, OP_REQUIRES(tuple.size() == ctx->num_outputs()), guards the later tuple[i] loop but not the index.

std::size_t index = ctx->input(0).scalar<int>()();

    OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, buf->Peek(index, &tuple));
evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-controlled tensor value assigned to `index` (signed int widened to size_t, so -1 → 18446744073709551615) and used directly as the position argument to `buf->Peek(index, &tuple)` with no bounds, negativity, or range check on any path in this code; the OP_REQUIRES_OK only checks the callee's return status after the harmful use. Trigger fully instantiated: attacker supplies input(0) with an out-of-range value; Peek consumes it as a raw queue position, producing an out-of-bounds read whose tuple contents are then emitted through ctx->set_output.

assumptions: Buffer::Peek's internal implementation is not shown; its call signature (`Peek(const std::size_t index, Tuple*)`) establishes that `index` is consumed as a queue position. Whether it internally bounds-checks is unquotable, and per the call-site rule the defect stands in this code either way.
ctx->input(0) is assumed attacker-reachable because it is a data-carrying parameter of a non-static OpKernel entry point; no documented precondition restricting input(0)'s range exists in this code.
limitations: If Buffer::Peek is in fact a bounds-checked accessor that returns InvalidArgument for out-of-range indices (not shown), the defect reduces to a robustness issue; however, no such contract can be quoted from the given code, so the unvalidated index passing remains the primary defect.

verdict.summary: In gf_text_get_utf8_line, the UTF-8/8-bit conversion loop writes into the fixed stack buffer szLineConv[2048] through index j, but the only loop guard (for (i=0; i<len; i++)) bounds i by the attacker-controlled line length, never j by the buffer size. In the 'non UTF8' expansion branch one input byte emits two output bytes (szLineConv[j]=...; j++; then the shared szLineConv[j]=szLine[i]; j++), so any line of >=1025 such bytes (e.g., all 0xC1) drives j past 2048, producing an out-of-bounds stack write with attacker-influenced bytes; szLineConv[j]=0 and strcpy(szLine, szLineConv) then overflow further. Trigger is fully instantiated by untrusted subtitle-file content via gf_fgets with unicode_type==0; no statement anywhere in the function bounds j, clamps it, or checks lineSize against 2048.

evidence.reason: Root cause: j (the write index into the 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv declared at line 5) is never compared against 2048 on any path; the loop bound 'i<len' caps only the input index by the attacker-controlled line length. Trigger: a subtitle line of >=1025 bytes whose high-bit bytes are each followed by a non-continuation byte (e.g., all 0xC1) takes the expansion branch, emitting two szLineConv writes per input byte (here, plus the fall-through 'szLineConv[j] = szLine[i]; j++;' at lines 53-54), so j exceeds 2048 and lines 18/53/56 write out of bounds with attacker-influenced values (0xc0|x and masked bytes). The subsequent strcpy(szLine, szLineConv) at line 57 copies the over-length string into the caller buffer, compounding the corruption. No bound, clamp, mask, or lineSize check exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: gf_fgets behaves like fgets: reads at most lineSize-1 bytes and NUL-terminates (assumed for the in-bounds read of szLine[i+1] at line 17 at i=len-1).
gf_utf8_wcstombs is a project-internal callee whose return-value semantics (including any failure sentinel) are not shown in this code; its return is consumed unchecked at line 79.
lineSize is assumed to be the true size of the caller buffer szLine; no statement in this code asserts or checks its relation to 2048.
limitations: Line 79 'szLineConv[i] = 0;' uses the unchecked return of gf_utf8_wcstombs; if the callee returns 2048 (exactly full) or a failure sentinel (e.g. (u32)-1), this is an OOB write, but the callee's return contract is not shown, so the trigger could not be instantiated from this code alone.

The UTF-16 byte-swap loop (lines 68-75) has no bound on i and relies solely on the double-NUL test at line 70; if gf_fgets fills the buffer exactly, szLine[i+1] reads one byte past the buffer and, if that stale out-of-bounds byte is nonzero, lines 71-73 write one byte past szLine. Because the triggering byte lies in memory this code never initializes, the trigger is not fully instantiated here.
If callers pass lineSize > 2048, even the non-expanding copy path (unicode_type==1) overflows szLineConv via line 53; this is the same missing j-bound as the primary finding.

verdict.summary: find_pattern_in_path() uses the unvalidated signed parameter 'len' both as the allocation size ('pat = alloc(len + 5)') and as the sprintf '%.*s' precision. With len < 0 (e.g. -1), alloc(len+5) succeeds with a 1-4 byte heap buffer while the negative precision is treated as omitted by sprintf, copying the entire NUL-terminated 'ptr' string plus the '\<'/'\>' decorations into it — a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled content. evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-data parameter len (int, line 4 of the signature) is used as the heap buffer size (alloc(len + 5)) and as the %.*s precision with no sign or range check anywhere in the function (the only guard, 'if (pat == NULL)', tests allocation failure, not size). Trigger: call with len = -1, ptr = 'A'*100, type not CHECK_PATH/FIND_DEFINE; alloc(4) succeeds, then sprintf treats the negative precision as omitted and writes 2 + 100 + 2 + 1 = 105 bytes into the 4-byte buffer — heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled bytes (also STRNCMP(startp, ptr, len) with negative len later casts to huge size_t). The missing guard 'if (len < 0) ...' was searched in all fix forms (check, clamp, mask, corrected comparison, bounds-safe helper) and appears nowhere on any path.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable vulnerability in this code. All sinks are guarded: segment indexing by the length check, array writes by the numTriggeredTopics==64 drain check, and substr bounds hold by construction since start never exceeds topic.size() on any internal path. Remaining risks (triggeredTopics overflow if drain() misbehaves, stack exhaustion from deep wildcard chains built by unshown subscribe code, and comment-acknowledged delivery of wildcard-topic messages to '#' subscribers) could not be triggered from statements in this code.

assumptions: drain() resets numTriggeredTopics below 64 (e.g., to 0) and clears the triggered flags; its implementation is not shown, and the ==64 guard at both write sites is correct only under this contract.
The initial (non-recursive) call passes start <= topic.size() and stop != npos; only recursive calls are visible in this code.
Topic nodes in the trie (children map values, wildcardChild, terminatingWildcardChild) are non-null, built by subscribe code not shown.
publish() is not invoked concurrently from multiple threads (globals numTriggeredTopics/triggeredTopics/messageId are unsynchronized).
limitations: If drain() ever left numTriggeredTopics >= 64, triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++] would write out of bounds (CWE-129/787); this depends entirely on the unshown callee and could not be instantiated.

Deep wildcard subscriptions (e.g., '+/+/+...' filters) combined with a long attacker-published topic cause recursion one frame per segment; with a ~65535-byte filter/topic this could approach stack exhaustion (DoS). The wildcardChild chain is produced by the subscribe path, which is not part of the given code, so the trigger is speculative here.

Messages published to topics containing wildcards are delivered to terminating-wildcard ('#') subscribers for each topic prefix before the lazy check aborts, as the comment acknowledges; impact analysis shows the '#' subscriber would receive the same message under any valid topic anyway, so no unauthorized disclosure or bypass results.

The single-character wildcard check does not restrict topics whose wildcard characters appear inside longer segments; such segments are literal (non-wildcard) per MQTT semantics, so this is not exploitable.

verdict.summary: InvertibleRWFunction::CalculateInverse is not vulnerable. The only attacker-influenced input, x, flows exclusively through arbitrary-precision Integer arithmetic into the fail-closed verification 'if (ApplyFunction(y) != x) throw ...', which runs immediately before the return on every path; any malformed, out-of-range, or non-residue x results in a thrown exception rather than a wrong result, memory error, or bypass. The historical CVE-2015-2141 forgery is closed by the quoted fix 'r = modn.Square(r)' inside the retry loop. No memory sinks (memcpy/fixed buffers/indices), no injection surfaces, no fail-open paths exist in the given code.

assumptions: DoQuickSanityCheck() (callee not shown) is assumed to perform key sanity checks on m_n, m_p, m_q, m_u; degenerate key material (e.g., m_n <= 1 making the Randomize range [1, m_n-1] invalid) is treated as owner-trusted key state, not attacker data.

ModularArithmetic::Square/Multiply/MultiplicativeInverse, Jacobi, ModularSquareRoot, CRT, and Integer arithmetic are standard arbitrary-precision bignum operations that cannot overflow fixed-width buffers; ModularSquareRoot of a non-residue returning a root of the negated value is caught downstream by the ApplyFunction check.
OpenMP pragmas are written in a non-standard nested form; treated as a build/compatibility concern with no security effect.
limitations: Attacker-controlled x outside [0, m_n) or not a quadratic residue mod n causes an exception (fail-closed) rather than any bypass; worst case is a rejected operation, not a vulnerability.
The do/while loop could spin only if gcd(r, n) > 1 for repeated RNG draws, which requires factoring the modulus; the trigger is not instantiable and r is independent of attacker input.
Code paths for key loading/decoding (e.g., DERDecode of the private key) are not shown; any defect there is out of scope for this snippet.

verdict.summary: xQueueGenericCreate computes the queue storage size as (size_t)(uxQueueLength * uxItemSize) where the multiplication is performed in UBaseType_t arithmetic (32-bit on standard ports) and widened to size_t only after wrapping. A caller-supplied uxQueueLength and uxItemSize whose product exceeds the UBaseType_t range (e.g. 0x40000 * 0x40000) wraps to a small value, so pvPortMalloc allocates a block of sizeof(Queue_t)+wrapped_size while prvInitialiseNewQueue records the unwrapped uxItemSize and uxQueueLength, causing out-of-bounds heap writes on every subsequent enqueue. The only overflow check is configASSERT, a compile-time-optional macro with no halting definition in this code, so no guard reaches the sink in production builds.

evidence.reason: The product uxQueueLength * uxItemSize is computed in UBaseType_t width and cast to size_t only after the multiplication (line 14), so it wraps/truncates before sizing the allocation. Trigger: uxQueueLength=0x40000, uxItemSize=0x40000 gives a wrapped xQueueSizeInBytes of 0; pvPortMalloc(sizeof(Queue_t)+0) (line 28) returns a minimal block, and line 46 passes the UNWRAPPED uxQueueLength/uxItemSize to prvInitialiseNewQueue with a zero-byte storage area, so every item write overflows the heap block. The only guard is the line-17 configASSERT, which is a compile-time-optional macro whose halting definition is not in this code, and no unconditional bounds check on the product exists on any path.

assumptions: UBaseType_t is 32 bits, as on standard FreeRTOS 32-bit ports; on 16-bit ports the wrap threshold is lower and the defect is easier to trigger.
configASSERT is defined per FreeRTOS convention in the user's FreeRTOSConfig.h and is frequently left as a no-op in production builds; the given code contains no definition that halts execution.

prvInitialiseNewQueue (not shown) stores uxItemSize and uxQueueLength as the queue's item size and length per its universally known FreeRTOS role; the defect stands at this call site regardless, since this code passes attacker-derived unwrapped sizes alongside an allocation sized from the wrapped product.
limitations: If configASSERT is compiled in and defined to halt, the line-17 check mathematically detects the overflow before allocation, blocking the trigger; this protection is configuration-dependent and not enforceable from the given code.

The out-of-bounds write itself lands in queue send/copy code outside the given snippet; the instantiated defect in this code is the wrapped product sizing the allocation at line 28 and the undersized-storage argument passed at line 46.

verdict.summary: InvertibleRWFunction::CalculateInverse performs only arbitrary-precision Integer arithmetic with no memory, copy, size, index, format, path, or command sinks. Every attacker-relevant failure path is fail-closed: the blinding loop exits only on a nonzero inverse ('} while (rInv.IsZero());'), the Jacobi-symbol adjustment branch is present for the mixed/zero cases, the OpenMP sections are barrier-separated before CRT, and the final 'if (ApplyFunction(y) != x) throw Exception(...)' verification rejects any miscalculated or out-of-domain result before it is returned. No trigger with a security impact could be instantiated from the inputs this code consumes.

assumptions: Internal callees not shown (modn.MultiplicativeInverse, modn.Square/Multiply, ModularSquareRoot, CRT, Jacobi, Integer::Randomize, ApplyFunction, DoQuickSanityCheck) are assumed to be the documented Crypto++ bignum helpers; no quote of their bodies is available in the given code.
m_p, m_q, m_n, m_u are assumed to be a coherent private key loaded by key-loading code outside this function; this function contains no statements that load or mutate them.

The caller-supplied rng is assumed to be a functioning RandomNumberGenerator; no precondition documenting this appears in the given code, but rng only seeds the blinding factor r, which is range-clamped by 'r.Randomize(rng, Integer::One(), m_n - Integer::One());'.
limitations: Degenerate key material (e.g., m_n <= 1) could make the blinding do-while loop or the Randomize range behave pathologically; no statement in this code instantiates such a key, so the trigger is speculative (key loading is not shown).

A hostile or broken RandomNumberGenerator could in principle loop if it deterministically emitted a non-invertible r; not instantiable from this code's own flow, and r is drawn from [1, m_n-1], so failure requires the RNG to hit p or q on every draw.

The fail-closed backstop 'if (ApplyFunction(y) != x)' depends on the correctness of the not-shown ApplyFunction; if that callee were itself wrong, this check would not detect it, but no evidence of that exists in the given code.

This is the post-fix Crypto++ Rabin-Williams inverse routine; the historical mixed-Jacobi-symbol miscalculation is already handled by the quoted 'if (Jacobi(cp, m_p) * Jacobi(cq, m_q) != 1)' branch, and the verification check would throw on any residual error.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow/wraparound in the bitmap-size computation: attacker-controlled width/height parsed from '#define' lines (guint, up to 2^32-1 via negative %d values) flow unchecked into size = bytes_per_line * hh (32-bit unsigned product) and then into g_malloc(size). The only guard, if (!ww || !hh), rejects zero only. A crafted XBM (e.g. width 8, height -2) makes size wrap to -2, so g_malloc receives a sign-extended ~2^64-byte request and the process aborts (g_error), an attacker-induced denial of service; a wrap to a small positive value instead returns a buffer far smaller than the returned *width/*height describe, a heap-overflow precursor for the consumer.

evidence.snippet:
size = bytes_per_line * hh;
		bits = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: bytes_per_line (int, from attacker width) is multiplied by hh (guint, attacker height, e.g. (unsigned int)(-2) = 4294967294 from a '#define ..._height -2' line) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic; the wrapped result is assigned to int size with no range check on any path (if (!ww || !hh) only rejects zero) and passed straight to g_malloc. Instantiated trigger: width 8 + height -2 + 'static unsigned char bits[] = {' gives bytes_per_line=1, size = -2, g_malloc(0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE) fails and g_error aborts the process parsing the attacker's file.

Origin of the tainted values: value is parsed from an attacker-supplied file line via sscanf(line,"#define %s %d",...) and cast to guint without any range validation, so ww and hh can each reach 2^32-1 (e.g. -2 -> 4294967294); these feed the overflowing multiplication at line 87.

assumptions: MAX_SIZE is a fixed macro; since line and name_and_type are both char[MAX_SIZE], the %s length analysis (token <= MAX_SIZE-9 after the strlen(line) == MAX_SIZE-1 rejection) holds for any value.

next_int() is not shown; the code's own guard 'if ((value = next_int (fstream)) < 0)' treats a negative return as failure, and any non-negative return is truncated to unsigned char before storage, so its internals cannot cause memory corruption here.
g_malloc aborts on allocation failure and returns NULL only for size 0 (documented GLib semantics); 'if (!bits)' catches the size-0 case.
int/guint are 32-bit with two's-complement wrap on the int assignment (mainstream compiler behavior).
limitations: Consumer-side heap overflow: when the product wraps to a small positive value (e.g. bytes_per_line=0x4000 with hh=0x40001 gives size=0x4000), the function returns a 16KB buffer together with *width/*height describing a bitmap orders of magnitude larger; the out-of-bounds read/write would occur in the caller's rendering code, which is not given, so this impact link is not instantiated here.

NULL out-parameters: *width/*height/*data are dereferenced unconditionally (lines 117-119) while x_hot/y_hot are NULL-checked; a NULL out-param is a caller programming error with no trust-boundary content, recorded as robustness only.

Transient allocation of up to ~2GB (e.g. ww=2, hh=2147483647, 'static unsigned char' header gives bytes_per_line=1, size=0x7FFFFFFF) from a ~60-byte file — bounded by INT_MAX; memory-exhaustion amplification folded into the primary finding.
version10p loop under-fills by one byte per line when padding=1 (bytes advances 2 per iteration but only 1 byte is written at line ends) — a data-layout correctness issue, not memory safety.

Refuted: an odd size in the version10p loop (which would cause a 1-byte overflow via 2*ceil(size/2) writes) is impossible — bytes_per_line is provably always even in that branch (padding=1 adds 1 to an odd (ww+7)/8; padding=0 forces ww%16 in {0,9..15}, making (ww+7)/8 even).

verdict.summary: parse() trusts every offset, index, and count field of a caller-supplied ELF file. e_shoff/e_phoff/e_shstrndx/e_shnum/e_phnum and section sh_offset/sh_name are used directly as pointer offsets and indices into an mmap of the file with no bounds check against st.st_size, producing deterministic out-of-bounds reads (crash/disclosure) and, at strcpy(&name[15 - 6], "[...]"), an out-of-bounds write whose destination pointer name = elf_map + shstrtab.sh_offset + shdr[i].sh_name is fully attacker-controlled. Additionally, dynamic/dynstr are uninitialized stack ints used as section indices whenever the file has no '.dynamic'/'.dynstr' section, and count = sh_size/sizeof(Dyn) drives an attacker-scalable OOB read loop.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink. name is elf_map + shstrtab.sh_offset + shdr[i].sh_name (line 183), both offsets raw 32/64-bit file fields with no bounds check anywhere; the only guard here, strlen(name) > 15, bounds the string LENGTH, not the pointer location. Trigger: a crafted ELF whose shstrtab.sh_offset/sh_name place name outside the mapped file; strlen then reads out of bounds, and strcpy writes "[...]"+NUL (6 bytes) at name+9, an attacker-chosen address — memory corruption primitive.

Primary out-of-bounds read. e_shoff, e_phoff, e_shstrndx are raw file fields used as offsets/indices into the mmap with no validation against st.st_size or e_shnum; e.g. a 64-byte file with e_shoff=0x7FFFFFF0 makes shdr point ~2GB past the 1-page mapping and shstrtab = shdr[e_shstrndx] reads unmapped memory. No guard on any path; only fd/fstat/MAP_FAILED are checked.

verdict.summary: This is the fixed form of TensorFlow's SparseDenseBinaryOpShared Compute. Every attacker-controlled index reaching the dense-side gather is bounds-checked: `if (!FastBoundsCheck(idx[d], rhs_ref.dimension(d)))` flags failure and `OP_REQUIRES(ctx, indices_valid, ...)` returns before `rhs_ref.coeff(idx)` executes on every iteration and every branch, so no out-of-domain access is reachable. Shape/rank consistency (indices columns vs sp_shape length, rank 1-5, dense-broadcast-only compatibility via VecGreaterEq && b.IsValid, nnz-sized allocations) is enforced by quoted checks, and the integer-division-by-zero path is guarded by the quoted `dense_gathered_flat(i) != 0` check when the op is a Div. Remaining items are speculative or crash-only and are recorded in notes.

assumptions: FastBoundsCheck(value, limit) implements 0 <= value < limit (TensorFlow core utility with documented semantics); it therefore rejects negative and >=-limit indices, including idx = -1 and idx = INT64_MAX.

Eigen's broadcast TensorRef coefficient access maps an output index within the broadcast dimension to the input index by modulo of the input dimension, so `rhs_ref.dimension(d)` is exactly the domain consumed by `rhs_ref.coeff(idx)`.

Tensor dtypes of the inputs match the op's registration (T for sp_values, int64 for sp_indices/sp_shape); this is enforced by the TensorFlow op framework before Compute runs, not by statements in this code.
`TensorShape(shape_vec)` accepts non-negative dims; its behavior on negative or overflow-producing dims is internal and not shown, so no claim about a crash there is instantiated.
`internal::SubtleMustCopy` returns the copied value unchanged (it only forces a load); all sanitization is done by the FastBoundsCheck guard that follows.
limitations: Width confusion candidate: nnz is int64_t but the gather loop uses a 32-bit counter (`for (int i = 0; i < nnz; ++i)`). With nnz >= 2^31 the counter overflows to a negative value, producing an out-of-bounds read via `indices_mat(i, d)` (~17 GB before the buffer) and potentially an out-of-bounds write via `dense_gathered_flat(i)`. Not promoted: the trigger requires roughly 40 GB of attacker-supplied tensors to be successfully allocated (sp_indices >= 17 GB plus nnz-sized values, output, and temp allocations all succeed first) — an environmental resource precondition no statement in this code produces — and the impact beyond a same-process crash requires the wild negative address to land on mapped, security-relevant data, a link that is neither quotable in this code nor characterizable. Realistically the outcome is a SIGSEGV of the process executing the attacker's own model; recorded as a robustness/width defect, not a primary vulnerability.

Crash-only candidate: sp_shape containing negative or element-overflowing dimension values reaches `TensorShape(shape_vec)` (and the `BCast` machinery) before any validation; if those internals CHECK-fail, the process aborts. The failing behavior lives entirely inside a callee not shown, and the characterizable impact is a crash at equal privilege with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification — not instantiated as a vulnerability here.

The sticky `indices_valid` flag (declared before the nnz loop) only causes over-rejection: once any row sets it false, subsequent otherwise-valid rows also fail with InvalidArgument. This is spurious-error behavior, not a security defect; the guard still fires before every `rhs_ref.coeff(idx)` use.

verdict.summary: The MPEG video demuxer's partial-start-code accumulation uses a fixed 8-byte window on ctx->hdr_store (`memcpy(ctx->hdr_store + ctx->bytes_in_header, start, 8 - ctx->bytes_in_header)` and the 8-byte `mpgviddmx_next_start_code(ctx->hdr_store, 8)` scan, plus `ctx->hdr_store[current+3]` with current up to 7), but nowhere in this function is hdr_store guaranteed to be allocated or to hold at least 8-11 bytes at that point. hdr_store is only grown on the reaggregation and VOS-accumulate paths, whose sizes are derived from packet sizes and can be smaller than 8; the loop-top `if (remain<5) memcpy(ctx->hdr_store, start, remain)` and the copy_last_bytes `memcpy(ctx->hdr_store, start+remain-3, 3)` write into hdr_store with no allocation check at all (it can still be NULL on the first tiny packet). An attacker supplying the demuxed stream can drive a heap out-of-bounds write of up to 7 attacker-controlled bytes past a small hdr_store allocation.

evidence.snippet:
if (ctx->bytes_in_header) {

			memcpy(ctx->hdr_store + ctx->bytes_in_header, start, 8 - ctx->bytes_in_header);
evidence.reason: Unguarded fixed-size accumulation into ctx->hdr_store: the copy writes 8 - bytes_in_header (up to 7) bytes at offset bytes_in_header (up to 4), requiring >= 8 allocated bytes, but no statement on any path in this function allocates or verifies hdr_store to that size before this point — the only growth paths (reaggregation prologue and the VOS/VOL EOS accumulate) size hdr_store from packet sizes that can be < 8. When hdr_store was never allocated (first packet < 5 bytes hits `if (remain<5) memcpy(ctx->hdr_store, start, remain)` with hdr_store == NULL) this is a NULL write; when allocated smaller than 8 it is a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled stream bytes. The 8-byte fixed store is a buffer size miscalculation (CWE-131) with no enforcing guard anywhere.

Origin of the defect: this path stores up to 4 bytes into ctx->hdr_store and sets bytes_in_header up to 4 without ever allocating or size-checking hdr_store; on the first packet hdr_store is NULL, and thereafter hdr_store_size/alloc are not updated, so the later 8-byte accumulation copy (evidence 1) operates on an unallocated or undersized buffer.

assumptions: gf_m4v_parse_frame/gf_m4v_parse_config return sizes within the current buffer; the code only 'guards' size vs remain with asserts (compiled out in release), so `memcpy(pck_data, start, size)` and `start += size; remain -= size` would read out of bounds if the parser overreports — callee not shown, trigger not instantiable here.
gf_filter_pck_new_alloc returns a correctly sized buffer of (u32)size for the memcpy of size bytes — standard container semantics.
mpgviddmx_next_start_code returns an index within the scanned length or negative; used consistently with that contract.
limitations: size/remain mismatches after gf_m4v_parse_frame rely on the not-shown parser honoring the buffer bounds; if violated, further OOB reads occur at `memcpy(pck_data, start, (size_t) size)`.

asserts (assert(remain>=size), assert(ctx->resume_from <= ctx->hdr_store_size), assert(remain>=current)) are the only protection on several pointer advances and are compiled out in release builds; no independent trigger was instantiated for those invariants in this code's own flow.

The NULL-write variant (hdr_store never allocated when the first packet is <5 bytes) is a crash of the demuxer process; the heap OOB write variant requires a multi-packet sequence producing a small (<8 byte) hdr_store allocation, which is reachable via the packet-size-derived allocation expressions but depends on interleaving of the accumulate paths.

verdict.summary: The Example::Initialize function sizes num_examples from the attacker-fed example_weights tensor but never validates the length of the independently attacker-fed example_labels tensor before indexing it in the per-example loop, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (example_labels(example_id)) whenever the labels tensor is shorter than the weights tensor.

evidence.snippet:
example->example_weight_ = example_weights(example_id);
    example->example_label_ = example_labels(example_id);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: example_id iterates 0..num_examples-1, where num_examples = example_weights.size() (line 46), but example_labels comes from a separate input tensor (line 48) whose size is never checked against num_examples anywhere in the code; a labels tensor smaller than the weights tensor makes example_labels(example_id) read past the end of the labels buffer.

Origin of the tainted value: example_labels is fetched as an independent attacker-controlled tensor with no size validation (unlike sparse_example_indices at line 11, sparse_feature_indices at line 19, and example_weights at line 39), and flows directly to the unguarded indexed access at line 65.

assumptions: CreateSparseFeatureRepresentation, CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation, and ComputeSquaredNormPerExample are internal callees whose bodies are not shown; their behavior (including whether CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation validates dense_features_inputs.size() against num_dense_features) is assumed, not verified.

num_sparse_features/num_sparse_features_with_values/num_dense_features are graph/kernel attributes; treating them as attacker-data in a malicious-graph scenario is an assumption about the threat model, though no documented precondition constrains them in this code.
limitations: num_features_ = num_sparse_features + num_dense_features (line 6) can overflow signed int only with ~INT_MAX-scale attribute values, and num_features_ is consumed only in code not shown — impact not instantiated here.

dense_features_inputs (line 52-53) is not size-checked in this code against num_dense_features, but the list is consumed inside CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation (not shown); if that callee indexes it unvalidated the defect would be there, but the harmful use is not in the given code.
example_labels_t->flat<float>() on a non-float tensor would CHECK-fail inside Eigen (crash of the op process only, no corruption).

The OOB-read values are written into example_label_ and would influence subsequent training computations in the not-shown update path; the primary security impact claimed here is the heap OOB read itself.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability: array indexing is bounded by the quoted loop guard and UBYTE-width component count, memset lengths match their allocations, and the only unguarded precondition (unchecked AllocMem return) requires non-attacker-inducible allocation failure.

assumptions: m_pEnviron->AllocMem is assumed either to throw/abort on failure or to return a valid pointer; its semantics are not shown. If it can return NULL on failure, both memsets (lines 11 and 16) dereference the unchecked result.
m_pFrame->ComponentOf(i) is assumed to return a non-NULL Component for every i in [0, m_ucCount); the callee is not shown. If it can return NULL, comp->SubXOf() at line 20 dereferences it.
UpsamplerBase::CreateUpsampler is assumed to return a valid pointer or throw; a NULL return would be stored into m_ppUpsampler[i] and dereferenced later in code not shown.
m_ucCount is assumed consistent with the frame's actual component count (set in code not shown); within its declared UBYTE width the code's own bounds are safe either way.
sizeof(struct Line *) == sizeof(class UpsamplerBase *) == sizeof(class Upsampler *) as pointer types; the type-name mismatch between lines 15 and 16 is therefore benign.
limitations: Candidate C1 (unchecked AllocMem result, CWE-476): the guard is genuinely absent (lines 10-11 and 15-16 check only the member's prior NULL-ness, never the returned pointer), but the trigger requires allocation failure. Allocation sizes are bounded by the UBYTE component count to at most ~16KB, so an attacker cannot force OOM through input; the failure is environment-induced and the impact is only a crash of the decoding process itself, with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification. Recorded as a robustness limitation, not a vulnerability in this code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable memory writes are guarded: the column-0 index b is validated by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, b > -1 && b < N, ...)' immediately before 'sparse_handles_t(b) = handle;' on every path, the gap-fill loop's own bound 'for (int64_t b = 0; b < N; ++b)' bounds its writes, and the output-copy loops are bounded by 'i < num_entries' and 'd < rank' against tensors sized {num_entries, rank-1} and {num_entries}. InputSt.IndicesValid() additionally runs before any index is consumed. Remaining issues (negative dims masked by a zero dim reaching TensorShape, int truncation of rank at >=2^31-element shapes, and O(N) gap-fill work decoupled from input size) are trigger-instantiable but their impact chains depend on unshown callee behavior or are by-design contract work, so they are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: SparseTensorsMap::AddSparseTensor and SparseTensor::Create are assumed to return a failure Status on invalid arguments rather than crash; their internal behavior is not shown in the given code.
GetMap with OP_REQUIRES_OK is assumed to either return a valid map pointer or an error Status; no NULL map dereference path is reachable from the given statements.

Attacker model: tensor content (indices, values, shape) of the op inputs is treated as attacker-controlled per discipline 4; deployment reachability (e.g., remote serving) is not assumed for impact claims.
limitations: Shape vector {0, -k} (zero first dim masking a negative later dim) passes the overflow-detection loop because 'MultiplyWithoutOverflow(0, -k) == 0' is not < 0; the negative dim then reaches 'TensorShape tensor_input_shape(input_shape_vec);' whose behavior for negative dims is not shown. If TensorShape CHECK-fails on negative dims (TF's typical behavior), this is an input-triggered process-abort DoS; if it accepts, TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape later rejects it cleanly. Impact not characterizable from given code.

Similarly, a shape vector longer than TF's maximum dimension count reaches the same TensorShape constructor with no rank cap in this function; any crash depends on unshown TensorShape limits-checking.

'int rank = input_shape->NumElements();' and 'for (int i = 0; i < input_shape_vec.size(); i++)' use int against int64 sizes; wraparound requires feeding >=2^31 shape-vector elements (tens of GB), so the trigger is not practically instantiated.

The gap-fill loop performs O(N) map insertions where N = sparse_shape[0] is decoupled from input size (empty indices allowed), but the op's contract requires producing N handles and first allocates an 8*N-byte handle tensor, so this is by-design work with constant-factor overhead (borderline CWE-400, not a defect in this code).

'MultiplyWithoutOverflow(new_num_elements, input_shape_vec(i))' result is truncated to int; some products >INT_MAX truncate to non-negative ints and are not flagged. Harmless here because new_num_elements is never consumed downstream (only the overflow flag is), but the check is not a reliable shape validator.

verdict.summary: Both attacker-controlled 'index' attribute reads are range-checked in execution order against the correct context bound (num_inputs/num_outputs, reject-side '<=' verified at edges index=-1, 0, bound-1, bound), and every indexed use of that index occurs after its check on the only path. Failure sentinels of GetNodeAttr and MakeShapeFromShapeProto are tested before their results are used, and 'resource' pointers are NULL-tested before dereference. No fully instantiated defect exists in the given code.

assumptions: InferenceContext::input/set_output/input_handle_shapes_and_types/set_output_handle_shapes_and_types index their per-input/per-output arrays sized by num_inputs()/num_outputs() — assumed standard TensorFlow semantics, not shown in this snippet.
AddNodeInternal (not shown) constructs node_context from the node's declared inputs; its exact behavior is an assumption.
_Arg/_Retval ops are assumed to have one output/one expected input per TensorFlow op registration, code not shown.
limitations: Speculative C1: for the kRetvalOp branch, node_context->input(0) and node_context->input_handle_shapes_and_types(0) use literal index 0 with no check that node_context->num_inputs() > 0; if an attacker-supplied function body could contain a _Retval node with an empty input list AND AddNodeInternal builds a zero-input context AND InferenceContext::input() only DCHECKs (release no-op), this would be an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Trigger preconditions all lie in code not given, so it is not a confirmed vulnerability here.
Speculative C2: CHECK_NOTNULL(GetContext(node)) aborts if AddNodeInternal succeeded but did not register a context — an internal-inconsistency crash, not attacker-instantiable from the shown flow.

CHECK macros in this code (CHECK_NOTNULL) abort the process on malformed models loaded by the operator; if models from untrusted clients are processed by a shared server this is at most a robustness/DoS consideration outside what the shown statements instantiate.

verdict.summary: SparseFillEmptyRowsOpImpl validates only ranks/row-counts of its input tensors but never checks that indices' second dimension matches dense_shape's length, nor that dense_shape's element values are non-negative, before passing the raw tensors into functor::SparseFillEmptyRows. An attacker-supplied indices matrix with fewer columns than dense_shape's rank (or a negative dense_shape entry) passes every quoted OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC check and reaches the functor, causing an out-of-bounds read / invalid memory access in the host process. The code's own TODO comment admits the missing shape checks.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC(context,
                       FunctorType()(context, default_value_t, indices_t,
                                     values_t, dense_shape_t, done),
                       done);
evidence.reason: Sink: the functor is invoked with attacker-controlled tensors (indices_t, values_t, dense_shape_t) whose mutual consistency is never validated. Concrete trigger: indices_t = matrix [3,2], values_t = vector [3], dense_shape_t = vector {5,4,3} passes all checks at lines 20, 24, 28, 33, 39, 45 (none compares indices_t.dim_size(1) to dense_shape_t.NumElements() nor validates dense_shape values), so the functor indexes indices(i, d) for d up to 2 — past the 2-column indices matrix — producing a heap out-of-bounds read; negative dense_shape entries likewise reach the functor's row/index arithmetic unvalidated.

Origin of the defect: the developer comment explicitly concedes the missing consistency checks ('add shape checks between values, indices'); the only additional check present (dense_shape_t.NumElements() != 0) rejects merely empty shapes, not rank mismatches or negative shape values, so the attacker-supplied inconsistency reaches the functor call unguarded.

assumptions: The internal functor::SparseFillEmptyRows consumes indices along the dense rank implied by dense_shape's length and uses dense_shape's element values for output sizing/indexing; this is the op's defining contract, and per the analysis rules the defect is attributed to this call site because this wrapper is the trust-boundary intake point and passes out-of-domain arguments with no validation on any path.
limitations: The precise faulting statement inside functor::SparseFillEmptyRows is not shown; severity is derived from the characterizable out-of-bounds read rather than a quoted in-functor access.
The 'dense rank > 0' TODO item is effectively covered by the combination of IsVector(dense_shape_t.shape()) and NumElements() != 0, so no separate finding was raised for it.

verdict.summary: All attacker-supplied metadata (dims shape, length, tensor rank) is validated by quoted, execution-ordered OP_REQUIRES guards before the vec<bool>() access and the rank dispatch switch; every reachable rank is handled, so no memory-safety, bounds, or fail-open defect exists in this code.

assumptions: The dtype of the 'dims' input is constrained to DT_BOOL by the op registration (not shown); this code itself performs no dims.dtype() check. Even without that constraint, vec<bool>() reads dim_size(0) <= 8 bytes from a buffer holding dim_size(0) elements of at least 1 byte each, so access stays in bounds regardless of dtype.

HandleReverseCase<Device, T, NDIMS> is an internal callee not shown; it is assumed to consume the validated dims map of exactly NDIMS == input_dims elements and the OP_REQUIRES_OK-checked output pointer.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK macros return from Compute on failure, which is the standard TensorFlow contract.
limitations: Candidate: missing dims.dtype() == DT_BOOL check before dims.vec<bool>() could allow a non-bool tensor to be reinterpreted as bool, producing garbage axis-reversal flags and (if the framework also lacked the dtype constraint and Tensor::base's dtype CHECK) at worst a crash of the caller's own process. No out-of-bounds access is reachable because the number of bytes read never exceeds the buffer size; impact is incorrect computation at equal privilege, so it is recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability in this code.

The switch has no default arm; if a hypothetical rank outside 0..8 passed the quoted 'input_dims <= 8' guard, Compute would return without setting output 0. Rank is a non-negative int and rank > 8 is rejected before the switch, so this path is unreachable as written.

verdict.summary: The per-channel calibration loop iterates i in [0, depth) where depth = input_max.NumElements() is attacker-controlled, and indexes transposed_input.chip<0>(i) without any check relating depth to input's last dimension; when depth exceeds that dimension the chip reductions read past the end of the input tensor buffer, and the OOB-derived min/max values are disclosed through the output_min/output_max tensors. A second manifestation of the same missing-bound class: input_min_data[i] is guarded only by input_min.dim_size(0) == depth rather than NumElements, so an input_min of shape [depth, 0] passes validation and yields an out-of-bounds/NULL read at the scale computation.

evidence.snippet: const size_t depth = input_max.NumElements();
evidence.reason: Origin of the unvalidated bound: depth is taken solely from the attacker-controlled input_max tensor's element count and is never related to the shape of input.

Out-of-bounds read: transposed_input.dimension(0) equals input's LAST dim (input.flat_inner_dims<qint32>() then shuffle({1,0})), but the loop bound is depth from input_max.NumElements(). With input shape [2,5] and input_max shape [8], i=5..7 make chip<0>(i).minimum()/maximum() read past the end of the input tensor buffer; the OOB-derived values flow via ranges[i] and out_min_max into output_min->flat<float>()(0) and output_max->flat<float>()(0). The only shape checks (input_min.dim_size(0)==depth, input_max.dim_size(0)==depth) constrain other tensors and cannot prevent this.

evidence.snippet:
float scale =
          std::max(std::abs(input_min_data[i]), std::abs(input_max_data[i]));
evidence.reason: Guard/quantity mismatch: input_min_data[i] is read for all i < depth, but the validating statement checks input_min.dim_size(0) == depth, not input_min.NumElements(). An input_min of shape [depth, 0] passes the check with zero elements, so input_min_data[i] reads out of bounds of the flat buffer (or dereferences the null/empty-buffer pointer), and the read value reaches the output through scale, ranges[i], and out_min_max.

assumptions: Eigen's Tensor chip/minimum/maximum reductions perform no release-mode bounds check on the chip index, per standard Eigen semantics (universal known library behavior).
Tensor::flat<T>().data() returns a pointer to the tensor's raw buffer of NumElements()*sizeof(T) bytes, so indexing beyond NumElements() is out of bounds.

The op's input tensors (content and shapes) cross a trust boundary: a graph/session can construct or dynamically reshape these tensors, and the kernel itself validates some shape relations, proving shapes are runtime variables.
limitations: Wrong dtype for input (non-qint32-compatible) or input_min/input_max (non-float), or input rank < 2, triggers CHECK failures inside Tensor::flat/flat_inner_dims — a crash-only path with no corruption (robustness/DoS).
If input_min's shape is [depth, 0], data() may be nullptr, in which case candidate 2 manifests as a NULL dereference (CWE-476 crash) rather than an OOB read; the defective use site is unchanged.
On LLP64/MSVC targets 1L << 31 overflows a 32-bit signed long (UB, yielding a negative divisor and incorrect ranges) — a correctness issue only, no memory-safety effect.
The MSVC OpenMP branch omits reduction(max:out_min_max) and is_non_negative is written unsynchronized; both are benign data races on monotonic/float scalars with no memory-safety consequence.
If all per-channel ranges are zero, out_min_max is initialized to std::numeric_limits<float>::min() (smallest positive normal), a minor calibration inaccuracy, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled argv/argv_eol index accesses in this 352 (WHOREPLY) handler are guarded by quoted argc comparisons with correct operators in execution order (argc < 8 early return; argc > 8; argc > arg_start+1/+2 ternaries), and the malloc/snprintf host-building is exactly sized. The only residual gap, the uncorrected '+ 1' on a possibly empty hopcount token at 'pos_hopcount = (argc > arg_start + 1) ? argv[arg_start + 1] + 1 : NULL;', requires the not-shown IRC message parser to emit an empty argv token, which no statement in this code produces or quotes, so its trigger is speculative.

assumptions: IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) behaves as the standard WeeChat macro (returns on argc < min); it is subsumed for all uses by the explicit 'if (argc < 8) return WEECHAT_RC_OK;' guard.
argv/argv_eol element indexing convention (which argv slot maps to which 352 parameter) is taken as given; only bounds matter and all bounds are guarded by quoted argc checks.

irc_channel_search/irc_nick_search/irc_nick_set_host/irc_msgbuffer_get_target_buffer semantics are not shown and are assumed to handle strings safely; this code passes them only in-bounds, non-NULL-guarded strings.
WeeChat's IRC message parser (not shown) determines argv tokenization; no statement in this code produces an empty argv element.
limitations: Speculative: 1-byte out-of-bounds read via 'pos_hopcount = (argc > arg_start + 1) ? argv[arg_start + 1] + 1 : NULL;' (line 30) if argv[arg_start+1] is an empty string; the index itself is bounds-checked, but the '+1' has no emptiness check. Trigger requires the unshown parser to emit an empty token (e.g., from a double space or empty trailing) — an internal-callee behavior that cannot be quoted here, so the trigger is not instantiated. Note the sibling ':' branch is protected by 'if (argv[arg_start][0] == ":")' before its '+1', showing the asymmetry.

Speculative: 'length = strlen (argv[4]) + 1 + strlen (argv[5]) + 1;' truncates into int only for ~2GB parameters; even then snprintf's size argument (the same malloc length) bounds the write, so no corruption primitive is reachable.

Unchecked strdup/malloc results (str_host is checked; ptr_nick->realname = strdup (pos_realname) is not) only fail on allocation failure not inducible by the attacker; degradation, no security impact.

verdict.summary: The only in-code attacker-data memory access (the Opt_name validation loop reading param->string[i]) is provably bounded by the quoted, execution-order-correct guards `if (!param->size)`, `if (param->size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1)`, and `i < param->size`. Other attacker values (release_agent path, source, subsys name) are only stored or compared here; their harmful consumption lies in code not given, and the remaining candidates (negative signed char into isalnum, NULL string via VFS contract violation, subsys_mask width, log forging via key) have triggers or impacts that cannot be instantiated from this code, so they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: fs_parse (not shown) is assumed to honor the kernel fsparam_string contract: for `opt == Opt_name` / `opt == Opt_release_agent`, `param->string` is non-NULL and `param->size == strlen(param->string)`; this code cannot quote that contract and its own flow never produces a NULL string with size > 0.
`cgroup_no_v1_named` is a boot parameter assumed false (default); its declaration/value is not in the given code.

`MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN` and the width of `ctx->subsys_mask` are defined in headers not shown; the name-length guard is internally consistent because the same macro governs the downstream buffer, but that buffer is not in the given code.
`param->key` is assumed non-NULL per VFS parse_param contract (unquotable here).
limitations: `char c = param->string[i]; if (isalnum(c))` passes a raw signed char to isalnum; an attacker-supplied name byte >= 0x80 becomes a negative non-EOF argument, outside isalnum's documented domain (undefined behavior, potential out-of-bounds read of the kernel ctype table). No unsigned-char cast, mask, or range check exists anywhere in the given code, but the actual OOB depends on the unshown kernel __ismask/_ctype implementation, so the impact could not be instantiated; a one-line `(unsigned char)c` cast would remove the concern.

`ctx->release_agent = param->string;` stores an unvalidated path with no capability or content check; historically this option feeds a call_usermodehelper execution path in cgroup release handling. That execution occurs entirely in code not given and no statement here passes the value into a memory, copy, or indexing operation, so no impact link could be quoted.

`ctx->subsys_mask |= (1 << i);` can truncate the bit for i >= 16 if the mask type is narrower than the number of compiled-in subsystems; both the mask width and CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT are outside the given code, and the effect is configuration-dependent correctness, not memory safety.

param->key containing a newline could forge the `invalfc(fc, "Unknown subsys name '%s'", param->key)` log line (CWE-117), but reaching this path requires a cgroup mount attempt whose privilege posture is not shown, so the trigger is not instantiated.

A NULL `param->string` with `param->size > 0` would NULL-deref inside the name loop, but only if the VFS/fs_parse contract for string parameters is violated; this code's own statements cannot produce that state.

verdict.summary: pgpPrtParams consumes an attacker-controlled packet blob, but every memory-facing use is channeled through decodePkt(p, (pend - p), &pkt), which receives a provably in-domain (pointer, exact remaining length) pair guarded by the loop condition p < pend in execution order; parsing failure and any over-advance of p both fail closed to rc = -1. All remaining candidates (out-of-range blen, zero-advance infinite loop, uninitialized pkt fields) can only be triggered by behavior of the internal callees decodePkt/pgpPrtPkt, which are not shown and therefore cannot serve as trigger producers for this code.

assumptions: decodePkt (project-internal, not shown) parses one packet from (buf, len) without reading past len and sets pkt.head == p and pkt.body/pkt.blen consistently on success; this contract is unquotable from the given code.
pgpPrtPkt consumes pkt.body/pkt.blen within the buffer and tolerates the digp value passed; pgpDigParamsNew accepts any pkt.tag value.
pkts/pktlen form a self-consistent buffer+length pair supplied by the caller (interface contract); only the buffer CONTENT is attacker data.
limitations: If the unshown decodePkt can succeed while setting pkt.blen beyond the remaining buffer, pgpPrtPkt would read out of bounds and p += (pkt.body - pkt.head) + pkt.blen would skip past pend; the trigger (a decodePkt bug) is not instantiable from the given code, so this is recorded as speculative.

If decodePkt can return success with (pkt.body - pkt.head) + pkt.blen == 0, the while (p < pend) loop would never terminate (CWE-835/400); per PGP packet grammar at least the tag byte is consumed, and decodePkt's actual behavior is an unshown-callee assumption.

The return value of pgpDigParamsNew is not NULL-checked; on allocation failure digp stays NULL and pgpPrtPkt(&pkt, NULL) is invoked. This is reachable only via allocation failure (fixed-size allocation), so it is a robustness issue, not an attacker-triggerable vulnerability.

The given listing already contains the historical rpm mitigation for signature-packet parsing (if (pkttype == PGPTAG_SIGNATURE) break;), matching post-CVE-2021-3521 upstream code; the historical overflow itself lived in the not-shown callee chain (decodePkt/pgpPrtPkt), not in the statements given here.

verdict.summary: The kernel entry validates tensor ranks and dense_shape non-emptiness, then delegates all element-level consumption to functor::SparseFillEmptyRows, which is not shown. Cross-tensor consistency checks (indices row count vs values length; index values vs dense_shape elements) are absent — the code's own TODO admits this — but every candidate's out-of-bounds impact would occur inside the unshown functor, so no impact link is characterizable or instantiable from the given code.

assumptions: functor::SparseFillEmptyRows is project-internal and not shown; its indexing behavior, buffer sizing, and preconditions are unknown and cannot be quoted, so no impact chain can be continued past `FunctorType()(context, default_value_t, indices_t, values_t, dense_shape_t, done)`.
OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC is the standard TF macro that invokes the done callback and returns on failure; taken as known framework semantics.
context->input(n) is assumed to return a valid (possibly empty) Tensor per TF framework contract; empty shapes are rejected by the IsMatrix/IsVector/IsScalar rank checks.
limitations: Missing cross-tensor validation, admitted by the code itself (`// TODO(ebrevdo): add shape checks between values, indices,`): indices_t.dim_size(0) is never checked against values_t.NumElements(), and index element values are never checked against dense_shape_t elements. If the unshown functor derives a loop bound from indices_t and indexes values_t, or sizes a scratch buffer from dense_shape_t and indexes it with index values, an attacker-supplied input (e.g., a 2x1 indices matrix with a 1-element values vector, or an index >= the corresponding dense_shape element) reaches the functor call with all rank guards passing, producing a heap out-of-bounds read/write in code not given. Trigger input is fully instantiated; impact is not, so this is not confirmable from the given code (would be CWE-125/CWE-787 at the functor, CWE-20 at the missing check site).

The TODO also notes a missing check that dense rank > 0; a rank-0 dense_shape vector passes `dense_shape_t.NumElements() != 0` only if nonempty, but degenerate sizing consequences again land in the unshown functor.

verdict.summary: In gst_flxdec_chain, the FLX_FRAME_TYPE branch computes the payload length as the unsigned subtraction flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize without verifying flxfh.size >= FlxFrameChunkSize. The only guard, 'if (avail < flxfh.size) goto need_more_data;', compares adapter availability with flxfh.size and is bypassed by any undersized attacker-supplied chunk header (size < 12 while avail >= 12), causing the subtraction to underflow to ~4.29 billion. gst_adapter_take then returns NULL (or a short buffer), which is immediately dereferenced via FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS ((FlxFrameType *) chunk) and ((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks, crashing the decoder process — a denial of service triggered by a malicious FLX file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-controlled flxfh.size (from the FLX frame chunk header) is subtracted from FlxFrameChunkSize without a lower bound; when 0 <= flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize the guard 'if (avail < flxfh.size)' (line 105) is trivially true-passed (avail >= 12 >= flxfh.size), the guint subtraction underflows to a huge value, gst_adapter_take returns NULL for the oversized request, and the result is dereferenced unconditionally at line 113/114 — NULL dereference / out-of-domain size at this call site. Trigger fully instantiated: attacker file supplies id=FLX_FRAME_TYPE, size=2.

assumptions: FlxHeaderSize, FlxFrameChunkSize, FlxFrameTypeSize are the standard FLX constant sizes (header 128, frame chunk 12); gst_adapter_take returns NULL when fewer than the requested bytes are available (documented GStreamer semantics); width/height in FlxHeader are 16-bit fields so width*height fits in guint (65535*65535 < 2^32), ruling out the allocation-overflow variant.
limitations: If flxh->depth > 8, flxdec->converter is never created (creation gated on 'if (flxh->depth <= 8)'), yet flx_colorspace_convert (flxdec->converter, ...) is called unconditionally — a NULL-converter call for a crafted deep-depth header; crash lands inside the unshown callee and is not simulated here as a primary.

Bounds handling inside flx_decode_chunks and flx_colorspace_converter (not shown) may contain further overflows with the attacker-derived chunk count and payload pointer; cannot be analyzed from this snippet.
The underflowed size could be a heap-buffer-size primitive rather than NULL if gst_adapter_take semantics differed; treated as NULL-deref DoS per documented take() behavior.
