verdict.summary: The capacity check for the fixed 64-entry triggeredTopics array runs only once at publish() entry; the per-segment loop and the tail can each append a topic pointer via triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++] with no re-check, so a single published topic matching more than (64 - numTriggeredTopics) untriggered nodes writes Topic* pointers out of bounds past the array, corrupting adjacent memory in the broker process.

Second unguarded write of the same counter: after the loop exhausts all segments of an exactly-matched topic, this tail append has no capacity check on any path, so when the loop's appends have already brought numTriggeredTopics to 64, this write lands at triggeredTopics[64] — the concrete one-past-end write in the simulated trigger.

The only capacity enforcement in the code: it establishes the array capacity of 64 and is correct in variable, unit, and operator, but its execution position (once per publish call, before the segment loop) is what the sink requires it to violate — a single publish call can append more than the remaining capacity across its loop iterations and tail without this check ever re-running.

assumptions: triggeredTopics is a 64-element array (inferred from the quoted 'numTriggeredTopics == 64' check and its comment); drain() resets numTriggeredTopics (callee not shown) — not required for the trigger, which needs only the entry check to be bypassed by per-loop increments.

The initial (non-recursive) call passes start=0, stop=npos; the code's own recursion (line 36) passes stop+1 <= topic.size(), so find/substr at lines 9-10 never receive out-of-domain positions (computed maximum start == size, which both accept).

limitations: Exponential call amplification via the wildcardChild recursion (line 36): each loop iteration spawns a recursive call that rescans remaining segments, so a wildcard-child chain of depth k against a k-segment topic yields ~2^k calls (CWE-400); requires a deep '+ '-subscription trie whose construction is not shown, so the trigger precondition could not be fully instantiated from the given code alone.
Deep recursion stack exhaustion likewise depends on wildcard-child chain depth in the unshown trie.
The entry check uses '== 64' rather than '>= 64'; this only matters after the primary overflow has already occurred and is not an independent defect.

assumptions: Eigen coeffRef on an Eigen::Map performs unchecked raw indexing (data[col*rows + d]) in release/TF builds; this is standard documented Eigen semantics per discipline 3.

out_backprop_mat.coeffRef(d, out_index) on the read side is in-bounds because out_index is bounded by the b/r/c loop bounds against the matrix size out_cols*out_rows*out_batch; this was verified, not assumed.
limitations: num_elements_in_pooling_cell (lines 96-97) can overflow int64 or become 0 when a very negative start is used, causing Inf/NaN to be written, but this has no effect beyond the OOB write already reported (division only executes inside the same loops).
A start value larger than the clamped end (e.g., seq[0]=in_rows) causes the inner loops to skip, producing no write and no denial of service.

verdict.summary: DecodeImageAPNG reads fcTL chunk fields at fixed offsets up to chunk.p+33 (png_get_uint_32/png_get_uint_16/chunk.p[32]/chunk.p[33]) without validating that the file-declared chunk.size is at least 34 bytes; a truncated fcTL chunk (e.g., length field 4 => 16-byte heap buffer) causes a heap out-of-bounds read of up to ~18 bytes, a memory-safety violation reachable by any crafted APNG/PNG file.

evidence.reason: Sink: fixed-offset reads of up to chunk.p[33] from a heap buffer whose size is the attacker-controlled chunk length field. The only size check in the function (chunkIHDR.size == 25, line 39) covers IHDR only; no statement checks chunk.size >= 34 for fcTL, and the range checks at lines 153-155 run after the reads and constrain the values, not the buffer extent. Trigger: file with valid signature, IHDR(size 25, w=h=1), then an fcTL chunk with length field 4 (buffer of 16 bytes): line 143 reads p[16..19] OOB, lines 144-149 read up to p[33] — heap out-of-bounds read.

Origin of the tainted value: read_chunk fills chunk.p/chunk.size from raw file bytes (size = declared length + 12, as proven by chunkIHDR.size == 25 for the 13-byte IHDR data). The only guard applied before the fcTL field reads is a non-NULL assert on chunk.p; chunk.size is never validated against the fixed offsets 12..33 later consumed at lines 142-149.

assumptions: read_chunk (not shown) is assumed to allocate exactly chunk.size bytes at chunk.p and to accept chunks of arbitrary declared size/type; this is corroborated by the given code itself (chunkIHDR.size == 25 for 13-byte IHDR data, type bytes at p[4..7], data at p+8, and a generic isAbc/processing_data branch for arbitrary chunk types), but its exact minimum-size and error behavior cannot be quoted.
processing_start/processing_finish/processing_data are not shown; the trigger assumes processing_start returns false (success) for a syntactically valid IHDR so the chunk loop is entered (line 60).
cMaxPNGSize is referenced but not defined in the given code; its numeric value is unknown.
limitations: Integer overflow: 'rowbytes = w * 4' and 'imagesize = h * rowbytes' (lines 53-54, 32-bit unsigned int) and the 'x0 + w0 > w' wraparound (line 154) could yield OOB access via the frame copy loop, but only if cMaxPNGSize >= 2^30 — the bound cannot be quoted, so this trigger is speculative.

fdAT branch: 'png_save_uint_32(chunk.p + 4, chunk.size - 16)' (line 181) underflows for chunks smaller than 16 bytes, planting a huge pseudo-length later consumed by processing_data; the over-read would occur inside the unshown callee, and the size<16 window may be excluded by read_chunk's unshown minimum.
'isAbc(chunk.p[4..7])' (lines 187-188) and 'memcpy(chunk.p + 8, "IDAT", 4)' (line 182) need chunk.size >= 8/12 respectively; safe only if read_chunk guarantees a minimum chunk size.
'delete[] chunkIHDR.p' (line 209) may free an uninitialized pointer if the first read_chunk fails before assigning chunkIHDR.p (CWE-457 / invalid free) — depends on unshown read_chunk error handling.
Memory leaks on early-return paths (e.g., JXL_FAILURE at line 84) are not treated as security findings.

verdict.summary: In the IRC 352 (WHO reply) handler, when argv[8] equals "*" the code sets arg_start=9 and immediately reads argv[arg_start][0] without first checking argc > 9. A server sending a 352 numeric with exactly 9 space-split tokens and a literal "*" in the flags position makes the handler read argv[9] — one past the last argument — and dereference it, crashing the client (NULL-terminated split array yields a NULL-pointer dereference; DoS from a malicious server).

evidence.snippet:
arg_start = (strcmp (argv[8], "*") == 0) ? 9 : 8;
        if (argv[arg_start][0] == ':')
evidence.reason: The guard `if (argc > 8)` only guarantees argc >= 9, i.e. argv[8] is the last valid element. When argv[8] == "*", arg_start becomes 9 and `argv[arg_start][0]` reads argv[9] — beyond the argc-bounded argument array — before any of the later `argc > arg_start` checks (lines 24-25, 30-31) execute. Trigger fully instantiated by server-controlled input: the raw line `:s 352 me #c u h srv n *` produces argc = 9 and argv[8] = "*", so argv[9] is the NULL terminator and dereferencing it crashes the user's client (remote denial of service). The missing guard is a bounds check of argc against arg_start before line 21, which appears nowhere on any path.

assumptions: argv/argv_eol are the space-split tokens of the raw IRC message (argv[0] is the prefix, argv[1] the numeric) and argc is the token count, inferred from the handler's own indexing (argv[3]=channel, argv[4]/argv[5]=user/host, argv[7]=nick, argv[8]=flags); the split routine is not shown.

The split array is NULL-terminated at index argc (standard WeeChat string-split semantics), so the out-of-domain argv[9] slot holds NULL and the crash is a NULL-pointer dereference; if it were not NULL-terminated the defect would instead be a heap out-of-bounds pointer read/dereference (CWE-125) — the defect at line 21 stands either way.
limitations: Potential integer overflow of `int length` (strlen sums) would require a single IRC message with >2GB tokens, which no statement in this code can produce; not exercised.
strdup of pos_realname returning NULL on allocation failure only yields a NULL display field with no security effect.
Impact is a crash/DoS of the user's client triggered by server data; no memory WRITE primitive was found in the simulated trigger.

verdict.summary: This scatter-update kernel contains the full set of guards for its attacker-derived inputs: the element count is bounded to the Index type before the truncating cast ('N_big <= std::numeric_limits<Index>::max()'), params' first dimension is bounded to Index's range so the functor's row-domain check '[0, params->dim_size(0))' is representable, the division/remap sink is covered by 'if (N > 0)' plus the StartsWith shape-prefix check executed before updates.shaped({N, num_updates / N}), and the scatter functors' index validation is both documented by this code's error message and post-checked via 'OP_REQUIRES(c, bad_i < 0, ...)' on both branches. No reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect was instantiated; the remaining candidates rely on the not-shown functor internals violating their documented contract and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The functor contract is documented in this code by the error message 'indices... is not in [0, params->dim_size(0))' returned when bad_i >= 0: ScatterScalarFunctor/ScatterFunctor return a negative sentinel on full success and the flat position of the first out-of-range index otherwise, without writing at an out-of-range row. The 'params->dim_size(0) <= std::numeric_limits<Index>::max()' guard exists precisely to keep that domain representable in Index.
Kernel registration (not shown) constrains the indices tensor dtype to match the Index template parameter; indices.flat<Index>() would otherwise be a dtype mismatch, not a raw reinterpretation.
LookupResource sets the out-param only on an OK status, which OP_REQUIRES_OK checks before v->tensor() is dereferenced.
limitations: On CPU, the scatter functor may apply earlier in-bounds updates to the resource variable before returning bad_i, so a failing op can leave the variable partially mutated; this is callee-internal (loop order not shown), writes stay in bounds, and the attacker could write those same valid values with a legitimate op, so it is not a security impact.

The DIV-by-zero validation ('ValidateInput<T>(updates)') runs only for isCPUDevice, so GPU scatter-div by zero produces inf/NaN in params instead of an InvalidArgument error; this is a numerical/behavior divergence with no memory-safety consequence.

The error-path reads 'indices_flat(bad_i)' and 'SliceDebugString(indices.shape(), bad_i)' rely on the functor returning bad_i < N when bad_i >= 0; if the not-shown functor ever returned an out-of-range bad_i this would be an OOB read on the error path, but no statement in the given code can produce such a value.

Rank arithmetic 'indices.dims() + params->dims() - 1' could in principle overflow int only at absurd ranks far beyond any framework-supported tensor rank; not triggerable on this code's actual input surface.

verdict.summary: qtm_decompress performs the match-run copy on the window-wrap path (match_offset > window_posn) without any check that window_posn + match_length <= qtm->window_size. match_length and match_offset are fully attacker-controlled via decoded symbols (selector 6), and the only clamp (lines 112-113) exists solely on the non-wrap branch, so an attacker-crafted Quantum stream writes past the end of the heap-allocated window buffer (out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-influenced content), and window_posn += match_length can itself advance past window_size.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the wrap-path copy writes match_length bytes starting at window[window_posn] with no bound on window_posn + match_length versus qtm->window_size; the quoted guard at line 98 bounds only j (the read offset), not the write extent, and the clamp that does bound writes (lines 112-113) is on the else branch only. Instantiated trigger: attacker decodes literals until window_posn = window_size - 2, then a selector-6 match with match_length = 5 and match_offset = window_size + 2 gives j = 4 (passes the line-98 check), and the runs at lines 105/108 write window[window_size], window[window_size+1] and window[window_size+2] — out-of-bounds heap writes with attacker-decompressed content.

Origin of the tainted values: match_length and match_offset are computed directly from symbols and bit-fields decoded out of the attacker-controlled compressed stream; no range check is applied to either before they reach the unguarded copy sink at lines 105/108.

assumptions: QTM_GET_SYMBOL / QTM_READ_BITS decode attacker-controlled bits from the compressed input stream into sym/extra/selector (standard Quantum-format decoding; the stream contents are attacker data since this function is the decompressor of an untrusted file).

QTM position_base/extra_bits tables permit offsets at and beyond window_size (required by the format's offset encoding); exact table constants live in a header not shown, but the trigger only needs match_offset = window_posn + j with small j >= 1 and match_length >= 3, both trivially representable.
qtm->window is a heap buffer of exactly qtm->window_size bytes allocated by the setup code (not shown).
limitations: Speculative: if QTM_FRAME_SIZE could exceed qtm->window_size, the literal write window[window_posn++] (line 59) would also be out-of-bounds because frame_end is clamped only against frame_start + QTM_FRAME_SIZE (lines 47-49), never against window_size; the constant relation is not given, so this is recorded, not counted.

Speculative: after window_posn += match_length (line 116) exceeds window_size on the clamped else branch, qtm->o_end = &window[window_posn] (line 120) stores an out-of-bounds pointer; exploitation requires later reads through o_ptr/o_end, which are partially guarded by the frame-alignment error return (lines 124-127). Same missing invariant as the primary finding.
Minor: the input re-alignment loop 'do { QTM_READ_BITS(i, 8); } while (i != 0xFF);' (line 131) consumes unbounded attacker input up to file end; bounded by input size, recorded as low-impact.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety, injection, authz, or fail-open sink is reachable with an instantiated impact chain. The asymmetric type check (input2->type unverified) causes only in-bounds value misinterpretation; the unchecked negation of model-controlled zero_point is signed-overflow UB whose wrapped value feeds only arithmetic inside a not-shown callee; the silent no-op for non-quantized input1 leaves output untouched but its consumer is not in this code.

assumptions: QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp (internal, not shown) is assumed to always write its out-params; its behavior for scale <= 0 is unverified.
The TFLite interpreter is assumed to pass non-NULL tensors and to dispatch this quantized kernel only for appropriate types; neither contract is documented or asserted in this code.

reference_ops::ComparisonWithScaling / BroadcastComparison4DSlowWithScaling semantics (shape matching, output sizing) are not shown and treated as internal-trusted callees receiving tensor-derived (not raw attacker offset/size) arguments.
limitations: C1 (speculative, not a vulnerability here): model-controlled params.zero_point == INT32_MIN makes '-input1->params.zero_point' (lines 4-5) signed-overflow UB (CWE-190); the wrapped offset only feeds fixed-point arithmetic in a not-shown callee with no memory/index sink, so no security impact is instantiated.

C2 (correctness only): line 3 checks input1->type but never input2->type, so GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) reinterprets a mismatched-type buffer; since every tensor element is >= 1 byte and the shape reflects the true element count, all reads stay in bounds — wrong comparison values, no OOB access.

C3 (impact not instantiated): if input1->type is neither uint8 nor int8 the function silently returns without writing output (uninitialized/stale tensor, CWE-457), but the consumer of the output tensor is outside this code and the dispatch contract is not shown.

C4 (speculative): no NULL check on input1/input2/output; a NULL tensor can only arrive via interpreter behavior not produced by any statement in this code, and the result would be an equal-privilege in-process crash with no corruption.

verdict.summary: net_bind frees the addrinfo list with freeaddrinfo(servinfo) while the loop-exit pointer ptr still references a node in that list, then calls getsockname(fd, ptr->ai_addr, &ptr->ai_addrlen) and net_port_get/net_address_get on the freed memory — a use-after-free write/read on the normal successful bind path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: freeaddrinfo(servinfo) frees the addrinfo node that ptr (set by the loop's break) points to, including its ai_addr buffer; no copy, deferral, or reallocation exists anywhere on the path. Trigger: any successful bind (loop reaches 'break' with fd >= 0 and ptr non-NULL) executes freeaddrinfo and then getsockname writes the bound sockaddr (16/28 bytes) into the freed heap buffer and overwrites the freed ai_addrlen — heap use-after-free write; net_port_get/net_address_get subsequently read the same freed memory.

assumptions: net_port_get and net_address_get are internal callees not shown; they are assumed to read the sockaddr they are passed, which is itself freed memory on this path.
freeaddrinfo frees the whole list including ai_addr buffers (POSIX semantics), making ptr dangling.
limitations: Secondary: &ptr->ai_addrlen is size_t* while getsockname expects socklen_t* (type/width mismatch, harmless on LP64 in practice since getsockname reads the length first); subsumed by the primary UAF.
close(fd) at the error label may see fd == -1 only if the loop never opened a socket and ptr != NULL, which cannot occur; no security impact.
*port is a data-carrying parameter but is only consumed via snprintf(strport, sizeof(strport), "%hu", *port), which bounds it.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled data reaches a memory, size, index, or injection sink without a quotable guard. Port formatting is bounded by snprintf with sizeof(strport); the getaddrinfo/getsockname results are length-checked against the destination union before use; fd lifecycle has no double-close or use-after-free path.

assumptions: cfg_getstr(cfg_getsec(cfg,"general"),"bind_address") and the "ipv6" bool are operator/admin configuration, not attacker-supplied data across a trust boundary.

net_port_get() and net_address_get() (project-internal, not shown) safely consume &naddr; this code's own guard 'naddr_len > sizeof(naddr)' bounds the filled structure before those calls, and net_address_get is passed sizeof(addr) matching its INET6_ADDRSTRLEN destination.
getaddrinfo/getsockname standard semantics per discipline 3: outputs are well-formed addrinfo/sockaddr structures with consistent lengths.
limitations: close(fd) on the error path may be called with fd == -1 when socket() failed on the last loop iteration — a benign failed close, no security effect.
setsockopt SO_KEEPALIVE/SO_REUSEADDR/IPV6_V6ONLY failures skip addresses silently; robustness only.
If the internal helpers net_port_get/net_address_get mis-handle naddr beyond the checked length, that defect would reside in the not-shown callee; this code passes in-domain arguments.

verdict.summary: This Reverse-op kernel consumes two attacker-controlled tensors but validates every value it passes to the only memory-touching sink: 'dims' must be a rank-1 vector (TensorShapeUtils::IsVector check), must have exactly as many elements as input has dimensions (input_dims == dims.dim_size(0)), and rank is capped at 8 (input_dims <= 8) so the fully enumerated switch (cases 0-8) always matches with an exact-size bool vector and a same-shape output; the scalar path never reads 'dims', and allocate_output is status-checked via OP_REQUIRES_OK. The remaining theoretical triggers (reversal of tensors with a zero-size non-first dimension, or a non-bool 'dims' dtype) require behavior inside the not-shown HandleReverseCase callee or an external op-def type contract, so they are not instantiated vulnerabilities in this code.

assumptions: The op registration constrains input 1 ('dims') to dtype DT_BOOL; this contract is external to the shown code, and Tensor::vec<bool>() itself CHECKs dtype and aborts (crash-only) if violated.

HandleReverseCase<Device, T, NDIMS> (not shown) consumes the passed dims.vec<bool>() map of exactly NDIMS booleans and the output tensor allocated with input.shape(); no statement inside that callee is visible, so its internal behavior is assumed consistent with the in-domain arguments this code provably supplies.
context->input(0) and context->input(1) return valid tensors per the framework contract for this non-optional-input op.
limitations: Candidate (dismissed): an input with a zero-size non-first dimension (e.g. shape [2,0] with dims [true,true]) passes all quoted checks and reaches HandleReverseCase with 0-element tensors; any out-of-bounds would occur entirely inside the not-shown callee/Eigen, which receives in-domain arguments (vector size == NDIMS == rank, output shape == input shape), and Eigen's reverse assignment iterates only the output's (empty) range — no OOB is instantiated in this code.

Candidate (dismissed): a non-bool 'dims' tensor reaching dims.vec<bool>() cannot be produced by this code's own flow (op-def dtype contract); if it occurred, the result is a CHECK abort in vec<bool>() — a controlled crash with no corruption.

Candidate (dismissed): switch fallthrough leaving 'output' unwritten for rank > 8 — blocked by the quoted OP_REQUIRES(context, input_dims <= 8, ...) which returns Unimplemented before the switch; rank 0 goes to the scalar branch.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived inputs (tensor shapes, indices, dense values) flow only into project-internal callees (ValidateIndices, MakeSplits, WriteSplits, WriteValues) whose behavior is not shown; no memory, copy, indexing, injection, or security-state sink exists in the given code. The one unguarded arithmetic statement (dim_size(0) - 1 can underflow to -1 when the first nested_splits tensor has zero rows) has no in-code sink, so its impact cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: ValidateIndices, MakeSplits, WriteSplits, and WriteValues are project-internal functions whose implementations are not shown; their bounds handling, memory safety, and return semantics are assumptions.

The contract `DCHECK_GT(params_nested_splits_in.size(), 0); // Enforced by REGISTER_OP.` is taken at face value as a documented precondition enforced by op registration; DCHECK is a no-op in release builds, but the comment documents enforcement outside this code.
SPLITS_TYPE is assumed to be a signed integer type (e.g., int32/int64), making `dim_size(0) - 1` at dim_size 0 evaluate to -1 rather than wrapping.
limitations: Potential signed underflow: `SPLITS_TYPE num_params = params_nested_splits_in[0].dim_size(0) - 1;` yields -1 when the attacker supplies a first nested_splits tensor with dim_size(0)==0; no guard exists in this code, but num_params is consumed only by the not-shown ValidateIndices callee, so whether -1 causes out-of-bounds behavior (vs. all indices being rejected, fail-closed) cannot be determined from the given code.

All actual bounds computation and value copying (MakeSplits, WriteValues) occur in callees not shown; if those functions mishandle the attacker-derived indices_in, params_dense_values_in, or value_slices, the vulnerability lives there and this code fragment cannot confirm or refute it.

verdict.summary: MklRequantizePerChannel never checks that the min/max vector length (depth) matches the input tensor's channel dimension, so an attacker-chosen mismatch between input shape [N,H,W,C] and min_vec size D passes all quoted guards and feeds a D-element scales vector to mkldnn's per-channel reorder (mask 2), which indexes scales by channel up to C — an out-of-bounds heap read whose leaked floats are multiplied into the readable output tensor. Separately, input_requested_min/max are read with flat<float>()(0) with no non-emptiness check, so an empty tensor crashes the process executing the untrusted graph.

evidence.snippet:
mkldnn::primitive_attr reorder_attr;
      reorder_attr.set_output_scales(2, scales);
evidence.reason: Sink: mask 2 selects per-channel scaling indexed by the input's channel count (input.dim_size(3) after TFShapeToMklDnnDimsInNCHW), but scales is sized only from depth = input_min_vec.NumElements(). No check anywhere relates depth to the channel dim, so with input [1,2,2,64] and min/max vectors of length 16, the reorder reads scales[16..63] past the 16-float heap buffer; the OOB floats scale the attacker-readable output tensor (heap info disclosure). With empty min/max vectors depth==0 passes every quoted guard and every channel lookup is OOB.

evidence.snippet: size_t depth = input_min_vec.NumElements();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted count: depth is taken solely from the attacker-controlled min vector; the subsequent OP_REQUIRES checks compare each vector's dim_size(0) to this same value (self-consistency) and never to input.dim_size(3).

Unguarded element-0 access on an attacker-shaped tensor: with requested_min (and identically requested_max, lines 14-16) of shape [0], NumElements()==0 and the TensorMap read at index 0 dereferences a null/zero-length buffer, crashing the process executing the attacker's graph (remote DoS). No emptiness check exists on any path, and these reads run before even the input.dims()==4 check.

assumptions: Op registration constrains input tensor dtype to qint32 and requested_min/max dtypes to float, so flat<qint32>()/flat<float>() type CHECKs are not attacker-triggerable here.

mkldnn's per-mask output-scale semantics (scales indexed by the masked dimension's extent) is the documented behavior of the external library; whether mkldnn additionally validates the scales count at primitive creation is not shown or quotable, so the call site at line 51/82/91 is treated as the defect per callee rule.
limitations: Depth > INT_MAX (int i loop counter vs size_t depth) requires an ~8 GB min_vec tensor and yields at most an uncaught std::bad_alloc — no amplification beyond the input's own size; not treated as a vulnerability.
requested_min == requested_max == 0 produces inf/NaN scales and garbage output but no memory-safety effect.

If mkldnn's ReorderPd creation does validate scale-count vs channel count, the mismatch would throw mkldnn::error and be converted fail-closed by the catch block; the confirmed empty-tensor read (CWE-476) stands independently.

verdict.summary: The i2c md command handler parses attacker-supplied console arguments but every memory- and index-sensitive sink is guarded: argv accesses are protected by argc checks, the chip offset length by 'if (alen > 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;', the stack buffer linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] by the clamp 'linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;', and the device pointer by an 'if (ret) return' check after i2c_get_cur_bus_chip. The do/while loop terminates because linebytes equals min(nbytes, LEN) and strictly decreases nbytes. No unguarded sink reachable from the command's input surface was found.

assumptions: The globals i2c_dp_last_chip/addr/alen/length are assumed zero-initialized statics (definition not shown); zero is in-domain for all of them, and they are only rewritten at the end of this function from validated values.
get_alen(argv[2], DEFAULT_ADDR_LEN) is assumed to return its result as a value comparable as uint; the quoted guard 'if (alen > 3)' catches any -1/UINT_MAX error sentinel as well.
DISP_LINE_LEN is assumed >= 1 (header constant not shown); loop termination argument depends on it.
Behavior of internal callees i2c_get_cur_bus_chip, i2c_set_chip_offset_len, dm_i2c_read, i2c_read is not shown; this code passes only in-domain arguments (alen <= 3, linebytes <= DISP_LINE_LEN).
limitations: Resource consumption: 'length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL)' with a huge value (e.g. ffffffff) makes the do/while loop perform ~2^32/DISP_LINE_LEN I2C reads. Work is exactly proportional to the explicitly requested dump length and is the documented function of 'i2c md'; the console operator is the issuing party, so this is command semantics, not attacker-amplifying consumption (CWE-400 dismissed).

chip and addr are passed unvalidated to internal i2c functions; any out-of-bounds consequence would occur inside callees not shown and this code passes no out-of-domain argument to them (chip is by definition a free-form I2C device address).

On the CMD_FLAG_REPEAT path, alen and length are loaded from i2c_dp_last_* globals without re-validation; the stored values were validated by the same guard in a prior invocation (or are zero initially), so no trigger value can be instantiated.

verdict.summary: AutoParallel::Initialize indexes each apply-gradients node's input list with a hard-coded per-op position (e.g., 9 for ApplyAdam) from the gradient_pos table, but never checks the node's actual input_size(). A malicious GraphDef (GrapplerItem) containing an apply-gradients node with fewer inputs causes input(idx) to read and mutable_input(idx) = ... to write past the end of the repeated field's heap storage — out-of-bounds read and out-of-bounds write in the process optimizing the attacker-supplied graph.

evidence.reason: Root cause: gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] (up to 9) is used as a repeated-field index with no input_size() check. Trigger: attacker-supplied item.graph with node op="ApplyAdam" and input_size()=1 — line 67 reads input(9) out of bounds (heap OOB read whose garbage string is copied into the new div node) and line 70 writes through mutable_input(9) out of bounds (heap OOB write of div_node->name()). No bounds, clamp, or error check on input_size() exists anywhere in the function.

Origin of the taint: any node in the attacker-controlled GraphDef whose op() string matches the apply-gradients set is registered (by name only, with no arity validation) into apply_gradients_nodes_, feeding the unbounded index use at lines 67/70.

assumptions: AddNodeDivConst/AddNodeDiv/IsDequeueOp/ComputeTransitiveFanin and NodeName are TensorFlow-internal helpers not shown; they are assumed to allocate/find/parse per their signatures. The two ComputeTransitiveFanin results are checked with TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR.
item.MainVariables() is assumed to return non-null NodeDef pointers; only its emptiness is checked (line 11).
Protobuf repeated-field accessors input(i)/mutable_input(i) only DCHECK the index; in release builds an out-of-range index performs a raw out-of-bounds read/write.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: NULL dereference of dequeue_node at line 104 — unreachable when dequeue_node == nullptr because input_nodes is only filled inside 'if (dequeue_node)' (line 84), making the loop body at line 103 unreachable; construction guard verified.
Candidate dismissed: gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] default-constructing 0 on a missing key — the 11 map keys exactly match the 11 set members, so the lookup always hits.
Unchecked return of AddNodeDivConst (line 48) could in principle be NULL, but no statement in this code produces that failure value; speculative only.

verdict.summary: njs_await_fulfilled consumes only one trust-boundary value (the resolved promise value, a well-typed njs_value_t) which flows exclusively into fixed-width, type-safe copies and a JS function call. All VM frame/level state mutations are provably restored by the unconditional restore block executed before every post-interpreter exit, and each path frees the async context at most once. Potential issues (unchecked vm->top_frame->function->context and ctx->await dereferences, scope write at ctx->index, context leak on the memory-error path) depend on values produced by code not shown or on allocation failure, so no trigger is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) is assumed to return a pointer to a valid njs_value_t (undefined sentinel) when nargs <= 1; this is the documented njs helper contract, not shown in the given code.

ctx, ctx->await, ctx->index, ctx->pc, and ctx->capability are assumed valid and in-domain: they are produced by njs_vmcode_await / the promise job scheduler, which are not shown; no statement in the given code creates or validates them.

njs_function_call on ctx->capability->resolve/reject is assumed not to synchronously execute queued promise reaction jobs; if it did, the subsequent njs_async_context_free could be a use-after-free, but promise-job semantics (discipline 3 well-known behavior) queue reactions instead.
The bytecode operand behind ctx->index is assumed to be compiler-generated (operator-supplied script), not attacker-supplied data.
limitations: The memory-error early-return path ('if (njs_is_memory_error(vm, &vm->retval)) { return NJS_ERROR; }') returns without calling njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx), leaking the async context and its suspended frame; triggerable only under VM memory exhaustion, not attacker-instantiable here, so recorded as a robustness/leak concern, not a vulnerability.

No NULL or validity check exists in this fragment for vm->top_frame->function->context, ctx->await, or ctx->index; a NULL/dangling context would crash the VM. The producer of these values is outside the given code, so the trigger is speculative.
njs_async_context_free and njs_function_call are not shown; their exact free/copy semantics are assumed per standard njs behavior.

verdict.summary: InferShapesForFunctionSubNode reads node_context->input(0) for a _Retval node without ever checking that the node/context has at least one input. An attacker-supplied graph (SavedModel/GraphDef) containing a _Retval node with zero inputs passes the only checks present (the 'index' attr is validated only against outer_context bounds) and reaches an out-of-bounds read at line 52, whose garbage ShapeHandle pointer is then dereferenced by ShapeHandleToProto.

evidence.reason: The sink node_context->input(0) is invoked with no check of node_context->num_inputs() anywhere in the function. Trigger: attacker-provided function graph contains a '_Retval' node (type_string check at line 34 matches) with zero inputs; AddNodeInternal builds a context with num_inputs()==0; the 'index' guard at lines 42-46 validates only index against outer_context->num_outputs(), so the call reaches line 52 and indexes an empty input vector — out-of-bounds read whose garbage ShapeHandle is dereferenced by ShapeHandleToProto.

assumptions: outer_context is built by trusted refiner machinery; its num_inputs()/num_outputs() are internal, and the index guards at lines 14 and 42 are verified correct (operator <= is the right bound, correct variable and unit).

InferenceContext::input(0) on a context with zero inputs performs an unchecked container index in release builds (its DCHECK is compiled out); this rests on universally known vector-indexing semantics, not shown code.
The behavior of the internal accessor input_handle_shapes_and_types(0) (line 57) for an out-of-range index is not shown in this code.
limitations: CHECK_NOTNULL(GetContext(node)) on line 4 could abort the process, but GetContext reads internal refiner state just populated by AddNodeInternal on line 3; no attacker-instantiable trigger was identified beyond loading the model itself, so this is robustness-only.

The secondary candidate at line 57 (input_handle_shapes_and_types(0) with zero inputs) likely bounds-checks internally in the real implementation and returns nullptr, but that callee is not shown; the primary defect at line 52 stands independently.

verdict.summary: SetUnknownShape consumes the attacker-controlled index output_port by passing it to GetUnknownOutputShape(node, output_port) as the very first statement, before the only validation in the function (the bounds check 'output_port < 0 || output_port >= ctx->num_outputs()') and before the context NULL check execute. A negative or too-large output_port therefore reaches the callee unvalidated; per the call-site rule the defect is here, producing an out-of-bounds index access / crash in the host process processing the untrusted data. The later check correctly guards only the subsequent ctx->set_output(output_port, shape) use, not the earlier one.

evidence.reason: Root cause: use-before-validation of output_port. The sink at line 3 passes the raw, attacker-controlled index output_port to GetUnknownOutputShape unconditionally as the function's first side-effecting statement; the only bounds guard ('if (output_port < 0 || output_port >= ctx->num_outputs())') and the ctx NULL check appear at lines 5-8, i.e., strictly AFTER the first use in execution order. Instantiated trigger: SetUnknownShape(node, -1) (or any port >= num_outputs) executes GetUnknownOutputShape(node, -1) with the out-of-domain index before the check at line 8 can reject it, causing an out-of-bounds index access / crash in the process consuming the untrusted data.

evidence.snippet: Status SetUnknownShape(const NodeDef* node, int output_port) {
evidence.reason: Trust-boundary origin: output_port is a data-carrying index parameter of a non-static entry point (declared int, so negative values are representable); its content is caller-controlled and no documented, quotable precondition constrains it at entry, making it attacker-data per the attacker model.

assumptions: GetUnknownOutputShape is not shown; its characterization as an indexed per-output lookup consuming output_port rests on its signature and name (it returns the ShapeHandle for output #output_port). Per the call-site rule, the defect at the call site stands even though the actual out-of-bounds access would land inside the callee, but the exact in-callee access is unquoted.
The caller of this non-static function may be an internal graph-conversion path processing an attacker-supplied GraphDef; the code itself is treated as the last line of defense for output_port.
limitations: NULL-dereference candidates for 'node' inside GetContext/GetUnknownOutputShape were not instantiated: both callees are not shown, and this code passes no provably out-of-domain pointer beyond possibly-NULL, with no quotable caller contract either way.

The value 'shape' returned by GetUnknownOutputShape on an error/missing-context path is produced by a not-shown callee and stored via ctx->set_output; no in-code statement demonstrates it can be an invalid handle, so this is not a confirmed defect.

The precise in-callee impact of the out-of-range index (out-of-bounds read vs. immediate crash) cannot be quoted from the given code; either way it constitutes an attacker-reachable memory-safety/DoS defect at the call site, hence severity medium rather than high.

verdict.summary: The op builds TensorSlice requests (start/length for dimension 0) purely from attacker-controlled row_remapping values (min_old_row/max_old_row, lines 25-34 and 117-127) and passes them to tensor_slice.SliceTensorShape() and reader.LookupSlice() without ever validating them against the checkpoint tensor's actual row count tensor_shape.dim_size(0); the only shape-vs-count check (line 98) covers the column dimension and only when col remapping is absent. An attacker supplying row_remapping = [0, 100] against a 5-row checkpoint tensor makes the code construct and load a slice of length 101 (rows [0,101) of 5 rows), driving out-of-bounds slice computation/reads in the slice machinery; with values [0, INT64_MAX] the expression max_old_row - row_start + 1 (line 121) signed-overflows and feeds a negative length to slice.set_length. Defect is at the call site per the unvalidated attacker-derived offset/length rule; the quoted guard new_row < num_rows_ && new_col < num_cols_ && new_row >= 0 && new_col >= 0 correctly protects the output write, but no guard of any form bounds the slice extent.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, reader.LookupSlice(old_tensor_name, tensor_slice,
                                                 &loaded_tensor_t));
evidence.reason: Sink: LookupSlice (and SliceTensorShape at lines 146-147) consumes tensor_slice, whose dimension-0 start and length are derived only from the attacker-controlled row_remapping tensor, with no validation anywhere in this code that the slice lies within the checkpoint tensor's first dimension (tensor_shape.dim_size(0)). Trigger: row_remapping=[0,100] with a 5-row DT_FLOAT checkpoint tensor yields slice start=0, length=101, which is passed into the slice shape computation and data-read/copy call — an out-of-domain, attacker-derived offset/length handed to an indexing/copy operation.

Origin of the faulty values: slice bounds are computed exclusively from min_old_row/max_old_row, which are min/max of unvalidated attacker-supplied int64 row IDs (lines 25-34). No clamp, mask, min/max with tensor_shape.dim_size(0), or rejection exists. Additionally, with row_remapping=[0, INT64_MAX] the expression max_old_row - row_start + 1 overflows int64 and passes a negative length to slice.set_length — the same missing bound as the root cause.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap (callee not shown) is assumed to resize *id_present to remapping.size() and map old_id -> vector index; the in-code guards row_remapping.size() == num_rows_ and col_remapping.size() == num_cols_ then make the row_id_present[i]/col_id_present[j] indexing at the end in-bounds. If the callee sizes differently, that indexing would be an additional OOB read, but the callee body is not given.

max_rows_in_memory_, num_rows_, num_cols_ are OpKernel attributes set by the same untrusted party that supplies the input tensors (TF op threat model); no in-code statement bounds max_rows_in_memory_.

BundleReader/TensorSlice internal behavior (whether an out-of-range slice causes a CHECK failure or an out-of-bounds read) is not shown; per the call-site rule the defect stands regardless of which occurs inside the callee.
limitations: The min/max sentinel logic (lines 26-32) unconditionally overwrites min/max while negative, but simulation shows it converges either to a value >= 0 or leaves both negative (skipping slice creation entirely); no in-code out-of-domain value results from this quirk beyond the already-reported missing bound.

ckpt_path is an attacker-controlled filesystem path; opening an attacker-chosen checkpoint is the op's documented purpose, so path use alone is not counted as a vulnerability absent an attacker-writable-planting scenario.

Slice loops with huge max_old_row and small positive max_rows_in_memory_ cause attacker-scalable memory growth of the tensor_slices vector (unbounded consumption); this shares the same missing bound and is not counted as a separate finding.

The output_matrix write, loaded_tensor reads, and initializing_values reads were verified safe via the quoted guards at lines 190-192 and the initializing_values_index < size check; these dismissals rest on guards quoted in this code.

verdict.summary: In ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd, the decrypt path computes ilen = aes->src_len - authsize with no check that src_len >= authsize; a caller-supplied command with src_len < authsize underflows the unsigned int to a ~4GB value that is immediately used as the skip length in scatterwalk_ffwd (walking past the input scatterlist, OOB read) and later as the data length in ccp_init_data (DMA of ~4GB, memory corruption). Independently, dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len underflows when iv_len > 32 and the attacker-derived offset and length are passed unvalidated into ccp_set_dm_area against the 32-byte context workarea (OOB write at the call site). Neither iv_len nor src_len is bounds-checked anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Integer underflow at the sink: aes->src_len and aes->authsize are caller-supplied command fields (attacker-data at this handler's trust boundary); no statement in the function checks src_len >= authsize before the subtraction. Simulated trigger: decrypt action, src_len=0, authsize=16 gives ilen=0xFFFFFFF0, which is consumed immediately by scatterwalk_ffwd as a ~4GB skip over the input SG (out-of-bounds read) and later by ccp_init_data(&src, cmd_q, p_inp, ilen, ...) after 'if (ilen > 0)' evaluates true, DMA-mapping/reading ~4GB and writing engine output to the destination — memory corruption. The only guards executed earlier are on iv, key, key_len, and authsize; none bounds src_len or ilen in any form.

evidence.snippet:
dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len;
	ret = ccp_set_dm_area(&ctx, dm_offset, aes->iv, 0, aes->iv_len);
evidence.reason: Second underflow sink: aes->iv_len is never validated (the preceding comment explicitly calls the 96-bit IV an 'assumption'), while the context workarea was allocated at lines 97-98 as CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES (32 bytes). With iv_len = 40, dm_offset = 32 - 40 = 0xFFFFFFEC, and both the out-of-domain offset and length are passed into the memory-copy call ccp_set_dm_area with no check on any path — an out-of-bounds write primitive at this call site (defect is here even though the copy completes inside the callee).

assumptions: CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES is 32 bytes (the standard CCP register-block size); the key copy at line 82 (dm_offset = CCP_SB_BYTES - key_len with key_len clamped to {128,192,256} bits) is safe under this constant, but the iv_len subtraction at line 103 is unguarded for any iv_len > 32 regardless of the exact constant.

The ccp_cmd fields originate from the kernel crypto API / CCP command interface; per the trust model of this handler, those data-carrying fields are treated as attacker-data since no caller precondition is documented or checked in the given code.
limitations: Encrypt-path tag write (ccp_get_dm_area(&final_wa, 0, p_tag, 0, authsize)) and the aad_len skip in scatterwalk_ffwd at lines 54-55 depend on the caller's scatterlist geometry (dst sized src_len+authsize, src covering aad_len); this code never validates those, but the SG layout is produced by the caller and could not be disproven as a contract — impact chain not fully instantiated here.
The precise byte-level write of the iv_len candidate lands inside ccp_set_dm_area, which is not shown; the defect recorded is the provably out-of-domain offset/length passed at the call site.

Memory-allocation failure paths (ccp_init_dm_workarea returning error) only cause early returns; no fail-open security-state issue observed — tag comparison at crypto_memneq fails closed with -EBADMSG.

verdict.summary: ax25_release() calls ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) on the STATE_0, STATE_1/2 and non-SEQPACKET paths (lines 22, 32, 74), after which the unconditional `if (ax25_dev)` block dereferences the destroyed ax25_cb via `del_timer_sync(&ax25->timer)` and the following four timer addresses (lines 77-81). The only guard, `if (ax25_dev)` (line 76), constrains the local ax25_dev pointer's NULL-ness, not ax25's lifetime, so it does not cover the sink. A local user triggers it by creating an AF_AX25 SOCK_SEQPACKET socket, binding it (ax25_dev non-NULL), and closing it while in AX25_STATE_0, yielding a use-after-free write on freed kernel slab memory.

evidence.reason: Use-after-free: the else-branch (and identically the STATE_0 case at line 22 and STATE_1/2 case at line 32) destroys the ax25 control block with ax25_destroy_socket(ax25), then execution falls through to the `if (ax25_dev)` block, which forms &ax25->timer and del_timer_sync()s five timers inside the destroyed object. `if (ax25_dev)` guards only the ax25_dev pointer, not ax25's lifetime; no statement between any destroy call and line 77 keeps ax25 alive. Trigger: unprivileged local user closes a bound SEQPACKET ax25 socket in AX25_STATE_0; ax25_dev is non-NULL so the block executes and dereferences freed memory (UAF write).

Origin of the tainted lifetime on the easiest trigger path: a SEQPACKET socket that is merely created and bound sits in AX25_STATE_0, so close() enters this case and destroys ax25 at line 22; control then continues to the timer-deletion block at lines 76-81 that uses the destroyed object.

assumptions: ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) releases/frees the ax25_cb once its remaining references are dropped; the callee body is not shown — the contract is inferred from its name, from the code's own caching of ax25_dev at line 14 BEFORE any destroy call, and from the destroy-then-use structure. If the object were provably pinned by a reference not visible here, the UAF would not fire; this residual uncertainty is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.

The matching ax25_dev reference hold (taken at bind) and the semantics of ax25_dev_put/dev_put_track are not shown; the double-put concern for the STATE_1/2 path (ax25_disconnect at line 29 possibly already putting the device) could not be verified and was not counted as a finding.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference candidate at line 40 (`ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL]`): the code itself treats ax25->ax25_dev as nullable (`if (ax25_dev)` at line 76) yet dereferences it unguarded in the STATE_3/4 switch. Rejected as SPECULATIVE: no statement in the given code produces state 3/4 together with a NULL ax25_dev (the NULLing producer, e.g. device-removal/disconnect code, is not shown).

del_timer_sync(&ax25->t1timer) at line 78 cancels the t1timer deliberately started at line 59 (`ax25_start_t1timer(ax25)`), aborting the AX25_STATE_2 shutdown handshake; no memory-safety consequence could be instantiated from the given code — protocol-logic issue only.
Unlocked windows between release_sock(sk)/lock_sock(sk) (lines 19-21, 28-30) allow concurrent timer callbacks, but the impact depends on timer bodies not shown; not counted.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg dereferences the network-supplied buffer without verifying that at least a header's worth of bytes remain: msg->hdr->length is read (line 26) even when buf_len < sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr), and (*attr)->length (line 42) is read whenever msg_len > 0, allowing a 2-byte attribute-length read up to 3 bytes past the end of a buffer whose remaining length is 1-3 bytes. Both out-of-bounds reads are directly triggerable by a crafted STUN datagram.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop guard is 'msg_len > 0' (only 1 byte required) while the body immediately dereferences (*attr)->length at p_attr+2, needing 4 remaining bytes. Trigger: buf_len = 25 with hdr length field = 5 passes the line-27 equality check; after one 4-byte attribute, msg_len = 1 and p_attr = buf+24 (last byte); line 42 then reads buf+26..buf+27, 2 bytes past the buffer end. The line-45 check runs after the read and cannot prevent it.

evidence.snippet:
msg_len = pj_ntohs(msg->hdr->length);
    if (msg_len != buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr)) {
evidence.reason: msg->hdr->length is read from buf before any check that buf_len >= sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr); with a 1-3 byte datagram this reads past the buffer (buf+2..buf+3), and the size_t subtraction buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) wraps, but only after the OOB dereference has occurred. No minimum-length guard exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: pjstun_msg_hdr is 20 bytes and pjstun_attr_hdr is 4 bytes (type + length) per the STUN layout implied by the code's field accesses at offsets 0-1 (type) and 2-3 (length); pj_ntohs is standard byte-swap.
buf/buf_len originate from a network-received datagram, making them attacker-data; this function is the trust-boundary intake point for STUN messages.
limitations: The OOB-read values (attribute length, message header length) flow only into length comparisons and are not returned or logged verbatim, so disclosure is limited to adjacent heap memory influencing an error/no-error comparison; impact is primarily a memory-safety violation (potential crash on unmapped pages), hence low severity.

The early exit when attr_max_cnt is reached while msg_len > 0 (lines 36, 60-62) returns PJ_SUCCESS with a truncated parse; this is a robustness/protocol-accuracy issue, not a security-state misrepresentation, since no verification or authorization decision rests on the parsed attributes here.

verdict.summary: mobi_decode_infl applies attacker-controlled insert/delete rules to a fixed buffer, but every memory sink is preceded by a combined range guard ('pos < 0 || l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX' for insert, the s-variant for delete) whose arithmetic reduces to '*decoded_size + 1 <= INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX' independently of the attacker-steered pos, covering both memmove read and write extents and the decoded[pos] access. Negative pos (from 'pos -= c - 10' and 'pos--'), pos past the end, negative l, and a full buffer are all rejected before any dereference on every path; wrapped pos values from signed underflow are also caught by 'pos < 0 || l < 0'. No unguarded sink remains.

assumptions: The caller allocates 'decoded' with at least INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes and sets *decoded_size to a length within [0, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX] — this producer (inflate step) is not shown; the code's own guards still re-derive the effective bound for every memory access, and a decoded_size >= INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX is rejected at the first insert/delete iteration.
INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX is a positive constant larger than any *decoded_size the internal producer can emit.
debug_print is a debug macro typically compiled out in release builds.
limitations: debug_print("Out of buffer in %s at pos: %i\n", decoded, pos) passes the raw buffer to %s; if decoded were not NUL-terminated this could overread on the error path (debug-only output, fixed format string, no disclosure primitive instantiated).

Extreme rule inputs (~238 MB of bytes in 11..19) can drive 'pos' to signed-int underflow (UB) before the guard; the wrapped values are always rejected by 'pos < 0 || l < 0' before any dereference, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable — robustness only.

A 32-bit pointer wrap in 'd + l' would require *decoded_size near INT_MAX at entry, which only a violation of the unshown inflate producer's contract could produce; not instantiable from the rule input in this code.
The delete-branch guard is stricter than necessary (rejects deletes when the buffer is exactly full) — a correctness quirk, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: AutoParallel::Initialize declares 'const NodeDef* dequeue_node;' without an initializer. When the attacker-supplied graph's training fanin contains no dequeue op (fully attacker-controlled via the GrapplerItem/GraphDef content), the loop body never assigns it, and 'if (dequeue_node)' reads an uninitialized stack pointer into control flow; a non-null garbage value is then dereferenced via 'dequeue_node->name()' and passed to ComputeTransitiveFanin, causing a wild-pointer dereference in the process optimizing the attacker's graph (denial of service / potential memory-safety impact).

evidence.reason: Root cause: 'const NodeDef* dequeue_node;' (line 79) is declared uninitialized and is only assigned inside 'if (IsDequeueOp(*train_node))'. Trigger: an attacker-authored graph whose transitive fanin of the fetch nodes contains no dequeue op leaves dequeue_node indeterminate; line 88 'if (dequeue_node)' then reads the uninitialized value into control flow, and lines 89-90 'dequeue_node->name()' dereference a wild pointer when the stack garbage is non-null, crashing/corrupting the process that ingests the attacker's graph. No initialization, NULL sentinel, else-arm, or post-loop check exists on any path.

assumptions: GrapplerItem (graph, fetch, init_ops, MainVariables) content originates from a user-submitted GraphDef across a trust boundary, making node names, op types, input lists, and graph topology attacker-data.

ComputeTransitiveFanin and IsDequeueOp are internal callees not shown; IsDequeueOp returning false for all fanin nodes of a graph without queue-based input pipelines is the ordinary, attacker-instantiable case.
AddNodeDivConst/AddNodeDiv return valid NodeDef pointers whose names this code itself inserts and re-looks-up consistently.
limitations: Lines 67/70 call protobuf repeated-field accessors 'input(gradient_pos[...])' and 'mutable_input(...)' with constant indices (2..9) without checking input_size(). A malformed ApplyAdam-family node with fewer inputs than the op signature could cause an out-of-bounds access inside protobuf release-mode accessors, but producing such a node requires bypassing TensorFlow's op-signature validation before grappler runs — a precondition not instantiated by this code's own statements, so it is recorded as speculative.

The uninitialized stack bytes at dequeue_node are environment-dependent; if they happen to be zero, execution degrades to skipping the input-node computation (still an uninitialized read, CWE-457), while non-null garbage yields the wild-pointer dereference described in the evidence.

verdict.summary: A minimal device release callback that derives the enclosing rtrs_clt_sess from the core-provided device pointer via container_of and frees it with kfree. No attacker-controlled content, sizes, indices, or strings are consumed; the only pointer arithmetic uses a compile-time offset, and the single-free precondition is enforced by the device core's refcount protocol, which this function cannot bypass.

assumptions: dev is supplied by the kernel device core when the device's refcount drops to zero; it is trusted internal state, not attacker data across a parse or protocol boundary.
container_of computes clt = dev - offsetof(struct rtrs_clt_sess, dev); the offset is a fixed compile-time constant, so no attacker-controlled pointer scaling exists.
limitations: Double-free would require the device core to invoke release twice or the object to be freed elsewhere before release runs; no statement in this function can produce a second kfree, so this trigger is speculative and rests on behavior outside the given code.
A NULL or mistyped dev reaching the callback would corrupt memory, but this code contains no path that produces such a value; it originates solely from trusted core bookkeeping.

verdict.summary: All loop counters are 32-bit signed ints ('auto i = 0', 'auto start_offset = 0') while their bounds are 64-bit, attacker-shape-controlled values (flat_segment_id.size(), big_stride). With a tensor whose flattened trailing-dims product or segment-id numel exceeds INT32_MAX, the counters undergo signed overflow and wrap negative; the signed comparisons keep the loops alive, and output_flat()/flat_input()/flat_segment_id() are then indexed with negative indices, causing out-of-bounds reads and an out-of-bounds tstring write (heap corruption) or a crash of the shared TensorFlow process.

evidence.reason: start_offset is a 32-bit signed int (auto start_offset = 0) but big_stride is int64 and equals the product of the input's trailing dims, fully attacker-controlled. With input shape [1, 2147483649] and segment_id [1] (id 0, num_segments 1), after start_offset reaches INT_MAX=2147483647, start_offset++ overflows to INT_MIN=-2147483648; the signed comparison (int64)INT_MIN < 2147483649 stays true, so output_index = -2147483648 and offset = -2147483648. output_flat(output_index).append(...) then writes through an out-of-bounds tstring (heap corruption) and flat_input(offset) reads out of bounds — no numel/stride cap exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.snippet:
for (auto i = 0; i < flat_segment_id.size(); i++) {
      OP_REQUIRES(
          context,
          ((flat_segment_id(i) < num_segments) && (flat_segment_id(i) >= 0)),
evidence.reason: The validation loop's counter i is a 32-bit signed int while flat_segment_id.size() is a signed 64-bit Eigen Index derived from the attacker-chosen segment_id shape. With more than 2^31-1 segment-id elements, i++ at INT_MAX wraps to INT_MIN, the signed comparison INT_MIN < size() remains true, and flat_segment_id(i) on this line reads out of bounds inside the guard itself, also leaving segment ids beyond index INT_MAX unvalidated and looping until an OOB-read value fails the check or the process segfaults.

assumptions: GetOutputShape (line 31) is assumed to build output_shape as [num_segments] + input trailing dims, so output_flat.size() == num_segments * big_stride; the helper is not shown.

GetStrides/GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets (lines 52-54) are assumed to return big_stride = product of input dims [segment_dims, input_dims) and relative_offset_set.size() == flat_segment_id.size() with in-range offsets; helpers not shown.
Eigen TensorMap operator() and flat<T>() indexing are assumed to perform no bounds checks in release builds (universally known Eigen semantics).
flat_segment_id.size() returns Eigen's signed 64-bit Index, making 'i < flat_segment_id.size()' a signed comparison that negative wrapped counters still satisfy.
limitations: Triggering requires very large tensors (>= ~2^31 elements, i.e., tens of GB for tstring inputs); on typical hosts the allocation may fail and the op then aborts cleanly via OP_REQUIRES_OK, but on large-memory ML hosts the trigger is instantiated.

Negative num_segments with an empty segment_id tensor reaches GetOutputShape (line 31) with a negative dimension; whether that CHECK-crashes or fails allocation depends on the not-shown helper, so no impact was instantiated.

A potential int64 overflow of num_segments * big_stride versus TensorShape's element-count handling inside the not-shown GetOutputShape/allocator could desynchronize output_index from the allocation, but this behavior is not shown and was not instantiated.

The OOB accesses land ~64GB before the tensor buffers, so in practice the most likely immediate result is SIGSEGV (DoS of the shared TF process); heap corruption/disclosure occurs if that range is mapped.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader validates the input length with `length < sizeof(bh)`, where bh is a POINTER, so only 4/8 bytes are required before blobheader fields (totlen, min_version, version, hdrsize, flags — at least 10 bytes of fields) are read. An attacker-supplied state blob of exactly the pointer width with totlen equal to its own length passes all checks, and bh->min_version / bh->version are then read out of bounds, leaking adjacent heap bytes into the exported header values.

evidence.snippet: if (length < sizeof(bh)) {
evidence.reason: The only length guard compares `length` against `sizeof(bh)` — the size of the blobheader POINTER (4 or 8 bytes), not `sizeof(*bh)`. It therefore permits buffers shorter than the blobheader struct that lines 14-33 read, making every subsequent field access unguarded.

Out-of-bounds read sinks. Trigger: attacker supplies an 8-byte blob (64-bit) with bytes 0-3 = 00 00 00 08; line 7 passes (8 < 8 false), line 14 passes (ntohl(totlen)==8==length), then bh->min_version is read at struct offset 8 and bh->version at offset 9 — past the end of the 8-byte buffer — and the OOB byte is exported via *hdrversion. On 32-bit, length=4 makes hdrsize/flags/version/min_version reads all OOB. No statement in the function bounds length against the struct size.

assumptions: blobheader contains at least totlen(uint32), hdrsize(uint16), flags(uint16), min_version(uint8), version(uint8) — 10+ bytes — so sizeof(blobheader) > sizeof(blobheader*); the struct definition itself is not shown.

verdict.summary: A remote VNC client can set dlen = 0xFFFFFFFF in the ClientCutText message; the handler computes 'return 8 + dlen' in uint32 arithmetic, which wraps to 7. The framing layer then invokes protocol_client_msg with len = 7 for the next message; both 'if (len == 1)' and 'if (len == 8)' fall through, so 'client_cut_text(vs, read_u32(data, 4), data + 8)' is reached with a ~4GB attacker length (and read_u32(data,4) itself reads one byte past the delivered data), causing a massive out-of-bounds read in the server process. The same corrupted expected-length lets a wrapped follow-up message drive the SET_ENCODINGS loop ('read_s32(data, 4 + (i * 4))' / 'memcpy(data + 4 + (i * 4), &val, sizeof(val))') up to offset 262143 with only a few bytes delivered, a heap out-of-bounds write. evidence.reason: Root cause and sink. dlen is fully attacker-controlled; the only guard is 'if (dlen > 0)' (emptiness), with no cap, clamp, or overflow check on '8 + dlen'. With dlen = 0xFFFFFFFF, '8 + dlen' wraps to 7; the handler is next invoked with len = 7, both len checks fall through, and 'client_cut_text(vs, read_u32(data, 4), data + 8)' is called with an ~4GB size against a 7-byte message (read_u32(data,4) already reads byte 7 out of bounds), yielding a large out-of-bounds read / DoS / potential disclosure in the server. The same wrapped expect reaching SET_ENCODINGS turns 'memcpy(data + 4 + (i * 4), &val, sizeof(val))' into a heap out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: The not-shown VNC io loop invokes protocol_client_msg with len equal to the byte count the handler last returned (the code's exact-equality checks 'if (len == 1)', 'if (len == 4)', 'if (len == 8)' and 'vnc_read_when(vs, protocol_client_msg, 1)' document this framing contract); the OOB-read magnitude at client_cut_text additionally depends on that internal callee's copy behavior.
VNC authentication/handshake occurs outside this snippet; all message fields reaching this handler are treated as unauthenticated network input.
A non-wrapping huge dlen (e.g. 0x7FFFFFF0) also makes the server buffer ~2GB per 8-byte message (memory-exhaustion amplification), under the same framing contract.
limitations: The audio default arm 'printf ("Invalid audio message %d\n", read_u8(data, 4));' executes at len == 4 and reads byte 4 of a 4-byte message — a 1-byte out-of-bounds/uninitialized read. Its trigger is instantiated, but the leaked byte goes only to the server process's stdout, which the remote client cannot observe, so no attacker-visible disclosure or corruption link could be quoted; treated as a minor robustness defect, not a driver of the verdict.

Return values of protocol_client_msg converted to negative int (dlen in (0x7FFFFFF7, 0xFFFFFFF8]) would be treated as errors by a typical io loop; that fail-safe behavior is an assumption about the not-shown caller.

verdict.summary: The function validates only input1's type (`input1->type == kTfLiteUInt8 || input1->type == kTfLiteInt8`) and never checks input2->type or output->type, creating a type-confusion surface; however, all data accesses remain within each tensor's own shape/data allocation (1-byte reads/writes into buffers allocated per shape), so no out-of-bounds access, memory corruption, or other security impact is instantiated within this code. requires_broadcast is assumed to be computed by the caller from actual shape equality; this code neither computes nor asserts it.

limitations: Missing type checks: only input1->type is validated; input2->type and output->type are never checked, so an input2 of a non-quantized type (e.g. float32) is reinterpreted as uint8/int8 and output is written as bool regardless of its declared type. Instantiated impact is limited to incorrect comparison results, not memory corruption, because 1-byte interpretation of any shape-sized buffer stays in-bounds.

If the caller passed requires_broadcast=false while input1 and input2 have different shapes, the not-shown non-broadcast callee could index input2 out of bounds; this trigger precondition cannot be instantiated from the given code and the OOB would occur entirely inside the unshown callee.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled 16-bit JPEG segment length is converted to signed int len = (data[2]<<8|data[3]) - 2, which can be negative (-2 or -1); the unchecked negative len is passed as fread's size_t count, wrapping to ~SIZE_MAX and causing a sequential out-of-bounds stack write past uchar data[0x10000] until EOF.

At the sink 'fread (data, 1, len, ifp);' the negative int len converts to size_t ~SIZE_MAX, so glibc fread copies file bytes past the 64KB stack buffer data[0x10000] until EOF — an attacker-scalable stack out-of-bounds write (memory corruption).

assumptions: ifp/dng_version/info_only are interface context; all file bytes read via fread are attacker-supplied (this function is the parser at the trust boundary).
glibc/POSIX fread semantics: with huge nmemb it repeatedly reads/copies bytes into the destination buffer until EOF or error (standard library behavior, discipline 3).
limitations: Uninitialized stack reads (data[7], data[1+data[0]*2], data[3+data[0]*2]) occur when len is shorter than the fixed offsets; these stay within the 64KB array bounds, so they are a CWE-457 robustness/decode-fidelity issue, not the verdict driver.
jh->bits underflow at 'jh->bits -= data[3+data[0]*2] & 15;' can produce negative bits whose harmful use occurs in decode code not shown; impact chain not instantiated here.
make_decoder_ref is an internal callee not shown; no defect proven at its call site beyond what the primary overflow already covers.

Minor memory leaks on some early-return paths (e.g. orders/pattern arrays) are non-security robustness issues

verdict.summary: In the JPEG-LS run-mode path, the run length decoded from the attacker's compressed bitstream (LONG run = DecodeRun(...)) is used as the loop bound `while(run)` without ever being clamped to the remaining line length. If the decoded run exceeds the remaining samples, `*lp[cx]++ = a[cx] << preshift;` writes past the end of the line buffer while `length--` goes negative; the subsequent `if (length)` (non-zero test, not > 0) and `while(--length)` then drive billions of further out-of-bounds writes, giving attacker-controlled heap corruption.

With run > length (e.g. length=3, run=1000), the 4th iteration writes one column past the line buffer and the loop continues writing attacker-influenced values (a[cx] << preshift) far out of bounds. length then goes negative, and the follow-on checks `if (length)` (line 80, tests non-zero, not > 0) and `while(--length)` (line 152) keep the decoder writing out of bounds for ~2^31 iterations — heap corruption with attacker-scalable magnitude. verdict.summary: The S3M order-list copy loop writes attacker-controlled bytes into the fixed-size array header->ord with index j bounded only by the file-supplied ordnum (up to 65535) and no destination-capacity check anywhere in the code, causing an out-of-bounds heap/struct write of attacker-controlled content and length when a crafted S3M file declares ordnum larger than ord's capacity and omits the 255 terminator byte.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted count: the 16-bit file-supplied ordnum directly sizes the orders allocation and, without any clamp, becomes the maximum index j used to write header->ord[j++] in the copy loop at lines 78-84.

verdict.summary: In mobi_decode_infl, the delete path executes 'if (dir == '<') { pos--; }' without any lower-bound check, so a crafted rule byte string can drive pos to -1 (e.g. rule bytes {3, 'X'} with *decoded_size == 0). The subsequent bounds check 'l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX' is vacuous with respect to pos because d + l = decoded + *decoded_size, so the code reads decoded[-1] (out-of-bounds read, also leaked via debug_print) and, when the pre-buffer heap byte matches the rule character, memmove writes one byte at decoded[-1] (heap underflow write); a following insert writes an attacker-chosen byte at decoded[-1] via 'decoded[pos] = c', and repeated deletes scale the underflow deeper.

evidence.reason: Root cause: pos is decremented with no floor. With pos == 0 (initial *decoded_size == 0 and rule byte 3 setting mod='d', dir='<'), pos becomes -1. The guard 'l < 0' only catches pos > *decoded_size, and 'd + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX' evaluates to decoded + *decoded_size, which is independent of pos, so it cannot detect the negative pos. Trigger instantiated: rule = {0x03, 'X'} drives pos to -1 and passes the check.

Sink: with pos = -1, 'decoded[pos]' reads decoded[-1] (unconditional out-of-bounds heap read; the byte value is printed via debug_print on the mismatch path). If the pre-buffer byte equals the rule character c (1/256, retryable per crafted file), 'memmove(d, s, l)' with d = decoded-1 and l = *decoded_size+1 writes one byte out of bounds before the buffer, and (*decoded_size)-- drives the size to -1; a subsequent insert ('decoded[pos] = c' at line 37) writes an attacker-chosen byte at decoded[-1].

assumptions: INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX is a positive constant (defined outside this snippet) and the decoded buffer has at least that capacity; the upper-bound check semantics do not depend on its exact value for the pos<0 defect.

rule, decoded content, and *decoded_size originate from the parsed MOBI file (index inflation records), making them attacker-controlled per the trust-boundary model; this function is the intake point for that data.
limitations: The out-of-bounds WRITE at decoded[-1] requires the heap byte immediately preceding the buffer to equal the rule's delete character (probability 1/256 per attempt; attacker can retry with re-crafted files or groom the heap). The out-of-bounds READ at decoded[pos] with pos = -1 is unconditional once the two-byte rule {3, c} is processed.

debug_print calls format the binary 'decoded' buffer with %s (lines 23, 33, 46, 50); if logging is enabled and the buffer is not NUL-terminated this can over-read past the buffer, and line 50 discloses the OOB byte decoded[-1]. Treated as a secondary consequence of the primary defect, not a separate finding.
No deeper impact (RCE) is claimed; the demonstrated primitive is a heap-buffer underflow read/write with attacker-scalable depth via repeated matched deletes.

verdict.summary: The promise-fulfillment callback consumes attacker content only as typed njs values handled via safe typed operations; all raw memory/index uses rely on engine-internal fields (ctx->index, ctx->await, ctx->capability) not derived from attacker data anywhere in this code. ctx->index, ctx->await, ctx->capability, ctx->pc, and ctx->capability->resolve/reject are valid non-NULL values produced by the not-shown async-context creation machinery.

On the NJS_AGAIN path, 'function->context = NULL; function->await = NULL;' execute unconditionally while ctx remains alive for the next fulfillment; any harmful consumer of function->await after suspension is not shown, so the impact chain is uncharacterizable.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg parses an attacker-supplied STUN message with a loop that stores one attribute pointer per 4 message bytes into the fixed-size array msg->attr, but never checks msg->attr_count against the array capacity. A crafted packet whose body is thousands of minimal 4-byte attributes drives attr_count far past the array, and line 40 (*attr = (pjstun_attr_hdr*)p_attr;) writes attacker-buffer pointers out of bounds, corrupting the pjstun_msg struct and adjacent memory (CWE-787/CWE-129).

assumptions: pjstun_msg.attr is a fixed-capacity array of attribute pointers (PJSTUN_MAX_ATTR, ~16 per pjstun.h); its definition is not part of the given code, but no bound check on attr_count exists in the code regardless of capacity, and the loop permits up to ~16,383 iterations (msg_len up to 65535, 4 bytes per attribute).
sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr)=20 and sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr)=4 per the STUN header layouts used by pjlib-util; the code's own arithmetic (buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr)) treats them consistently.
buf and buf_len carry a received network packet (STUN runs over UDP), so packet content and length are attacker-controlled per discipline 4.
limitations: Minor out-of-bounds READ at line 41: (*attr)->length is read before the line-44 length check, so a packet with buf_len = 21..23 (msg_len 1..3) reads up to 3 bytes past the buffer. Instantiable but negligible disclosure; dominated by the OOB write.

msg->hdr->type and msg->hdr->length (lines 10, 25) are read with no buf_len >= sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) check; a datagram shorter than 20 bytes causes a small OOB read before the msg_len check rejects it. Subsumed by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: All iteration over attacker-scalable int64 bounds (flat_segment_id.size(), big_stride, relative_offset_set.size()) is performed with 32-bit signed int counters (`int i`, `auto i = 0`, `auto start_offset = 0`). With a segment_id tensor of more than 2^31 elements (fully attacker-controlled shape/content in this op kernel), the validation-loop counter at line 42 overflows: after i = INT_MAX, i++ wraps to INT_MIN, the promoted comparison `-2147483648 < size` still holds, and `flat_segment_id(i)` performs an out-of-bounds read 8 GiB below the tensor buffer, crashing the process. Same width-confusion class at the write sink: `auto start_offset = 0` and `auto i = 0` deduce to 32-bit signed int but iterate over the int64 bounds `big_stride` and `relative_offset_set.size()` (both derived from attacker-controlled tensor shapes). After wrap, negative indices hit `flat_segment_id(i)` (OOB read feeding output_index) and `output_flat(output_index)` (out-of-bounds tstring::append write at lines 61-63). assumptions: flat<T>() accessors return Eigen TensorMaps whose size()/operator() use 64-bit DenseIndex, so size() is int64 and the int counters can wrap; this is the standard TensorFlow/Eigen contract on 64-bit builds.

The semantics of GetOutputShape, GetStrides, and GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets (not shown) are unknown; the analysis of whether relative_offset_set.size() equals flat_segment_id.size() and how big_stride is computed rests only on their names and this code's usage, not on quotable code.

The validated range for flat_segment_id is [0, flat_segment_id.size()) but the use loop indexes it over [0, relative_offset_set.size()); proving a mismatch (and hence use of unvalidated segment ids at the output write) requires the semantics of the unshown GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets/GetStrides, so this candidate remains unproven.

The fully-instantiated trigger (C1) requires a segment_id tensor of >2^31 elements (≈8 GiB) plus a matching tstring input (tens of GiB RAM); feasible on large hosts and consistent with TensorFlow's accepted CVE class for int-counter-vs-int64-size loops, but resource-heavy.

The inner-loop OOB-write variant additionally requires relative_offset_set.size() or big_stride to exceed 2^31 while the validation loop completes, which depends on the unshown helpers; the OOB read in the validation loop is the concretely simulated impact.
Line 27 prints `input_dims` (rank) where the dimension size is meant — cosmetic error-message defect only.

verdict.summary: The RequantizePerChannel kernel validates the size of input_requested_min twice and never validates input_requested_max, so an attacker can pass an empty requested_output_max tensor and cause a heap out-of-bounds read at input_requested_max.flat<float>()(0), with the read value returned via the output_max tensor. Separately, depth (from input_min_vec.NumElements()) is never checked against the input tensor's channel dimension, so set_output_scales(2, scales) hands mkldnn a scales vector shorter than the channel count, producing an attacker-scalable heap out-of-bounds read during the reorder.

evidence.reason: Copy-paste validation bug: the OP_REQUIRES intended to check the requested_output_max tensor instead re-checks input_requested_min.NumElements() == 1, so input_requested_max's element count is never validated on any path.
