Trigger: attacker feeds input_requested_max as an empty float tensor (NumElements 0); the guard at line 31 evaluates input_requested_min (1 == 1) and passes, then line 34 reads flat<float>()(0) from a zero-element buffer — an out-of-bounds read (Eigen TensorMap operator() is unchecked in release builds). The garbage value flows into input_requested_max_float and is returned to the attacker via output_max->flat<float>()(0) = input_requested_max_float, leaking heap memory contents.

evidence.snippet:
mkldnn::primitive_attr reorder_attr;
      reorder_attr.set_output_scales(2, scales);
evidence.reason: scales is sized by depth = input_min_vec.NumElements(), but no statement in the code ties depth to the channel dimension of the 4D input tensor (the only size checks are input.dims() == 4 and input_max_vec.NumElements() == depth). Trigger: attacker feeds input of shape [1,1,1,1000] and min/max vectors of 10 floats each; all guards pass, set_output_scales(2, scales) registers a 10-entry per-channel (mask 2) scale set for a 1000-channel reorder, and the subsequent reorder execution indexes scales[c] for c up to 999 — a heap out-of-bounds read whose length is fully attacker-controlled via the tensor shape.

evidence.snippet:
const Tensor& input_min_vec = ctx->input(kInputMinVecIndex);
      size_t depth = input_min_vec.NumElements();
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted size: depth is taken directly from the attacker-supplied input_min_vec tensor's element count and is used to size the scales vector, yet is never validated against the input tensor's channel dimension before being consumed by reorder_attr.set_output_scales(2, scales) at line 61.

assumptions: Eigen TensorMap operator() (used by Tensor::flat<float>()(0)) performs only a debug-mode DCHECK bounds check and is unchecked in release builds, per its universally known semantics.

mkldnn primitive_attr::set_output_scales with mask 2 consumes one scale per channel of the reorder destination, indexed by channel position, without validating the vector length against the destination channel count (mkldnn as used by this TensorFlow version).

The op's input tensors are supplied at session execution time by a party across a trust boundary from the process operator (standard TensorFlow op-kernel model); no shape/type constraint outside this Compute function is quoted in the given code and none is relied upon for the triggers.
limitations: std::vector<float> scales(depth) with attacker-chosen depth can throw std::bad_alloc, which the catch clause (mkldnn::error only) does not handle; however the attacker must first allocate a min_vec tensor of comparable size, so this is an allocation-failure/environment condition with ~1x amplification, not a vulnerability.

If both requested min and max are 0.0, requested_min_max is 0 and scales become Inf/NaN, producing NaN output tensor values — numerical corruption of the op's own output only, no memory-safety, disclosure, or bypass impact.
The QINT8 branch checks input_requested_min_float < 0.0f while the message references requested_output_max — a wrong-variable logic bug that only adds a redundant constraint and does not fail open.

Passing a non-float tensor for input_requested_max would trigger a dtype CHECK failure inside flat<float>() before reaching the OOB read; the primary trigger uses a correctly typed but empty tensor, so this does not gate the vulnerability.

verdict.summary: ConstantFolding::MulConvPushDown performs an unchecked attribute-map lookup, conv_node->attr().at("data_format"), on a Conv2D/Conv3D NodeDef from the graph being optimized. Because 'data_format' is an optional attribute with a default, an attacker-supplied GraphDef can contain a Conv2D/Conv3D node without it; reaching this line (all earlier checks pass) throws std::out_of_range, which is uncaught and aborts the optimizing process - a denial of service against any service that runs grappler on untrusted models. No existence check (find/count/GetNodeAttr status) exists anywhere on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the attacker-controlled NodeDef attribute map is accessed with .at("data_format"), which throws std::out_of_range when the key is absent, with no presence check (find/count/GetNodeAttr status test) anywhere in the function. Trigger: a crafted GraphDef whose Conv2D node (one Mul input constant, one Conv2D input constant, matching shapes, single consumer) omits the optional 'data_format' attribute passes every earlier check and reaches this statement, throwing an uncaught exception that terminates the process optimizing the untrusted graph.

Origin of the tainted value: conv_node is selected from the attacker-supplied graph, and the only validation performed on it is an op-type check (IsConv2D/IsConv3D), which never verifies the presence or content of the 'data_format' attribute; the node's unvalidated attr map then flows to the unchecked .at() lookup at line 80.

assumptions: protobuf Map::at() throws std::out_of_range for a missing key, per standard STL-compatible container semantics (discipline 3).
The graph passed to the grappler optimizer is attacker-supplied (TensorFlow's documented threat model: untrusted models optimized by a server process).
Semantics of not-shown internal callees (NodeMap::GetNode, IsReallyConstant, IsValidConstShapeForMulConvPushDown, GraphProperties) were not relied on to produce or dismiss the primary trigger.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference via node_map_->GetNode(...) (lines 16-17 dereferenced at 19-20; lines 43-44 dereferenced at 45-46): GetNode's failure sentinel (nullptr for unresolved or '^'-mangled input names) is produced by a callee not shown, and whether a GraphDef with dangling inputs survives upstream graph construction is not demonstrated by this code, so the trigger is not instantiated; recorded as speculative.

Reaching the .at() sink requires non-empty shape properties for the malformed Conv2D node (lines 55-70); whether GraphProperties populates properties for a node missing 'data_format' depends on shape-inference code not shown. Per GUARD ANCHORING this unquotable upstream behavior cannot serve as a guard, and TensorFlow's real-world security fixes for this exact line confirm the crash is reachable; confidence reflects this residual uncertainty.

verdict.summary: ImmutableExecutorState::Initialize looks up a FrameInfo via raw std::map operator[] using the attacker-controlled Enter node's "frame_name" attribute (frame_info_[frame_name].get(), line 84) instead of the EnsureFrameInfo() accessor used at every other frame lookup (lines 9, 41, 136). On a map miss, operator[] inserts a null unique_ptr, so the unchecked dereference at line 90 (frame_info->parallel_iterations) is a NULL pointer dereference. An attacker-supplied GraphDef containing an Enter node whose frame_name does not correspond to any registered control-flow frame (e.g., an Enter unreachable from the graph source, which this code explicitly processes — see line 127) crashes the model-loading/serving process (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Root cause: frame_info is obtained by frame_info_[frame_name].get() where frame_name is the raw, attacker-controlled node attribute string (line 83), not the cf_info-derived name used to populate the map. std::map::operator[] default-inserts a NULL unique_ptr on a miss, so frame_info can be nullptr, and line 90 dereferences it with no null check, EnsureFrameInfo call, or error return between the lookup and the use. Trigger: an attacker GraphDef with an Enter node whose "frame_name" attribute names no registered frame (e.g., an Enter not reachable by the control-flow walk) reaches line 84 with frame_info == nullptr and crashes at line 90, denying service to the process loading the model.

Origin of the mismatch: the frame_info_ map is populated in this code exclusively from cf_info.unique_frame_names (this loop) and from cf_info.frame_names[id] (line 41, via EnsureFrameInfo). No statement in this code ever inserts an entry keyed by a node's raw "frame_name" attribute before the line-84 lookup, so an attribute value that does not coincide with a cf_info frame name produces a map miss and a null pointer; the code's own use of EnsureFrameInfo everywhere else (lines 9, 41, 136) confirms the absence of this guard at line 84 is the defect.

assumptions: BuildControlFlowInfo (not shown) is assumed to register control-flow frames only for nodes it visits when walking the graph from its source; its behavior is unquotable, so neither the claim that it guarantees every Enter's raw frame_name attribute is a registered key nor the opposite claim can be verified from the given code.

EnsureFrameInfo (not shown) is assumed to return a valid, newly created FrameInfo on a miss (as its use at lines 9, 41, 136 implies); whether it initializes the nodes member cannot be quoted (the explicit assignment at lines 9-10 suggests it does not).
The attacker is the originator of the GraphDef/model file from which the Graph is built (standard TensorFlow model-loading trust boundary); the process loading it is the impacted party.
params_.create_kernel is assumed to succeed for an Enter node with well-formed attributes, so execution reaches line 84.
limitations: Candidate (speculative, not primary): outputs_required[e->src_output()] at lines 146/148 is indexed with an attacker-derived slot guarded only by `if (e->src_output() >= 0)` (line 145) with no upper bound against `new bool[n->num_outputs()]` (line 140) — a heap out-of-bounds write would occur if a data edge with src_output >= num_outputs can reach this code; whether Graph construction (not shown) rejects such edges could not be verified from the given code, so the malformed-edge state could not be instantiated here.

root_frame_info_ = frame_info_[""].get() (line 12) is the same unguarded raw map-lookup pattern; the root frame is presumed registered by BuildControlFlowInfo and root_frame_info_ is not dereferenced within this code, so no in-code impact chain exists.
enter_frame_info_[id] = frame_info (line 102) can store a null FrameInfo for downstream consumers; those consumers are not shown.
cf_info.frame_names[id] (line 40) would be an out-of-bounds read if the not-shown BuildControlFlowInfo does not size the vector to num_nodes; this contract is unquotable.
frame_info->nodes->push_back(item) (line 132) relies on the nodes member being initialized for frames created via EnsureFrameInfo at line 41; EnsureFrameInfo's body is not shown.

verdict.summary: fiber_switch's argument-copy path is correctly guarded: the 'if (len >= 15)' branch packs excess arguments into an array and the else branch pairs 'mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2)' exactly with a copy of len values into stbase[1..len], so every stack write is in bounds for all admitted len (0..14); argc field is capped at 15. Remaining concerns (negative len, callinfo pointer layout after 'c->ci--', NULL from internal callees) cannot be triggered by any statement in this code and are recorded as assumptions/limitations.

assumptions: mrb_stack_extend(mrb, room) guarantees at least room slots from the context's stbase; it is a project-internal function not shown, but the code's own comment 'for receiver and (optional) block' documents this sizing intent and the extend amount matches the subsequent copy length exactly.
fiber_switch_context(mrb, c) makes c the current context (mrb->c == c) so the subsequent mrb_stack_extend applies to c->stbase; the call is placed in execution order before all stack writes.
fiber_check and fiber_check_cfunc return a valid, non-NULL context and raise on invalid fibers; their implementations are not shown.
The caller passes len >= 0 and a pointing to at least len mrb_values (mrb_ary_new_from_values and the copy loop read len elements from a); this contract is not documented inside the given code.
The callinfo array layout (dummy callinfo below ci, capacity for c->ci[1]) is established by fiber-creation code not shown; the comment 'pop dummy callinfo' documents the convention.
MRB_PROC_ENV(c->cibase->proc) is non-NULL and its ->stack has at least one element; cibase->proc is set by the fiber creation code not shown.
CALLINFO's argc field can represent values 0..15 (CALL_MAXARGS), which the len=15 packing branch respects.
limitations: Negative len: if a caller passed len < 0, the copy loop is skipped (e < b) and c->cibase->n would receive a negative value consumed later by mrb_vm_exec; neither the negative producer nor the harm occurs inside this code, so the trigger is not instantiated here. No 'len < 0' check exists anywhere in the function.

The NULL guard 'if (!c->ci->proc)' checks the pre-decrement c->ci->proc, while mrb_vm_exec later consumes the post-decrement c->ci->proc and the sink uses c->cibase->proc; whether these can be NULL/invalid depends on fiber_init (not shown), so no trigger is provable from this code.

'c->ci[1].stack[0] = value;' writes through an unchecked adjacent callinfo on the vmexec/non-CREATED path; bounds depend on callinfo capacity managed elsewhere and no violation is producible by statements in this code.

If len could exceed the actual number of elements at a, mrb_ary_new_from_values(mrb, len, a) and the copy loop would over-read a; this is a caller contract that this code does not check, but no over-read is producible by this code's own flow.

verdict.summary: All memory operations in check_passwd are bounded by hash_len, the same expression that sizes the calloc(hash_len * 2) allocation; passwd/length reach only hash-input parameters of digest callees and never a size, index, or offset sink in this code. No trigger with a security impact could be instantiated.

assumptions: digest_length(d) returns a positive length matching the digest's output size (internal callee, not shown).
read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd write at most the passed hash_len bytes into passwd2_sum (bound passed at call site).
pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 writes exactly keylen bytes to passwd1_sum and PBKDF2_SALT_LEN <= PBKDF2_LENGTH (compile-time constants).
digest_free(d) tolerates d == NULL on the PBKDF2 path where d is never allocated (callee not shown; barebox digest_free checks for NULL).
The unseen caller of this static function passes a passwd buffer at least length bytes long and interprets ret == 1 as authenticated.
limitations: digest_free(d) is called with d == NULL on the CONFIG_PASSWD_CRYPTO_PBKDF2 path (d is only assigned in the else branch); if digest_free dereferences NULL this is a deterministic NULL deref, but the callee is not shown and the crash is not attacker-gated nor higher-privilege — speculative (potential CWE-476).

strncmp on the password hash uses early-exit comparison, giving a theoretical timing side channel on hash-prefix match length (CWE-208); impact on the PBKDF2 path is masked by the constant heavy PBKDF2 work, and leaking a derived-hash prefix does not yield the password.
If digest_length(d) or PBKDF2_LENGTH could be 0, calloc(0,1) plus strncmp(...,0)==0 would set ret=1 (auth bypass); no statement in this code can produce hash_len == 0.

The length parameter is passed to digest_digest/pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 without validation; a caller passing length larger than the actual passwd buffer would cause an OOB read inside the callee, but the caller and callee signatures are not shown, so this is a contract issue, not an instantiated defect.
On the -ENOMEM early return, digest_free(d) is skipped, leaking the digest allocation — a resource leak with no security impact here.

verdict.summary: In LoadAndRemapMatrix's Compute, min_old_row/max_old_row are derived from the attacker-controlled row_remapping tensor without any validation against the checkpoint tensor's shape (or for arithmetic overflow). With row_remapping = {0, INT64_MAX}, slice_length = max_old_row - row_start + 1 overflows int64_t to INT64_MIN; row_start then wraps to INT64_MIN and on the next iteration slice_length computes to 0, so the while loop never terminates while tensor_slices grows without bound — a small attacker input causes an infinite loop and unbounded memory consumption (DoS/OOM).

evidence.reason: Slice-length sink: with attacker-controlled row_remapping = {0, INT64_MAX} (num_rows_ = 2), min_old_row = 0 and max_old_row = INT64_MAX reach this loop unvalidated. First iteration: max_old_row - row_start + 1 = INT64_MAX - 0 + 1 overflows int64_t to INT64_MIN, so a negative length is stored into the slice and row_start += slice_length wraps row_start to INT64_MIN. Second iteration: max_old_row - row_start + 1 wraps to 0, so row_start never advances and the loop never exits while tensor_slices.push_back grows the vector without bound. No statement in the code bounds min/max_old_row against tensor_shape.dim_size(0) or checks slice_length > 0.

Origin of the tainted values: min_old_row and max_old_row are computed directly from the attacker-controlled contents of row_remapping (only the vector's size is checked against num_rows_ on line 9). Arbitrary int64 values, including INT64_MAX, are accepted; the only filter is the >= 0 test, so 0 and INT64_MAX pass through to the slice-construction loop as min_old_row and max_old_row.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap (internal callee, not shown) is assumed to size row_id_present/col_id_present to the input vector's length; the quotable size checks (lines 9 and 42-43) then bound the initializing-loop indexing.
max_rows_in_memory_ takes its default (<= 0) in the simulated trigger; any positive value still produces the same overflow path via std::min.
int64 arithmetic wraps in two's complement (the declared width is int64_t and no earlier check bounds the values below the wrap scale, so the wrap is exercised by the code as written).
limitations: Slices built from unvalidated min/max_old_row that exceed tensor_shape.dim_size(0) are passed into TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape and BundleReader::LookupSlice with no range validation in this code; whether those callees return an error, CHECK-crash, or read out of bounds is not shown, so that impact chain is not characterizable here (the same missing guard as the primary finding).

Loop counters use int against int64 bounds (e.g., 'for (int i = 0; i < row_remapping.size(); ++i)'); triggering the wrap requires >= 2^31-element (multi-GB) input/allocations which allocation limits make impractical to instantiate.
ckpt_path is an attacker-controlled filesystem path passed to BundleReader (arbitrary-file-open surface), but no concrete defect within this code was instantiated from it.
Cells intentionally left uninitialized during column remapping are filled by the initializing_values loop; no uninitialized-output leak was instantiated under the assumed RemapVectorToMap semantics.

verdict.summary: The error label 'beach' unconditionally executes 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' even when obj is NULL. obj is NULL on the paths reached via 'if (!prelink_range) goto beach;' (obj never allocated) and via 'R_FREE (obj); goto beach;' after a failed prelink plist parse. Loading an attacker-supplied malformed kernelcache Mach-O therefore dereferences NULL and crashes the process loading the file (denial of service).

evidence.reason: The sink 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' at line 67 dereferences obj with no NULL check on any path into the label. obj is NULL when beach is reached from line 15 (obj was initialized to NULL at line 11 and never allocated on that path) or from line 31 (after 'R_FREE (obj)' set it to NULL). Writing through the NULL pointer crashes the process loading the attacker-supplied file — an attacker-instantiated denial of service (CWE-476).

Origin of trigger path A: for a Mach-O without a derivable prelink info range, get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 returns its failure sentinel NULL; the branch jumps to beach while obj is still NULL (line 11), reaching the NULL dereference at line 67.

Origin of trigger path B: when the prelink plist at the attacker-influenced offset/size fails to parse, r_cf_value_dict_parse returns NULL (sentinel checked here); 'R_FREE (obj)' sets obj to NULL before 'goto beach', again reaching the NULL dereference at line 67.

assumptions: R_FREE frees the pointer and sets it to NULL (standard radare2 macro), so obj is NULL after 'R_FREE (obj)' on line 30.

get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 and r_cf_value_dict_parse can return NULL on malformed input; this is evidenced by this code's own failure-sentinel checks at lines 14 and 28, though the callees themselves are not shown.
limitations: Lines 26-27 pass the attacker-influenced prelink_range->range.offset and .size into r_cf_value_dict_parse without bounds validation in this code. The callee is not shown and typically consumes via RBuffer (clamped) reads, so no out-of-bounds impact could be instantiated; recorded as a potential upstream-validation gap, not a confirmed finding.

Minor resource leaks with no demonstrated attacker-scalable impact: the r_buf_ref reference taken at line 2 is never released on the '!main_mach0' early return (lines 6-8), and rebase_info (line 10) is never freed on beach paths.
The write at line 67 is to a NULL/near-NULL address only; no memory corruption or disclosure was instantiated — impact is denial of service of the process loading the malicious file.

verdict.summary: In the NE entry-table parsing loop, the index 'off' grows past EntryTableLength before each read of bin->entry_table: the bundle_type read can occur at off == EntryTableLength (off-by-one after the while-loop increment), and on the movable path the segnum/segoff reads execute before the only EntryTableLength check (which itself uses '>' instead of '>='), with all other bounds checks comparing the wrong unit (file size via tableat + off, on a stale pre-increment off). A crafted NE file therefore causes heap out-of-bounds reads in the process parsing it (crash/DoS, potential heap-content disclosure into entry addresses).

evidence.reason: Root cause: check-after-use. 'off += 2' then '*(bin->entry_table + off)' reads the table at an index not yet validated; the only domain check 'if (off > bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength)' runs after the read (and uses '>' so off == Length still passes, letting r_read_le16 read indices Length and Length+1). Trigger: EntryTableLength=3, entry_table={2,0xff,X}, file larger than tableat+6 → off goes 0→1→2→3→5 and entry_table[5] is read 3 bytes past the buffer before the check breaks; all inputs are attacker-supplied NE file bytes and header fields.

Off-by-one OOB read: the while guard 'off < bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength' bounds only the pre-increment off; after 'off++' the read at 'bin->entry_table + off' can occur at index == EntryTableLength. Trigger: EntryTableLength=1, entry_table[0]=nonzero, file extending beyond tableat → off becomes 1 and entry_table[1] is read one byte past the buffer; the file-size check on line 30 uses the stale pre-increment off and the wrong unit.

assumptions: bin->entry_table is allocated/bounded by bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength at parse time (allocation not shown); the code's own comparisons at lines 29, 59 and 67 treat EntryTableLength as the table's valid index domain, which is the basis for calling these reads out-of-bounds.
bin->segment_entries contains at least SegCount entries, so the guarded index computations at lines 64 and 72 stay in range.
r_list_get_n and r_read_le16 behave as standard container accessor / little-endian 2-byte reader per discipline 3.
limitations: Memory leaks of 'segments' (and 'entries' contents) on early-return paths (lines 46-49, and entry freed at 53 is fine but segments leak) are resource-management issues, not security impacts.

The disclosed OOB bytes only reach output as components of entry->paddr addresses (weak info-leak potential); the reliably instantiated impact is denial of service via crash of the process parsing the malicious NE file.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled data (server-supplied CAP LS capability list) is copied into the fixed 256-byte buffer exclusively via g_strlcat calls bounded by sizeof(buffer), which truncate and NUL-terminate safely; the format string passed to tcp_sendf is a literal, buffer+9 is always in-bounds due to the unconditional 9-byte prefix, and all loop bounds are fixed or NUL-sentinel-terminated. No memory-safety, injection, or amplification defect is reachable.

assumptions: tags_data is assumed non-NULL at every call site (message dispatch layer contract); this code contains no NULL check or assertion for it, so a NULL would crash at tags_data->timestamp — recorded as an unquotable interface contract, not a defect of this function.

tcp_sendf is assumed to be a printf-style wrapper with literal-format and bounded-string semantics consistent with its name; the only argument passed is a NUL-terminated buffer of at most 256 bytes, so no out-of-domain argument crosses the call site.
limitations: Truncation: a very long capability list is silently truncated at 255 characters in the outbound CAP REQ (g_strlcat clamps); this is a functional/cosmetic limitation with no memory-safety or security impact.

Speculative: a NULL tags_data parameter would cause a NULL dereference at tags_data->timestamp, but no statement in this code produces or documents that value; trigger precondition could not be instantiated from the given code.

verdict.summary: The attacker-influenced length 'len' reaches the copy loop and mrb_stack_extend, but the destination write is guarded by 'mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2);' executed before the copy, sizing the buffer from the same expression as the copy length (max written index len < len+2). The read side '*a++' and the env/callinfo derefs lack in-code guards, but no trigger precondition for those (len exceeding the caller's array, NULL env, invalid ci[1]) can be instantiated by any statement in this code; all such candidates are speculative on unshown callers/callees.

assumptions: mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) guarantees capacity for len+2 stack slots from the fiber's ci stack base (c->stbase for a MRB_FIBER_CREATED fiber); this internal callee is not shown and its guarantee is assumed per standard mruby semantics.
Callers of fiber_switch pass a consistent (a, len) pair built by the VM's argument-passing protocol; no statement in this code enforces or documents this contract.
mruby fiber initialization gives a CREATED fiber a dummy callinfo above cibase (so 'c->ci--' cannot underflow) and a proc with a non-NULL env; both are set in code not shown.
The width of the callinfo field 'n' is assumed wide enough for realistic argument counts; the declared type is not visible in the given code.
limitations: C1 (CWE-125, OOB read of 'a' in 'while (b<e) *b++ = *a++;'): no guard bounds 'len' against the actual size of the caller's array, but a mismatched (a, len) pair can only be produced by a caller not shown; trigger not instantiated in this code.
C2 (CWE-476, NULL deref): 'MRB_PROC_ENV(c->cibase->proc)->stack[0]' has no NULL check on the env; triggering requires a fiber whose proc lacks an env, producible only by code not shown.
C3: 'c->ci[1].stack[0] = value;' writes through a callinfo slot past the current one with no in-code validity check; whether ci[1] is allocated/initialized depends on VM internals not shown.
C4 (CWE-191): 'c->cibase->n = len;' may truncate if 'n' is narrower than mrb_int, but the required argument count exceeds any reachable call surface in the unshown callers.
C5 (CWE-190): 'len+2' overflow or negative 'len' requires a caller passing extreme values no statement here can produce.

verdict.summary: xfrm_migrate writes found/migrated state pointers into fixed-size stack arrays x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] and x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] indexed by nx_cur/nx_new, which are incremented once per loop iteration up to the attacker-supplied num_migrate. No statement in this code bounds num_migrate (or the counters) against XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, so an XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE request with more matching states than XFRM_MAX_DEPTH causes an out-of-bounds pointer write past the 6-element arrays, corrupting the kernel stack.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop is bounded by attacker-controlled num_migrate with no check against XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6), and nx_cur/nx_new are incremented per iteration without any bound. Trigger: with num_migrate = 7 (or more) and 7 matching states pre-created by the attacker, at iteration i=6 nx_cur = 6, so 'x_cur[nx_cur] = x' (line 25) writes one pointer past the end of the 6-element stack array x_cur (and 'x_new[nx_new] = xc' at line 29 does the same for x_new) — an out-of-bounds write of a state pointer into the kernel stack frame.

evidence.snippet:
struct xfrm_state *x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH];
	struct xfrm_state *x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH];
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the destination arrays are fixed at XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6) entries, while the write counters nx_cur/nx_new are driven by the caller-supplied num_migrate with no bound in this code, creating the size mismatch that the out-of-bounds writes at lines 25 and 29 exploit.

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is the kernel constant 6, giving x_cur/x_new an index domain of 0..5.

xfrm_migrate_check(m, num_migrate) is an internal callee whose body is not shown; per guard anchoring, no bound it might impose on num_migrate can be claimed, and no such bound is quotable anywhere in the given code (the historical upstream fix for this exact defect added a num_migrate > XFRM_MAX_DEPTH rejection inside xfrm_migrate_check, confirming it was absent).

xfrm_migrate is the netlink migration intake path (non-static, driven by user-supplied XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE data), so num_migrate and the migrate entries are attacker-data per discipline 4; the attacker can also pre-create matching states via XFRM_MSG_NEWSA to satisfy the find precondition.
limitations: Triggering requires the attacker to have created at least XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 states matching the migrate entries; this is instantiated by the same trust boundary (SA creation via the same netlink subsystem), not by a caller contract.
A negative num_migrate simply skips the loop (i < num_migrate is false at i=0), so no underflow path exists at this sink.

verdict.summary: This is a libvirt test-suite callback consuming compiled-in test fixtures (no trust-boundary input). All NULL sentinels (rc, src, xml) are checked before first use in execution order; the invariant chain 'if (!data->expect) erc = -1;' -> rc/erc mismatch -> early return, plus 'if (src && !data->expect) return -1;', plus the checked '!(xml = virBufferContentAndReset(&buf))', provably guarantees data->expect and xml are non-NULL at the STRNEQ and %s uses. Format strings are static; g_auto/g_autofree/g_autoptr handle all cleanup paths. No memory-safety, injection, or trust-boundary defect is present.

assumptions: virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute returns 0 only on success and does not set *src on failure — internal callee not shown; however, even if it returned -1 with src set, the quoted check 'if (src && !data->expect) { ... return -1; }' still prevents any NULL use.
virDomainDiskSourceFormat's return convention (< 0 on failure) is the project-documented contract; the return value is checked with '< 0'.
data->backing and data->expect originate from a static test-case table in the same test binary, i.e. internal-trusted, not attacker-data per discipline 4.
limitations: Candidate 'NULL deref at STRNEQ(xml, data->expect) when expect==NULL' could not be instantiated: with expect==NULL, erc is forced to -1, so a successful parse (rc=0) mismatches erc and returns -1 at the first check; a failed parse leaves src==NULL and returns 0. The later fprintf of data->expect is likewise unreachable with expect==NULL.
The branch 'if (src && !data->expect)' appears to be dead code under the rc/erc invariant, but unreachable code cannot constitute a defect.
This is test code with no network, guest, or lower-privileged input surface; findings restricted to test-harness robustness would not carry security impact.

verdict.summary: load_buffer leaks two owned resources on error paths: the RBuffer reference taken at line 2 is never released when MACH0_(new_buf) fails (early 'return false' at line 7 bypasses the r_buf_free at beach), and the RRebaseInfo allocated at line 10 is never freed on any of the four 'goto beach' paths (beach frees fbuf, obj, prelink_range, prelink_info and main_mach0, but not rebase_info). Both triggers are instantiated by attacker-supplied malformed kernelcache/Mach-O files, and per-invocation leaks are attacker-scalable to memory exhaustion in long-running consumers.

evidence.reason: Early return on parse failure. fbuf was reference-counted at line 2 ('RBuffer *fbuf = r_buf_ref (buf);'); this 'return false' exits without r_buf_free(fbuf) and without reaching the beach cleanup at line 66, so the buffer reference taken for attacker-supplied file data leaks on every rejected file — attacker-scalable retention.

The error-path cleanup frees fbuf and main_mach0, and every goto beach (lines 15, 21, 31, 41) pre-frees prelink_range/obj/prelink_info, but no statement on any path frees rebase_info (allocated at line 10). Trigger: attacker file parses as Mach-O so rebase_info is allocated, then get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 returns NULL (line 14's own error arm) — the heap object with attacker-influenced chained-fixup data is leaked.

evidence.snippet: RRebaseInfo *rebase_info = r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0 (fbuf, main_mach0);
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked value: rebase_info is allocated here from attacker-derived Mach-O data and is only stored into obj->rebase_info on the success path (line 46); on all four error paths reaching 'beach' it is never released.

assumptions: r_buf_ref increments the RBuffer refcount and r_buf_free decrements/frees it (standard r2 buffer semantics); the caller of load_buffer does not retain ownership of the reference taken at line 2.
RRebaseInfo allocated by r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0 is heap memory owned by this function until transferred at line 46; internal callee not shown.
get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 returning NULL for a malformed file is instantiated by the code's own error arm at line 14 ('if (!prelink_range)'), which documents that sentinel as reachable.
limitations: r_cf_value_dict_parse (lines 26-27) receives attacker-derived offset/size from prelink_range; whether the parser bounds-checks its reads is internal and not shown — potential out-of-bounds read inside the callee could not be instantiated from this code.

swizzle_io_read(obj, io) (line 60) is internal; whether it safely handles obj->rebase_info == NULL (possible when line 10's allocation fails, since the return is not checked before line 46) could not be verified.

Impact of the two leaks is a per-invocation retention primitive; turning it into memory exhaustion requires the host process (r2 library consumer, fuzzing harness, batch-analysis service) to process repeated attacker files — assumed reachable for a library entry point but not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled sinks in this Samba VFS fsctl handler are guarded by quoted, execution-order-correct checks: in_data[0] read is preceded by in_len >= 1; BVAL reads require exact in_len == 16; sid_parse is bounded by in_len < 8 rejection plus MIN(in_len - 4, SID_MAX_SIZE); the shadow-copy output allocation is sized from the same expression used for the writes and gated by the max_out_len < *out_len check; offset+length wrap is rejected. The only theoretical defect — uint32 truncation of labels_data_count = num_volumes*2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL)+2 causing a heap overflow in the label loop — requires ~71.5 million snapshot volumes produced by an unshown VFS backend and an attacker-writable snapshot root, neither instantiable from this code.

assumptions: Caller allocates in_len valid bytes at _in_data and honors the out_data/out_len contract; no NULL in_data with in_len >= 1 is producible from this code.

SMB_VFS_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA, sid_parse, sid_to_uid, create_volume_objectid, push_file_id_16, srvstr_push behave per Samba's documented contracts (srvstr_push writes at most its dest_len argument; sid_parse validates the encoded SID length).
limitations: Speculative: uint32 truncation of labels_data_count at line 'labels_data_count = (shadow_data->num_volumes * 2 * sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL)) + 2;' could yield a small *out_len and heap buffer while the loop writes num_volumes*60 bytes, but triggering it requires num_volumes >= ~71.5 million snapshots, a value produced entirely by the unshown shadow-copy VFS backend (shadow_data->labels would also need ~71M allocations), and attacker-writable snapshot directories — no statement in this code produces or permits these preconditions.

FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID may report *out_len smaller than the 48 bytes it fills (e.g., max_out_len < 48), truncating the client-visible reply; this is a protocol-correctness concern (acknowledged by the in-code comment), not memory corruption in this code.
FSCTL_FIND_FILES_BY_SID is a stub that always returns NT_STATUS_OK without listing files; it makes no authorization decision on the parsed SID, so this fail-open stub has no security effect here.

If shadow_data->labels is non-NULL but shorter than num_volumes (a backend contract violation), shadow_data->labels[i] in the loop would read OOB — the array/num_volumes consistency is enforced only inside the unshown VFS backend.

verdict.summary: SetupWriters dereferences parser-produced box pointers (trak->Media, trak->Media->information, ->sampleTable, stbl->SampleSize, stbl->TimeToSample, stbl->ChunkOffset) with no NULL validation on any path. A malformed MP4 whose trak lacks mdia/minf/stbl, or whose stbl lacks stsz/stts/stco/co64, makes these attacker-controlled parsed fields NULL, crashing the media-processing process (denial of service). The code itself treats sampleTable as nullable via a later check on line 63, proving the earlier unguarded derefs are the defect.

evidence.reason: Chained unguarded dereference of attacker-file-derived parsed box pointers. A crafted MP4 with a trak box lacking mdia (or mdia/minf lacking stbl) leaves trak->Media (or ...->information->sampleTable) NULL; line 19 dereferences it before any check. The function's own later guard 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable' (line 63) proves these values can be NULL, yet no check protects this earlier sink in execution order.

writer->stbl->SampleSize and writer->stbl->TimeToSample are dereferenced with no NULL check; an attacker-crafted stbl missing the stsz or stts boxes leaves them NULL, producing a NULL-pointer dereference at line 31 or 33. (The nb_entries==1 check correctly bounds entries[0], but nothing bounds the pointers themselves.)

evidence.snippet: if (writer->stbl->ChunkOffset->type == GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_STCO) {
evidence.reason: stbl->ChunkOffset is the parsed stco/co64 box pointer; an attacker-crafted stbl containing neither box leaves it NULL, and this unconditional dereference of ->type crashes. No NULL check on ChunkOffset exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: gf_isom_get_track(movie->moov, i+1) is an index-based accessor over movie->moov->trackList, the same list whose count bounds the loop (lines 11-12), so trak is non-NULL; its internal implementation is not shown.

The upstream isom parser populates structure fields only for boxes present in the file (so absent boxes leave NULL pointers); this is behavior of code not shown, but the in-code NULL guard on 'trak->Media->information->sampleTable' at line 63 corroborates that these parsed fields can be NULL.
mw, writers, and the box pointers movie->moov->trackList entries are a consistent in-memory parsed state (no concurrent mutation assumed).
limitations: Lines 41/47: early 'return GF_OUT_OF_MEM' on gf_isom_box_new failure leaks the current writer and previously added writers; triggerable only by allocation failure an attacker cannot induce — robustness, not a security defect here.

Line 52: mw->total_samples (u32) accumulates parsed sampleCount values; a wrap is not reachable at a memory-safety sink in this code (progress counter only) and sampleCount is bounded by the parser's table allocations — no instantiated impact.

Line 13: a NULL return from gf_isom_get_track would crash at line 18, but the loop bound 'trackCount = gf_list_count(movie->moov->trackList)' with 'i < trackCount' keeps the 1-based index in range of the same list, so the trigger is not instantiated.
No memory-corruption (write) primitive was found; the instantiated impact is denial of service via NULL-pointer dereference in the process consuming the attacker's file.

verdict.summary: The frame index parameter of the exported decoder gif_internal_decode_frame is used to index gif->frames before any range validation: gif->frames[frame].display is read at line 19 with no prior check, and the only bounds statement, 'if (frame > gif->frame_count_partial)' (line 24), executes after the first use and uses '>' instead of '>=', so frame == frame_count_partial also passes and gif->frames[frame] is read and written throughout the function. Any out-of-range frame value produces an out-of-bounds read (and, at the exit label, out-of-bounds writes for the off-by-one case).

evidence.reason: First use of the attacker-controlled parameter frame (unsigned int, non-static exported function, no quotable precondition) with zero prior validation. Simulated trigger: caller passes frame = 0x7FFFFFFF; this statement executes before any check and reads gif->frames[0x7FFFFFFF].display far out of bounds (CWE-129/CWE-125).

The only range guard on frame: it is positioned after the first use (line 19), so it cannot protect that read, and its operator '>' (should be '>=') lets frame == gif->frame_count_partial pass, so gif->frames[frame].frame_pointer/.transparency/.disposal_method/.virgin are read and .opaque/.virgin are written at the exit label for an out-of-range index.

assumptions: Declarations/sizes of gif->frames, gif->local_colour_table, gif->global_colour_table, gif->width/height are in the gif_animation struct, which is not shown; capacity of the frames allocation is assumed to be tracked by fields not referenced here.

gif_skip_frame_extensions, gif_interlaced_line, lzw_decode_init, lzw_decode, and the bitmap callbacks are internal callees not shown; their documented behavior (advancing buffer_position in bounds, returning interlace lines < height, returning LZW_OK/LZW_OK_EOD on success, non-NULL buffers) is assumed per discipline 3 and cannot be quoted.
limitations: colour_table[colour]: the LZW stack can emit colour values 0-255 while a local colour table may declare as few as 2 entries (colour_table_size = 2 << (flags & 7)); no 'colour < colour_table_size' check exists anywhere, but whether the access is out-of-bounds versus reading uninitialized entries depends on the (not shown) array declarations, so the trigger's memory-safety consequence is not fully instantiated.

colour_table[gif->background_index] in the clear-image memset uses an index from the logical-screen descriptor against a possibly local colour table with no size check; same dependency on unshown array declarations.

The exit-label writes gif->frames[frame].opaque = ... / .virgin = false become out-of-bounds WRITES only if the frames allocation ends exactly at frame_count_partial entries; the allocation code is not shown.

Deep recursion via the GIF_FRAME_RESTORE disposal chain (alternating RESTORE/KEEP frames) can scale recursion depth linearly with file size (potential stack exhaustion, CWE-674/CWE-400); the overflow point depends on stack limits and per-frame stack usage, so it is environment-dependent.
The direct 'return GIF_INSUFFICIENT_MEMORY;' statements bypass the gif_decode_frame_exit label, skipping buffer_position restoration and bitmap callbacks; correctness issue only.

verdict.summary: readconf_main() runs at startup consuming only operator-originated data (build-time config file list, root-owned configuration file with in-function ownership/mode verification, uname/euid). All memory and format sinks are guarded by quotable checks in execution order (NULL tests with PANIC_DIE before *t='X', before pw->pw_gid, before fstat; %.256s precision bounds nodename; strncmp/offset pairs consistent). The sprintf tail-append onto big_buffer and the unchecked expand_string return before Ustrtol lack guards, but their triggering values (near-buffer-length build-time file path; failing admin expansion) are not attacker-reachable, so no vulnerability is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: log_write with LOG_PANIC_DIE terminates the process (universal Exim semantics); relied on only to confirm control flow, not to dismiss a memory-sink guard.
string_nextinlist copies list items into big_buffer bounded by big_buffer_size (standard documented Exim helper behavior); big_buffer_size is large relative to any build-time config path.

get_config_line, readconf_handle_option, read_named_list, parse_extract_address, unpick_ratelimit, regex_must_compile, expand_string are internal callees whose failure behavior is per discipline 3 not assumable; none receives a raw unvalidated size/index/offset from this code (only string pointers), so no call-site defect arises here.
uts.nodename is NUL-terminated on POSIX systems.
limitations: Unguarded sprintf tail-append: 'uschar *suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename);' followed by sprintf(CS suffix, ".%ld.%.256s", ...) writes up to ~279 bytes at the end of filename inside big_buffer with no capacity check (CWE-120/676 pattern). Not a vulnerability here only because filename comes from the compile-time config_main_filelist, which this code never sizes from external input; in a build with an unusually long configured path it would overflow. A length-bounded format is the missing guard.

Unchecked expand_string result: 'uschar *s = expand_string(host_number_string);' lacks the 'if (s == NULL) log_write(... PANIC_DIE ...)' guard present for spool_directory/log_file_path/pid_file_path; a failing expansion yields Ustrtol(NULL, &end, 0) and a NULL dereference crash at startup (CWE-476 pattern). Trigger is admin misconfiguration of a root-owned, mode-verified config file, not attacker data, and impact is a same-privilege crash with no corruption, so recorded as robustness, not vulnerability.

host_number accepts negative values: 'if (n > LOCALHOST_MAX)' checks only the upper bound, so 'host_number = n' can be set negative from a config value like "-5". Downstream use of host_number is not shown, so no impact link can be instantiated.

When CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID is defined but CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE is not, 'config_file' is read before it is ever assigned on the first loop iteration (CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID-only arm reads config_file == NULL in its 'if (config_file == NULL)' test and the finally-try block); under that build combination the first-iteration flow is incoherent — a build-configuration correctness bug, not attacker-triggerable, and the common default build does not compile these arms.

verdict.summary: SetupWriters dereferences parsed-file-derived box pointers without validating them: the guard at line 17 checks stbl, SampleSize, ChunkOffset and SampleToChunk but omits stbl->TimeToSample (dereferenced at lines 39-40) and trak->Media->mediaHeader (dereferenced at line 26). An attacker-supplied MP4 whose stbl lacks an stts box (or whose mdia lacks mdhd) makes the writer dereference NULL during the write path, crashing the process — a denial of service on untrusted input.

evidence.snippet:
if (writer->stbl->TimeToSample->nb_entries==1) {
			writer->constant_dur = writer->stbl->TimeToSample->entries[0].sampleDelta;
evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference: TimeToSample comes from the attacker-controlled parsed sample table, and the only validation in the function (line 17: 'if (!stbl || !stbl->SampleSize || !stbl->ChunkOffset || !stbl->SampleToChunk)') omits TimeToSample while explicitly guarding its sibling boxes — proving missing mandatory boxes are a reachable state in this structure. An MP4 with stsz/stco/stsc but no stts passes line 17 and reaches line 39 with TimeToSample == NULL, crashing the process.

evidence.snippet: writer->timeScale = trak->Media->mediaHeader->timeScale;
evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference: trak->Media is proven non-NULL by lines 16-19, but trak->Media->mediaHeader is never checked anywhere in the function (the line-17 guard does not mention mediaHeader). A parsed track whose mdia lacks an mdhd box reaches this dereference with mediaHeader == NULL, crashing the process during the write path.

assumptions: The box parser that produced mw->movie (not shown) leaves stbl->TimeToSample and trak->Media->mediaHeader NULL when the corresponding stts/mdhd boxes are absent from the input file; this leniency cannot be quoted from the given code, but the line-17 guard against NULL SampleSize/ChunkOffset/SampleToChunk from the same structure establishes that missing-box NULLs are a real, parse-surviving state this code must defend against.

gf_isom_get_track(movie->moov, i+1) is assumed to return a valid track for 1..gf_list_count(movie->moov->trackList); a NULL return would crash at line 16, but no attacker-reachable path producing it was instantiated.

Media_SelfContainedType, Media_IsSelfContained, gf_isom_box_new, gf_isom_box_array_del_parent and CleanWriters are project-internal callees whose semantics are not shown and are not relied on as guards.
limitations: Early returns 'return GF_OUT_OF_MEM' at lines 47 and 53 skip CleanWriters, leaking TrackWriter objects and previously added writers; triggerable only by allocation failure, so robustness, not security.
mw->total_samples (u32) can wrap when summing attacker-controlled sampleCount values across many tracks; impact is a corrupted progress counter only.
The NULL derefs cause a crash/DoS, not memory corruption; no out-of-bounds write or read primitive is instantiated by the simulated triggers.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImage reads the attacker-controlled animation frame count Frames (up to 2^32-1) from the MAT file header and loops that many times via 'if(--Frames>0){ ... goto NEXT_FRAME; }' with no bound anywhere. Each pass leaks one QuantumInfo (AcquireQuantumInfo result is never released - no RelinquishQuantumInfo exists in the function) and permanently appends a non-empty image to the list (surviving the final cleanup that only removes rows==0||columns==0 images), so a ~200-byte crafted 4D-matrix MAT file drives billions of iterations, unbounded memory retention and CPU consumption, exhausting the decoding process.

evidence.reason: Sink: the loop back-edge is driven solely by the attacker-controlled Frames counter; no bound, cap, or blob-size check exists on any path, so each of up to 2^32-1 iterations leaks a QuantumInfo (line 236, never released) and retains one image in the list, causing memory/CPU exhaustion from a single small file.

evidence.snippet: Frames = ReadBlobXXXLong(image2);
evidence.reason: Origin: the frame count is read verbatim from the attacker-supplied matrix header (DimFlag==16 path) as a full 32-bit value and reaches the loop at line 413 unvalidated.

evidence.snippet: quantum_info=AcquireQuantumInfo(clone_info,image);
evidence.reason: Amplification mechanism: this allocation executes on every NEXT_FRAME iteration (the goto at line 417 lands above it) and the previous QuantumInfo is overwritten without any RelinquishQuantumInfo anywhere in the function, leaking memory once per frame.

assumptions: The MATHeader struct declaration is not in the given code; SizeX/SizeY widths are presumed 32-bit only because they are assigned from 32-bit blob readers (ReadBlobLSBLong/MSBLong return 32-bit values).
z2qtype[] is not shown; assumed to have at least 4 entries since z is constrained to 0..3 by the quoted DimFlag arms.

Internal callees (DecompressBlock, CalcMinMax, FixLogical, FixSignedValues, InsertComplexDoubleRow/FloatRow, ImportQuantumPixels) are not shown; their buffer usage was checked only via the ldblk*8-sized BImgBuff invariant, which holds for all quoted read lengths.
limitations: Candidate heap over-read via 32-bit wrap: 'ldblk = (ssize_t) (8 * MATLAB_HDR.SizeX)' (and the 4x/2x variants) can wrap modulo 2^32 if SizeX is a 32-bit field (e.g. SizeX=0x20000000, miINT64 gives ldblk=0 or 8 while image->columns=SizeX, so ImportQuantumPixels would read far past the ldblk*8-byte BImgBuff). Not fully instantiated: the MATHeader field width cannot be quoted from the given code (guard anchoring fails), and the impact additionally requires SetImageExtent to succeed allocating a >=8.6 GB pixel cache for a >=0x20000000-column image - an environment capacity condition the attacker cannot force. If the real struct uses 32-bit fields, this is a real CWE-190/CWE-125 defect worth fixing independently.
'image->colors = one << image->depth' with depth==64 shifts a size_t by 64 (undefined behavior); on common targets this yields colors=1 with no demonstrated security impact.

clone_info and quantum_info are leaked on ThrowReaderException/early-return paths after CloneImageInfo/AcquireQuantumInfo; a fixed small leak per invocation, not attacker-scalable within one file, so not promoted to a vulnerability.
The ping-mode path swaps columns/rows and 'goto done_reading' (author-marked 'BAD'); it reports swapped dimensions in ping mode, but no memory-safety impact could be instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: In njs_object_iterate_reverse, the array branch bounds its index with 'from < array->length', but the string branches use args->from/args->to (int64_t, attacker-reachable index parameters with no documented/enforced precondition in this code) in raw pointer arithmetic: 'p = string_prop.start + from' (byte-string) and 'p = njs_string_offset(string_prop.start, end, from)' followed by njs_utf8_prev/next (UTF-8), with no check that from <= length-1 or to >= 0 anywhere on any path. If from exceeds the string length (or to is negative), njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) and the p-- walk read out of bounds past the end (or before the start) of the heap string buffer, an out-of-bounds read whose content is surfaced to the iterator handler.

evidence.reason: Root cause: pointer p is computed as string_prop.start + from with no bound of from against length (string_prop.size). The array branch enforces 'from < array->length' (lines 27-28) before indexing; the string branches have no analogous check on any path. Trigger: from > length-1 (or to < 0) makes p point past the buffer (or before start) and njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) reads *p out of bounds on every loop iteration while p-- walks the OOB region — heap out-of-bounds read, values passed to the handler.

Same missing bound in the UTF-8 branch: from is not validated against the string's character count before njs_string_offset/njs_utf8_next position p, and njs_utf8_prev(p) then reads out of bounds when from exceeds the string length (p at/past end) — the guard that exists for arrays ('from < array->length') is absent here.

evidence.snippet:
from = args->from;
    to = args->to;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted indices: args->from and args->to (int64_t) enter this function with no documented or checked precondition bounding them to [to, length-1] of the value being iterated; they flow unvalidated into the pointer arithmetic at lines 80 and 107.

assumptions: njs_string_prop returns the string's character count (length) and byte size (string_prop.size) with string_prop.start pointing at the byte buffer; njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) copies/reads one byte at *p; njs_utf8_prev/njs_utf8_next read/decode bytes around p — standard njs semantics relied on per callee-semantics discipline.

The values from/to are produced by njs iterator call sites not shown in this snippet; no statement in this code bounds them, so they are treated as attacker-data per the GUARD ANCHORING discipline (this code is judged as the last line of defense).
limitations: If the (not-shown) callers of njs_object_iterate_reverse always clamp from to [to, length-1] (as the array callers effectively do by iterating up to length-1), the trigger from > length-1 or to < 0 cannot be instantiated; that clamp is not quotable from this code, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.

njs_value_property_i64 and njs_array_indices are internal callees whose behavior on out-of-range indices is not shown; they are treated as characterizable lookups per discipline 3, not as defect sites.

A NULL-dereference variant (njs_string_offset returning NULL for from past the end, then njs_utf8_next(NULL, end)) is subsumed by the same missing bound; if the OOB read cannot be instantiated, this would reduce to a robustness issue.

verdict.summary: print_media_desc validates the output buffer only for the 'm=' line's media/transport components ('if (len < media.slen+transport.slen+12+24)'), but the format-token loop writes ' ' plus fmt[i].slen attacker-controlled bytes for each of fmt_count tokens with no bounds check against end. A parsed SDP message with format tokens longer than the ~29-byte slack causes pj_memcpy at line 29 to write past buf+len, corrupting adjacent memory; the negative (end-p) lengths subsequently passed to print_bandw/print_attr extend the corruption.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop copies attacker-controlled fmt[i].slen bytes for each of fmt_count attacker-controlled tokens, advancing p with no comparison against end or len anywhere in the loop. Trigger: SDP with media.slen+transport.slen+36 <= len passing the line-9 check, but a single fmt token longer than the remaining ~29 bytes of slack, e.g. len=64, 'm=audio 5000 RTP/AVP ' leaving 44 bytes and fmt[0].slen=100 → pj_memcpy writes ~56 bytes past the buffer.

Root cause: the only capacity check in the function miscalculates the required buffer size — it accounts for media.slen, transport.slen and fixed overhead (36) but omits every fmt token (' ' + fmt[i].slen per token, fmt_count tokens), so it passes while the fmt loop at lines 27-31 overflows. This is the incorrect buffer-size calculation (CWE-131) that enables the out-of-bounds write.

evidence.snippet: printed = (int)print_bandw(m->bandw[i], p, end-p);
evidence.reason: Downstream consequence of the same overflow: once the fmt loop pushes p past end, end-p is negative and is passed as a length (converted to a huge unsigned size), turning the bandwidth/attribute printing loops (lines 45-51, 54-60) into further unbounded writes. Same trigger; no independent guard exists on these paths once p has exceeded end.

assumptions: m is a pjmedia_sdp_media populated from a parsed SDP message; in PJSIP usage SDP originates from a network peer, so media/transport/fmt strings, their lengths, and fmt_count are attacker-data (no precondition on m is documented or checked in this code).
pj_memcpy(p, src, n) copies exactly n bytes; pj_utoa returns the number of characters written (standard PJSIP semantics, characterizable callee).
m->desc.port is at most a 5-digit value and port_count at most 10 digits, so the fixed 36-byte reserve in line 9 does cover the non-fmt portions of the 'm=' line.
limitations: Integer overflow of the line-9 sum media.slen+transport.slen+36 would require slen values near SIZE_MAX; SDP token lengths cannot plausibly reach that scale, so this secondary path is not counted as a trigger.
A NULL m->desc.fmt[i].ptr dereference or crash-only impact was not separately classified: the primary trigger already produces out-of-bounds writes of attacker content, which is memory corruption.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in inbound_cap_ls: the server-controlled capability list extensions_str is split into an unlimited number of tokens (g_strsplit(..., " ", 0)) and every token matching a known capability is appended to the fixed 256-byte stack buffer via unbounded strcat calls with no length check. A malicious IRC server sending ~20 repeated capability names (e.g. 'identify-msg' 20 times: 9 + 13*20 = 269 bytes incl. NUL > 256) writes out of bounds past buffer[256], corrupting the stack with attacker-influenced content.

This is a libvirt unit-test callback whose entire input surface is a compiled-in test fixture struct (data->backing, data->expect, data->rv) supplied by the in-tree test driver; no value crosses a trust boundary, and every observable sink (fprintf with static format strings, string comparison) consumes only fixture data or checked helper outputs. No attacker-reachable memory, injection, or security-state defect exists.

assumptions: Behavior of internal callees virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute, virDomainDiskSourceFormat, and virBufferContentAndReset is not shown; their outputs are treated per standard semantics (return code checked at line 12, NULL checked at lines 15-16 and 25).
args is assumed non-NULL and pointing to a valid testBackingParseData fixture, per the test-driver callback contract this signature documents; no attacker can influence the callback argument.
limitations: Line 8 ('int erc = data->rv;') dereferences args without a NULL check; if the test driver passed NULL it would crash the test process. Trigger is not attacker-instantiable (same trust domain, fixture-driven) and the impact is an equal-privilege process crash only, so it is a robustness note, not a vulnerability.

The comparison 'if ((rc = virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute(data->backing, &src)) != erc)' conflates failure codes (any negative rc vs exact erc) and the 'src && !data->expect' branch at line 19 is partially redundant — test-logic quality issues with no security effect.

verdict.summary: In the decrypt path, ilen is computed as aes->src_len - authsize with no check that src_len >= authsize; for a decryption command with src_len (e.g., 0) smaller than authsize, the unsigned subtraction wraps to a near-SIZE_MAX value (0xFFFFFFF0), which is then used as the byte length for scatterwalk_ffwd (line 62) and ccp_init_data (line 148), causing out-of-bounds scatterlist traversal and copying far past the source buffer — kernel memory corruption driven entirely by command-field content at this handler's entry point. No check on aes->src_len exists anywhere in the function (only key_len, authsize, and non-NULL pointers are validated).

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned integer underflow at 'ilen = aes->src_len - authsize;'. The only guards on aes fields are the key_len check (lines 24-27), non-NULL key/iv checks (lines 21, 29), and the authsize switch (lines 34-45, which ensures authsize >= 4); there is no check that aes->src_len >= authsize. Trigger instantiated by simulation: aes->action = DECRYPT, aes->authsize = 0 -> authsize = 16 (line 33), aes->src_len = 0 -> ilen = 0xFFFFFFF0 at line 61, immediately consumed as the walk length by scatterwalk_ffwd at line 62, driving an out-of-bounds scatterlist traversal of ~4 GiB.

Impact link: the wrapped value ilen = 0xFFFFFFF0 passes the 'if (ilen > 0)' check at line 144 and is passed as the data length to ccp_init_data at line 148, which maps and copies data from the source SGL for that length — out-of-bounds read of the caller's buffer and out-of-bounds writes into the driver's DMA workareas, i.e., memory corruption in kernel context.

evidence.snippet: struct ccp_aes_engine *aes = &cmd->u.aes;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: aes->src_len is a data-carrying field of the caller-supplied cmd parameter, consumed at this handler's entry point with no validated precondition (the comment at lines 50-51 explicitly admits input lengths of 0 as in-domain), making the underflow trigger reachable from this function's own input surface.

assumptions: struct ccp_aes_engine fields src_len, aad_len, authsize, iv_len are unsigned integers per the kernel header (not shown); the underflow at line 61 depends on that unsignedness.

The exact dispatch path by which cmd->u.aes is populated (ccp_perform_cmd / ccp-crypto API wrappers, potentially reachable by unprivileged users via AF_ALG) is not shown; per the analysis discipline, unquotable caller contracts are treated as attacker-data, so aes->src_len is attacker-data.

ccp_init_data, scatterwalk_ffwd, ccp_set_dm_area, and ccp_get_dm_area are project-internal callees not shown, but their memory-consuming role (SG walk / data map-and-copy / dm-area copy at a given offset and length) is used only after identifying the out-of-domain argument (wrapped ilen) passed at this call site.
limitations: Speculative: aes->iv_len is unvalidated; 'dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len;' (line 103) underflows and ccp_set_dm_area (line 104) would write out of bounds if iv_len > 64. The comment at lines 93-96 documents the 96-bit IV assumption, and no statement in this code enforces iv_len; the trigger requires the not-shown caller to supply iv_len > 64, so it is recorded as speculative rather than primary.

Contract-dependent: on encrypt, the tag is written into p_tag inside the destination SGL (line 58 computes p_tag; the ccp_get_dm_area call near the end ignores its return value) with no dst length check; the code quotes the documented expectation 'It is expected that the input and output SGs will be valid' (lines 50-51), and the trigger requires the caller to violate SG lengths, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
The ignored return value of ccp_get_dm_area on the encrypt tag path is an error-handting/hardening concern with no demonstrated memory-safety trigger in this code.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start() never checks fread() return values or end-of-file, so once the parsed stream hits EOF with a stale marker tag in (0xff00, 0xffff] other than 0xffda, the do-while loop has no reachable exit and spins forever. A 2-byte attacker file (SOI only, "FF D8") fully instantiates the trigger: fread returns 0, data[] is unchanged, tag stays 0xffd8 forever, yielding unbounded CPU consumption / permanent hang in whatever process parses the attacker-supplied file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the return values of both freads are discarded, so at EOF data[] retains stale content and tag never changes. The only in-loop guard, `if (tag <= 0xff00) return 0;`, covers only tags <= 0xff00 and does not detect the short read. Trigger: attacker supplies a file containing only the 2-byte SOI (FF D8) or any JPEG stream truncated before SOS with last-read marker e.g. 0xffe1/0xffd8; each iteration re-reads nothing, tag stays constant and != 0xffda, so the loop at line 40 never terminates — unbounded CPU work from a tiny input.

evidence.snippet: } while (tag != 0xffda);
evidence.reason: Loop exit condition is reachable only when tag == 0xffda, but tag is derived solely from data[0..1], which are only updated by the unchecked fread on line 13. After EOF with a stale tag in (0xff00, 0xffff] and != 0xffda, this condition is permanently false and no other statement on any path terminates the loop — the defective sink of the infinite-loop trigger.

assumptions: struct jhead's field widths (huff[], free[]) are not shown in the given code; huff is indexed up to [5] on lines 43/45 and free/huff by c<4 on line 31 — assumed declared with sufficient elements, so no OOB struct write is claimed.
merror (line 49) is assumed to terminate on a NULL allocation; its body is not shown.

make_decoder_ref (line 31) semantics are not shown; assumed to parse a Huffman table without catastrophic in-call behavior; the call site passes dp bounded to [data, data+len) by the line-30 loop guard.
ifp is an ordinary stdio stream over the attacker-originated image file; fread returns 0 at EOF without modifying the buffer (documented C semantics).
FORC(n) expands to a bounded for-loop over c; dng_version/zero_after_ff are globals as written.
limitations: Uninitialized/stale stack reads beyond len (CWE-457/908): lines 20-25 read data[0..7] and lines 34-35 read data[1+data[0]*2] / data[3+data[0]*2] with no check that len covers those indices; a SOF with declared length 2 (len=0) or a truncated SOS feeds uninitialized bytes into jh->bits/high/wide/clrs/psv. Within this code every derived value stays in a bounded domain (sraw masked with '& 3' on line 20, clrs checked on line 42, wide <= 65535, indices <= 513 inside the 0x10000 array), and the consumers of the returned jh fields are callers not shown, so the disclosure/corruption impact chain is not instantiated here.

Potential stack over-read inside the not-shown make_decoder_ref (line 31): dp is only bounded at loop entry by `dp < data+len`; a truncated Huffman table near the end of a length-wrapped 65535-byte DHT segment (len = (0)-2 wraps to 65534) could make the callee read past data[0x10000]. The callee's read extent is not quotable from the given code, so this is not counted as a finding.

jh->bits can be driven negative (line 35) and jh->clrs can be up to 258 on the info_only path (line 41 returns before the line-42 check); their downstream uses (ljpeg_row shifts, caller buffer sizing) are in code not shown.
jh->clrs == 0 passes the `jh->clrs > 6` check (operator is >, not >=), producing calloc(0,4) at line 48; merror/caller handling of a zero-size row is not shown.
Verified safe: len's maximum reachable value after the ushort wrap on line 15 is 65535, which is within `uchar data[0x10000];` (65536 bytes), so the line-17 fread never overflows the buffer.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability found. Every dereference of the attacker-controlled string is guarded by a NUL check on the same pointer in execution order (lines 10 and 22), the same-codepoint/same-length property keeps the s += clen scan from skipping past the terminator, and the only stack write is a size-bounded vim_snprintf into buf[NUFBUFLEN-sized] storage; no out-of-domain argument is passed to any callee.

assumptions: mb_cptr2char_adv/mb_ptr2char (Vim mbyte helpers) decode one character without consuming the terminating NUL, i.e. clen never advances past the string end; standard Vim behavior but internal callees not shown.
ga_concat/ga_concat_esc grow the garray correctly for the literals and clen ≤ 4 bytes passed to them.
vim_snprintf honors its size argument and NUL-terminates buf (standard documented semantics).
limitations: same_len (int) can overflow only if the input contains ≥ 2^31 identical consecutive characters (≥2GiB run); even then the sole effect is a mis-signed count printed through the bounded %d — no memory-safety or security impact, and the trigger is not practical to instantiate.

A theoretically shorter re-encoding of a matching codepoint (impossible in canonical UTF-8; overlong forms are longer) would be needed to make s += clen skip the NUL; no input value instantiates this, and the *s != NUL check would still bound subsequent reads.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled data reaches this dma-buf attach callback; all consumed values are driver-internal state or framework-contract pointers. The only code defect is a memory leak of the kzalloc'd attachment on the dma_get_sgtable error path (returns -EINVAL without kfree(a)), but the triggering failure is a DMA-API/environment condition that this code's own flow cannot produce from any attacker input, so it is a robustness issue, not an instantiated security vulnerability.

assumptions: dmabuf->priv is the fastrpc_buf this driver set at export time (framework contract; not asserted in this snippet, but its only writer is this driver, so it is internal-trusted rather than attacker-data).
dma_get_sgtable semantics are standard: returns 0 or negative errno; failure depends on the buffer's DMA mapping properties, which are fixed at buffer creation and not attacker-modifiable here.
limitations: Memory leak (CWE-401-class robustness defect): if (ret < 0) { dev_err(...); return -EINVAL; } returns without kfree(a), leaking the kzalloc'd struct on every failed dma_get_sgtable call. Not counted as a vulnerability because the failure precondition is an environment/DMA-API condition that no attacker input in this code's surface can induce or repeat at scale.
The error return discards ret and always reports -EINVAL — cosmetic error-reporting inaccuracy, no security effect.
No detach-side counterpart is shown; lifetime of a beyond attachment->priv is the framework's contract, unverifiable from this snippet.

verdict.summary: All buffer writes are bounds-guarded: the entry check 'if (len < (pj_size_t)m->desc.media.slen+m->desc.transport.slen+12+24) return -1;' covers the m=-line's fixed overhead (computed maximum 27 bytes < 36-byte margin), the fmt loop uses 'end-p > fmt[i].slen' (exactly ensuring room for the leading space plus the copy), and the CRLF uses 'end-p >= 2'. Later print_* helpers receive the in-domain pointer p and exact remaining length end-p with negative returns checked. No reachable out-of-bounds write exists in this function.

assumptions: pj_utoa(unsigned port, p) writes at most 10 digits and returns the digit count with no extra terminator (port and port_count are unsigned per pjmedia types); the 36-byte margin in the entry check exceeds the computed 27-byte fixed overhead regardless.

The internal helpers print_connection_info, print_bandw, and print_attr honor the passed maximum length (end-p) and return a negative value on overflow; their implementations are not shown, but this code passes in-domain arguments (p provably <= end, length = exact remaining space) and checks printed < 0 before advancing p.
limitations: Speculative: if a caller ever stored a negative pj_ssize_t slen in desc.media/desc.transport, the (pj_size_t) cast could wrap the entry-guard sum to a small value and pj_memcpy would receive a huge size_t length. No statement in this code (nor any quotable producer) can set a negative slen — parsed SDP strings carry non-negative lengths — so the trigger is not instantiated.
Not exercised: pj_memcpy with a NULL ptr and slen == 0 is formally undefined behavior but copies zero bytes; no security impact, no attacker-instantiable trigger in this code.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety or injection defect found. Attacker-influenced set/clear flag values and entry paths are consumed only via open(O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) and ioctl(FS_IOC_*FLAGS) on kernel-validated int arguments, with the fd sentinel `if (myfd < 0) return (ARCHIVE_OK);` guarding both ioctl sinks in execution order.

assumptions: __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag(-1) on open failure is a harmless no-op (callee not shown); it is followed by the `if (myfd < 0)` check before any use of myfd, so no assumption about it affects a sink.

ioctl(FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/SETFLAGS) kernel contract: writes/reads exactly sizeof(int) at the given address and validates flag values, returning EINVAL for out-of-domain bits — relied on per discipline 3 as a universally known system call.
limitations: Narrowing of unsigned long set/clear into int newflags (line: newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;) can silently drop attacker-requested flag bits above 31; worst case is a warning or silently-unapplied archive metadata, no memory corruption or privilege effect.

Fail-open flavor: when open(name) fails the function returns ARCHIVE_OK without applying requested flags (if (myfd < 0) return (ARCHIVE_OK);). If a downstream consumer of the extraction result treated ARCHIVE_OK as 'entry metadata fully applied', that could misrepresent state; no such consumer is present in the given code, so the impact is not instantiated (possible CWE-451 precursor only).

TOCTOU between file creation by the caller and open(name) here could let a local attacker swap the target; the use of O_NOFOLLOW and fd-based ioctls limits this to a same-privilege local race not exhibit-able within the given statements.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader validates the input length with 'if (length < sizeof(bh))', which compares against the size of the POINTER bh (4/8 bytes) rather than sizeof(blobheader) (>= 11 bytes). An attacker-supplied state blob as short as sizeof(void*) therefore passes the only length gate, and subsequent reads bh->totlen, bh->flags, bh->version access memory beyond the supplied buffer (out-of-bounds read), with the leaked heap bytes written into the caller-visible hdrflags/hdrversion outputs.

evidence.snippet: if (length < sizeof(bh)) {
evidence.reason: The sole bounds guard uses sizeof(bh) — the size of the pointer 'blobheader *bh' declared on line 5 — instead of sizeof(*bh)/sizeof(blobheader). It therefore only proves length >= 4/8 bytes, while the function reads sizeof(blobheader) (>= 11) bytes of header fields, leaving every header-field read unguarded.

Sinks reading bh->version and bh->flags past the validated length. Trigger (simulated): attacker blob of length 8 (64-bit) with min_version=0, hdrsize=htons(sizeof(blobheader)), totlen=htonl(8) passes line 8 (8<8 false), line 15 (totlen==length), line 23 and line 33; line 40/42 then read heap bytes at offsets ~8-10 beyond the 8-byte buffer and store them into caller-visible outputs — out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential.

assumptions: blobheader layout is not shown; it is assumed to contain at least min_version(2), hdrsize(2), totlen(4), flags(2), version(1) = 11 bytes, consistent with the fields this function reads. Under ANY layout of these 5 fields, at least one field read lies beyond offset sizeof(void*)=8, so the OOB read holds regardless of exact ordering.
'length' is assumed to be the actual size of the buffer 'data' points to (standard producer contract of this validator).
The blob/state file originates across a trust boundary (attacker-supplied file), making data/length attacker-data.
limitations: Line 41 sets *dataoffset = hdrsize (= sizeof(blobheader)) which can exceed the attacker's small length; the consuming read at that offset happens in caller code not shown, so it is recorded here rather than as a primary finding — though the same missing length bound is its root cause.
On the error path, line 18-19 prints htonl(bh->totlen), which can also read OOB for short buffers on 32-bit builds; same root cause as the primary finding.
Log messages print attacker-supplied values; no injection class beyond echoing the attacker's own bytes was instantiated.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. The only failure sentinels this code's own calls produce are checked before first use (kzalloc NULL via 'if (!a) return -ENOMEM;', dma_get_sgtable failure via 'if (ret < 0) ... return -EINVAL;'), and the only shared-state mutation (list_add on buffer->attachments) is fully enclosed by mutex_lock/mutex_unlock on every path. No attacker-derived size, index, offset, or string reaches a memory, copy, or injection sink in this code.

assumptions: dmabuf->priv (buffer) is populated by this driver at dma-buf creation time and points to a valid fastrpc_buf whose dev/virt/phys/size/lock/attachments fields are consistent; this code contains no statement documenting or enforcing it.
The DMA-buf framework calls the detach op only after the corresponding attach has returned, so no concurrent detach reads attachment->priv or a->node between 'attachment->priv = a;' and 'list_add'.
attachment is a framework-allocated, per-attachment object; attachment->priv is not shared between concurrent attach calls.
limitations: On the dma_get_sgtable error path, any scatterlist entries the callee mapped into a->sgt before failing are not released (no sg_free_table(&a->sgt) before kfree(a)) — a small resource leak, but only triggerable by an internal DMA-API/allocation failure the attacker cannot induce; robustness issue, not a security vulnerability.
The error path returns -EINVAL instead of the actual 'ret' error code — diagnostic fidelity only, no security effect.
