If a future caller could pass a dmabuf whose priv was not a valid fastrpc_buf, dereferencing 'buffer->dev' etc. would fault, but no statement in this code can produce that state and it would be a kernel-internal contract violation.

verdict.summary: The ex_substitute() implementation guards every memory/index sink reachable from attacker-influenced values: the multi-line match clamp 'if (nmatch > curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count - sub_firstlnum + 1)' precedes 'ml_get(sub_firstlnum + nmatch - 1)', the loop-top check 'if (lnum > curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count) break;' precedes 'ml_get(sub_firstlnum)', the temporary buffer is allocated from the exact expressions later copied ('new_start_len = needed_len + 50' and the 'needed_len > (int)new_start_len' reallocation guard), and the 'lastone' short-circuit ('skip_match || ... ||') prevents dereferencing a stale 'matchcol' in 'sub_firstline[matchcol]'. The only unguarded arithmetic, 'eap->line2 += i - 1' with an attacker-supplied count, can wrap the line number, but the wrapped value never reaches a memory or security sink here: the substitution loop 'for (lnum = eap->line1; lnum <= line2 ...)' cannot execute when line2 is wrapped below line1, and 'curbuf->b_op_end.lnum = line2' is gated on 'sub_nsubs > start_nsubs', which the skipped loop leaves unchanged. No primary candidate with an instantiated trigger and impact chain survives.

assumptions: eap->line1/eap->line2 are validated against buffer bounds and ordering by the ex-command dispatcher (do_one_cmd, not shown); no such precondition is quotable in the given code, so inverted ranges reaching the ':%s/\n//' join fast path are recorded as unproven.

Internal callees (vim_regexec_multi, vim_regsub_multi, getdigits, skip_regexp_ex, alloc, ml_get/ml_replace/ml_append/ml_delete, do_join, regtilde) are assumed to honor their standard Vim contracts: regexec returns in-range positions, allocation returns NULL on failure, getdigits parses a non-negative long. Their implementations are not shown.

The ex-command string is treated as operator-entered; file content under edit is treated as untrusted data that reaches this code only through regexec-derived columns, all of which are bounded as analyzed.
limitations: Signed integer overflow at 'eap->line2 += i - 1;' (long count from getdigits, e.g. ':s/p/s/9223372036854775807e') wraps line2 negative; the upper-bound clamp 'if (eap->line2 > curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count)' does not repair it. Impact chain not instantiated: the loop 'for (lnum = eap->line1; lnum <= line2 ...)' cannot run with line2 < line1, so no ml_get/index/write consumes the wrapped value, and 'curbuf->b_op_end.lnum = line2' is unreachable because sub_nsubs stays equal to start_nsubs. A lower-bound/overflow clamp on the count would be the one-line fix; recorded as a robustness gap, not a vulnerability.

'sublen' is obtained from a first 'vim_regsub_multi' call and used to size new_start, while a second call writes the substitution; a '\=' expression whose second evaluation is longer than the first could overflow new_end. This depends on the unshown callee and on an operator-authored substitution expression (not cross-boundary attacker data), so it is speculative.

joined_lines_count = eap->line2 - eap->line1 + 1 (join fast path) could underflow only if the dispatcher delivered line1 > line2; range validation is not shown and this code contains no statement producing such a range, so the trigger is not instantiated.

Multiple out-of-memory paths ('goto outofmem') are handled without double-free or use-after-free: vim_free/VIM_CLEAR NULL the pointers and regmatch.regprog is always initialized by a successful search_regcomp before any path reaching 'vim_regfree(regmatch.regprog)'; early returns before search_regcomp never call it.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new reads a 2-byte bootstrap-method count from buffer[6..7] (R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) with offset=6) without any check that the attacker-controlled attribute size sz is at least 8 bytes; the only bounds check in the function (if (offset >= sz) break;) appears later and never guards this read, producing a heap out-of-bounds read when a short attribute passes r_bin_java_default_attr_new.

evidence.reason: Root cause: offset is advanced to 6 unconditionally and R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) dereferences buffer[6..7] with no check that sz >= 8 anywhere in the function (the only sz comparison, if (offset >= sz) break;, occurs later inside the loop and never guards this read). Trigger: attacker-supplied Java class attribute with sz < 8 that yields a non-NULL attr from r_bin_java_default_attr_new (the code checks only if (attr), i.e., NULL, not size), causing a heap out-of-bounds read of the parser process.

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new is an internal callee not shown; it is assumed to return a non-NULL attr for at least some attributes with sz < 8 (its NULL/failure semantics and any internal size validation cannot be quoted from the given code).
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT is assumed to read two bytes at the given buffer offset (standard radare2 macro semantics).

r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new is assumed to bounds-check against the length sz - offset passed to it; it receives a correct in-domain remaining length because the guard if (offset >= sz) break; guarantees offset < sz at the call.
limitations: attr->size = offset can exceed sz when a returned bsm->size overshoots the remaining buffer (offset += bsm->size on line 19 with no clamp); the oversized attr->size is stored as metadata whose consumers are not shown, so downstream impact is not instantiated here.

A NULL bsm with bsm->size == 0 leaves offset unchanged for successive iterations, but the loop is bounded by num_bootstrap_methods (max 65535 from a USHORT read), so this is only wasted work, not an amplification primitive.
A ut64 wrap of offset += bsm->size returning below sz would require a ~2^64-scale size from the callee and is not exercised by any value this code's own constants produce.

verdict.summary: fname_match handles its attacker-influenced input (the filename subject 'name') safely: every use of 'name' is guarded by 'if (name != NULL)', and the allocation result 'p' from home_replace_save is sentinel-checked ('p != NULL') before its first use in vim_regexec, with exactly one vim_free(p) and no dangling pointer returned (match is only ever set to 'name' or NULL). No size, index, copy, format, command, or authz sink exists in the function. The remaining failure modes (NULL rmp, invalid rmp->rm_prog, non-NUL-terminated name) are caller/producer preconditions whose violation this code's own flow cannot instantiate, so they are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: vim_regexec(regmatch_T*, char_u*, colnr_T) consumes the subject string safely for arbitrary NUL-terminated subjects and requires a valid rmp->rm_prog; both are project-internal contracts not quotable from the given code.
home_replace_save(NULL, name) returns a heap pointer or NULL and performs only string-prefix replacement; its failure path is the NULL sentinel checked in this code.
'name' is assumed NUL-terminated by its producer (not shown); this function never writes to or resizes 'name'.
limitations: NULL rmp: 'rmp->rm_ic = p_fic || ignore_case;' and both vim_regexec calls dereference rmp without a NULL check; trigger requires an internal caller passing NULL, which no statement in this code instantiates — robustness issue, not attacker-reachable.
Invalid/NULL rmp->rm_prog: no validation before vim_regexec; a crash inside the regexp engine would require the (unshown) caller to pass an uncompilled regmatch_T — speculative per STEP 4(a).
A non-NUL-terminated 'name' would cause an out-of-bounds read inside vim_regexec, but the producer of 'name' is outside this code; the defect, if any, is at the producer.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled lengths, offsets, and output budgets consumed by this FSCTL handler are guarded in execution order by quoted checks: in_len>=1 before in_data[0] (SET_SPARSE), in_len<8 rejection plus MIN(in_len-4,SID_MAX_SIZE) before sid_parse (FIND_FILES_BY_SID), in_len!=16 and offset+length<offset wrap rejection before the 16-byte reads/writes (QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES), and max_out_len<*out_len rejection with the output buffer talloc-allocated from the same *out_len expression before the label-copy loop (GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA), whose per-iteration writes are additionally bounded by srvstr_push dest_len. The only theoretical defect, uint32 truncation of labels_data_count, requires ~10^8+ shadow-copy volumes that no statement in this code or attacker input surface can produce.

assumptions: The smbd fsctl plumbing guarantees _in_data is a valid buffer of in_len bytes and non-NULL when in_len>0 (interface contract; no statement in this code enforces it).

SMB_VFS_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA returns a num_volumes consistent with its labels array and at filesystem-snapshot scale; sid_parse, srvstr_push, push_file_id_16, and create_volume_objectid behave per their documented Samba semantics (bounded push, 16-byte writes).
sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) is a small compile-time constant, so the labels_data_count arithmetic is computed at sizes far below any overflow.
limitations: Speculative: labels_data_count = (num_volumes*2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL))+2 could truncate as uint32 if num_volumes reached ~10^8-10^9; no code path here or attacker input produces such a volume count, and the resulting allocation would fail first.

If max_out_len < 64 in FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID, the code still fills a 64-byte local buffer but clamps *out_len; the consumer copies only *out_len bytes from the 64-byte allocation, so no out-of-bounds access is instantiated (the in-code comment itself flags this as a question).

FSCTL_SET_SPARSE reads in_data[0] when in_len>=1 without a NULL check on _in_data; a NULL pointer with in_len>0 would require the caller (smbd) to violate its buffer contract, which is not producible by statements in this code.

verdict.summary: The function contains no attacker-reachable sink: the only copy with external data (kstrdup of args.name) is guarded by 'if (args.name)', and all buffer sizes are compile-time constants or stored caller-supplied values with no in-code use. The unchecked vzalloc/kstrdup return values can only yield NULL under environment-induced allocation failure, with any dereference occurring in a callee not shown.

assumptions: The declared width of args.es_pid in struct vidtv_s302m_encoder_init_args is not given; 'cpu_to_be16(args.es_pid)' could truncate if the field is wider than u16, but the value is only stored, never used as an index or size in this code.
Consistency between args.src_buf and args.src_buf_sz (that sz matches the actual buffer size) is a caller contract; no statement in this code documents or enforces it.
The args.head linked list is assumed acyclic; a cyclic list would make the while-loop non-terminating, but the list is constructed by this driver's own init code, not by external input.
limitations: Unchecked allocation: 'e->encoder_buf = vzalloc(VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ);' (and 'e->name = kstrdup(args.name, GFP_KERNEL);') do not test the failure sentinel before 'return e'. On allocation failure, a NULL encoder_buf or name escapes as a successful init and would be dereferenced later in vidtv_s302m_encode (callee not shown). Trigger requires environment/OS allocation failure that an attacker cannot induce through any input this code consumes, so this is a robustness defect, not an attacker-triggerable vulnerability.
Minor: if 'ctx = kzalloc(priv_sz, GFP_KERNEL);' fails after a successful kstrdup, 'kfree(e);' leaks e->name; a small leak on an allocation-failure path with no security effect.

verdict.summary: block_insert's allocation expression exactly matches the bytes copied in every branch (insert/append × TAB-split/non-TAB × is_short/is_MAX), negative 'spaces' is clamped to 0 before allocation, and the allocation result is NULL-checked before any write; no reachable out-of-bounds write could be instantiated from this code's own data flow.

assumptions: block_prep (not shown) sets bdp->textcol, bdp->textlen, bdp->endspaces such that textcol+textlen stays within the line and endspaces >= 0; if it could return negative endspaces, the 'ts_val - spaces' memset size and alloc term could disagree, but no statement in this code produces that value.
ml_get(lnum) returns a NUL-terminated line for lnum in [oap->start.lnum+1, oap->end.lnum]; the loop bound 'lnum <= oap->end.lnum' is the only guard on lnum.
mb_head_off(oldp, oldp+offset) with offset within the line returns a small non-negative value; the subtraction only shrinks offset consistently for both the memmove length and oldp advance.
limitations: Potential integer overflow of the alloc expression (sum of line length, spaces, s_len, ts_val) requires values near INT_MAX, which Vim's column cap (MAXCOL) and not-shown line-length limits prevent; not instantiated here.

Stale loop-carried 'spaces'/'count' when a later line takes the is_MAX append branch: traced both sides of the byte accounting; the alloc expression and the copy sequence still match exactly, so it is a style hazard, not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: set_fflags_platform guards every sink in execution order: the fd is validated ('if (myfd < 0) return (ARCHIVE_OK);') before both ioctl calls, the GETFLAGS result is tested ('if (ioctl(myfd, ...GETFLAGS..., &oldflags) < 0) goto fail;') before any read of oldflags, and cleanup closes myfd only when the fd was opened locally ('if (fd < 0) close(myfd);'). The unsigned-long-to-int flag truncation carries no memory-safety consequence, and the fail-open ARCHIVE_OK returns are graceful degradation of metadata restoration, not security-state misrepresentation. The only speculative issue is a TOCTOU/symlink race on the path-based open(name) when fd<0, whose window (file creation) lies in code not shown and cannot be instantiated here.

The XM file loader trusts attacker-controlled counts and sizes without bounds checks: rows*channum*6 overflows 32-bit int producing an undersized heap allocation that the pattern decode loop then overflows (lines 277/372-378); instr[y].size-4 underflows for size<4 causing a stack-buffer overflow in f.read (line 420); patnum is never clamped, so the pattern loop writes phead[y] past the fixed array (line 257); smp[g+s] is written past MP_MAXSAMPLES because the only bound check runs after the writes; and nbu[] (raw file bytes 0-255) indexes the 16-entry smpReloc array, and pc indexes past the patdata-sized heap buffer.

evidence.snippet: phead[y].patternData = new mp_ubyte[phead[y].rows*header->channum*6];
evidence.reason: Integer overflow (CWE-190) leading to out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787). rows and channum are attacker-controlled uwords read at lines 263 and 49 with no clamp anywhere (contrast the explicit clamps for ordnum/insnum at lines 56-59). With rows=channum=26755, rows*channum*6 = 4,294,974,150 wraps the 32-bit int promotion to 6,854, the allocation succeeds, and the decode loop at lines 301-378 writes patternData[bc..bc+5] for bc up to 4,294,974,150-equivalent cells, overflowing the buffer from cell ~1142 onward with attacker-derived slot bytes.

evidence.snippet:
header->channum = LittleEndian::GET_WORD(hdrBuff+4);
	header->patnum = LittleEndian::GET_WORD(hdrBuff+6);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: channum and patnum are read raw from the file with no upper-bound validation (no clamp like the ordnum clamp at line 56 or the insnum check at line 58), feeding both the allocation-size overflow at line 277 and the unbounded phead[y] loop at line 257.

Unsigned underflow (size<4 makes size-4 wrap to ~0xFFFFFFFC) passes a huge count to f.read targeting the 29-byte stack buffer; the only guard is 'size < 29', which does not establish size >= 4. An attacker-supplied 0.104 XM with an instrument size dword of 0 and >29 bytes remaining overflows the stack buffer with attacker-controlled file content (CWE-191/CWE-787).

patnum (attacker uword up to 65535) is never checked against the pattern array capacity — no 'patnum > MP_MAXPATNESSES' rejection exists anywhere, unlike the analogous insnum check at line 58. phead is a pre-allocated fixed array (allocated before patnum is read, so it cannot be sized for it), so phead[y].len/rows/patdata/effnum/patternData writes for y beyond the fixed capacity are out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787).

The per-instrument sample header loop writes smp[g+s] (including f.read(&smp[g+s].name,1,22) at line 567 with attacker bytes) with no bound on s+instr[y].samp before the loop. The only guard, 'if (s>=MP_MAXSAMPLES) return MP_OUT_OF_MEMORY;' at line 625, executes after s++ in a later loop, so s can be MP_MAXSAMPLES-1 entering the next instrument, and g up to 15 produces indices up to MP_MAXSAMPLES+14 — out-of-bounds heap writes (CWE-787).

nbu[] is copied raw from file bytes (line 473) with values 0-255 and used to index smpReloc, declared 'mp_sint32 smpReloc[MP_MAXINSSAMPS]' (line 4). No mask, clamp, or range check on nbu exists anywhere (the memset at line 466 zeroes values, not the index), so nbu[sc]=255 reads up to 956 bytes past the 16-entry stack array — out-of-bounds read whose value flows into the sample-number mapping (CWE-125/CWE-129). Same defect at lines 228-232 in the 0.102/0.103 path.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(slot,buffer+pc,5);
						pc+=5;
evidence.reason: pc is advanced up to 5 bytes per cell for rows*channum cells but is never compared against phead[y].patdata, the attacker-controlled size used to allocate 'buffer' at line 288. With patdata=1, rows=2, channum=1, the memcpy at line 341 (and buffer[pc] reads at line 307) read past the end of the heap buffer — out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125).

assumptions: mp_uint32/mp_sint32 are 32-bit and mp_uword is 16-bit, so mp_uword*mp_uword*6 promotes to a 32-bit int that wraps at line 277.
f.read copies up to min(count, remaining file bytes), so a huge count still overflows the destination when the attacker supplies enough file bytes.

module->phead/instr/smp are fixed-capacity arrays allocated before parsing (only NULL-checked at line 17); their capacity constants (MP_MAXPATNESSES etc.) are not shown in this excerpt — the patnum finding additionally relies on this, but the verdict rests on the self-contained integer-overflow, stack-overflow, and OOB-read findings.
limitations: hdrsize<4 wraps header->hdrsize to ~0xFFFFFFFC (line 36), producing a ~4GB allocation and 4GB memset at lines 42-43 with no NULL check on hdrBuff — attacker-inducible memory exhaustion/DoS (CWE-400), not promoted to a primary finding because the dominant impact is resource exhaustion rather than corruption.

In the MODPLUG 'text' chunk, module->allocateSongMessage(len+1) is unchecked and len+1 wraps to 0 for len=0xFFFFFFFF, followed by memset(module->message, 0, len+1) and f.read(module->message, 1, len); whether this yields a NULL/small buffer depends on the non-shown allocateSongMessage callee, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
In the 0.102/0.103 path, smpReloc entries for sc >= instr[y].samp can be read uninitialized at line 229 when samp < MP_MAXINSSAMPS (CWE-457) — the OOB index issue dominates and is reported instead.
rows*channum*6 arithmetic is technically signed-overflow UB; on every real 32-bit-int target it wraps as simulated.

verdict.summary: The only memory-access sink, p[x], is guarded by the quoted bounds check 'if (bx * lprn->nBw + x >= bpl) break;' which precedes the read in execution order and constrains the exact same byte-offset expression used to form p, with the correct >= operator — this is the fix for ghostscript bug 701785 and it is present. Remaining candidates (vertical row index not bounded against ImageBuf size, possible negative y0 from C modulo, division by zero if maxY==0, int overflow in index arithmetic) all require buffer-size, device-parameter, or caller-argument facts that are not in this code and could not be instantiated, so they are recorded as limitations rather than confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: ImageBuf's allocation size is not shown; the analysis assumes it holds at least maxY = BlockLine/nBh*nBh scan lines and that the caller keeps y0+bh within that range, which cannot be verified from the given code.
lprn->nBh, nBw, and BlockLine are set by device-parameter handling code not shown; validation of these values (e.g., nBh >= 1, BlockLine >= nBh) is assumed but unquotable here.

r, h, bx are parameters of an internal print-page helper; their concrete producing loop (which in the real gdevlprn.c derives them from bounded page-geometry loops) is not shown, so no quotable precondition constrains them in this code.
gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line(pdev) is assumed to return a valid non-negative byte count per scan line.
limitations: Vertical bounds: y0 = (r + h - bh) % maxY can be as large as maxY-1, so the row index y0+y can reach maxY+bh-2; no statement in this code bounds it against ImageBuf's size. Not confirmed because the allocation and the caller's guarantees on r and h are not in the given code (trigger precondition uninstantiated).
Negative y0: if a caller passed r + h - bh < 0, C99 '%' yields a negative y0 and p[x] would read before ImageBuf. No statement in this code produces such r,h; speculative.

Division by zero: if BlockLine < nBh (maxY == 0) or nBh == 0, 'y0 = (r + h - bh) % maxY;' or 'maxY = lprn->BlockLine / lprn->nBh * lprn->nBh;' divide by zero. Depends entirely on unshown parameter-setting code.
Potential signed int overflow in '(y0 + y) * bpl + bx * lprn->nBw' for extreme page sizes; at the required scale the ImageBuf allocation itself would fail first, and that allocation is not shown.

verdict.summary: xfrm_migrate writes attacker-derived state pointers into fixed-size stack arrays x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] and x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] inside a loop bounded by the caller-controlled num_migrate parameter, with no statement in this code bounding num_migrate, nx_cur, or nx_new to XFRM_MAX_DEPTH. With num_migrate > XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and entries matching existing states, nx_cur reaches XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and the loop writes one element past the array end (x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] = x), a kernel stack out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: The loop bound is the attacker-controlled num_migrate parameter, and nx_cur is incremented once per successful lookup with no comparison against XFRM_MAX_DEPTH anywhere in this code. When num_migrate exceeds XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and the finds succeed, the iteration with nx_cur == XFRM_MAX_DEPTH executes x_cur[nx_cur] = x, writing a struct xfrm_state pointer one element past the end of the stack array declared as struct xfrm_state *x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] (line 9). The same overflow occurs at x_new[nx_new] = xc (line 35) if xfrm_state_migrate also succeeds. No clamp, bounds check, break, or loop ceiling exists on any path.

evidence.snippet: struct xfrm_migrate *m, int num_migrate,
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: num_migrate is an int parameter of the non-static, exported xfrm_migrate (netlink XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE path), so its content is attacker-data. The only purported validation is the call xfrm_migrate_check(m, num_migrate) (line 14), whose body is not shown; nothing in the given code demonstrates it constrains num_migrate to <= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, so per last-line-of-defense analysis the bound is absent in this code.

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is the kernel constant 6; the given code declares the arrays with this size but does not show its value.

xfrm_migrate_state_find returns a non-NULL state when the attacker-supplied entry m[i] matches an existing state; this is the callee's normal success path, explicitly handled by this code's own branch at line 30, and the attacker controls the entry content needed to match.
xfrm_state_migrate returns a new state on success (relevant only for the secondary x_new overflow; the primary x_cur overflow does not depend on it).

In upstream Linux, the not-shown xfrm_migrate_check does bound num_migrate to XFRM_MAX_DEPTH; however, that enforcement is outside the given code and per the analysis rules is an assumption that cannot demote the candidate — it is recorded here, not relied upon.
limitations: The out parameter err is always assigned at line 14 before any goto out, so no uninitialized-return defect exists.
A negative num_migrate simply skips the loop (i < num_migrate fails immediately) — no wrap or under-read is triggered by it.
The restore_state cleanup helpers (xfrm_states_put/xfrm_states_delete) would also consume the over-range counts, but this is the same root cause as the primary write and adds no independent finding.

verdict.summary: __u16 truncation of stream_len and outlen/inlen causes sctp_make_reconf to allocate a far smaller chunk than the data subsequently appended via sctp_addto_chunk, producing a large heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled stream_list content (e.g. stream_num=65535: stream_len wraps 131070→65534, outlen wraps 65550→14, chunk sized 14 bytes, then 65534 bytes are copied into it).

evidence.snippet: __u16 stream_len = stream_num * sizeof(__u16);
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the product stream_num * sizeof(__u16) reaches 131070 for stream_num=65535 but is truncated to the __u16 65534 on assignment; no guard on stream_num exists anywhere in the function.
Second __u16 truncation: outlen = (16+65534) wraps to 14, so the chunk is allocated with only outlen+inlen = 14 bytes of payload capacity, decoupled from the copy lengths used later.

Sink: with stream_num=65535, out=true, in=false, the chunk holds 14 bytes (line 15) but 16 bytes are appended at line 27 and then 65534 attacker-controlled bytes from stream_list are appended here — a ~64KB heap out-of-bounds write; the if(stream_len) test checks only non-zeroness and bounds nothing. The in=true path (lines 41-42) is symmetric.

assumptions: sctp_make_reconf(asoc, len) allocates a chunk whose payload area is exactly len bytes and returns NULL on failure (standard kernel helper); the if(!retval) check therefore covers only allocation failure, not capacity.

sctp_addto_chunk(chunk, len, data) appends exactly len bytes of data to the chunk's payload area (skb_put+memcpy) without an internal bounds check against the chunk's declared size; the size/copy mismatch is created entirely in this code.

stream_num and stream_list content originate from the user-supplied SCTP reset-streams request (srs_number_streams/srs_stream_list), so their values are attacker-controlled at this function's entry surface; no caller-side cap on stream_num is quotable from the given code.
limitations: Minor: outreq.param_hdr.length = htons(outlen) publishes the truncated length (14) rather than the bytes actually appended — a protocol-consistency symptom of the same truncation, not a separate vulnerability.
A stream_num of exactly 32768 makes stream_len wrap to 0, silently dropping the stream list; this produces only incorrect behavior with no memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImageV4 only checks the ReadBlob error sentinel (count == -1) when reading pixel rows, so a truncated MAT v4 file (EOF returns count = 0, or any partial read) passes the check and the code calls ImportQuantumPixels / InsertComplexDoubleRow / InsertComplexFloatRow on a heap buffer whose contents were never read from the file and are never initialized in this code; the uninitialized heap bytes are written into the decoded image and disclosed to the party that supplied the file.

evidence.reason: The pixel-row read only rejects the error sentinel -1; ReadBlob returns 0 at EOF and partial counts on truncated files, so ImportQuantumPixels (line 170) consumes the full depth/8*image->columns buffer even though no bytes were read. Trigger instantiated: a 20-byte header declaring nRows=4, nCols=1 with EOF before pixel data yields count=0, passes the check, and uninit heap contents are committed to the output image via SyncAuthenticPixels. No length check, EOF check (only at line 200, after the loops), or initialization of pixels exists anywhere in this code.

Same missing short-read guard in the complex-pixel loop: with HDR.imagf==1 a truncated file gives count=0 (not -1), and the never-filled pixels buffer is passed as (double *) or (float *) to InsertComplexDoubleRow/InsertComplexFloatRow, importing uninitialized heap data into the image.

assumptions: ReadBlob semantics assumed standard for ImageMagick: returns number of bytes read, 0 at EOF, -1 only on error; the pixel-row consumers (ImportQuantumPixels, InsertComplex*Row) import a full image->columns-wide row from the supplied buffer without knowledge of count.

The quantum pixel buffer returned by GetQuantumPixels is assumed to be at least depth/8*image->columns bytes (sized by SetQuantumDepth from the same columns/depth at line 154) and is not initialized by any statement in this code; any zeroing inside the not-shown allocator is an unquotable contract and is not relied on.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read in the complex loop when HDR.Type[1] is 2/3/4 (buffer holds 2 or 1 bytes/pixel while InsertComplexFloatRow receives a float *): depends on the not-shown callee's consumption and on SetQuantumDepth's allocation extent, so the trigger could not be fully instantiated.

Ping path SeekBlob(image, HDR.nCols*ldblk, SEEK_CUR) at line 109 uses ldblk after digit extraction (value 0..9, the M digit) instead of an element size, so ping mode fails to skip pixel data and misparses subsequent bytes; demonstrated impact is misparsing only, not memory corruption.
status of SetQuantumDepth (line 154) is overwritten and unchecked before GetQuantumPixels; reachable only via allocation failure, not attacker-instantiated here.
(int) image->columns truncation in FixSignedValues (line 173) requires image widths > 2^31 to survive SetImageExtent; trigger not instantiated.

verdict.summary: On the ctx allocation-failure error path, out_kfree_buf releases the vzalloc()ed encoder_buf with kfree(); vzalloc memory must be freed with vfree(), so the code's own error path performs an invalid free (kernel BUG/OOPS, potential allocator corruption). No vfree()/kvfree() or any correct deallocator for encoder_buf exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
out_kfree_buf:
	kfree(e->encoder_buf);
evidence.reason: Mismatched deallocator at the sink: the pointer freed here was produced by vzalloc() at line 16, so it is vmalloc-area memory; kfree() is valid only for kmalloc/kzalloc slab objects or NULL, making this an invalid free. The path is reached solely through the code's own error handling (lines 31-33: ctx = kzalloc(priv_sz, GFP_KERNEL); if (!ctx) goto out_kfree_buf;), a state produced by this code's statements. A STEP 5 search found no vfree/kvfree, no alternate free of encoder_buf, and no slab reassignment anywhere on any path, so the defect is unguarded.

evidence.snippet: e->encoder_buf = vzalloc(VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ);
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: this single assignment is the only producer of e->encoder_buf, and every non-NULL value it can hold at line 63 is vmalloc-space memory that must be released with vfree().

assumptions: Kernel allocator semantics per discipline 3: memory from vzalloc() must be freed with vfree(); kfree() accepts only kmalloc-family slab pointers or NULL.

The error path at line 33 executes only when the kzalloc at line 31 returns NULL; whether an unprivileged attacker can force that failure (system-wide memory pressure coinciding with driver init) is an environment property assumed, not provable from this snippet.
The declared width of args.es_pid is not shown, so no truncation claim against cpu_to_be16(args.es_pid) can be anchored.
Callers of this non-static constructor are not shown; no statement in this code derives any args field from external/attacker content.
limitations: kstrdup(args.name) at line 14 trusts the caller for NUL termination (no check in this code); since this init-time constructor receives only driver-internal values and no attacker-reachable invocation exists in this code, the non-terminated-string trigger is not instantiated.
The kstrdup result at line 14 is unchecked, so e->name may be NULL; kfree(NULL) at line 66 is safe and nothing dereferences it here - benign.

The while (args.head->next) walk at lines 52-53 would spin forever on a cyclic chain or dereference a malformed head; that requires a caller to hand in a broken encoder list, which no statement in this code produces - contract issue, not instantiated.
args.src_buf and args.src_buf_sz are stored unvalidated at lines 25-26 but consumed only inside the not-shown encode callback; no memory, copy, or indexing sink on them exists in this code.
The out_kfree_e path (vzalloc failure at line 17-18) frees only kzalloc/kstrdup objects and is correct.

verdict.summary: The BootstrapMethods attribute parser bounds-checks its buffer accesses: the header read is guarded by 'if (offset + 8 > sz)' and every per-iteration use of buffer + offset is guarded by 'if (offset >= sz) break' in execution order, so attacker-controlled class-file content cannot drive an out-of-bounds access at any sink in this function.

assumptions: r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new (not shown) is assumed to validate its own reads against the size argument (sz - offset) passed to it and to set bsm->size from parsed content; this code passes only in-domain arguments (in-bounds pointer, exact remaining length), so any defect in that callee is outside this code.
r_list_newf and r_list_append are assumed not to fail except on allocation failure, which an attacker cannot induce.
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT is assumed to read exactly 2 bytes at the given offset (standard radare2 big-endian read macro), which the 'offset + 8 > sz' guard covers with margin.
limitations: When r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new returns NULL, offset is not advanced and the loop retries the identical call up to num_bootstrap_methods times (max 65535) — bounded CPU amplification only, not attacker-scalable to unbounded work; recorded as a minor robustness note, not a vulnerability.
attr->size = offset could truncate if the RBinJavaAttrInfo size field is narrower than ut64; the field type is not shown and the trigger requires a multi-gigabyte class file, so this is speculative.
buf_offset + offset can wrap ut64 with a huge bsm->size, but it is only a reported logical offset, never used as a memory access, so no security impact.

verdict.summary: cvtchar parses an attacker-supplied capability string, but every read of sp halts at or before the NUL terminator (case '\0', isdigit halting on 0, (c != '\0') tests) and every value passed to the save_char/save_string sinks is provably contained in [0,255] by the unsigned char declaration, UChar narrowing casts, and the c &= 0x1f mask; the octal accumulation 8*c + digit wraps modulo 256 (defined behavior) with no memory-safety effect. Residual risks are caller-side (len=2 past a '^' at end of string, len=0 on NUL input) and occur in code not shown.

assumptions: UChar is a narrowing cast to unsigned char; save_string and save_char are buffer-append helpers that manage dp growth and accept a char-domain argument; their implementations are not shown.
sp points to a NUL-terminated string; the caller of cvtchar consumes the returned len to advance sp; the caller's loop is not shown.
limitations: If the string ends with '^' followed by NUL, len=2 is returned and an unseen caller doing sp += len would read past the terminator — impact depends entirely on unshown caller code.
len=0 is returned when *sp is NUL; a caller loop of the form while (*sp) sp += cvtchar(sp) could stall, but the caller is not shown.

The octal arm accepts non-octal digits 4-9 (isdigit instead of an octal digit test) and values above 255 wrap modulo 256, producing an incorrect converted character value; this is a parsing-accuracy defect with no memory-safety consequence since c remains a valid unsigned char.
dp is a global whose NULL/validity and the growth behavior of save_string/save_char cannot be verified from this code; all arguments this code passes to them are in-domain.

verdict.summary: __u16 truncation of outlen/inlen in sctp_make_strreset_req: (sizeof(outreq) + stream_len) wraps modulo 65536 for large stream_num (e.g., 32767 gives outlen=14 while the true payload is 65550), so sctp_make_reconf allocates a 16-byte chunk payload but sctp_addto_chunk subsequently copies stream_len (65534) attacker-supplied bytes from stream_list into it, a massive kernel heap out-of-bounds write reachable from an unprivileged SCTP socket stream-reset request.

evidence.reason: Root cause: outlen/inlen are declared __u16, so (sizeof(outreq) + stream_len) — up to 16+65534 = 65550 for stream_num=32767 — truncates to 14, and the chunk is allocated with only SCTP_PAD4(14)=16 bytes of payload while later copies total 16+65534 bytes.

evidence.snippet:
if (stream_len)
			sctp_addto_chunk(retval, stream_len, stream_list);
evidence.reason: Sink: with stream_num=32767, out=1, stream_len=65534, the chunk from line 15 holds a 16-byte payload already filled by the line-26 copy; this call copies 65534 attacker-controlled bytes into it, a heap out-of-bounds write of ~65518 bytes. No bounds check on stream_num, stream_len, or outlen exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: sctp_addto_chunk copies exactly its size argument into the chunk's payload area and does not itself enforce tailroom bounds (not shown; standard copy semantics per discipline 3)
sctp_make_reconf allocates the chunk payload sized from its second argument (line 15) — the only sizing statement in this code
The caller allocates stream_list with stream_num __u16 entries, so the 65534-byte read from stream_list is in-bounds (the write side overflows regardless)
stream_num is derived from userspace stream-reset request data (setsockopt/SCTP_STREAM_RESET path); no kernel-side validation is quotable from this code
limitations: The line-6 truncation stream_len = (__u16)(stream_num * 2) for stream_num >= 32768 causes under-copy rather than over-copy of stream_list and a misstated param_hdr.length; not promoted since the primary overflow at lines 12/29 subsumes the impact

If sctp_make_reconf's internal skb allocation plus sctp_addto_chunk's skb_put were to include hard tailroom enforcement, the primitive degrades from heap overwrite to kernel panic (skb_over_panic) — still an unprivileged, attacker-triggered denial of service, but the exact callee behavior is not shown

verdict.summary: luaG_runerror forwards an interpreter-internal format string and CallInfo state to internal Lua helpers; no attacker-derived value reaches a sink within this code, and all candidate triggers (format-string control, NULL msg, GC stale ci) rest on callers or callees not shown.

Callers of luaG_runerror pass constant format literals and trusted varargs (standard Lua interpreter practice, not quotable here).
The Lua GC does not free the closure of the currently executing CallInfo frame (runtime invariant, not quotable in this snippet).

verdict.summary: In the NE entry-table parser, the moveable-segment branch reads an attacker-controlled 8-bit segment number (segnum, 1-255) from the file's entry table and indexes bin->segment_entries[segnum - 1] guarded only by `if (segnum > 0)` — with no upper-bound check against ne_header->SegCount (the sibling Fixed branch performs `bundle_type < SegCount`). An attacker-crafted NE file with small SegCount and a large segnum causes a heap out-of-bounds read whose value is disclosed as the reported entrypoint paddr (or crashes the parser).

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing upper-bound guard on segnum. segnum is an attacker-controlled byte read from the file's entry table (line 57) with reachable values 1-255; the only check is `if (segnum > 0)` (line 60), which constrains only the lower bound. The array's domain is established by this code's own sibling check `if (bundle_type < bin->ne_header->SegCount)` (line 64) guarding the identical `segment_entries[... - 1]` indexing in the Fixed branch — but the `else if (bundle_type == 0xff)` arm never executes it. Trigger: NE file with SegCount=1, a moveable bundle (bundle_type=0xff), and segnum=200 → `bin->segment_entries[199].offset` is a heap out-of-bounds read at attacker-chosen offset; the leaked heap value flows into entry->paddr, appended and returned as a reported entrypoint (memory disclosure), and may segfault.

assumptions: bin->entry_table, bin->segment_entries, bin->alignment, and bin->ne_header fields are populated by not-shown parsing of the same attacker-supplied NE file; their contents are treated as attacker-data per discipline 4.

r_list_get_n is assumed to return NULL for an out-of-range index (standard radare2 container accessor semantics); the code handles NULL via `s? s->paddr: 0` at line 23, so the csEntryPoint path is safe.
limitations: Reads from bin->entry_table (lines 33/38/57/59/66) are bounds-checked against `tableat + off + 4 >= r_buf_size (bin->buf)` — a different object (bin->buf) than entry_table, and `off` can exceed EntryTableLength inside the inner loop without re-check of the outer while bound. The allocation size of bin->entry_table is not shown in this code, so a concrete out-of-bounds read relative to that allocation cannot be fully instantiated here; also the moveable arm reads entry_table[off+5] (line 59) while the guard at line 42 validated only through index off+4. These are potential secondary OOB reads but rest on an unquotable allocation size.
When segnum == 0 in the moveable branch, an entry with paddr = 0 is still appended (R_NEW0 default) — a misreported entrypoint address, cosmetic/non-security output, not counted as a finding.
Entry allocation is O(file size) (off advances ≥3 per appended entry), so no attacker-scalable amplification (CWE-400) beyond input size was found.

Unchecked MALLOC result is an allocation-failure-only NULL dereference, i.e., robustness, not a security vulnerability.

verdict.summary: In _gnutls_server_select_suite, the loop 'for (i = 0; i < datalen; i += 2)' reads data[i + 1] before any even-length validation of the attacker-supplied cipher-suite list. The only odd-length guard ('if (datalen % 2 != 0) ... return GNUTLS_E_UNEXPECTED_PACKET_LENGTH;') executes later in the function, after the reads, so a malicious client sending an odd datalen (e.g. 1 byte) causes a one-byte out-of-bounds read past the buffer; the out-of-bounds byte is then compared against safe-renegotiation and fallback SCSV constants, potentially invoking _gnutls_ext_sr_recv_cs or returning GNUTLS_E_INAPPROPRIATE_FALLBACK based on adjacent memory — a misrepresentation of the peer's signaled security capabilities.

evidence.reason: The loop bound 'i < datalen' permits i = datalen-1 when the attacker-supplied datalen is odd, so 'data[i + 1]' reads one byte past the peer-provided cipher-suite buffer (e.g. datalen=1, i=0, reads data[1]). No guard before this loop rejects odd lengths or bounds i+1 against datalen. If the out-of-bounds byte matches the SCSV minor constant, _gnutls_ext_sr_recv_cs(session) is invoked and the session records safe-renegotiation support the peer never sent.

The only odd-length validation exists but is placed after the data[i + 1] reads (lines 17 and 30) and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites consumes the odd-length data, so in execution order it never protects the out-of-bounds read; the fix is to reject odd datalen before the first loop.

assumptions: server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites, _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites, and _gnutls_remove_unwanted_ciphersuites are internal callees not shown; their return values are used only under quoted 'if (ret < 0)' / 'if (ret <= 0)' checks, and whether ret is bounded by sizeof(cipher_suites)/MAX_ALGOS and even is assumed, not quotable.

GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR/MINOR and GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR/MINOR are 2-byte SCSV constants as suggested by the comments (e.g. {0x00, 0xff}); the exact values do not affect the out-of-bounds read itself.
limitations: Potential overflow of pk_algos[MAX_ALGOS] or out-of-range cipher_suites_size would require the not-shown internal callees to violate their sizing contracts (they receive sizeof/size arguments); speculative — not counted.

If the 1-byte OOB read stays within a larger surrounding allocation, the direct disclosure is limited to the value influencing the SCSV comparisons and subsequent handshake state/return value (peer-observable behavioral side channel and security-state misrepresentation), not a returned byte.

evidence.reason: Loop reads data[i+1] (also at line 30 for TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV) with only i < datalen as the bound. With attacker-supplied odd datalen (e.g. 1), the last iteration has i = datalen-1 and data[i+1] = data[datalen] reads one byte past the ciphersuite field — an out-of-bounds read. No check on datalen appears anywhere between function entry and this loop.

This is the only parity guard for datalen, and it is the correct check — but it executes AFTER the SCSV loop (lines 13-39) that already performed the out-of-bounds read, so it fails in execution order to protect the first use of data[i+1].

assumptions: data/datalen are the parsed ClientHello ciphersuite-list bytes; datalen derives from a 2-byte handshake length field, so unsigned wrap of i (i += 2) is not reachable at declared widths.

server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites, _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites, _gnutls_remove_unwanted_ciphersuites, and _gnutls_ext_sr_recv_cs are internal callees not shown; their returned sizes (cipher_suites_size <= MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE, even) are assumed in-domain and could not be verified by quoting.

Whether data[datalen] lands inside the caller's larger handshake-message allocation is caller-layout-dependent (not shown); the defect is judged at this function's own boundary contract of datalen valid bytes.
limitations: datalen == 0 and odd datalen reaching the later selection loops are rejected at lines 78-81 in execution order; those loops are guarded.
The SCSV handling (renegotiation protection and TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV) fails closed via gnutls_assert_val returns; no fail-open authz or downgrade issue found.

verdict.summary: In _gdContributionsAlloc, the cleanup path uses an unsigned int loop counter u with `while (u >= 0)`, which is always true; after `u--` the index wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF, causing an out-of-bounds read of res->ContribRow[u].Weights and gdFree() of the garbage pointer (invalid free / heap corruption) whenever any per-row allocation fails or overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) sets overflow_error.

When the first gdMalloc of Weights returns NULL (produced by line 26, checked here), the cleanup loop reads res->ContribRow[0xFFFFFFFF].Weights — an out-of-bounds read far past the ContribRow heap block — and passes the garbage value to gdFree, an invalid free (heap corruption); the loop also never terminates normally. No signedness fix, wrap test, or bound on u exists anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: u is unsigned, making the later `u--` / `while (u >= 0)` cleanup loop wrap instead of stop.

assumptions: overflow2(a,b) is an internal libgd helper (not shown) assumed to return nonzero when a*b overflows; the primary defect does not depend on its exact semantics, since a NULL gdMalloc result alone triggers the same path.
gdMalloc is assumed to be the standard libgd allocator returning a pointer or NULL; its NULL return is the failure sentinel this code explicitly handles at line 28.
line_length and windows_size are treated as attacker-data (derived from image geometry / public scaling API parameters); no documented precondition on them is quotable in this code.
limitations: The trigger requires either a gdMalloc failure at line 26 (attacker can influence the requested size via windows_size and exhaustion via many iterations of attacker-controlled line_length, but a deterministic memory-exhaustion trigger is not fully instantiated from the given code alone) or overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) being true, i.e. windows_size around 2^28 — the producer of windows_size is not shown.
Minor resource leak: on the error path (line 34 `return NULL`), res->ContribRow (allocated at line 17) and res itself are not freed.
Potential uninitialized read of Weights when overflow_error==1 was examined and dismissed: `overflow_error == 1 ||` short-circuits before the Weights access.

verdict.summary: do_i2c_md takes the display length from argv[3] via hextoul into a uint and assigns it to int nbytes with no validation; for length >= 0x80000000 nbytes is negative, and the one-sided clamp 'linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes' passes the negative value straight through, so an attacker-supplied size (e.g., -1) is passed to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read as the byte count filling the fixed stack buffer linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] — an out-of-domain size into a memory-writing call with no guard anywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Sink: linebytes sizes the read into the fixed buffer linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] (declared line 67), but the ternary clamps only the upper bound ('nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN'); with nbytes = -1 (attacker length 0xffffffff) it yields linebytes = -1, which is passed unvalidated to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read — an attacker-derived raw size into a memory-writing call, an out-of-domain length for a 16-byte stack buffer.

if (argc > 3)
			length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);
evidence.reason: Origin: the attacker-controlled argv[3] is parsed into uint length with no range check anywhere; line 65 'nbytes = length;' then converts it to int, so any length >= 0x80000000 becomes a negative nbytes that produces the negative linebytes at the sink (lines 70-76).

assumptions: DISP_LINE_LEN is 16 (stack buffer size); get_alen returns -1 on malformed address spec (its failure sentinel); hextoul parses the full 32-bit hex range including 0xffffffff.

dm_i2c_read/i2c_read are contractually 'read len bytes into buffer' operations; in U-Boot's I2C core a negative int length stored into a narrower (u16) message-length field reappears as ~65535, making the callee-side effect an out-of-bounds write past linebuf — per the call-site rule the defect stands here regardless of that internal width.
Both DM_I2C and non-DM_I2C builds were analyzed; the defect exists on each (line 73 / line 75).
limitations: alen == -1 fail-open: get_alen's error sentinel passes 'if (alen > 3)' and the DM guard 'alen != -1' merely skips setting the offset length, so a malformed address spec still produces a 'successful' dump at an unintended/default address — misrepresentation within the console user's own privilege; no memory-unsafe sink instantiated.
chip and addr are unbounded/unvalidated (truncated device selector, device-side offset only) — misaddressing of the I2C device, no host memory-safety effect shown.

Huge positive lengths (up to INT_MAX) cause up to ~2^27 I2C transactions — a slow operation self-inflicted by the console user who already controls the shell; not treated as attacker-scalable amplification.

The only check, pat->data[i][index]==-1, covers the blank sentinel but not the domain: any other negative value passes the '<0x10' branch and indexes fxColors[] out of bounds (below zero), and any value >= 0xe0 falls into the final else with no upper bound and indexes extFxColors[value-0xe0] out of bounds. } else {
            ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Text,uiColors[extFxColors[pat->data[i][index]-0xe0]]);

The pattern cell values consumed via patCache originate from an attacker-supplied song file (trust boundary), so out-of-domain effect values such as -2 or 0x1FF are within this code's input surface per discipline 4; the file-load statement itself is not shown.
noteName() return-string length is unknown (internal callee not shown); assumed short in evaluating the sprintf bound.
limitations: sprintf into static char id[32] could overflow only with extreme row/channel counts (e.g., patLen or chans near 10 digits) or an unbounded noteName() string; the quoted guard 'if (i<0 || i>=e->song.patLen) return;' bounds i only by file-controlled patLen, and no quotable bound on chans or noteName length exists — trigger not fully instantiated.

The effects loop 'for (int k=0; k<e->song.pat[j].effectRows; k++)' uses file-controlled effectRows with no check against the pattern's column width, but DivPattern's row width is not shown, so an OOB at pat->data[i][index] could not be proven.
