The trigger value is concrete, but its only consumer is the unshown ValidateIndices, so the security impact of -1 could not be instantiated from the given code; recorded as incomplete validation (CWE-191) rather than a primary finding.
The dims() > 0 check is applied only to split tensor [0]; scalar split tensors at deeper levels would be consumed inside the unshown MakeSplits — impact not instantiable here.
Positional context->input(list_size) indexing could mis-fetch inputs if the framework's input-count validation were absent; framework enforcement is not shown, so this remains an assumption.

verdict.summary: DecodeImageAPNG computes rowbytes = w * 4 and imagesize = h * rowbytes in 32-bit unsigned ints (lines 53-54). The only guard, 'if (w > cMaxPNGSize || h > cMaxPNGSize)' (line 43), bounds w and h individually and never their product, so for attacker-chosen IHDR dimensions such as 2048x524288 the product wraps (h*rowbytes = 2^32 -> imagesize = 0). 'frameRaw.p = new unsigned char[imagesize]' then allocates a 0-byte buffer while 'frameRaw.rows[j] = frameRaw.p + j * rowbytes' points every row far out of bounds. The OOB row pointers are passed to processing_data call sites (lines 174/190) for decoding (out-of-bounds write into the undersized heap block) and are dereferenced directly at 'f[4 * x + 3]' (line 114) in the frame-copy loop (out-of-bounds read whose bytes become output pixels). Secondary: delay_den is parsed from an fcTL chunk (line 147) with no zero check anywhere and divided at line 78, giving a division-by-zero crash (DoS).

evidence.reason: Root cause: w and h are attacker-controlled unsigned ints from the IHDR chunk (lines 40-41); 'imagesize = h * rowbytes' is 32-bit unsigned arithmetic whose product wraps for dimensions individually permitted by 'if (w > cMaxPNGSize || h > cMaxPNGSize)' (line 43). Instantiated trigger: w=2048, h=524288 -> rowbytes=8192, imagesize = 524288*8192 = 2^32 which wraps to 0, so 'new unsigned char[imagesize]' allocates 0 bytes while rows[j] = p + j*8192 points every row out of bounds, producing heap out-of-bounds accesses at the processing_data call sites and the f[4*x+3] read.

Consuming sink of the overflowed allocation: f = frameRaw.rows[y] = frameRaw.p + y*rowbytes lies outside the undersized (wrapped-imagesize) heap block, so f[4*x+0..3] reads out of bounds; the read heap bytes are stored into the output image pixels (information disclosure) or fault. The bounds checks on w0/h0 (lines 151-153) only guarantee y < h and x < w0, i.e. indexing inside the logical image, not inside the physical allocation.

evidence.snippet: bundle.duration = delay_num * 1000 / delay_den;
evidence.reason: Secondary confirmed defect: delay_den is parsed from an attacker-controlled fcTL chunk (line 147) with no zero check anywhere (the validation at lines 151-153 omits delay_den), so an fcTL with delay_den = 0 reaches this integer division by zero and crashes the decoding process on attacker-supplied input (denial of service).

evidence.snippet: delay_den = png_get_uint_16(chunk.p + 30);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted divisor: attacker-controlled 16-bit value read from the fcTL chunk; the value 0 passes every subsequent check in the function and is consumed as a divisor at line 78.

assumptions: cMaxPNGSize is not defined in the given code; the overflow trigger requires it to be at least 46341 (so that w*h*4 can exceed 2^32). In the project this code originates from (libjxl apng.cc) it is 8,000,000, which amply satisfies this.

read_chunk allocates chunk.p as a heap buffer whose length is chunk.size, filled from the file stream; inferred from the code's own uses (chunkIHDR.size == 25 for a 13-byte IHDR payload, chunk.size passed as the byte length to processing_data at lines 174/190, chunk.p deleted with delete[]).

processing_start/processing_finish/processing_data return 0 on success, inferred from the control flow (nonzero is treated as an error at the processing_data call sites); processing_start initializes png_ptr/info_ptr (declared uninitialized at lines 7-8), presumably via reference parameters not shown.
CHUNK.size and the CHUNK struct layout are not shown; assumed unsigned and >= 12 for any chunk.
limitations: Lines 142-149 read chunk.p[12..33] of an fcTL chunk without verifying chunk.size >= 34; a crafted fcTL with a short payload would make these heap out-of-bounds reads. Kept speculative because the exact buffer size produced by read_chunk (not shown) is an assumption.

Line 179 'png_save_uint_32(chunk.p + 4, chunk.size - 16)' underflows when chunk.size < 16, writing a wrapped ~4 billion length into the synthesized IDAT header; the size actually passed at line 181 (chunk.size - 4) stays in range, and the wrapped length is only consumed inside processing_data (not shown), so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

Line 57 'new png_bytep[h * sizeof(png_bytep)]' over-allocates (h*8 pointer elements instead of h, ~512MB for h = 8,000,000) from a ~30-byte file — resource amplification/DoS of the decoder, but bounded by cMaxPNGSize and one allocation per call.
Early returns at lines 44, 84-86 and the IEND break at lines 137-139 leak chunk.p / frameRaw.p; leaks only, no security impact beyond bounded memory retention.

verdict.summary: All variable-length memory operations in squashfs_opendir are provably guarded. The check `if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) ... goto corrupted;` executes before both `read_directory_data(dire->name, &start, &offset, dire->size + 1);` and `dire->name[dire->size + 1] = '\0';` in the same iteration with no bypass path; edge testing shows size=255 yields a 256-byte copy plus NUL at index 256, exactly fitting the SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 bytes of name space in `char buffer[sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1]`, while size>=256 is rejected by the `>=` operator. `if(dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT) ... goto corrupted;` bounds the inner loop before it begins. `dire->name` is NUL-terminated before strdup. The only unguarded use is dereferencing the unchecked `*i = read_inode(block_start, offset);` result, but a NULL return cannot be produced by any statement in the given code, so that trigger is not instantiated; no memory-safety, injection, authz, or fail-open defect is reachable.

assumptions: Struct definitions for squashfs_dir_header/squashfs_dir_entry, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT are not shown; count and size are assumed unsigned (standard SquashFS definitions), and name is assumed a trailing flexible/zero-length array so offsetof(name) <= sizeof(struct) (the buffer-fit argument holds for any layout satisfying this).

Internal callees are not shown: read_directory_data is assumed to validate (start, offset) against the directory table and return FALSE when data is exhausted (this, plus res==FALSE checks, is what terminates the outer loop for oversized declared sizes); read_inode is assumed not to return NULL; check_name is assumed to reject '/', '.', '..' per its comment; check_directory and squashfs_closedir are assumed to behave as named; MEM_ERROR is assumed to abort.
sBlk.s.directory_table_start is assumed initialized from the parsed superblock before this function runs.
limitations: Unchecked `*i = read_inode(block_start, offset);` is dereferenced at `dir->mode = (*i)->mode;` with no NULL test anywhere in the function; if the (not shown) read_inode can return NULL on malformed input, this is a NULL-dereference crash/DoS in the process unpacking the attacker's image. The trigger depends on unshown callee behavior, so it is not confirmed as a vulnerability in this code.

Attacker-derived block_start/offset/start are passed into read_inode/read_directory_data without validation in this code; any out-of-bounds access would land inside those not-shown callees, so the impact chain cannot be instantiated here.

The inner loop is bounded by dir_count rather than remaining declared size (bytes), so a directory can consume more entries than its inode declares; each entry is still fully validated, making this a parsing-robustness quirk, not a memory-safety defect.
Roughly 30-50x allocation amplification (struct dir_ent plus strdup per ~7-byte on-disk entry) is proportional to the attacker's supplied directory data and not unbounded retention.

verdict.summary: The DXF group-90 vertex count maxVertices is attacker-controlled from the parsed file and only checked with `if (maxVertices>0)`. The allocation `new double[4*maxVertices]` computes the element count in 32-bit int; for maxVertices = 1073741825 (0x40000001) the product wraps to 4, so a 4-element heap buffer is allocated while the initialization loop `for (int i=0; i<maxVertices; ++i)` (and later vertex writes guarded only by vertexIndex<maxVertices) writes up to 4*maxVertices elements — an immediate, attacker-scalable out-of-bounds heap write at i=1.

evidence.reason: The allocation size `4*maxVertices` is computed in int and overflows for attacker-supplied maxVertices > INT_MAX/4 (e.g. 1073741825 wraps the product to 4), producing a 4-element buffer; the very next loop iterates maxVertices times writing 4 elements per iteration, so `vertices[i*4] = 0.0` at i=1 is an out-of-bounds heap write, continuing for ~2^30 iterations — attacker-driven memory corruption from a crafted DXF file (group code 90).

evidence.snippet:
maxVertices = toInt(groupValue);
        if (maxVertices>0) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: maxVertices is taken directly from the parsed DXF group value; the only guard is `maxVertices>0`, which imposes no upper bound, allowing values up to INT_MAX whose quadrupled count overflows at the allocation site (line 9).

assumptions: Member types (maxVertices/vertexIndex as 32-bit int, vertices as double*) are not shown; inferred from `toInt`, `for (int i=0; i<maxVertices;`, and the index arithmetic. If maxVertices were 64-bit the overflow would require a correspondingly larger value but the same missing upper bound remains.

groupCode/groupValue are member state populated by the DXF parser from the input file; treated as attacker-data per the trust-boundary model since this function is the intake point for LWPOLYLINE group data.
Member initial values (maxVertices, vertices, vertexIndex) are set outside this snippet; assumed initialized such that group 10/20/30/42 before any group 90 hits the `vertexIndex>=0` guard.
limitations: Denial of service via huge non-wrapping maxVertices (e.g. 100,000,000 → ~3.2GB allocation): `new` throws std::bad_alloc which is not caught here; impact is an aborted parse of the attacker's own file — crash-only at equal privilege.

For values where 4*maxVertices wraps negative (e.g. maxVertices = 0x20000001), the allocation throws rather than corrupting; only the positive-wrap cases yield corruption, and they exist (e.g. 0x40000001, 0x40000002).
The index expression i*4 itself overflows int for i >= 2^29, but the out-of-bounds write at i=1 occurs long before, so this adds no separate finding.
Signed overflow is formally undefined behavior in C++; the analysis assumes the typical two's-complement wraparound observed in practice on mainstream compilers.

verdict.summary: All attacker-derived offsets (ESIL-parsed ptr, op->src[i]->delta, op->ptr) pass through explicit maxstackframe bounds checks (±8192) in both branch arms before reaching get_stack_var/r_anal_function_set_var; the backward ESIL scan is bounded by 'addr >= esil_buf + 1' and the minimum in-buffer length guaranteed by the strstr match; no memory, copy, or indexing sink consumes an unbounded attacker value. assumptions: reg and sign parameters are treated as internal-trusted: the function is static and this code contains no statement deriving them from the analyzed binary; no in-file quote documents caller contracts, so this classification rests on radare2's architecture rather than a quoted guard.

r_num_get, r_strf_var, r_str_isnumber, R_ROUND, and the sdb type-lookup helpers (r_type_func_args_type, r_type_func_args_count, r_type_func_args_name, r_type_get_bitsize, r_anal_cc_max_arg, r_anal_cc_arg) are assumed to behave as keyed/safe lookups per discipline 3; their internals are not shown.

The wrapped index reaches r_type_func_args_type(anal->sdb_types, fname, i). The impact chain is not instantiated: the callee is a string-keyed sdb lookup (not a memory/index/copy operation at this call site), and loop termination relies on the unshown callee returning NULL for the out-of-range index (the 'if (!tp) break;' arm). If fcn->bits or anal->bits were a positive value < 8, 'const int bytes = (fcn->bits ? fcn->bits : anal->bits) / 8' would be 0 and R_ROUND(sum_sz, bytes) could divide by zero; no statement in this code produces such a bits value (arch plugins supply 8/16/32/64), so the trigger is not instantiated here.

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN = 256 and struct squashfs_dir_entry ends with the name member (standard squashfs definitions; not shown in the given code). The buffer-fit arithmetic holds for any trailing-name layout, with slack if name is a fixed array.

read_directory_data, check_name, squashfs_closedir, MEM_ERROR, and TRACE are project-internal callees not shown; their semantics (e.g., table-bounds checking of the start/offset cursor, rejection of '/', '.', '..') are assumed, not verified.

If the (unshown) read_inode can return NULL on a corrupted inode, a crafted filesystem would NULL-dereference and crash unsquashfs. The trigger precondition cannot be instantiated from the given code, so this is recorded as a robustness/DoS limitation, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Raw attacker-derived directory-table cursor (start = sBlk.s.directory_table_start + (*i)->start, offset = (*i)->offset) is passed to read_directory_data with no validation in this code; any out-of-bounds consequence would occur entirely inside the unshown callee.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability. The only directly user-writable value, runtime->control->appl_ptr (settable via the mmap control page and persisting after munmap), is provably bounded by the quoted modulo 'runtime->control->appl_ptr % runtime->period_size' before use in snd_pcm_lib_write/snd_pcm_lib_writev, and the mmap_count guard diverts the mapped case. The silence-fill arithmetic (size = (8*(period_bytes - buffer_used) + 7) / width) has no in-function bounds check, but establishing an actual out-of-bounds write requires properties of code not shown (exact allocation size of runtime->oss.buffer, sample-alignment invariant of runtime->oss.buffer_used, period_ptr <= period_bytes, width/period_size != 0), so those candidates are recorded as limitations rather than confirmed defects.

The allocation size of runtime->oss.buffer is not shown; whether it equals period_bytes exactly (making the round-up silence fill potentially exceed it when buffer_used is not sample-aligned) cannot be established from the given code.

If period_bytes < buffer_used or period_bytes < period_ptr were reachable, the subtractions would underflow to huge sizes passed to snd_pcm_format_set_silence; the enforcing/producing statements are not in this code, so this is speculative.
Division by zero in '/ width' or '% runtime->period_size' would require an invalid runtime->oss.format or a zero period_size, whose validators are not shown.
Concurrent snd_pcm_oss_sync callers can race on the substream->f_flags save/restore around the DRAIN ioctl, but this only misrestores a nonblocking flag with no memory-safety or privilege impact.

verdict.summary: udf_expand_file_adinicb uses disc-derived, unvalidated i_lenEAttr/i_lenAlloc in memset/memcpy operations without any bounds check: if i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE, PAGE_SIZE - i_lenAlloc wraps and memset writes far past the mapped page; memcpy(kaddr, i_data + i_lenEAttr, i_lenAlloc) reads past the embedded udf_inode_info buffer (heap disclosure into the file page) and writes past the page if i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE; memset(i_data + i_lenEAttr, 0, i_lenAlloc) writes past the inode allocation. Trigger: crafted UDF image with an in-ICB inode declaring oversized lengths, followed by a write that expands the file.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: i_lenAlloc and i_lenEAttr are attacker-controlled (disc-image-derived) lengths/offsets with no bounds check on any path in this function. With i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE the memset size PAGE_SIZE - i_lenAlloc wraps to a huge unsigned value causing an out-of-bounds write past the kmap'd page; memcpy copies i_lenAlloc bytes from i_data + i_lenEAttr, reading past the embedded inode buffer (kernel heap data lands in the file page and is disclosed on read) and writing past the page when i_lenAlloc > PAGE_SIZE.

evidence.snippet:
memset(iinfo->i_data + iinfo->i_lenEAttr, 0x00,
	       iinfo->i_lenAlloc);
evidence.reason: Same unbounded length: memset of i_lenAlloc bytes at offset i_lenEAttr into the fixed embedded buffer of udf_inode_info writes past the inode allocation whenever the crafted disc image declares i_lenEAttr + i_lenAlloc larger than the buffer.

evidence.snippet: struct udf_inode_info *iinfo = UDF_I(inode);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: iinfo->i_lenAlloc, iinfo->i_lenEAttr and inode->i_size are populated from the mounted UDF disc image (attacker data across the trust boundary); this function performs no validation of them before using them as copy sizes and offsets.

assumptions: The on-disk inode parser that fills iinfo->i_lenAlloc / iinfo->i_lenEAttr is not shown; any bounds enforcement there is an assumption and was not relied upon — no quotable check exists in the given code.
Types assumed per the kernel UDF definition: i_lenEAttr/i_lenAlloc are 32-bit unsigned, and i_data is a fixed-size embedded buffer in udf_inode_info sized from the filesystem block size.
limitations: Restore-path memcpy at line 59 (memcpy(iinfo->i_data + iinfo->i_lenEAttr, kaddr, inode->i_size)) is an unbounded copy with attacker-controlled inode->i_size and would be an OOB write, but it is reached only when filemap_fdatawrite() returns an error (line 54); inducing a controlled writeback failure is environmental and could not be instantiated as a deterministic trigger in this code, so it is recorded as an unguarded sink with a speculative trigger.
WARN_ON_ONCE(!inode_is_locked(inode)) (line 8) documents a locking precondition but asserts nothing about data lengths and does not protect any sink.

verdict.summary: The pattern-editor effects loop is bounded only by the module-file-controlled field e->song.pat[j].effectRows; index=4+(k<<1) is never checked against the pattern row width before the accesses pat->data[i][index] and pat->data[i][index+1], so a crafted module with a large effectRows value drives an out-of-bounds heap read (and int wrap of k<<1 for very large values) in the process that opens the file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the only loop bound is the attacker-controlled song field e->song.pat[j].effectRows (loaded from the module file) and index=4+(k<<1) is never validated against the pattern row's finite width before the array access pat->data[i][index] at line 194. Second sink of the same defect: pat->data[i][index+1] is read with the unvalidated index=4+(k<<1) derived from the unbounded, file-controlled effectRows loop, both in the comparison and in the sprintf; no statement on any path bounds index+1 within the pattern row.

assumptions: e->song fields (patLen, effectRows, pattern cell data, chanShow, insLen) originate from the loaded module file and are consumed here without clamps; no bound on effectRows is visible in this code.

DivPattern row width and the patChanX/volColors/fxColors/extFxColors array sizes are internal declarations not shown; the OOB-read defect holds for any finite row width because effectRows is unbounded in the loop.
chans and patCache are caller-supplied with no precondition documentable from this code.
limitations: sprintf into static char id[32] (lines 87,118,130,155,161,195,199,203,249,251): worst case is 8 hex digits plus fixed text plus digits(i)+digits(j); overflowing 32 bytes requires i or j at ~1e9 scale (patLen/chans unbounded in this code), which would first cause OOB reads at pat->data[i][0] — the write-overflow trigger past that point is not instantiated, so it stays speculative.

patCache[j] NULL dereference, patChanX[chans]/patChanX[j] writes, and e->song.pat[j]/chanShow[j]/chanCollapse[j] reads require chans to exceed caller-side array sizes; the caller is not shown and no quotable contract or in-code producer of such chans exists.
noteName(...) returns a string of unknown length into sprintf(id,"%s##PN_%d_%d",...) (line 87); its callee semantics are not shown, so no trigger could be instantiated.

verdict.summary: update_process_times consumes only an internal timer-mode flag (user_tick) and kernel globals; no attacker-derived sizes, indices, pointers, or strings reach any sink, and all callees receive in-domain arguments.

assumptions: account_process_tick and other kernel-internal callees treat user_tick as a mode flag per kernel convention; no data-carrying attacker input reaches them via this function.

verdict.summary: Sysfs store handler correctly bounds the attacker-controlled write length: the guard 'if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) return 0;' executes before the only copy (strscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1)) and provably caps the strscpy count at the destination array size, so no out-of-bounds write, read, or injection is reachable.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a compile-time constant >= 1 (it dimensionizes drc_name in this code); its exact value is not shown.
The sysfs/kernfs framework delivers a NUL-terminated, page-sized buffer in buf — a framework contract not quotable from the given code; strscpy's write side is bounded regardless.
dlpar_add_slot (not shown) is assumed to validate the DRC name string; this code passes it an in-bounds, NUL-terminated buffer of at most MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 characters.
limitations: Behavior of dlpar_add_slot on an empty or malformed name (e.g., nbytes == 0 yields drc_name = "") cannot be verified from the given code.

Returning 0 instead of a negative error when nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a minor semantic wart (the write is silently not performed); no security state is mispresented and no impact link exists in this code.

verdict.summary: snd_pcm_oss_sync divides by 'width' at two sinks without checking that snd_pcm_format_physical_width() returned a non-zero width. For an invalid/width-less runtime->oss.format the lookup returns its unknown-format sentinel 0 (or a negative error that widens into unsigned long width), so an unprivileged user triggering SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC on /dev/dsp causes a kernel division-by-zero fault (local DoS). No guard on width exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Root cause: line 25 assigns the result of snd_pcm_format_physical_width(format) to unsigned long width with no check for the lookup's unknown-format sentinel (0 or negative error); line 30 divides by width. Trigger: an unprivileged /dev/dsp user sets runtime->oss.format to a width-less value, leaves buffer_used > 0, and invokes sync — make_ready succeeds, params_lock is taken, width = 0, and 'size = (8 * (period_bytes - buffer_used) + 7) / width' executes a division by zero, oopsing the kernel.

Second unguarded division sink: in the period_ptr > 0 arm, 'size * 8 / width' divides by the same unchecked width produced at line 25; with width == 0 the same division-by-zero fault is reachable on this alternate path. No statement on any path bounds width away from zero.

assumptions: snd_pcm_format_physical_width() returns 0 for a format with no physical width and a negative error for out-of-range formats (kernel lookup-table semantics); this sentinel is what makes width == 0 producible.
runtime->oss.format is attacker-influenceable via OSS ioctls on the same open /dev/dsp instance (ioctls implemented in code not shown); this is the input surface, not a caller contract.
snd_pcm_oss_make_ready succeeding implies a prepared runtime; runtime pointer itself is treated as non-NULL for a registered playback/capture substream.
limitations: Speculative (dismissed): modulo-by-zero at 'size = runtime->control->appl_ptr % runtime->period_size;' if period_size == 0 — period_size is set only inside the unshown snd_pcm_oss_make_ready; no quoted statement here produces period_size == 0, so the trigger precondition is not instantiated.

Speculative (dismissed): unsigned underflow of 'runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.buffer_used' (or period_ptr) producing an oversized size passed to snd_pcm_format_set_silence (out-of-bounds write). The invariant buffer_used/period_ptr <= period_bytes is maintained only in the not-shown OSS write path; no producing statement in this code violates it.

The int-to-unsigned-long widening at line 25 converts a hypothetical negative physical_width error into a huge divisor, causing an undersized (not overflowing) silence fill; no separate corruption primitive was instantiated from it.

verdict.summary: The function is a pure hash computation over a struct with a fixed-size name array. The only subscripted access, id->name[i], is provably bounded by the loop condition 'i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN && id->name[i]', which uses the array's exact declared size with a strict '<' operator and short-circuits before the read at i == NAME_MAXLEN. All hash arithmetic is on unsigned long (well-defined wrap) and the result is masked to LONG_MAX before return. No memory write, copy, allocation, or attacker-derived offset/size sink exists; no trigger is instantiable within this code.

assumptions: The caller passes a valid, non-NULL struct snd_ctl_elem_id pointer; this contract is not asserted or documented anywhere in the given code, so a NULL dereference cannot be triggered by any statement in this code and is recorded as a contract assumption.
limitations: Speculative: a caller passing NULL for id would crash the kernel context (CWE-476-like), but the trigger is only a caller contract violation not producible by this code's own flow.

Speculative: attacker-crafted IDs could collide in the returned hash, potentially lengthening traversal in the (not-shown) hashtable lookup; the impact link lies in code not given, and traversal cost is bounded by the number of existing control elements, so no attacker-scalable amplification is provable here.

verdict.summary: All sinks are guarded: the sk dereference at refcount_add is protected by `if (sk && sk_fullsock(sk))` (fixing the historical NULL-deref pattern), pskb_put is bounded by `tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)` with the correct <= operator, the frags[] write in __skb_fill_page_desc is bounded by `skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS`, the page-frag region is guaranteed by the checked skb_page_frag_refill with allocsize = ALIGN(tailen) >= tailen, and the stale esp->esph after cow is re-derived from esph_offset captured before skb_cow_data. The only unprovable preconditions (range of esp->tailen, skb_cow_data tailroom contract) originate in code not given and are recorded as assumptions.

assumptions: esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen, esp->proto, esp->esph are computed by the caller (esp6_output_tail / esp6_output), which is not part of the given code; their ranges and the invariant that fill_trailer writes no more than tailen bytes cannot be quoted here and are treated as unverifiable contracts.

skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) is assumed to honor its documented kernel contract of providing at least tailen bytes of tailroom in *trailer on success; its failure sentinel (negative return) is checked in the given code.
skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC) is assumed to guarantee allocsize bytes from pfrag->offset on true return; its failure is checked in the given code.
No concurrent writer modifies skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags or pfrag between the bounds check and __skb_fill_page_desc; the skb is single-owner on the xfrm output path.
limitations: The NULL-dereference candidate on skb->sk (the historical CVE-2017-7541 pattern in this exact function) is not a vulnerability here because the guard `if (sk && sk_fullsock(sk))` is present in the given code.

A negative or integer-overflowing esp->tailen (e.g. tailen < 0 passing `tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)` and reaching pskb_put, or ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) wrapping) is speculative: the producing computation for tailen is not in this code and no statement here can instantiate such a value.

esph_offset is computed from esp->esph - skb_transport_header(skb) under the assumption esp->esph points into the same linear skb area, set by the not-shown caller; if that contract were violated the pointer difference would be arbitrary, but no path in this code instantiates it.

verdict.summary: add_slot_store copies nbytes attacker bytes into the stack array drc_name (memcpy at line 11) without NUL-terminating it, then calls strchr on drc_name (line 13). Because the guard at line 8 only bounds nbytes (nbytes <= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1) and no statement writes drc_name[nbytes] = '\0' or zeroes the array, strchr scans past the copied data into uninitialized stack memory and can run past the end of drc_name (kernel out-of-bounds read); if a '\n' is found beyond the array, *end = '\0' at line 16 writes out of bounds. Even in the in-bounds case, dlpar_add_slot at line 18 consumes uninitialized stack bytes as the device name.

evidence.reason: Root cause: memcpy copies exactly nbytes attacker-controlled bytes into the MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN stack array but never terminates it (no drc_name[nbytes] = '\0' or zero-initialization exists anywhere in the function). Trigger: attacker supplies a sysfs write of nbytes < MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN whose bytes contain no '\n' and no NUL (e.g. 8 bytes 'mydrc00'). strchr at line 13 then scans past the copied bytes into uninitialized stack and, with no NUL guaranteed in the array, can read past drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] (kernel OOB read, CWE-125); if strchr finds '\n' beyond the array, *end = '\0' at line 16 writes out of bounds; in all branches where a terminator is absent from the input, dlpar_add_slot(drc_name) consumes uninitialized stack bytes (CWE-908). The only guard, 'if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) return 0;', bounds only the copy length, not string termination.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a positive compile-time constant >= 2 (its exact value does not affect the trigger, which works for any nbytes in [1, MAX-1]).
Whether the kernfs/sysfs layer NUL-terminates buf beyond nbytes is outside the given code and is not relied upon: memcpy copies exactly nbytes bytes, so any such terminator never reaches drc_name.
limitations: The out-of-bounds write variant (strchr finding '\n' past the array end) additionally depends on residual stack contents past drc_name lacking an earlier NUL/'\n'; the out-of-bounds read and the uninitialized-name consumption do not depend on this and are fully instantiated by the attacker input alone.

Exploitability for privilege escalation depends on kernel stack layout and compiler optimizations of strchr, which are outside the given code; the finding is classified on the memory-safety defect itself.

verdict.summary: The code uses the safe mkstemp API for its temp file, sizes the sprintf destination and the read-back buffer from the same expressions consumed by the sinks, and NULL-checks the procedure body before use. The only out-of-domain path ((int)len truncation or ftell failure with a multi-gigabyte procedure file) cannot be produced by any party across a trust boundary, since the temp file is created O_EXCL with 0600 permissions and only the operator's own editor writes to it.

assumptions: myfread (internal, not shown) is assumed fread-like: reading at most len bytes into the len+1 buffer; if it can read more than len bytes the read-back would overflow, but no statement in this code produces such a value.
omAlloc/omStrDup/omFree and si_wait are internal Singular allocator helpers; their failure behavior (e.g., omAlloc returning NULL) is not shown.

pi (procinfo*) is assumed to be a valid pointer to a procedure record loaded in the current session; the code dereferences pi->language and pi->data.s.body without a pi NULL check, but no caller can be shown to pass NULL from this code.
limitations: Integer truncation: 'long len=ftell(fp);' followed by 'omAlloc((int)len+1)' truncates len above INT_MAX and omits a ftell(-1) sentinel check; a >2GB edited procedure file would cause an out-of-bounds write at 'pi->data.s.body[len]='\0';'. Speculative: the mkstemp file has 0600 permissions, only the operator's editor writes it, and no code path produces a 2GB length or a failed ftell on this regular seekable file.
system(p) executes the EDITOR/VISUAL environment variable; this is by design the operator's own editor setting, not a cross-boundary attacker value, so no CWE-78 trigger is instantiated.
The 'else { PrintS("cannot fork\n"); }' arm is unreachable for pid==-1 because 'if (pid!=0)' captures -1; fork failure results in si_wait(&pid) on a non-existent child — robustness only.
write(f,...) return value is unchecked and the omStrDup'd editor string is never freed (memory leak) — no security impact.

verdict.summary: All sinks in this kernel interrupt-entropy routine are provably guarded: the only computed index is masked with `& 3` against a 4-element array (`fast_pool->pool[cycles & 3]`), all pool writes use constant indices 0-3, NULL `regs` is handled by an explicit ternary (`regs ? instruction_pointer(regs) : _RET_IP_`), shift-by-32 hazards are excluded by width-dependent ternaries, and every pool copy uses sizeof of the exact object passed. The only externally influenced values (irq number, cycle counter, jiffies) feed XOR entropy mixing by design and never reach an unguarded memory, index, size, or injection sink.

assumptions: get_reg(fast_pool, regs) is an internal callee not shown; assumed (per upstream Linux drivers/char/random.c) to tolerate regs == NULL and return a finite value, consistent with this code calling it exactly when cycles == 0 and possibly regs == NULL.
get_irq_regs() and jiffies/random_get_entropy() are standard kernel-internal producers returning valid pointer-or-NULL and monotonic timer values respectively.
irq_randomness is a zero-initialized per-CPU static (BSS), so fast_pool->pool and fast_pool->count start at zero; no uninitialized-read hazard.

crng_fast_load, __mix_pool_bytes, credit_entropy_bits, and fast_mix are internal callees whose sizing/counting semantics are upstream kernel functions; all arguments passed here are in-domain (sizeof-matched buffers, small integer credit).
limitations: Candidate 'fast_pool->count grows unbounded if crng_fast_load keeps failing' is a scalar counter only ever compared with >= 64 and reset to 0; it never indexes memory, so no security impact.
irq_flags parameter is unused dead code — cosmetic, not a security issue.
Potential timing/entropy-quality observations (e.g., interrupt-timing side channels) are design properties of interrupt entropy collection, not defects in the given statements.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks in esp6_output_head are guarded in execution order: the tailroom path is gated by 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)', the page-frag descriptor write by 'nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' and 'allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE' (which bounds tailen since data_len >= 0), the frag-space use by the checked skb_page_frag_refill failure path, and the cow path by the 'nfrags < 0' check on skb_cow_data. The only candidate without an in-code fix, an unsigned wrap of 'ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, ...)', requires a ~4GB paged skb that no statement in this code can produce and is not instantiable.

assumptions: esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen, esp->proto and esp->esph are populated by the in-file caller esp6_output() (not shown); tailen >= tfclen + 2 and tailen > 0 are caller contracts with no quotable enforcement in this code.
skb_page_frag_refill() is treated as a standard kernel helper that, on success, guarantees allocsize bytes of available space at pfrag->offset in pfrag->page and returns false otherwise.
skb_cow_data() is treated as documented: it returns a negative error on failure and, on success, leaves *trailer with at least tailen bytes of tailroom.
ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE, L1_CACHE_BYTES, and MAX_SKB_FRAGS are assumed to have their normal kernel definitions (page-scale frag bound, cache-line, and maximum skb fragment slot count).
limitations: Speculative (not a vulnerability in this code): 'allocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES)' can wrap unsigned int if skb->data_len + tailen exceeds 0xFFFFFFFF, which would defeat the 'allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE' check. Instantiating this requires an skb carrying ~4GB of paged data; no statement in this code produces such a value and socket send-buffer/GSO accounting observed here (refcount_add(tailen, &sk->sk_wmem_alloc)) bounds realistic skbs far below that scale.

The returned nfrags is incremented twice on the frag path ('skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags = ++nfrags;' followed by 'nfrags++;'); this matches the upstream convention where the caller treats the result as frag-count-plus-one for the linear head. No sink in this code consumes it as a memory index, so it is noted as informational only.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. All entropy-mixing sinks use fixed-size buffers with sizeof-derived lengths and constant indices (pool[0..3]); the attacker-influenced irq value reaches only an in-bounds XOR data write; the possibly-NULL regs pointer is NULL-checked at its use site (ip = regs ? instruction_pointer(regs) : _RET_IP_); width-sensitive shifts are guarded by constant sizeof comparisons; and seed is consumed only on the success path of arch_get_random_seed_long.

assumptions: Behavior of internal callees not shown (get_reg, fast_mix, crng_fast_load, __mix_pool_bytes, arch_get_random_seed_long, credit_entropy_bits) is assumed to honor their standard kernel contracts: get_reg tolerates a NULL regs (the real kernel implementation does), arch_get_random_seed_long fills seed only when returning true, and __mix_pool_bytes consumes the given length from a sufficiently large pool.
struct fast_pool is assumed to contain at least pool[4], count, and last members, matching the fixed indices and comparisons used.
limitations: Speculative: when cycles == 0 and get_irq_regs() returns NULL, regs is passed unchecked to get_reg(fast_pool, regs); a NULL dereference would occur only if the unshown get_reg dereferences regs unconditionally. The real kernel get_reg handles NULL regs, regs is not attacker-derived, and the impact chain breaks inside the callee, so this is not confirmed as a vulnerability here.
The ternary (sizeof(ip) > 4) ? ip >> 32 : get_reg(fast_pool, regs) never calls get_reg because ip is declared __u64 (sizeof always 8) — dead code, no trigger exists.

Mixing attacker-observable values (irq, jiffies, cycles) into the entropy pool is by design; XOR-based mixing with a constant 1-bit credit does not let an attacker subtract entropy, so no RNG-poisoning defect is instantiated.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks consuming positional/length data are guarded by quoted, execution-order-verified checks (len > 0 before ptr[len-1], col > 0 before ml_get_cursor()-1, col > mincol loop bound). The only unguarded flow — the '!revins_on &&' wrapper disabling the start-of-buffer check, allowing Insstart.lnum/cursor.lnum to reach 0 and u_save to receive -1 — has no trust-boundary attacker (trigger is the operator's own keystrokes/options at equal privilege) and its impact chain terminates inside unshown internal callees (ml_get(0), ml_get_buf(buf,0,TRUE), u_save(-1,·), do_join), whose behavior may not be assumed. Recorded as a robustness limitation.

assumptions: Behavior of unshown project-internal callees (ml_get, ml_get_buf, u_save, do_join, replace_pop, get_sw_value, getvcol, del_char) is not assumed; in particular no assumption that ml_get(0) or u_save(-1) reads or writes out of bounds.

Cursor and Insstart invariants (lnum within [1, ml_line_count]) are maintained by the surrounding editor framework, not by statements in this code.

Potential division by zero in 'want_vcol = (want_vcol / ts) * ts;' when p_sta && in_indent and get_sw_value(curbuf) returns 0; the non-p_sta arm is guarded by the quoted 'get_sts_value() != 0'. Even if triggered, the result is a same-privilege crash of the operator's own process.
The insert-extra-spaces loop 'while (vcol < want_vcol)' is bounded per iteration by a single column and overall by the previous character's virtual column; no attacker-scalable amplification found.

*inserted_space_p is assumed non-NULL per internal caller contract; the pointer is supplied by Vim's insert-mode key dispatch, not by external data.

Candidate: index -1 at ptr[len - 1] — rejected by quoted 'len > 0' short-circuit.

Candidate: dec_cursor() past buffer start in the do/while delete loop — rejected by quoted bottom-of-loop condition 'curwin->w_cursor.col > mincol' evaluated before each subsequent iteration's dec_cursor.
Candidate: unbounded loop in 'while (vcol < want_vcol)' — rejected: each ins_char/ins_str of a single space strictly increases vcol, terminating at want_vcol.

verdict.summary: This CLI option parser consumes only local command-line arguments. Every string sink uses a fixed format string, the index sink argv[jas_optind] is bounded by the quoted guard 'while (jas_optind < argc)', and the only size-bearing call site passes the buffer's declared bound OPTSMAX alongside the buffer ('addopt(cmdopts->inoptsbuf, OPTSMAX, jas_optarg)'). Parsed numeric values (atoi/strtoull results) are stored but never consumed by any memory, index, or injection sink within this code, so no trigger with an instantiated security impact exists here.

assumptions: jas_getopt/jas_optarg/jas_optind behave getopt-like (internal callee not shown); in particular that a missing argument to a JAS_OPT_HASARG option does not yield an option code with jas_optarg unset.
addopt (not shown) is a bounded append honoring the OPTSMAX bound passed at the call site; if it ignores that bound the overflow would be a defect in addopt, not at this call site.
badusage() terminates the process (suggested by its use after cmdopts_destroy on error paths).
cmdopts_t.inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf are declared with at least OPTSMAX bytes.
get_default_max_mem_usage() returns a sane value.
limitations: strtoull(jas_optarg, 0, 10) for --memory-limit performs no endptr/error check, so a non-numeric argument silently yields 0; whether 0 means 'unlimited' downstream is decided in code not shown — impact not instantiated here.

atoi(jas_optarg) for debug-level and cmptno can wrap/truncate (e.g. cmptno overflow to negative), but those values are consumed by image-decode/render code not given; any out-of-bounds component indexing would be a defect there.

If jas_getopt can return a HASARG option code with jas_optarg unset, atoi(NULL)/addopt(NULL) would crash — requires unprovable callee behavior, and the impact would be a crash of the user's own process at equal privilege.
Potential overflow of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf via repeated -o/-O depends entirely on the unseen addopt implementation, which receives the correct bound.

verdict.summary: On the dual-transport-stream probe path, em28xx_duplicate_dev() allocates a second em28xx device (dev->dev_next) and marks a board slot; if the subsequent em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) fails, the code jumps to err_free, which frees only dev->alt_max_pkt_size_isoc and dev. dev->dev_next is never freed or kref-released, and its em28xx_devused slot bit is never cleared. A malicious USB device that enumerates with a dual-TS em28xx VID:PID, passes the first init, then fails the second init can repeat this cycle to leak kernel memory per attempt and permanently exhaust the EM28XX_MAXBOARDS slot array, making the driver reject all devices until reboot.

evidence.reason: The error unwind path frees only dev and its alt_max_pkt_size_isoc buffer; no statement on any path releases dev->dev_next (allocated after em28xx_duplicate_dev(dev) == 0 succeeded and proven live by kref_init(&dev->dev_next->ref)) or clears dev_next's em28xx_devused slot, causing an attacker-scalable kernel memory leak and permanent slot exhaustion on repeated failed dual-TS probes.

Origin of the trigger: at this point dev->dev_next is an allocated, kref-initialized object (line 214 success check, line 215 kref_init). When the device causes this init to fail, control jumps to err_free, which frees dev while dev_next remains allocated — the missing unwind is the defect.

assumptions: em28xx_duplicate_dev allocates dev->dev_next, assigns it a devno, and sets the corresponding em28xx_devused bit (callee not shown; the object's existence and devno are evidenced by the success check at line 214 and dereferences at lines 215 and 227).

em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) can be made to fail by device-controlled behavior (I2C/register responses); the callee is not shown, but the code itself anticipates and branches on this error return.

USB core contracts: altsetting/endpoint/config->interface arrays are sized by the core to match the descriptor counts used as loop bounds (lines 58, 62, 132); probe callbacks receive non-NULL intf/udev.
card[] is sized EM28XX_MAXBOARDS (declaration not shown); INPUT(0) references a fixed-size board input array member.
limitations: usb_set_intfdata(intf, dev) at line 162 leaves a dangling interface data pointer when init fails and dev is freed at line 288; no consumer of intfdata after a failed probe is visible in this code, so a use-after-free impact could not be instantiated.

retval from media_device_register (line 281) is ignored and the function returns 0 unconditionally (line 284); a failed registration is reported as probe success, but the consumer of the failed media_dev is not shown.

Resources potentially acquired by a successful em28xx_init_dev(dev, ...) (e.g., i2c adapter registration) are not visibly unwound before kfree(dev) on the err_free path; the callee is not shown, so no use-after-free could be proven.
dev_next's em28xx_devused bit is never cleared on the error path; this is part of the same missing unwind as the primary CWE-401 finding.

verdict.summary: Integer wrap in `malloc(n1 + 1)` (and its mirror `malloc(n2 + 1)`): the length fields n1/n2 are read from the attacker-controlled PYC file into ut32 without any bound; the value 0xffffffff (get_st32 returning -1 for file bytes ff ff ff ff) makes `n1 + 1` wrap to 0, so malloc(0) returns a non-NULL chunk that passes the NULL check, and `rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, n1)` then copies up to all remaining file bytes into the zero-size allocation — a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled content. The only length check, `if (size != n1)`, runs after the overflowing copy.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: `malloc(n1 + 1)` computes the allocation size in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic; n1 is an unbounded attacker-controlled length from the PYC file (line 16). With file bytes ff ff ff ff, get_st32 returns -1, stored in ut32 n1 as 0xffffffff, so `n1 + 1` wraps to 0 and malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal chunk that passes `if (!s1)`. `rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, n1)` then writes min(n1, remaining-file-bytes) attacker bytes into the zero-size allocation: heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption). The `if (size != n1)` guard on the next line executes only after the overflowing copy and cannot prevent it. Trigger fully instantiated by a crafted PYC whose magic_int & 0xffff exceeds 62061 followed by a complex object whose first length field is 0xffffffff.

Mirror instance of the same defect: n2 is read from the attacker-controlled file via get_st32 (line 38) with no bound; n2 = 0xffffffff wraps `n2 + 1` to 0, malloc(0) passes the NULL check, and rz_buf_read copies the remaining file bytes into the zero-size s2 allocation. Triggered with a first field that is small and satisfiable and a second length field of ff ff ff ff.

Origin of the tainted value: magic_int is parsed from the attacker-controlled PYC header; any magic whose low 16 bits exceed 62061 (e.g. Python 2.5+ magic 62131) selects the get_st32 path, which decodes a full signed 32-bit length field straight from file bytes into ut32 n1 with no range validation before its first use at the malloc on line 22.

assumptions: get_st32/get_ut8 are project-internal byte-decoders not shown; assumed to return the raw 4-byte/1-byte little-endian value from the attacker-controlled buffer, with get_st32 returning a signed st32 (so file bytes ff ff ff ff yield -1, stored in ut32 as 0xffffffff). No statement in the given code documents or bounds their return range.
rz_buf_read has fread-like semantics: it copies min(len, available) bytes into the destination and returns the count copied; the write into the destination happens at/below this call site.
malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal chunk (glibc behavior), so the `if (!s1)` / `if (!s2)` NULL checks do not detect the wrapped zero size.
pyc->magic_int originates from the PYC file header parsed by the caller and is therefore attacker-controlled.
limitations: Memory leaks on error paths (lines 23-25 leak ret; lines 39-41 leak s1 and ret; lines 43-45 leak s1 and ret) are real (CWE-401) but the leaked amount per invocation is bounded by the input size, so this is not attacker-scalable amplification; it does not drive the verdict.

If rz_buf_read were to return a -1 failure sentinel, `size` (ut32) would equal 0xffffffff and the `size != n1` check would pass, making `s1[n1] = '\0'` a wild write 4 GiB past the buffer; this variant depends on unstated callee error semantics and on a ~4 GiB source for the size==n1 path, and is subsumed by the same missing bound on n1/n2.
The get_ut8 branch (magic <= 62061) is safe: get_ut8's return is width-bounded to 0-255, so malloc(n1+1) cannot wrap there.

verdict.summary: In the degenerate early-return branch (empty data or no splits), the code iterates i from 0 to num_batch_items inclusive and writes ngrams_splits_data[i] = 0, but the caller-side split-validation pass is skipped, so ngrams_splits_data[i] for i >= 1 still holds ngram-count values left by the same row being processed earlier in the second per-item ngram loop; the returned ngrams_splits tensor therefore misreports nonzero offsets for a zero-element ngrams tensor. A consumer using these offsets to slice the empty ngrams vector reads out of bounds. Root cause: the nulling loop runs to num_batch_items (i.e., splits_vec.size() - 1) instead of resetting only the valid range, while the reset path that re-zeroes the values in the normal flow (ngrams_splits_data[0] = 0; plus the cumulative loop) is not executed in this branch; no guard anywhere in the snippet prevents the stale-value leak.

evidence.reason: Trigger: with empty data (or empty splits), this branch iterates i = 0..num_batch_items inclusive and sets every ngrams_splits entry to 0. The write itself is in bounds, but it marks the tensor as all-zero only if every slot is actually reached; the reset loop's upper bound is derived from splits_vec.size() - 1 with no guard that it matches the actual logical batch count, and the branch skips the ngrams_splits_data[0] = 0 re-seed plus cumulative recomputation that the normal path performs, so any slot not covered by this loop retains the stale per-item ngram counts computed at line 65 and previously visible to the caller in the earlier per-item phase.

evidence.snippet: ngrams_splits_data[i] = ngrams_splits_data[i - 1] + num_ngrams;
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked value: this cumulative assignment writes per-item ngram counts (potentially large positive integers, including a forced 1 from the preserve_short_ branch) into ngrams_splits_data[i]. In the degenerate early-return branch these values are not recomputed or cleared (the loop that would overwrite them, lines 57-66, is bypassed), so ngrams_splits leaks nonzero offsets that point past the end of the empty ngrams tensor allocated at lines 69-74, yielding an out-of-bounds read in any consumer of the returned splits.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to return from Compute on failure (standard TF macro semantics) — quoted as the only validation mechanism present.
tensorflow::Tensor::flat<T>().data()/operator() are assumed to provide raw Eigen storage with no bounds clamping (standard TF semantics); no bounds check is present in this snippet.
get_num_ngrams(length, ngram_width) is an internal callee whose exact return value is not shown; the defect does not depend on its value — the stale-split leak occurs regardless.

The victim that consumes the returned ngrams_splits tensor (a downstream op or client reading the RT rows) is not shown; the out-of-bounds read lands there, so the security impact depends on that consumer indexing the empty ngrams tensor with the leaked nonzero offsets.
splits is assumed to be a 1-D tensor of SPLITS_TYPE; the flat<SPLITS_TYPE>() view's unchecked element access (splits_vec(i)) is in range for all i used (i <= num_batch_items = size-1).
limitations: A speculative out-of-bounds READ exists via `auto data_start = &input_data[splits_vec(i)];` (line 78) combined with `CreateNgrams(data_start, output_start, num_ngrams, ngram_width)` where `ngram_width = data_length + 2 * pad_width_` can be 0 when a row is empty and pad_width_ is 0, causing CreateNgrams to read data_start[0] — one element past the end of the (empty) row. This is in-bounds if splits are batch-major (guaranteed non-degenerate here only when data is non-empty) and reads within the flat data buffer, but it could read past the end of the flat tensor if splits_vec(num_batch_items) == input_data_size is validated — which it is (`prev_split == input_data_size` check at lines 35-38), so data_start stays within input_data bounds for non-degenerate inputs. Dismissed as in-bounds per the quoted validation; no surviving candidate.

A speculative out-of-bounds WRITE exists in the `CreateNgrams(data_start, output_start, num_ngrams, ngram_width)` call at line ~112 (preserve_short_ path) where `output_start = &ngrams_data[output_start_idx]` is taken after output_start_idx was incremented across the ngram_widths_ loop; if the cumulative count at line 65 double-counts (e.g., both an ngram-producing width and preserve_short_ add to num_ngrams while the second loop only increments output_start_idx for the widths), the output_start_idx could exceed the allocated ngrams tensor size (ngrams_splits_data[num_batch_items]). Tracing: line 65 sums get_num_ngrams over all widths and adds 1 if preserve_short_ and all counts are 0; the second loop (lines 77-105) increments output_start_idx by num_ngrams per width and writes 1 more ngram only when output_start_idx == ngrams_splits_data[i], i.e., exactly when the sum of num_ngrams was 0 — matching the +1 at line 63-64. So the total written equals the allocated total. No surviving candidate; recorded because the equivalence relies on the preserve_short_ +1 and the == comparison matching exactly.

A degenerate-branch inconsistency: when `splits_vec.size() == 0`, `num_batch_items == -1` and the nulling loop `for (int i = 0; i <= num_batch_items; ++i)` does not execute (0 <= -1 is false), so the freshly allocated ngrams_splits tensor contains uninitialized memory that is returned to the caller — a potential info leak of uninitialized heap memory via the output tensor. This is dismissed only because allocate_output for a zero-element tensor yields no readable elements (splits->shape() is empty, so the output has 0 elements); however, if splits->shape() were non-empty with size 0 this would leak uninitialized memory. Not instantiated as a trigger because splits_vec.size() == 0 implies splits->shape().num_elements() == 0, so ngrams_splits has zero elements — no bytes are readable. Dismissed.

verdict.summary: No instantiated security vulnerability. All memory/index sinks are guarded in execution order: the stack push checks 'if ( size >= MAX_STACK_DEPTH )' and NULL-checks the allocation; 'list' rejects the parse sentinel with 'if ( list < 0 )'; 'set' checks every InterpretImageProperties result before any arg1+7/arg1+9 pointer arithmetic; 'write' checks 'if ( _images == (Image *) NULL )' before cloning; the registry key buffer is sized and formatted with the same MagickPathExtent constant; and the final cleanup is double-free-safe because every branch that frees arg1/arg2 breaks immediately leaving NULL. Remaining concerns (NULL args from the dispatcher for multi-argument options such as 'set'/'print'/'read', one-shot string leaks if 'set' arguments were pre-interpreted, and internal callee semantics of ExpandFilenames/CloneImages/MagickNextImage) could not have their triggers instantiated from this code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The CLI dispatcher (not shown) supplies a non-NULL 'option' string beginning with '-' or '+' and passes non-NULL arg1n/arg2n for options declared to take that many arguments; this is the precondition under which '*option' (IfNormalOp macro) and 'arg1n' in the 'set'/'print'/'read' branches are dereferenced without local NULL checks.

ExpandFilenames(&argc,&argv) on success returns a freshly allocated argument array owning copies of the strings; this is required for 'argv[i]=DestroyString(argv[i]); argv=(char **) RelinquishMagickMemory(argv);' to be free-correct, and for the original arg1n pointer not to be freed twice by the final cleanup.

CloneImages(new_images,"-1",...) (the quoted '+clone' path 'arg1=AcquireString("-1")') interprets negative scene numbers relative to the list end inside the callee; an OOB would occur in code not shown.

InterpretImageProperties, DestroyString, RelinquishMagickMemory, AppendImageToList, and the CLIWandExceptionBreak/CLIWandExceptArgBreak macros (exception then break) behave per their documented/observed ImageMagick conventions.

MagickNextImage/MagickResetIterator iterate the wand over the image list such that the 'while (MagickNextImage(&cli_wand->wand) != MagickFalse)' loops with SetImageArtifact/SetImageProperty applied to _images operate on each image as intended; if the iterator instead walks a separate pointer, 'set' would apply only to the head image (correctness bug in callee-dependent semantics, unquotable here).
limitations: NULL-dereference candidates at 'arg1=InterpretImageProperties(_image_info,_images,arg1n,_exception)' in the 'set' branch, 'FormatLocaleFile(stdout,"%s",arg1)' in 'print', and 'argv = (char **) &arg1' in 'read' require the dispatcher to invoke a multi-argument option with missing arguments; no statement in this code produces that state, so the triggers are speculative (the top block's explicit 'if (arg1n != (char *) NULL)' guard shows the author anticipated NULL args for zero-argument options only).

The 'set' branch re-interprets arg1n/arg2n and the 'option:' sub-branch assigns 'arg2=(char *) NULL;', which would leak strings allocated by the function-top percent-escape block if 'set' did not carry NeverInterpretArgsFlag; the code comment states its arguments are not auto-expanded, the leak is at most one small string per invocation, and no corruption or scalable amplification results.

The 'argc/argv' glob expansion in the 'read' branch is only as safe as the not-shown ExpandFilenames callee; per discipline 3 its internal behavior cannot serve as a trigger producer, and the call site itself passes only a filename argument.
Same-privilege CLI invocation model: option/argument content originates from the operator's own command line, so even the speculative NULL-arg crashes would not cross a privilege boundary.

verdict.summary: No quotable defect in this code. The only index sink (argv[jas_optind]) is bounded by the quoted loop guard 'while (jas_optind < argc)'; the malloc result is checked before use; jas_optarg is non-NULL at every use because the option table declares JAS_OPT_HASARG for each argument-taking option; and the potential fixed-buffer overflow for inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf depends entirely on the internal addopt() callee (not shown), to which this code passes the explicit size bound OPTSMAX and no raw offset or unchecked size. atoi/strtoull results are stored into fields with no memory, index, or injection sink in this code.

assumptions: jas_getopt/jas_optarg/jas_optind follow the universally known getopt contract: jas_optarg is non-NULL only for options declared JAS_OPT_HASARG (declared in the quoted option table), and jas_optind stays in [0, argc].
addopt(), badusage(), and get_default_max_mem_usage() are project-internal callees whose bodies are not shown; their behavior is assumed, not verified.
OPTSMAX is assumed to match the declared size of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf in cmdopts_t; the struct definition is not shown.
limitations: Candidate (speculative): repeated or oversized --input-option/--output-option strings are appended to fixed buffers inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf via addopt(cmdopts->inoptsbuf, OPTSMAX, jas_optarg). Whether this overflows depends on bounds logic inside addopt(), which is not part of the given code; this code passes the size bound, so any defect would be in the callee. Could not instantiate the trigger within this code.

cmdopts->max_mem from strtoull(jas_optarg, 0, 10) and cmdopts->debug/cmptno from atoi(jas_optarg) are not range-validated, but no sink in this code consumes them; misuse, if any, occurs in code not given.

verdict.summary: Driver probe function for Xilinx EmacLite. All inputs originate from trusted firmware (device tree) and kernel allocation APIs; no network/peer attacker data reaches any sink. Every failure sentinel is checked in correct execution order: alloc_etherdev NULL, missing IRQ resource, devm_ioremap_resource error, of_get_mac_address error (with random-MAC fallback), and register_netdev error all route to a single safe cleanup path. The unchecked-looking MEM resource pointer is handled by devm_ioremap_resource's documented NULL contract (returns ERR_PTR(-EINVAL)) and the quoted IS_ERR check that precedes all uses of the mapping and of res->start.

assumptions: devm_ioremap_resource follows its documented kernel API contract: it returns IOMEM_ERR_PTR(-EINVAL) without dereferencing a NULL resource argument; the IS_ERR check at the call site then covers all subsequent uses.
Device tree / DTB content is trusted firmware configuration, not attacker data across a trust boundary per discipline 4.
Modern kernels hash %p pointers in dev_info output; on ancient kernels this would leak a fixed kernel address once per boot.
limitations: C1: platform_get_resource(ofdev, IORESOURCE_MEM, 0) result is not locally NULL-checked before devm_ioremap_resource; only safe because of the callee's documented NULL handling — a robustness hardening opportunity, not an exploitable defect, and the DTB source is trusted firmware.
C2: dev_info prints lp->base_addr via %p and ndev->irq — potential pointer disclosure in dmesg on kernels predating %p hashing; fixed constant per boot, no attacker-scalable retention.
C3: return value of xemaclite_mdio_setup is ignored; failure yields a PHY-less device, degradation with no security effect.
C4: ndev->irq assignment narrows resource_size_t to int; only reachable with a malformed trusted DTB, not attacker data.

verdict.summary: This 4-line plugin accessor checks its two pointer arguments with rz_return_val_if_fail(bf && bf->o, NULL) and then only clones an internally-built list. The single unguarded dereference (bf->o->bin_obj used as qo->fixups without a NULL check on qo) has no trigger instantiable from this code, and the only callee receives a plain internal list pointer, not attacker-derived sizes, offsets, or indices. No memory, injection, or trust-boundary sink is reachable with a concrete trigger.

assumptions: rz_list_clone(qo->fixups) is an internal radare2 helper not shown; its NULL-input behavior and clone semantics are assumed benign (returns NULL on NULL input) and cannot be verified from the given code.
bf->o->bin_obj is assumed to be set to a valid QnxObj by the plugin's load routine (not shown) whenever bf->o is non-NULL; no statement in this code enforces that contract.
limitations: C1 (speculative): if a load path exists where bf->o is non-NULL but bf->o->bin_obj is NULL, line 4 dereferences qo->fixups with qo == NULL, crashing the process (CWE-476-style NULL dereference). The precondition is not produced by any statement in this code, and the impact would be a crash of the same-privileged process parsing the file, so it is recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.
C2 (not instantiated): if rz_list_clone fails or returns NULL, the return value propagates to the unseen caller; the caller's handling is not shown, so no impact chain can be established here.

verdict.summary: In ga_concat_shorten_esc(), the run-counting loop advances s += clen using the byte length measured once at p (clen = s - p), while its guard *s != NUL checks only a single byte. When the string ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte whose raw fallback value equals the decoded codepoint c, mb_ptr2char(s) compares equal, s += clen steps past the NUL terminator, and the while condition dereferences *s out of bounds, producing an unbounded heap over-read (crash/DoS, and a count of adjacent bytes leaked into the printed message when the run exceeds 20).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop guard '*s != NUL' bounds only the byte at s, but the advance 's += clen' moves clen bytes, where clen was measured once at p (line 21) and never re-verified against the character actually matched at s. Trigger: str = {0xC3,0x83,0xC3,0x00} gives c=195, clen=2; at s=&str[2] the truncated lead byte 0xC3 falls back to raw value 195 == c, so s += 2 jumps past the NUL to &str[4]; the next '*s' evaluation is an out-of-bounds heap read that keeps scanning until a non-matching byte or a segfault.

evidence.snippet: ga_concat_shorten_esc(garray_T *gap, char_u *str)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: str is a content-carrying parameter of this non-static display helper (Vim displays attacker-influenced strings such as file names and option values); its byte content, including a trailing truncated multibyte lead byte, directly instantiates the out-of-bounds trigger in the run-counting loop.

assumptions: mb_ptr2char_adv/mb_ptr2char (Vim macros, not shown) decode the character at the pointer, advance by its byte length without ever reading past a NUL, and return the raw first byte for illegal/truncated sequences (utf_ptr2char fallback) — the trigger depends on this documented Vim behavior.
ga_concat/ga_concat_esc grow the gap array and escape non-printable bytes; their internal bounds handling is not shown.
NUMBUFLEN is large enough for the '%d' rendering of an int (line 32 uses vim_snprintf bounded by NUMBUFLEN).
Strings fed to this display helper (option values, file names) are attacker-influenced in the Vim trust model.
limitations: The else branch (lines 37-38) advances p by only 1 instead of clen, so multibyte characters are reprocessed and their continuation bytes emitted as escaped garbage — a display-correctness/misrepresentation bug, but the output is a diagnostic message only and non-printables are escaped, so no security impact was instantiated.
same_len is a plain int; overflow requires more than 2^31 consecutive identical characters (>4 GB string) — not instantiated.

The length of the out-of-bounds scan depends on adjacent heap contents; the actual crash site and any disclosure depend on the allocation layout, but the first OOB read at &str[len+1] is unconditional once the trigger string is displayed.
NULL str is correctly handled by 'if (str == NULL)' returning early (lines 10-14).

verdict.summary: cmdline_insert_reg() performs no memory copies, allocations, or string assembly; the only index assignment (ccline.cmdpos = new_cmdpos) is provably clamped to [0, cmdlen] by the quoted two-stage guard ('if (new_cmdpos >= 0)' followed by the min-clamp 'if (new_cmdpos > ccline.cmdlen) ... else ...'), and the register/expression inputs are character codes passed to internal callees, not raw offsets or sizes. No unguarded security sink exists in this code.

assumptions: Semantics of internal callees not shown are assumed standard: plain_vgetc() returns a character code, get_expr_register() returns a register name or ESC, cmdline_paste() performs its own register validation and buffer sizing, putcmdline()/redrawcmd() are display-only. If any of these mishandles its input, the defect lies in that callee, not at any call site here (no raw size/index/pointer is passed).

Keystrokes are treated as the operator's own input in a local editor session; even under the broader attacker model, the character code c is never used as a memory size, offset, or pointer in this code.
limitations: new_cmdpos is a global set by set_cmdline_pos() (not shown); while its value could be arbitrary, the quoted clamp in this function bounds the resulting ccline.cmdpos to [0, ccline.cmdlen] on every path, so the risk is contained here.
Recursive CTRL-R '=' entry is blocked by the quoted guard 'if (ccline.cmdfirstc == '=' || cmdline_star > 0)'; no residual issue found.

verdict.summary: Kernel timer-tick accounting routine. Its only input, user_tick, is a kernel-internal 0/1 flag; every sink it reaches (accounting callees and a wrapping per-CPU PRNG state add) accepts the full reachable value domain, so no bounds, NULL, injection, or authz precondition can be violated by any reachable value.

assumptions: Internal callees (account_process_tick, rcu_sched_clock_irq, scheduler_tick, run_posix_cpu_timers, irq_work_tick) are not shown; their semantics are assumed per discipline 3, and all arguments passed to them (a 0/1 flag or none) are in-domain scalars, not raw offsets/sizes/indices.
user_tick is produced by the kernel tick layer outside this snippet; its reachable content is the flag domain {0,1}, which is in-domain for every sink here.
limitations: net_rand_state (prandom) is a non-cryptographic PRNG; mixing jiffies-derived values cannot weaken a security property it never provided, so no weak-randomness finding applies.

this_cpu_add executes in IRQ context per the in-code comment ('this timer irq context must be accounted for as well'); no cross-CPU or preempted per-CPU access is reachable, so no race candidate is instantiated.

verdict.summary: The destructor deletes four member pointers with appropriate NULL guards (`if (player)` line 4, `if (mixer)` line 11) and `delete` on a possibly-null `listener` is a defined no-op. No attacker-controlled data enters the function, so no tainted value reaches any sink. Latent lifetime concerns exist (conditional `removeDevice` at line 6-7, freeing `player` while `mixer` may reference it; `delete[]` form on `audioDriverName`), but every impact chain requires callee or constructor code not shown and cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: Semantics of `mixer->removeDevice(player)`, `mixer->isActive()`, and `mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player)` are not shown; it is assumed removeDevice does not free `player` and does not free `mixer`.

Members `player`, `mixer`, `audioDriverName`, and `listener` are initialized by this class's constructor/methods (not shown); correct pairing of `new[]` with the `delete[]` on line 14 cannot be verified from the given code.
`mixer` is assumed not to be owned or referenced by external code beyond this destructor.
limitations: Speculative use-after-free: if `mixer->isActive()` returns false or `mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player)` returns true, `removeDevice` is skipped and `delete player;` (line 8) runs while `mixer` may still hold the pointer. Impact requires mixer (or its destructor, line 12) or an external holder to dereference the stale pointer — none of that is shown in this code, so the trigger's impact is not instantiated.
Speculative double-free: if the not-shown `removeDevice` implementation took ownership of `player`, lines 7-8 would double-free it; callee body not available, so not provable.
Speculative allocation-form mismatch: `delete[] audioDriverName;` (line 14) is only correct if the not-shown allocation used `new[]`.
No attacker-data input exists at this entry point (destructor, zero parameters), so no candidate could be triggered by an external party.

verdict.summary: TOCTOU race in pxa3xx_gcu_write: the free-list availability check `if (!priv->free)` is performed outside the spinlock, but the buffer is taken from the list later under the lock (`buffer = priv->free;`) with no NULL check on `buffer` before `priv->free = buffer->next;` dereferences it. A concurrent write() can consume the last free buffer between the check and the take, leaving `buffer == NULL`, causing a NULL pointer dereference in kernel context while the spinlock is held — a kernel oops and a permanently deadlocked device, a local denial of service.

evidence.reason: Sink: `buffer` is taken from the free list under the spinlock and immediately dereferenced via `buffer->next` with no NULL check. A concurrent invocation of this handler can empty the free list between the unlocked check at line 21 and this critical section, so `buffer` is NULL and `priv->free = buffer->next;` is a NULL dereference executed while holding priv->spinlock (oops + permanent deadlock of the device). Trigger fully instantiated by two concurrent write() calls with one free buffer.

Origin of the defect: the only availability check of the free list is executed outside the spinlock (and wait_free wakers are not serialized against the take), so it does not constrain the value later read under the lock at line 31; the check is not re-validated inside the critical section on any path.

assumptions: PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS equals the number of words in buffer->ptr, per the code comment 'Last word reserved for batch buffer end command' and the check `if (words >= PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS)`; if the array were smaller, line 49 would be an OOB write, but nothing in the given code indicates that.
Semantics of the internal callee pxa3xx_gcu_wait_free are not shown; the confirmed race trigger uses only the non-wait path (line 21 condition false), so the finding does not depend on them.
The device node's permissions gate which local users can reach the handler; any user able to open the device for writing is the attacker.
limitations: `int words = count / 4;` truncates a 64-bit size_t: on an LP64 build, count ≈ 0x300000000 yields words = -2^30, which passes the `words >= PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS` check (negative), `words * 4` wraps to 0 so copy_from_user succeeds with n=0, and `buffer->ptr[words] = 0x01000000;` writes ~4 GB out of bounds — a severe OOB write. However, this driver targets 32-bit PXA3xx ARM where count/4 ≤ 0x3FFFFFFF is always positive, so the trigger is platform-dependent and was not counted as primary.
`BUG_ON(priv->ready_last == NULL)` could in principle fire if ready/ready_last became inconsistent, but no path in the given code produces that state; speculative.
Non-atomic `priv->shared->num_writes++` and `num_words += words` are statistics only (acknowledged by the comment) with no security effect.

verdict.summary: ex_substitute's memory sinks (mch_memmove/STRCAT/ml_get/indexing) are covered by quoted guards that hold in execution order: the nmatch clamp against ml_line_count bounds multi-line fetches, the lnum-vs-line_count break bounds sub_firstline fetches, allocation failures branch to outofmem, and copycol=0 in the new_start finalize block (plus re-derivation from regmatch.endpos[0].col after multi-line swaps) re-establishes the column invariant on every path that advances sub_firstline to a different buffer line, so no reachable state feeds a stale or negative copy_len to (size_t)copy_len in mch_memmove.

assumptions: vim_regexec_multi reports \zs-adjusted startpos[] and endpos[] columns within the matched lines (documented Vim regex engine semantics); out-of-range endpos columns are not produced by the engine.
ml_get/ml_replace/ml_append/ml_delete maintain the ml_line_count invariant this code's clamps rely on.
getdigits on a digit string returns a non-negative value; the given code additionally rejects i <= 0 before use.
vim_regsub_multi returns the replacement length consistent with what it later writes at new_end.
limitations: joined_lines_count = eap->line2 - eap->line1 + 1 can be negative if a backwards range reaches this function; range validation lives in the Ex address parser (not shown, unquotable), so the trigger could not be instantiated from this code's own flow.
needed_len (int) could overflow only with multi-gigabyte single lines, beyond any scale the code as written can reach; speculative.
Text-property paths (adjust_prop_columns, adjust_props_for_split) and do_join, u_inssub, u_savesub semantics are internal callees not shown; no defect was provable at their call sites.

The stale-copycol candidate (negative copy_len cast to size_t in mch_memmove) was simulated through both a do_all and a do_count trigger; in every reachable ordering the finalize block's copycol = 0 or the post-swap re-derivation executes first, so it was dismissed as unreachable rather than guarded-elsewhere.

verdict.summary: This is PHP module-init code executing once at extension load. It consumes no attacker-derived data: all inputs are compile-time constants, static tables, and engine/library contracts. The sole NULL-able value (logh) is guarded by 'if (logh)' before dereference, and the memcpy size is sizeof of the destination struct type copied from the engine's own standard handler struct. No trust boundary is crossed and no memory, injection, or authz sink is reachable.

assumptions: zend_get_std_object_handlers() returns the engine's static zend_object_handlers struct — an engine contract relied on for the memcpy source; this function is not the last line of defense for engine-internal data.
php_snmp_object_handlers is a static zend_object_handlers large enough for the copy, per the memcpy size argument taken from that type.
limitations: netsnmp_register_loghandler may return NULL on allocation failure at module load; the quoted 'if (logh)' guard makes this harmless (robustness only, no security impact, not attacker-inducible).
php_snmp_properties is a persistent hash initialized here; its destruction in MSHUTDOWN is not shown, but no attacker-reachable defect is visible in this function.

verdict.summary: The only input, 'size', is bounded by 'if (unlikely(size > MAX_RW_COUNT)) return NULL;' before its only use, the kvmalloc call. The guard checks the exact variable, in bytes, with the correct operator, on the only path, in execution order; no arithmetic can wrap and no other sink exists. kvmalloc's documented NULL-on-failure and ZERO_SIZE_PTR-on-zero behaviors are handled by contract with callers not shown.

assumptions: MAX_RW_COUNT is the standard kernel constant (INT_MAX & PAGE_MASK, ~0x7ffff000); the comparison therefore caps accepted sizes at approximately 2 GiB.
kvmalloc(0) returns ZERO_SIZE_PTR and kvmalloc returns NULL on failure — standard documented kernel allocator semantics per discipline 3.
limitations: Callers of this static helper must NULL-check the returned pointer (kvmalloc failure or the size cap path both return NULL); a dereference defect could exist in caller code not shown, but no harmful use occurs in this snippet.
Allocation sizes up to MAX_RW_COUNT (~2 GiB) remain reachable; this is the kernel's intended cap and is memcg-accounted via GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT, so no unbounded amplification was instantiated.
