verdict.summary: sctp_setsockopt_auth_key validates the user-supplied key length against the full option length instead of the bytes remaining after the struct sctp_authkey header: the guard 'if (authkey->sca_keylength > optlen)' permits sca_keylength == optlen even though the key begins at offset 6 of an optlen-byte kmalloc buffer, so the key copy performed via sctp_auth_set_key reads up to 6 bytes past the allocation (into an adjacent slab object) — an unprivileged-triggerable kernel heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Sole guard on the attacker-controlled key length compares sca_keylength to optlen — the total allocation size including the 6-byte fixed header (sca_assoc_id[4] + sca_keylength[2]) that precedes sca_key — instead of the remaining capacity optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey). With sca_keylength == optlen (e.g. 126 with optlen 126) the check passes, so the key region spans offsets [6, 6+optlen) of an optlen-byte object, overrunning it by up to 6 bytes.

Origin of the mismatch: the buffer is sized and filled with exactly optlen total bytes, yet the user-supplied sca_keylength copied into it at offset 4 may be as large as optlen, so the key starting at offset 6 cannot fit. The over-domain value flows to sctp_auth_set_key(sctp_sk(sk)->ep, asoc, authkey) at line 35, which copies sca_keylength bytes from authkey->sca_key, reading past the end of this allocation.

assumptions: struct sctp_authkey (Linux UAPI header, not shown): __s32 sca_assoc_id at offset 0, __u16 sca_keylength at offset 4, flexible __u8 sca_key[] at offset 6, sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) == 8; sca_keylength is the byte length of sca_key.

sctp_auth_set_key (upstream, not shown) allocates a key of sca_keylength bytes and memcpy's sca_keylength bytes from authkey->sca_key; this code passes the attacker-derived length that exceeds the in-allocation capacity, so the OOB read is a defect at this call site regardless of where the copy lands.
sctp_auth_enable defaults to 1; if a deployment disables it, the function returns -EACCES before the sink.
limitations: A negative optlen is not rejected by 'optlen <= sizeof(struct sctp_authkey)' (int promoted to size_t) but kmalloc() then fails on the huge converted size and returns -ENOMEM before any copy — robustness only, no out-of-bounds access.
Passing asoc == NULL to sctp_auth_set_key (endpoint-wide key when sca_assoc_id == 0) is the documented upstream semantic; no raw size or index is passed at that call site.

The at most 6 leaked bytes become shared-key material and are not directly observable by the attacker; practical disclosure would require distinguishing HMAC output, so impact is bounded to the out-of-bounds read itself.

verdict.summary: The UTF-8 decode size is computed as (size_t)(p - parser->end), which is always negative inside the loop (guaranteed by 'while (p < parser->end)') and wraps to a SIZE_MAX-scale size_t, removing the decoder's only bound. An SMTP peer sending a line whose last byte is a UTF-8 lead byte (e.g. 0xF0) at parser->end-1 makes uni_utf8_get_char_n read continuation bytes past parser->end; if they decode validly, p += nch moves p past end, causing further OOB reads at *(mp-1) and in i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) (leaking past-buffer bytes into cmd_params), and poisoning parser->cur = p beyond the buffer for subsequent parsing.

evidence.snippet:
nch = uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, (size_t)(p - parser->end),
					  &ch);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the length argument is the inverted pointer difference. The loop guard 'while (p < parser->end)' guarantees p < parser->end, so 'p - parser->end' is negative and the (size_t) cast wraps it to a near-SIZE_MAX value, so uni_utf8_get_char_n reads continuation bytes past the line buffer. Trigger: SMTP peer sends a command line ending in a UTF-8 lead byte (e.g. 0xF0) at parser->end-1; the decoder OOB-reads up to 5 bytes past parser->end, and on valid continuation bytes 'p += nch' sets p past end, leading to OOB reads in the trim loop ('*(mp-1)') and in i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp), and to parser->cur being stored beyond the buffer.

assumptions: uni_utf8_get_char_n(buf, max_len, chr) decodes at most max_len bytes, returning bytes consumed, 0 for a sequence truncated within max_len, -1 for invalid UTF-8 — inferred from its name/signature and the code's handling of nch == 0 and nch < 0; the defect does not depend on details beyond 'max_len bounds the read', which is the very bound the wrapped argument destroys.
The SMTP command line content between parser->cur and parser->end originates from a network peer (this is an SMTP command/AUTH-response parser), so line bytes are attacker-data.
limitations: max_size == 0 disables the length check ('if (max_size > 0 && ...)'); if 0 means 'unlimited' by configuration convention this is intended, otherwise it is a hardening gap, not a memory-safety defect.

The OOB read is bounded by the maximum UTF-8 sequence length (~6 bytes) per trigger, but repeated lines and the poisoned parser->cur = p (past end) allow repeated/amplified out-of-bounds reads on subsequent parse passes.

verdict.summary: mkiss_close() tears down the ldisc-private structure safely as written within this snippet: the NULL guard 'if (!ax) return;' covers every later dereference of ax; the detach under disc_data_lock plus 'if (!refcount_dec_and_test(&ax->refcnt)) wait_for_completion(&ax->dead);' orders the teardown behind any refcount-holding users; kfree of rbuff/xbuff and free_netdev occur strictly after unregister_netdev (which by documented kernel semantics guarantees no further netdev callbacks), and kfree(NULL) is a no-op. Every candidate defect (UAF against receive_buf/write_wakeup, NULL ax->dev at netif_stop_queue/free_netdev, unreached completion, double close, refcount underflow) requires a value or a racing context produced only in sibling functions (mkiss_open/mkiss_get/mkiss_put) that are not part of the given code, so no trigger could be instantiated here.

assumptions: mkiss_open (not shown) sets tty->disc_data to a struct whose refcnt is initialized to at least 1 and whose 'dead' completion is initialized; the refcount_dec_and_test in this code depends on that unshown initialization.

mkiss_get/mkiss_put in sibling callbacks (mkiss_receive_buf, mkiss_write_wakeup) are assumed to refcount_inc under disc_data_lock and complete(&ax->dead) on the final put; this is the standard 6pack/mkiss ldisc pattern but the sibling code is not given and cannot be quoted as a guard.

mkiss_open (not shown) guarantees ax->dev is non-NULL whenever disc_data is set; no statement in the given code can produce a NULL ax->dev, so the free_netdev/netif_stop_queue sinks cannot be failed by any value this code creates.

The tty core serializes ldisc open/close and calls close at most once per ldisc instance, so a second invocation of mkiss_close (which would take the 'if (!ax) return;' arm anyway) is not reachable from this code.

unregister_netdev is relied on per its documented netdevice-API semantics: after it returns, no further driver callbacks (start_xmit/ndo_stop) run, which orders the subsequent kfree(ax->rbuff)/kfree(ax->xbuff)/free_netdev safely against concurrent transmit.
limitations: Potential use-after-free/race against mkiss_receive_buf / mkiss_write_wakeup / mkiss_xmit would require that those sibling callbacks fail to take a refcount (or that xmit is not flushed by unregister_netdev). Neither the racing user nor the post-free dereference exists in the given code, so the trigger is speculative and could not be simulated.
A hang at wait_for_completion(&ax->dead) would require a refcount holder that never drops its reference; no such holder is created by any statement in this code.

A NULL dereference at netif_stop_queue(ax->dev) or free_netdev(ax->dev) would require ax->dev == NULL, whose only possible producer (mkiss_open) is not shown and produces no such value in the given code.

verdict.summary: In do_arg_all(), the second loop indexes the argument list with AARGLIST(alist)[i] at the do_ecmd() call using i bounded only by count, which is clamped once (before the loop) to the stale pre-loop value opened_len. Autocommands fired inside the loop by do_ecmd()/win_split() can shrink (or free) the argument list — a possibility the code itself documents ('ARGCOUNT may change while doing this, because of autocommands') and guards against in the first loop ('i < alist->al_ga.ga_len'), but the second loop never re-checks ga_len. A BufReadPost/BufNewFile autocmd running ':argdel' or ':args' reduces ga_len below i, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (use-after-free read if ga_data was freed) whose garbage aentry_T contents (ae_fnum/ae_fname) are dereferenced by alist_name() and passed to do_ecmd(), yielding wild memory reads and a crash in the operator's Vim process from attacker-influenced configuration/data.

evidence.snippet:
(void)do_ecmd(0, alist_name(&AARGLIST(alist)[i]), NULL, NULL,
		      ECMD_ONE,
		      ((buf_hide(curwin->w_buffer)
			   || bufIsChanged(curwin->w_buffer)) ? ECMD_HIDE : 0)
						       + ECMD_OLDBUF, curwin);
evidence.reason: The sink: AARGLIST(alist)[i] indexes alist->al_ga.ga_data with i up to count-1, where count was clamped before the loop to the stale opened_len. No statement in this loop constrains i against the current alist->al_ga.ga_len, even though do_ecmd itself (and win_split above) fires autocommands that can shrink the arglist mid-loop (e.g. ':argdel' in a BufReadPost autocmd), producing a heap out-of-bounds read — and a use-after-free read if ':args' freed ga_data — whose garbage ae_fnum/ae_fname are dereferenced by alist_name() and consumed by do_ecmd().

Origin of the faulty bound: count is clamped to opened_len (captured at entry from the pre-loop ARGCOUNT), while the code's own comment acknowledges ARGCOUNT can change during the loop via autocommands. The clamp executes once before the loop, so in execution order it cannot see arglist shrinkage caused by do_ecmd()/win_split() autocommands; the only in-loop ga_len guard in the function (line 84 'if (i < alist->al_ga.ga_len') belongs to the first, window-closing loop and never executes for the sink at line 252.

assumptions: ARGCOUNT expands to curwin->w_alist->al_ga.ga_len and AARGLIST(alist)[i] expands to alist->al_ga.ga_data[i] per standard Vim macros.

alist_name() dereferences aep->ae_fnum / aep->ae_fname (standard Vim semantics, characterizable callee), so an out-of-bounds aentry_T read yields dereferenced garbage and a wild pointer passed to do_ecmd().

Trigger requires an autocmd (e.g. BufReadPost running ':argdel *' or ':args') that resizes the argument list; autocmds are plugin/user configuration reachable with attacker-supplied content per Vim's documented threat model, and the code itself documents that autocommands change ARGCOUNT during this function (lines 48-50, 177).
limitations: Counter imbalance: line 232 '--autocmd_no_enter;' followed by 'continue' at line 240 (win_split FAIL) skips the compensating '++autocmd_no_enter' at line 258, possibly leaving the autocmd-suppression counter skewed so WinEnter/BufEnter events fire where suppressed; trigger edge value (split failure exactly at i == count-1 with tab_drop_empty_window) is narrow and no security impact beyond unsuppressed autocmds was instantiated.
opened[i] accesses were verified safe: line 44 'opened = alloc_clear(opened_len);' sizes the array from the same bound that limits i (lines 82, 196 via the clamp at lines 178-179).
new_curwin dereference at line 104 is NULL-guarded by line 103 'if (new_curwin != NULL)'.
The out-of-bounds access is a read primitive; no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds WRITE was instantiated, so severity is assessed as medium rather than high.

The same unvalidated index is also forwarded to createStreamForEntry(index).

The symlink target `originalFilePath` is read verbatim from the attacker-controlled entry data stream and passed to File::createSymbolicLink with no containment validation against targetDirectory. The only symlink guard in the function (`followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no && hasSymbolicPart(...)`) is skipped when the caller selects FollowSymlinks::yes, so a subsequent archive entry whose path traverses the attacker-created link (e.g. 'lnk/authorized_keys' after a link 'lnk' -> '/home/user/.ssh') is written via FileOutputStream through the link, escaping the extraction directory (CWE-59).

assumptions: entries.getUnchecked is JUCE's explicitly unchecked array accessor; the bounds-checked form is not used at line 3. No jassert or range check on `index` exists in the given code.
hasSymbolicPart and createStreamForEntry are project-internal callees not shown; their behavior is assumed per JUCE semantics (directory-walk symlink detection, entry-stream construction).
isAChildOf is assumed to perform lexical path-containment resolution as in the JUCE implementation it belongs to; the check at line 16 blocks classic '../' zip-slip within this code.
limitations: Zip-bomb / unbounded decompression (line 57, `out << *in`) writes attacker-scalable uncompressed data with no size cap (CWE-400) — noted but not treated as the primary finding since severity depends on deployment disk constraints.

The CWE-59 chain requires the operator to invoke extraction with FollowSymlinks::yes; with FollowSymlinks::no the hasSymbolicPart check blocks traversal through archive-created links, though the attacker-directed symlink itself is still created unvalidated.

The line 3 out-of-bounds read requires a caller passing an index outside [0, entries.size()); per the analysis framework this parameter is the attack surface of an exported function, but no such caller is shown in the given code.

verdict.summary: In QEMU's Cadence GEM gem_transmit, the guest-controlled TX fragment length is copied into s->tx_packet, but every copy is preceded in the same loop iteration by the bound check 'tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet)' whose break arm skips the copy; the operator, variables, units and execution order were verified, so the classic oversized-descriptor heap overflow (CVE-2021-3409 shape) is not reachable in this version. Remaining candidates (descriptor-length/array-size and num_priority_queues clamps in not-shown helpers, potential infinite descriptor walk, uninitialized desc on failed DMA read) could not have their triggers instantiated from this code and are recorded as limitations/assumptions.

assumptions: gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) returns at most sizeof(s->tx_packet); the mask/assert enforcing this lives in the not-shown remainder of the file (it reads the guest-writable GEM_DMACFG TX buffer-size field), so this bound is an assumption for this snippet — but no statement in the given code produces a value exceeding the buffer either, so no trigger can be instantiated.
gem_get_desc_len(s, false) returns <= DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS (real code: 2 or 4 words for TX vs. a 6-word array); not quotable here.
s->num_priority_queues is clamped at realize time to the size of s->tx_desc_addr[]/queue arrays; the clamping statement is not in this snippet.
gem_get_tx_desc_addr / gem_get_tx_queue_base_addr return addresses derived from guest-writable registers but consumed only through address_space_read/write, which tolerate arbitrary hwaddr values.
address_space_read on unassigned memory fills the destination with zeros, so a bogus descriptor address leads to the 'tx_desc_get_buffer == 0' break rather than unbounded behavior.
limitations: Unbounded while loop: if a descriptor with used==0, last==1, wrap==1 sat in memory whose write-back is silently dropped (ROM or write-ignoring MMIO), the used-bit set via address_space_write would never persist and gem_transmit would loop forever, hanging the emulator under BQL. The precondition (write-dropped memory containing a favorable descriptor pattern) is not produced by any statement in this code, so the trigger is speculative here; if instantiated in a real board it would be a guest-triggered DoS (CWE-400/CWE-835).

If the first descriptor address_space_read fails, uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] is used uninitialized by tx_desc_get_used(desc); consequences are confined to a branch decision in the guest's own emulation with all copies still bounded by the quoted guard — robustness only.

The 'TX descriptor too large' break path leaves p and total_bytes advanced into the next priority-queue iteration without resetting them; the quoted per-iteration bound check still prevents any overflow, so this is behavioral oddity, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. The only attacker-length-sensitive sink, the memcmp against the table cache key, is guarded by an exact length-equality check on the same conjunction in execution order; all failure sentinels (tdc_acquire_share NULL, my_malloc NULL, mdl_ticket NULL, db.str NULL) are checked before first use on every path, and the retry_share loop is bounded by a timeout-protected wait.

assumptions: get_table_def_key returns a key/key_length consistent with table_list->db/table_name; it is a project-internal callee not shown, but its output is used only after the length-equality guard at the memcmp.

Under MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK, table_list->mdl_request.ticket is non-NULL — a caller contract documented by the comment 'Grab reference to the MDL lock ticket that was acquired by the caller'; no check exists in this code.
check_stack_overrun, tdc_wait_for_old_version, and open_table_get_mdl_lock behave per their documented internal semantics (return nonzero/failure sentinel on failure).
DBUG_ASSERT statements are debug-only and document internal invariants, not runtime guards.
limitations: A NULL mdl_ticket dereference (mdl_ticket->get_deadlock_weight() / table->mdl_ticket= mdl_ticket) is possible only if an internal caller sets MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK without having acquired table_list->mdl_request.ticket; this trigger cannot be instantiated from this code or from attacker-supplied SQL content.

Infinite retry_share looping would require tdc_wait_for_old_version to return success repeatedly without the flushed share ever being replaced; no statement here instantiates that state, and the wait is timeout-bounded.
Tables reached via the locked-tables path are assumed to have non-NULL table->file; a NULL file would require a state this code never produces.

verdict.summary: ha_maria::drop_table passes the caller-supplied table path 'name' — a data-carrying parameter of a non-static handler invoked for client DROP TABLE — directly into maria_delete_table_files() with no validation of any kind: the only nearby statement, DBUG_ASSERT(!file || file->s->temporary), constrains 'file', not 'name', and is compiled out in release builds. An attacker-influenced name containing traversal components therefore reaches a file-deletion routine unconstrained, allowing deletion of files outside the intended data directory.

evidence.snippet: (void) maria_delete_table_files(name, 1, MY_WME);
evidence.reason: Sink: the raw, unvalidated attacker-influenced path string 'name' is handed to the table-file deletion routine. No check on any path in this code constrains 'name' (no separator/'..'/canonicalization/emptiness check, no error arm; the DBUG_ASSERT on line 3 constrains only 'file'). Instantiated trigger: caller-controlled name such as "./db/../../secret/data" passes through untouched (assert no-op in release, ha_close() does not touch name) and is consumed as the deletion path, destroying attacker-chosen files outside the data directory — root cause: missing path validation at the deletion call site (CWE-22).

evidence.snippet: void ha_maria::drop_table(const char *name)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: 'name' enters as a content-carrying parameter of a non-static storage-engine handler called to service a client DROP TABLE. This code documents, asserts, or checks no precondition on 'name' (the only assert, line 3, is about 'file'), so its content is attacker-data per the handler-parameter rule.

assumptions: maria_delete_table_files() is a project-internal callee not shown; from its name and call context it is taken to delete the files for the table path given as its first argument (analogous to unlink/remove). The arguments 1 and MY_WME are taken as an error-verbosity level and a 'report errors' flag.

name is treated as attacker-controlled content because it is a data-carrying parameter of a non-static handler method and no precondition on it is documented or checked in the given code; the SQL-layer identifier restrictions that exist in the real MariaDB parser are not present here and therefore cannot serve as a guard.
file and file->s are handler-internal state; DBUG_ASSERT is a debug-only assertion compiled out in release builds.
ha_close() is taken to close the open handler, returning a status int that this code discards via (void).
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of file->s at line 3 (file non-NULL with s NULL) is speculative: no statement in this code and no attacker-data parameter instantiates that internal state; recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.

The ignored return value of ha_close() (line 4) followed by unconditional deletion has no demonstrated security impact link inside this code (no corruption, bypass, or disclosure step is shown); recorded as robustness.

Real-world exploitability depends on whether the unshown SQL resolution layer permits separator/traversal characters in the resolved name; that enforcement is not quotable from the given code, so it was not used to dismiss the candidate, but it does bound the confidence of the finding.

verdict.summary: raptor_xml_writer_start_element_common allocates the nspace_declarations heap array with a budget of attribute_count+1 entries (plus declared namespaces and xml:lang), but the attribute loop writes up to TWO entries per attribute (a namespace declaration plus the attribute qname), so any element whose attributes require namespace declarations writes struct nsd entries past the end of the heap buffer (heap out-of-bounds write, CWE-787). The dedup loop also uses element->attributes[j] instead of element->attributes[i], producing an out-of-bounds read of the attributes array once nspace_declarations_count exceeds attribute_count (CWE-125) and defeating dedup. Additionally, the xml:lang block sizes its buffer for the unescaped language length and hands the escape function a (pointer, length) window starting at buffer+10 with limit buf_length, extending past the buf_length+1 allocation, so any escapable character in attacker-controlled xml:lang causes further heap out-of-bounds writes.

evidence.reason: The allocation budget counts only 1 entry per attribute, but the attribute loop below writes up to 2 entries per attribute (namespace declaration plus qname). With attribute_count=2, an element name in an out-of-scope namespace and two attributes in distinct out-of-scope namespaces, nspace_max_count=3 while the loop produces 5 entries: writes at indices 3 and 4 are heap out-of-bounds writes.

Sink of the heap overflow: this unconditional per-attribute write uses nspace_declarations_count, which already includes an extra namespace-declaration entry per attribute; no check anywhere in the code compares nspace_declarations_count against the allocated nspace_max_count, so with 2 attributes needing namespace declarations the writes at indices 3 and 4 land past the 3-entry heap array. Simulated trigger: name->nspace out of scope, attributes[0]/[1] in distinct out-of-scope namespaces -> entries 0..2 in bounds, index 3 out of bounds.

Index confusion: the dedup loop iterates j over nspace_declarations_count but indexes element->attributes[j] (should be [i]). Once nspace_declarations_count exceeds attribute_count (2 attrs: count reaches 3 at i=1), element->attributes[2] is an out-of-bounds read of the attributes array, dereferenced via ->nspace. The typo also defeats duplicate detection, worsening the overflow.

The buffer is sized for the UNESCAPED language length (buf_length+1 = lang_len+12 bytes), but the escape call is given pointer p=buffer+10 with limit buf_length (lang_len+11), a window extending to buffer+lang_len+21, i.e. 9 bytes past the allocation. Simulated trigger: xml:lang="x\"y" gives lang_len=3, buf_length=14, malloc(15); the escaped output x"y is 8 bytes written at buffer[10..17], so bytes 15..17 are out-of-bounds writes, followed by OOB writes of the quote and NUL at bytes 18-19 via the unchecked *p++/*p.

assumptions: raptor_qname_format_as_xml and raptor_namespace_format_as_xml return a malloc'd string or NULL; the NULL return is checked at lines 32, 61, 73 and 99 (quoted) before any use.

raptor_xml_escape_string behaves like a characterizable escape-into-buffer-with-length function: with a non-NULL buffer it writes escaped output (up to its length limit) starting at the given pointer and returns bytes written; this underpins the xml:lang finding, whose (pointer,length) window defect exists at the call site regardless of the callee's truncation policy.
nstack is non-NULL in the namespace-serializing configuration this function exists for; all write blocks are nstack-guarded so a NULL nstack cannot reach the sinks.
element->name and element->attributes are non-NULL when attribute_count>0, consistent with the code's own dereferences.
struct nsd is a plain struct of declaration pointer, length and nspace pointer, so each OOB entry write corrupts adjacent heap memory with attacker-influenced pointer and length values.
limitations: Sign/width confusion: for(i = 0; i < element->attribute_count; i++) compares unsigned i against int attribute_count; a negative count would wrap to a huge unsigned bound and cause OOB reads of element->attributes, but no statement in this code produces a negative attribute_count, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

The RAPTOR_MALLOC result at line 112 is not NULL-checked before memcpy at line 116; this is only reachable on allocation failure an attacker cannot induce, so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The qsort comparator raptor_xml_writer_nsd_compare and the format/escape callees are not shown; the OOB-write findings (entries 1-3) do not depend on their internals, only the xml:lang finding relies on the characterizable escape-function semantics recorded above.

If the escaping of xml:lang were ever zero-length or the callee refused to write on overflow, the xml:lang overflow would not occur; the undersized nspace_declarations overflow remains fully instantiated regardless.

verdict.summary: In sftp_mkdir, if any of the chained calls buffer_add_u32/buffer_add_ssh_string/buffer_add_attributes/sftp_packet_write fails (peer-induced write failure or OOM), the error arm frees buffer and path, and control then falls through to the unconditional ssh_buffer_free(buffer)/ssh_string_free(path) at the end of the block, double-freeing both heap objects and corrupting the client process heap.

evidence.reason: The error arm at lines 31-34 frees buffer and path but has no early return, so execution falls through to lines 35-36 which free the same pointers again. Trigger: a remote SFTP peer closes the transport (or OOM occurs) so that sftp_packet_write at line 31 returns < 0; lines 32-33 perform the first free, lines 35-36 the second free of both objects — a double free (heap corruption). The missing guard is an early return (or else) after the frees in the error arm; it appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: sftp_dequeue(sftp, id) is assumed to match replies by request id and return NULL when no matching reply is queued; its internals are not shown.
ssh_buffer_free/ssh_string_free are assumed to be free()-style wrappers (universally known semantics of deallocation).
limitations: The while (msg == NULL) loop can consume unbounded server-supplied packets if a malicious server keeps sending non-matching replies, but the loop exits when the transport fails (sftp_read_and_dispatch < 0) and the consumption is bounded by the attacker's own connection, so it is not promoted to a CWE-400 finding.

The double free's most deterministic trigger is a peer-closed connection causing sftp_packet_write to fail; an OOM-only instantiation depends on environment, though the allocation chain at lines 28-31 is inside this code.

verdict.summary: BMP reader hardening checks cover all memory sinks: allocation is sized from the same bytes_per_line/columns expressions consumed by each bpp conversion loop (recomputed equal-or-smaller for cases 1,4,8,16,24,32 and the 32-bit alpha prescan), ReadBlob counts are equality-checked against the allocated/expected lengths, number_colors is bounded by GetBlobSize and 1<<bits_per_pixel, and dimension/allocation failures return via SetImageExtent/ResourceLimitError paths. The residual discarded IsValidColormapIndex return status cannot be graded because the sanitization (or lack of it) and the actual colormap subscript both occur in unshown callees (IsValidColormapIndex, SyncImage).

assumptions: IsValidColormapIndex (unshown internal callee) is assumed to sanitize or at least write *target on failure; this cannot be quoted from the given code — its discarded return status means the colormap index reaching SetPixelIndex/SyncImage is not provably in range from this code alone.
SyncImage and DecodeImage semantics (bounds behavior of colormap subscripting and RLE output writing) are unshown and treated as in-domain.
SetImageExtent is assumed to enforce pixel-count/resource limits for pathological column counts; its limits depend on unshown policy configuration.
limitations: Discarded validation status: in the 4bpp and 8bpp loops, (void) IsValidColormapIndex(image,(ssize_t)*p,&index,exception) ignores the failure return, and index is never initialized in this function; if the unshown callee does not write a safe value on failure, an attacker file with number_colors < pixel byte range (e.g., colors=2, pixel 0xFF) stores an out-of-range colormap index that SyncImage (unshown) would subscript. Trigger value is produced here, but the memory-unsafety link exists only inside unshown callees — speculative.

Potential bytes_per_line integer wrap (columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel+31) requires 32-bit size_t with columns ≥ ~2^27.6 and multi-hundred-MB allocations plus a ≥33MB blob to pass the length/GetBlobSize check; allocation failure (AcquireVirtualMemory NULL → ResourceLimitError) precedes any use — speculative.

Case 1 sets index 0/1 with no IsValidColormapIndex call while image->colors may be 1 (number_colors=1 passes the '<16 && > 2' check); harm again requires the unshown SyncImage to subscript without validation.

verdict.summary: push_pipe is a kernel-internal helper whose every memory sink is guarded: ring-slot writes are bounded by the pipe_full loop condition, the fast-path len extension is bounded by 'left -= PAGE_SIZE - off; if (left <= 0)' (off + size <= PAGE_SIZE, exact at left == 0), size is clamped to i->count and rejected when 0, and buf->flags is explicitly zeroed. No attacker-instantiable trigger exists within this code; all residual candidates depend on contracts of the not-shown data_start() or its callers.

assumptions: data_start(i, &iter_head, &off) is a project-internal callee not shown; its contract (iter_head indexes the buffer being filled, 0 <= off < PAGE_SIZE, and buf->len == off for the fill-target buffer) cannot be quoted and is treated as an assumption.

Callers (copy_page_to_iter_pipe etc., not shown) are assumed to pass per-call chunk sizes bounded well below SSIZE_MAX so that 'left = size' cannot go negative, and to maintain 0 <= i->iov_offset < PAGE_SIZE.

pipe_full(head, tail, max_usage) is assumed to require head - tail < max_usage, and the pipe core is assumed to maintain max_usage <= ring_size with ring_size a power of two, making '& p_mask' a valid free-slot test.

Exclusive write access to the pipe during ITER_PIPE fill (no concurrent producer advancing pipe->head) is assumed to be enforced by surrounding splice/readv locking not shown; the code reads pipe->tail once into p_tail, which is conservative for fullness.
limitations: Candidate: if a caller could produce i->iov_offset > PAGE_SIZE, 'left -= PAGE_SIZE - off' would underflow and the caller's subsequent page write at that offset would be out-of-bounds; no statement in this code produces such an offset, so the trigger is not instantiated.

Candidate: if i->count could exceed SSIZE_MAX, 'left = size' would be negative and 'buf->len = min_t(ssize_t, left, PAGE_SIZE)' would store a huge unsigned length; the import path that could set such a count is not shown.

Candidate: a race between a concurrent consumer advancing pipe->tail and the stale p_tail captured at function entry; the stale value only makes pipe_full more conservative, and no interleaving is exhibited in this code, so no memory-safety effect is provable here.
Allocation failure (alloc_page returning NULL) merely shortens the returned byte count (return size - left) with no security effect.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable security defect found. All memory, length, NULL, and lifetime sinks are protected by quoted, execution-order-verified guards: db.str NULL check before use, cache-key length equality (== key_length) before memcmp, explicit !share sentinel check returning before err_lock (preventing NULL deref and double-release), and checked my_malloc result. The sole unguarded use — mdl_ticket= table_list->mdl_request.ticket with no NULL check in the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK branch — is gated by an internal server flag and ticket produced by the server's own pre-locking code, not by attacker input, so its trigger is not instantiable from this code's input surface.

assumptions: get_table_def_key(table_list, &key) returns a key buffer of at least key_length bytes and key_length consistent with the key buffer; this internal callee is not shown. Even if it violated this, the memcmp is additionally bounded by the quoted guard 'table->s->table_cache_key.length == key_length' on the destination operand.

tdc_acquire_share on success returns a fully initialized TABLE_SHARE/TABLE with non-NULL ->file; the DBUG_ASSERT(table->file != NULL) is debug-only, but no statement in this code can produce a table with NULL file on a success path.
set_partitions_as_used(table_list, table) returns a valid mysql error code or 0; internal callee not shown.
table_list->alias.str is non-NULL for parser-produced TABLE_LIST entries; it is used only as a NUL-terminated string in my_strcasecmp/my_error, never as a length.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference of mdl_ticket at 'mdl_ticket= table_list->mdl_request.ticket;' and subsequent 'mdl_ticket->get_deadlock_weight()' when flags contains MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK but the caller never acquired the ticket. No NULL check exists on that branch (the check 'mdl_ticket == NULL' only guards the non-HAS_MDL_LOCK branch). Trigger is speculative: the flag and the ticket are produced only by internal server locking code, not by any attacker-controlled input in this code's surface.

The 'goto retry_share' loop can repeat if the table version keeps changing (rolling FLUSH TABLES by another privileged session); each iteration waits via tdc_wait_for_old_version, so this is not attacker-scalable unbounded amplification, only a potential wait under privileged concurrent DDL.
DBUG_ASSERT invariants (!table_list->table, table->file != NULL, pushed_cond == NULL) are debug-build only; no release-build check exists, but no path in this code instantiates their violation.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_block_allocate, when the bitmap scan finds a zero bit at or beyond 'size', the code jumps to 'out' without calling kunmap(page), leaking the kernel mapping acquired by 'pptr = kmap(page);' on every such call. Since size/offset and the bitmap content derive from a mountable (attacker-crafted) HFS+ image, a crafted filesystem (e.g., extent offset >= total_blocks, or zero tail bits in the last partial word) triggers this path on every allocation attempt, causing unbounded retention of scarce kmap slots on CONFIG_HIGHMEM systems (denial of service).

evidence.reason: The 'out' label only executes mutex_unlock and return start; the page mapped by 'pptr = kmap(page);' (line 22) is never unmapped on this path. Trigger: crafted image with size=100, offset=100, *max=8 and a zero bitmap word at curr: scan finds bit at start=100 >= size, jumps to out, leaking the kmap mapping; repeatable per allocation request (attacker-scalable resource retention).

evidence.snippet: pptr = kmap(page);
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked resource: the kernel mapping acquired here is released only at lines 57, 110, and 134; the found->start>=size->out path (lines 79-81) bypasses all three.

assumptions: read_mapping_page of a page at/beyond the allocation file's EOF returns a zero-filled page rather than an error (standard page-cache behavior); the trigger also works without it when the last in-file partial word has zero tail bits.
kmap/kunmap semantics per the kernel: on !CONFIG_HIGHMEM/64-bit builds kunmap is a no-op and the leak has no effect; the DoS impact is specific to 32-bit highmem systems.

size, offset, *max and bitmap content are attacker-data: they derive from on-disk HFS+ metadata of a mountable image, and this non-static function is an intake point with no documented range precondition in the given code.
limitations: Integer overflow: '(size + 31)' in the end computations (lines 29, 71) wraps for size >= 0xFFFFFFE1, underestimating 'end' and skipping the tail scan; combined with 'offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS' (line 58) wrapping to 0, the termination check 'if (offset >= size)' fails and the scan restarts from page 0, returning wrongly-located (CWE-190) allocations. All memory accesses remain page-in-bounds; the consequence is on-disk metadata inconsistency consumed by code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
'HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max;' (line 136) can underflow the u32 free-block count when the on-disk count is inconsistent; consequences land in allocation checks not shown in this code.
'*max' is left untouched on the early-return and bitmap-full paths; callers must treat start == size as the failure sentinel — a caller contract not shown.

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry builds the extraction target path directly from the attacker-controlled zip entry filename (line 14) without rejecting '../', absolute, or drive-letter paths, allowing a malicious archive to write or overwrite arbitrary files outside targetDirectory (Zip Slip); additionally, the symbolic-link branch passes unvalidated entry content as the link destination to File::createSymbolicLink with overwrite=true, enabling creation/replacement of symlinks at attacker-chosen locations pointing to attacker-chosen targets.

evidence.snippet: auto targetFile = targetDirectory.getChildFile (entryPath);
evidence.reason: Root cause / sink: entryPath comes from the zip entry filename (attacker-controlled) with only an isEmpty() check (line 11); no validation rejects '..' segments or absolute paths before getChildFile. Trigger: an archive entry named '../../../home/user/.bashrc' yields targetFile outside targetDirectory, which is then deleted (line 29) and overwritten with attacker content via 'FileOutputStream out (targetFile); out << *in;' (lines 46, 51), instantiated end-to-end from the zip content alone.

Origin of the tainted path: the archive entry filename is consumed directly (only backslash-to-slash normalization on non-Windows; raw, including absolute 'C:\...' forms, on Windows), establishing the trust-boundary crossing that feeds the line-14 sink.

evidence.snippet:
if (! File::createSymbolicLink (targetFile, originalFilePath, true))
            return Result::fail ("Failed to create symbolic link: " + originalFilePath);
evidence.reason: Secondary sink: originalFilePath is read verbatim from the decompressed entry stream (line 38) with no validation, and createSymbolicLink is invoked with overwrite=true, so an attacker-chosen symlink is created (replacing any existing file) at the possibly-escaped targetFile pointing to an attacker-chosen destination — an arbitrary link/overwrite primitive (CWE-59).

assumptions: File::getChildFile and File::createSymbolicLink are assumed to follow standard path-resolution semantics (relative '..' components resolve upward; an absolute argument names that absolute path), which is their documented JUCE behavior.

The zip entry metadata (filename, isSymbolicLink, fileTime) is produced by the ZipFile parsing layer not shown, but its content originates from the archive and is consumed here without further validation.
limitations: entries.getUnchecked (index) (line 3) is an unchecked accessor; an out-of-range index supplied by the caller would cause an out-of-bounds read/crash inside the not-shown container, but the index-supplying party is the same-privilege caller whose own process crashes — robustness issue, not a security vulnerability in this code.
Disk-space consumption from 'out << *in' (line 51) is bounded only by the archive content and is inherent to extraction; no separate amplification defect was instantiated.
On Windows (JUCE_WINDOWS), the filename is used raw (line 6), so backslash-based traversal forms also reach the sink unchanged; exploitation via that branch is identical to the simulated trigger.

verdict.summary: The size argument to uni_utf8_get_char_n is (size_t)(p - parser->end), a negative pointer difference (p < parser->end per the loop guard) converted to a SIZE_MAX-scale value instead of the remaining length (parser->end - p). A remote SMTP client can send a command whose last buffered byte is a multi-byte UTF-8 lead byte with no CRLF yet; the decoder is then authorized to read bytes past parser->end. If the past-end (stale/uninitialized) bytes form a valid sequence, p advances past end, bytes beyond the valid region are duplicated into cmd_params (info disclosure), and parser->cur is set beyond parser->end, breaking the parser invariant; if the buffer is exactly full this is a physical out-of-allocation read. No guard anywhere bounds the read or re-checks p <= end.

evidence.snippet:
nch = uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, (size_t)(p - parser->end),
						  &ch);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the callee's size bound is computed as (size_t)(p - parser->end) instead of (size_t)(parser->end - p). Since the loop guard (line 12) enforces p < parser->end, the difference is negative and the cast yields a huge value (e.g. (size_t)-1 = SIZE_MAX when p = end-1), so the UTF-8 decoder is told far more bytes are readable than exist and may read a multi-byte sequence past parser->end. Trigger: attacker sends a short command ending in a UTF-8 lead byte (e.g. 0xC2) with no CRLF buffered yet; the decoder reads at/after end, and on a valid continuation the loop overshoots (p += nch, line 31), after which `if (p == parser->end)` (equality-only) fails to catch p > end. No clamp, range check, or post-loop bound on p exists anywhere.

evidence.snippet:
parser->state.cmd_params = i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp);
	parser->cur = p;
evidence.reason: Instantiated impact inside this function: with p = end+1 after the decode overshoot, mp = p (line 52, no trailing-WSP byte past end stops trimming), so i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) copies the byte(s) past the valid data region into cmd_params (uninitialized/stale memory disclosure to command handling and logs), and parser->cur = p sets the cursor beyond parser->end, corrupting the parser invariant; if the buffer's valid data ends at the allocation end, the callee's read at end itself was an out-of-allocation read (crash of the network-facing process, i.e. remote DoS).

verdict.summary: This hardened BMP decoder enforces fatal, execution-order-correct guards on every attacker-controlled value reaching a memory sink: dimensions are validated before size arithmetic, number_colors is bounded by 2^bits_per_pixel and by GetBlobSize before the 4*colors allocation and read, the raster length is bounded by 'if (((MagickSizeType) length/8) > GetBlobSize(image))' before allocation/read, the pixel buffer rows*max(bytes_per_line, columns+256) is never smaller than any per-row consumption in any bpp case (verified arithmetically for 1/4/8/16/24/32), short reads and failed seeks are fatal, and every error arm after allocation frees pixel_info. Integer-wrap scenarios for bytes_per_line*rows are caught by the subsequent allocation failure before any use. No out-of-domain offset, size, or index reaches a sink.

assumptions: IsValidColormapIndex(image,index,&index,exception) — an internal validation callee not shown — is assumed to reject/clamp palette indices against image->colors before *index is used in SetPixelIndex; the call site does route every raw pixel byte through it.

DecodeImage(image,compression,pixels,image->columns*image->rows) — internal callee not shown; this code passes an in-domain size (columns*rows <= rows*max(bytes_per_line, columns+256) = buffer) and a buffer pointer, so any overflow would be internal to the callee.
AcquireVirtualMemory/AcquireQuantumMemory return NULL on failure (checked) and do not themselves overflow their internal row*column size computation.

QueueAuthenticPixels(image,0,y,image->columns,1,exception) returns a region of at least image->columns pixels and GetAuthenticIndexQueue returns a matching index queue; all index writes in cases 1/4/8 stay below image->columns.

limitations: Integer wrap of length=(size_t) bytes_per_line*image->rows requires a product >= 2^64 (columns and rows are each <= 2^31-1 from the signed 32-bit header reads); the wrapped-length path is caught because the following AcquireVirtualMemory request rows*max(bytes_per_line,columns+256) is at least the unwrapped product and fails, yielding a fatal error. Not triggerable as written.

The mask-shift loops 'while (((bmp_info.red_mask << shift.red) & 0x80000000UL) == 0)' terminate at shift <= 31 for any nonzero 32-bit mask; shift-by-32 UB is unreachable on the declared widths and would be a compiler-level UB, not a memory-safety primitive.

The file_size mismatch check '(if ((MagickSizeType) bmp_info.file_size > GetBlobSize(image))) ThrowMagickException(...)' is non-fatal (exception recorded, parsing continues), but bmp_info.file_size feeds no memory operation — only this comparison and a log line — so it is not a fail-open security decision.

In the RLE path, whether DecodeImage can succeed while leaving part of the pixels buffer unwritten (uninitialized data later read by the case 8 loop) depends on the not-shown callee and could not be instantiated from the given code.

Stale bmp_info.alpha_mask across multi-frame iterations (only re-read when bmp_info.size > 40) can mis-set image->matte for a subsequent frame; this affects only bit-mask cosmetics, not memory safety or an authorization decision.

On hypothetical 32-bit size_t/MagickOffsetType builds, columns*rows and start_position+14+bmp_info.size could wrap; the code declares ssize_t/size_t/MagickOffsetType widths for which these stay in range, so this behavior is not exercised as written.

verdict.summary: mcba_usb_start_xmit copies the skb's CAN data using the attacker-supplied DLC byte without validating it: 'usb_msg.dlc = cf->len;' feeds 'memcpy(usb_msg.data, cf->data, usb_msg.dlc);' where cf->len is an unvalidated u8 (0-255) inside the 16-byte can_frame. The only guard, can_dropped_invalid_skb(), validates the skb protocol and total length (skb->len == CAN_MTU), not the DLC byte. A frame with can_dlc up to 255 passes that check, causing a stack out-of-bounds write of up to ~247 bytes past the fixed-size usb_msg struct (and an out-of-bounds read past the 16-byte skb), i.e. kernel stack memory corruption.

evidence.snippet:
usb_msg.dlc = cf->len;

	memcpy(usb_msg.data, cf->data, usb_msg.dlc);
evidence.reason: The memcpy sink copies usb_msg.dlc bytes into the fixed-size stack struct usb_msg (payload area sized for classic CAN's 8 data bytes). usb_msg.dlc is assigned directly from cf->len (line 43), an attacker-controlled u8 DLC field of the transmitted CAN frame (0-255). No clamp, range check, or mask bounds dlc before the copy; the RTR-flag OR on line 48 happens after the memcpy and does not bound the length. A frame with can_dlc=255 (skb->len still 16 == CAN_MTU) passes can_dropped_invalid_skb on line 14, so the copy overruns usb_msg by ~240 bytes on the stack (kernel memory corruption) and reads past the 16-byte skb.

evidence.snippet: struct can_frame *cf = (struct can_frame *)skb->data;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: cf is a direct pointer into the transmitted skb, whose frame content (including the unvalidated DLC byte cf->len) originates from user space via the CAN socket interface, crossing a trust boundary into this kernel transmit handler.

assumptions: struct mcba_usb_msg_can is not shown; assumed to be a fixed-size (~14-byte) message with an 8-byte data payload per classic CAN. The overflow holds for any fixed destination smaller than 255 bytes, and the source-side OOB read (reading up to 255 bytes from the 16-byte skb) is independent of the destination layout.

can_dropped_invalid_skb() is treated per its standard kernel semantics: it validates skb protocol/packet-type and total length (CAN_MTU/CANFD_MTU) and returns true to drop invalid skbs; it does not inspect or clamp the frame's DLC byte.
The CAN core's send path (not shown) is not treated as a guard; no enforcement of dlc <= 8 is quotable in this code.
mcba_usb_get_free_ctx and mcba_usb_xmit are not shown; only their NULL check (line 18) and error return (line 53) are treated as known.
limitations: Possible double-free/use-after-free of ctx: the xmit_failed path (lines 59-60) calls can_free_echo_skb and mcba_usb_free_ctx after mcba_usb_xmit returns an error; if the unshown mcba_usb_xmit already frees ctx on some error paths, ctx would be freed twice. The behavior of mcba_usb_xmit on failure cannot be verified from the given code, so this candidate is speculative.
ctx->ndx is passed to can_put_echo_skb/can_free_echo_skb (lines 50, 59) without a quotable bound; its range is set by the unshown mcba_usb_get_free_ctx, so a defect there cannot be instantiated here.

Reaching the sink requires the ability to transmit on the CAN netdev (e.g., CAP_NET_RAW in the owning netns); the exact privilege posture of the attacker is deployment-dependent and not quotable from this code.

verdict.summary: In the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write path, data->block[0] (attacker-controlled block length from the smbus ioctl surface, up to 255) is used without any bounds check to compute dma_size = data->block[0] + 1, which then sizes desc->wr_len_cmd and memcpy(&dma_buffer[1], &data->block[1], dma_size - 1) into the fixed-size priv->buffer — an out-of-bounds write of up to 255 bytes past the SMBus block buffer, plus a DMA mapping of the same oversized length. A caller that pre-validates block[0] ≤ 32 would mask the trigger, but no such check exists in this code, and this function is the smbus_xfer intake handler; per guard-anchoring rules that caller contract is unquotable here.

verdict.summary: The archive extractor creates symlinks and hardlinks with fully attacker-controlled targets from archive entries without any validation: g_file_make_symbolic_link (file, archive_entry_symlink (entry), ...) passes the raw target string directly to the sink, and the link() path does the same for hardlink targets. evidence.reason: Sink: the symlink target is taken verbatim from the attacker-supplied archive entry (archive_entry_symlink) and passed straight to g_file_make_symbolic_link with no check anywhere in the code that the target is relative or confined to extract_data->destination. This instantiates the first half of the trigger: an attacker-chosen symlink is planted inside the extraction directory pointing at an arbitrary absolute path.

The hardlink branch (lines 134-140, link(oldname, newname)) shares the same unvalidated-target root cause, but write-through is blocked by G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION replacing the hardlink, so it only contributes to the link-planting primitive already covered by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: In unlzw(), the LZW prefix-chain decode loop writes through a downward-decrementing stack pointer with no lower-bound or chain-termination check. After a CLEAR code, clear_tab_prefixof() resets only the first 256 table entries while free_ent restarts at FIRST-1, so newly allocated entries can carry stale pre-CLEAR prefixes (oldcode = incode can exceed the new free_ent), allowing an attacker-crafted compressed stream to produce a cyclic or over-long prefix chain. The loop 'while ((cmp_code_int)code >= (cmp_code_int)256) { *--stackp = tab_suffixof(code); code = tab_prefixof(code); }' then writes attacker-derived bytes below the de_stack buffer without any guard, corrupting memory of the process decompressing the attacker-supplied file.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: unbounded out-of-bounds write. stackp starts at de_stack (line 113) and is decremented once per chain step; the loop exits only when the prefix chain drops below 256. No check anywhere bounds stackp above the buffer's lower end, and no check proves chain termination. The only code-range guard, 'if (code > free_ent) { ... gzip_error(...); }' (lines 115-135), is bypassed for codes < free_ent, whose prefix entries may be stale after a CLEAR.

Trigger producer: on CLEAR the table is only partially cleared (clear_tab_prefixof clears the first 256 entries per its comment at line 50) while free_ent is reset to FIRST-1, so subsequent entries allocated at lines 177-181 (tab_prefixof(code) = (unsigned short)oldcode, oldcode = incode) can store stale pre-CLEAR codes as prefixes, breaking the strictly-decreasing chain invariant and enabling a cyclic/over-long chain that drives stackp out of bounds at lines 141-145.

assumptions: read_buffer/read_error/gzip_error/write_buf semantics assumed per their names: gzip_error aborts processing (its call at lines 133-135 acts as a rejection path); write_buf writes outpos bytes.

Table/suffix buffer layout (de_stack adjacent to tab_suffix/tab_prefix) assumed from macro names tab_suffixof/tab_prefixof/de_stack; the underflow write is out-of-bounds relative to the stack area regardless of the exact shared-buffer layout.
limitations: outbuf[outpos++] at line 100 is guarded: outpos is reset to 0 whenever it reaches OUTBUFSIZ (lines 160-165) and only one byte is written per iteration, so no overflow there.
input() reads of inbuf are bounded by the inbits computation at line 78 (aligned to n_bits within insize) and the while condition at line 81; no over-read candidate survived simulation.
